‌



View 4 Images Phil Day, Superintendent Pharmacist at Pharmacy2U, has warned that not all medications are suitable for weekly pill organisers (Image: Getty)

Pill boxes may not be the only issue

The pharmacist also warned that it's not just organisers that can be an issue, sharing advice on some other problems that might occur. Which room you store your medications in and when you take them are also crucial considerations.

‌



Taking tablets out of their original packaging

While transferring a week's worth of medication or supplements into an organiser might seem harmless, some medicines rely on their original packaging to protect them from moisture, air and light. The pharmacist says that removing this protection may cause them to degrade and, in some cases, reduce their effectiveness.

‌



Certain medicines, including effervescent tablets and some dissolvable tablets, are moisture-sensitive and may be unsuitable for pill organisers. Because of this, it's recommended to check with your pharmacist before removing medication from its packaging.

Storing different tablets and capsules together

‌



Using a pill organiser can be a handy time-saver, but some medicines aren’t meant to be stored side by side. For instance, gelatine capsules can hold moisture that may transfer to nearby tablets and potentially reduce how well they work.

View 4 Images Storing gelatine capsules alongside standard tablets in the same compartment can cause moisture to transfer between pills (Image: Getty)

‌



Certain slow-release pills, which rely on special coatings to release ingredients gradually, can also have specific storage needs. Taking tablets out of their original packaging may also make them harder to identify, raising the risk of mix-ups or dosage mistakes.

Don't assume vitamins and supplements are always safe with prescription medication

‌



A supplement being sold over the counter doesn’t automatically mean it’s risk-free. Some vitamins, minerals and herbal remedies can affect how prescription medicines work.

For example, calcium and iron can reduce absorption of certain drugs used to treat an underactive thyroid. People on some blood thinners may also be advised to avoid vitamin K supplements and St John’s Wort, as they can interfere with treatment. Always let your pharmacist know about any supplements you take, even if you’ve been using them for years.

‌



Taking all y o ur medication at the same time

Taking all your tablets at once might seem convenient, but not all medicines should be taken together. Some need to be taken on an empty stomach, others with food, while certain medications need to be taken at different times to avoid clashes.

‌



Taking medicines at the wrong time or in the wrong combination can affect how well they work. Always follow the instructions and check with your pharmacist if you're unsure.

Storing pill organisers in the bathroom

Article continues below

A bathroom cabinet might seem like an obvious place to keep your medication, but the heat and humidity from showers and baths can make it unsuitable for some medicines. Unless the label says otherwise, medicines should generally be stored in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight, heat and moisture, and always out of the reach of children.

News.title: Gordon Ramsay's morning routine may lower your risk of cancer
News.content:
Gordon Ramsay's morning routine may lower your risk of cancer

Gordon Ramsay's morning drink habit could actually lower your risk of certain cancers

View 4 Images Gordon Ramsay has a method that could benefit your health (Image: Leon Bennett/Getty Images)

Chef Gordon Ramsay has shared his morning routine - and health experts say it may offer genuine benefits, including a potential reduction in cancer risk. During an episode of WIRED's 'Gordon Ramsay Answers The Web's Most Searched Questions' series, the Scottish chef shared what he eats for breakfast and what he has after a gym session.

‌



‌



Answering the question, the chef - who recently cemented his place in Hollywood with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in Los Angeles - was asked, “Does Gordon Ramsay drink coffee?” He replied: “I love coffee.”

‌



"First thing in the morning, I'll start off the day after a session in the gym, and I'll get a black coffee and a croissant. Then throughout the day, I'll have a flat white. Potentially with oat milk or skim milk."

‌



Is black coffee healthy?

While milk often comes down to preference and, in some cases, allergies, it's estimated that around 103 million cups of coffee are consumed in the UK each day. That's around 5 million more than in 2018, according to the British Coffee Association.

View 4 Images MASTERCHEF: GLOBAL GAUNTLET: Host/Judge Gordon Ramsay. MASTERCHEF: GLOBAL GAUNTLET "Eggs Benedict" airs Wednesday, May 20 (8:00-9:00 PM ET/PT) on FOX. (Photo by FOX via Getty Images)

Despite milk having some benefits, such as supporting bone strength, muscle repair and daily energy, you might wonder whether black coffee offers any advantages too - and the good news is, it does. Experts from Healthline state that there is "some evidence that drinking coffee may reduce your risk of developing certain types of cancer."

‌



It explained that one review of 28 studies on coffee and cancer risk found that the more coffee the study participants drank, the lower their risk of liver cancer and endometrial cancer. It added: "Another review observed similar findings, but also reported that coffee might reduce colorectal cancer risk. However, this study likewise noted that coffee had no effect on overall cancer risk."

It stresses that while these suggestions are promising, "more studies are needed to fully understand how drinking coffee may affect cancer risk."

‌



Interestingly, the expert at Healthline also says that "coffee contains small amounts of other vitamins, minerals, and polyphenols, the latter of which are beneficial plant compounds." And experts such as Professor Tim Spector and the late Michael Mosley have hailed the benefits of polyphenols.

What are polyphenols?

Polyphenols are a group of compounds found in plants. They boast a wide range of health benefits, thanks to their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.

‌



Experts at Zoe, the health firm and app founded by Professor Tim Spector, suggest that polyphenols may help lower blood sugar levels and reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes. It may improve heart health and function, thereby reducing the risk of heart disease - and it may even protect against cancer.

Zoe explains: "Experts believe the powerful antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties found in polyphenols might play a role in reducing the risk of cancer. Researchers think that polyphenols may block the activity of certain cancers by inhibiting the growth and development of cancerous cells.

‌



View 4 Images Gordon Ramsay takes a coffee break during filming for series two of Channel 4's "Gordon's Great Escape" in June 2011 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia (Image: Martyn Goodacre/Getty Images)

"In animal studies, scientists have shown that polyphenols combat free radical damage that is associated with cancer development. The results of animal studies are more consistent than studies with human volunteers, which have yielded mixed results. For that reason, researchers need to carry out more human studies before drawing any solid conclusions. "

‌



The amount of polyphenols in your coffee can vary depending on what type of coffee you are having. But Zoe suggests that filtered coffee has around 214 mg per 100 g or 100 ml.

It adds: "Unlike other nutrients, there is no set dietary allowance for polyphenol intake. So, to reap the most health benefits, it’s worth eating a selection of foods from each of these groups, rather than focusing on single contributions from individual foods or drinks. Plus, this will provide you with a variety of polyphenols."

‌



While studies suggest the compounds in black coffee may help lower the risk of certain cancers, and that polyphenols could also reduce the risk of cancer, drinking coffee is not a prevention or cure. Cancer risk is influenced by many lifestyle and genetic factors, and researchers emphasise that more human studies are needed before definitive conclusions can be drawn. Always consult a healthcare professional regarding diet and disease prevention.

How much coffee is too much?

View 4 Images Keeping healthy isn't just about what you eat or drink; Chef Gordon Ramsay also loves to keep fit by taking part in Ironman 70.3 (Image: Nigel Roddis via Getty Images)

‌



While there are some benefits to black coffee - some of which need to be studied more - Healthline notes that "too much caffeine - whether from coffee or other beverages like sodas and energy drinks - can cause uncomfortable side effects like insomnia, anxiety, rapid heart rate, stomach upset, headache, and nausea."

It suggests: "Generally, healthy adults should try to stick to 400 mg of caffeine per day or less. If the only caffeinated drink you have is coffee, that’s about 4 cups (960 mL)."

‌



4 to 5 cups may be 'safe'

Senior dietitian Tracy Parker from the British Heart Foundation (BHF) also warns: "Up to 400 milligrams (mg) of caffeine a day, or around 4 to 5 cups of tea or coffee, is generally considered safe for most adults.

"You may find consuming too much caffeine at once or over the day can cause anxiety, sleeping problems and a rapid heart rate (palpitations). If you’re pregnant, the NHS recommends limiting caffeine intake to 200mg a day or less."

Article continues below

She adds: "Although having a few cups of coffee a day is not bad for your heart, adding sugar, syrups, whole milk or cream to your drink adds calories and saturated fat, which can lead to weight gain and high cholesterol levels."

News.title: Heart doctor names best food to keep your arteries clean
News.content:
Heart doctor names best food to keep your arteries clean

This food will help you live longer and reduce your risk of heart attack and stroke.

View Image A leading heart doctor has named the type of food you should be eating if you want to maintain clean arteries (Image: Getty)

A heart doctor has named a food type that will help "keep your arteries clean". He said eating the food was one of five simple things people could do to keep their heart health and blood pressure in good condition. Dr Jeremy London also named the single worst thing you could possibly do for your entire body.

‌



‌



Dr London, who is board-certified in general surgery, vascular surgery and thoracic surgery, regularly gives simple but crucial health advice to his millions of followers on social media. He has recently flagged an early symptom on the front of your leg that your heart could be in trouble and named an everyday food that will "pull cholesterol out of your body".

‌



If your arteries become narrowed or blocked, this is known as atherosclerosis. It makes it difficult for blood to flow through them and increases your risk of heart attack and stroke. But lifestyle changes can help stop it getting worse. These are Dr London's five simple steps to keeping your arteries clean. He added: "Remember that atherosclerosis is a 'time of exposure' disease. So the sooner you get started the sooner you can decrease your risk of heart attack and stroke."

‌



1. Never smoke

"Smoking is the single worst thing you can do for your entire body," said Dr London. "That includes cigarettes, marijuana, vaping. They all damage the inner lining of the vessel wall, making it more vulnerable."

2. Focus on a whole foods diet

This is the food type Dr London flagged as helping keep your arteries clean. He said: "Adequate protein, fibre and macronutrients keep blood glucose and insulin levels much more stable."

There isn't really an official list of whole foods but it's simple to know if something is a whole food: the term generally describes foods that are left close to their natural state. Here are some simple examples of whole foods:

‌



fruit and vegetables

nuts and seeds

beans and lentils

milk, cheese and yoghurt

wholegrains

unprocessed meat and fish.

Meanwhile, foods like ready meals, processed meats or products with added sugars, salt, fats or any additives are not whole foods.

‌



3. Exercise consistently

"Shoot for 150 minutes total a week," said Dr London. "Be sure you're getting breathless a few times a week and don't forget resistance training — this helps maintain cardiovascular efficiency as well as adequate muscle mass."

4. Know your Apo B levels

"Apolipoprtoein B are the dangerous cholesterol particles in your bloodstream," Dr London explained. "Less dangerous particles, less chance for invasion of the vessel wall."

‌



In the UK, an Apo B blood test is not routinely offered on the NHS as part of a standard cholesterol check. Instead, it is typically requested selectively by specialists or GPs in specific situations, such as a strong family history of early heart disease. and some other related conditions.

5. Get a home blood pressure cuff

"Checking your blood pressure one time a year at the doctor's office just isn't enough and many times it's not accurate. Check your blood pressure at home and shoot for a number of around 120/80 and address it if it's elevated."

‌



The NHS says your blood pressure is usually considered high if it's either 140/90 or higher when checked by a healthcare professional or 135/85 or higher when checked at home.

News.title: 'I lost my mum, dad and sister to brain tumours - lightning struck three times'
News.content:
When her younger sister, Helen, died from an aggressive brain tumour in March 2024, Iola Williams was dumbfounded. She says: “I’d lost my dad, my mum and now my little sister to brain tumours. Lightning didn’t just strike twice in our family, it struck three times. It beggars belief.”

A great-grandmother, retired psychiatric nurse Iola, 68, says: “I feel like I’m dealing with a ticking time bomb. You can’t help but think who’s next? If it can happen three times, who’s to say there won’t be a fourth?” Iola’s father, William, and sister, Helen, both died within weeks of being diagnosed with glioblastoma - an aggressive form of brain cancer that carries a prognosis of 12 to 18 months.

According to the charity, Brain Tumour Research, around 3,200 people are diagnosed with a glioblastoma in the UK each year. Iola says: “In August 2004, Dad was doing some gardening for a lady, locally, and had a fit in her garden. She found him on the floor and immediately called an ambulance.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



“It was a shock and we assumed he’d had a stroke. But, by the time I got to the hospital, he’d been told it was a brain tumour. He was crying. I’d never seen my dad crying. It was heartbreaking.”

View 6 Images William and Eleanor Williams with their grandchildren Emma, Paula and Gareth

William, in fact, had six brain tumours. Given radiotherapy and chemotherapy, he died just eight weeks later, aged 72. Iola, of Llanfrothen, north west Wales, says: “Dad was fit and healthy. He’d been active all his life as a groundsman.

“As a family, we were left reeling. The speed at which it all happened was horrendous. He was gone in four weeks. But that’s the thing about brain tumours … they can be a death sentence. And they don’t give you much time to say goodbye.”

‌



In August 2013, Iola’s 74-year-old mum, Eleanor, was diagnosed with a brain tumour (not a glioblastoma). She says: “Eleven years earlier, Mum had breast cancer, which she recovered from with chemo and a mastectomy. But a little over a decade later, the cancer came back - this time as a brain tumour.

"The first symptoms we noticed were her headaches and her handwriting was not as beautiful as normal. She’d always had the most gorgeous script. As part of her treatment, she was placed on steroids, which thinned the lining of her bowel and led to sepsis. In August 2014 she died, 12 months after being diagnosed with a brain tumour.”

View 6 Images Eleanor Williams in hospital, after suffering symptoms

Iola, who has three children and seven grandchildren with her husband, Richard, 71, a retired golf club groundsman, says her family were devastated. “Mum was such a huge part of our lives, a wonderful grandmother and great grandmother,” she says. “It was a crushing loss to lose Mum.”

‌



When, in January 2024, Iola’s sister, Helen was diagnosed with glioblastoma on her 56th birthday, she says: “It felt like a cruel joke. She started having seizures, which didn’t stop and a CT scan revealed it was a brain tumour. I couldn’t believe it. “

And Helen opted out of having treatment. “She’d seen what it had done to our dad - how unpleasant it was, and ultimately how it hadn’t helped,” says Iola. “She died 12 weeks later, leaving behind a daughter, son and four granddaughters.”

Astonishingly, despite experiencing three brain tumours in a single family, doctors say they all struck at random. Iola explains: “Despite my father and sister having glioblastoma, doctors say the three tumours weren’t hereditary or genetic. They were completely random. It’s unfathomable.”

View 6 Images Helen and her son Gareth

‌



Now Iola, unsurprisingly, suffers from severe health anxiety. She says: “I’ve got grown up children, grandchildren and a great grandchild now and I fear for all of them - as I fear for myself. What’s to say it won’t happen a fourth time? I’ve already had three family members wiped out by the same thing. It's at the back of my mind all the time.”

Brain tumours are the leading cause of cancer death in people under 40 in Wales. Survival rates remain devastatingly low, with only 17.2% of patients there surviving five years or more after diagnosis, compared to 61.5% across all cancers.

In England, after swimmer Archie Goodburn, 25 - diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago - made a tearful TV appeal in August for investment in brain cancer research, Prime Minister Andy Burnham drew-up an action plan. Last month, he announced a new national brain cancer clinical lead and promised a review of brain cancer progress and action to get patients treatment sooner.

Meanwhile, pioneering research is currently underway at the Brain Tumour Research Centre of Excellence at Queen Mary University of London, focused on using glioblastoma stem cells to help develop unique, patient-specific treatments. Moved by Archie’s story, Iola says: “His story made me so emotional. I’ve been there three times. My heart went out to him.”

‌



View 6 Images Swimmer Archie Goodburn at the 2026 Commonwealth Games (Image: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

Now Iola is calling on the Senedd - the Welsh Government - to urgently invest in research into the devastating disease that can affect anyone, at any age. And she supports Brain Tumour Research’s manifesto for Wales - It’s Time to do Things Differently - which urges the Welsh Government to commit to improved access to clinical trials and increased investment into research to transform outcomes for brain tumour patients in Wales.

She says: “My message to them is to act now. People are dying all the time. And nothing has changed in 20 years. The prognosis, treatment plan and general lack of direction and hope were the same in 2024 for Helen as they were two decades ago.

“It’s frustrating but also really worrying. What if it comes up again in my family knowing there's no cure? It's always there at the back of my mind How many more frightened people need to die before something is done and funding is granted?"

‌



Cruel coincidence

Dr Karen Noble, director of research and policy at Brain Tumour Research, says Iola’s story is one of cruel coincidence. She says: “Iola’s story is devastating. To lose three members of one family is extremely rare and brain tumours are typically not hereditary.

View 6 Images Dr Karen Noble of Brain Tumour Research (Image: PA)

"Fast-growing and highly aggressive, glioblastomas are incredibly challenging to treat. They are diffuse, meaning the tumour cells invade healthy areas of the brain and, even when removed by surgery, glioblastoma will always come back

“Just one in three patients survives for more than a year following diagnosis and no new treatments for glioblastoma have been approved since 2005. Despite this, just 1% of the national spend on cancer research was allocated to brain tumours between 2002 and 2021.

‌



“Iola’s story reflects why we urgently need the Government to support an increase in the national investment in research into brain tumours to at least £45 million a year, in order to close the gap with funding levels seen for other cancer types such as leukaemia, where sustained investment over recent decades has made a huge impact on survival rates.”

Brain tumours

A brain tumour occurs as a result of an abnormal growth or spread of cells from within the brain, or its supporting tissues, that can damage the brain or threaten its function.

No single, definitive cause has yet been identified for primary brain tumours. Causes are likely to vary between individuals.

Some of the common warning signs of a brain tumour include headaches, nausea and vomiting, vision problems, seizure,; weakness or numbness, speech difficulties and cognitive changes.

*source Brain Tumour Research

*For more information and to donate, see braintumourresearch.org

News.title: Cook crispy bacon without a frying pan using mess-free hack that makes it tastier
News.content:
Cook crispy bacon without a frying pan using mess-free hack that makes it tastier

A bacon sandwich is hard to beat, especially when the meat is perfectly crispy with plenty of crunch — but cooking it in a frying pan can be a messy affair, and there is a better method

View 3 Images You can't beat perfectly crispy bacon for breakfast (Image: creacart via Getty Images)

The weekend has finally arrived, making it the ideal opportunity to indulge in a proper breakfast that you maybe don't have the luxury of enjoying during the working week. There's nothing better than a bacon sandwich, especially when the rashers are perfectly crispy with a satisfying crunch.

‌



‌



Although it doesn't take long to cook up a few strips, it can be quite a messy business. Fat and grease can spit everywhere while the bacon sizzles away in the frying pan, which is especially chaotic if you have a gas hob — and quite painful too.

‌



And there's nothing more disappointing than enduring all of that only to end up with limp, soggy bacon that has no bite whatsoever.

‌



View 3 Images The texture of bacon can be tricky to get right (Image: Getty)

Why you should ditch the frying pan

According to food blogger The Modern Nonna, there's a far cleverer method for cooking bacon than simply chucking it into any old frying pan.

While this is likely the go-to approach for most people, it comes with one significant drawback — it creates an enormous amount of mess, leading to a tedious clean-up job when you'd much rather be tucking in.

‌



By opting for a large, deep, cast-iron or stainless steel pot instead — the sort you'd typically use for making soup — you can ditch the mess entirely, get crispier bacon and spend less time scrubbing the hob afterwards, which is always a welcome bonus.

How to cook the perfect bacon

All you need is a pack of your favourite bacon and a large pot. There's no need to add any oil or butter beforehand, as the fat from the bacon will naturally release during cooking, creating a wonderfully textured result.

‌



A stainless steel pot is the top choice, but any heavy-bottomed pot with tall sides will do the job perfectly well. Add the bacon strips to the pan, then increase the heat to medium-high.

Cook for approximately seven minutes until nicely crisped up, then flip over and cook for a further couple of minutes on the opposite side.

‌



View 3 Images Cooking bacon in a large pot cuts down on mess (Image: Getty)

The cooking duration will vary depending on the thickness of your bacon, so monitor it closely to prevent burning. Once cooked, simply lift from the pan using tongs and place on kitchen roll to soak up any exces grease.

‌



Then, serve in a sandwich, as part of a full English, or however you prefer. Make sure to dispose of any solidified grease in the general waste bin and avoid tipping it down the sink at all costs.

Fans commenting on the recipe were full of praise for this clever trick, with one person writing: "I used to dread the messy cleanup after cooking bacon on the stove which is why I started making bacon in the oven, but this hack is awesome! Perfectly crispy bacon with minimal fuss!"

Article continues below

Another said: "OMG this is brilliant! Worked like a charm and the clean up was so much easier. Thank you!"

News.title: 'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?
News.content:
"Move on!" That's Theresa May's frank instruction to Andy Burnham.

She spent years wrangling with the EU to try to forge a decent Brexit deal before being shoved out of her job by her party. Her leadership was broken by Britain's relationship with Brussels. Now she is warning the current resident of No 10 not to risk the same.

In a rare interview, Baroness May - who presided over negotiations with the EU between 2016 and 2019 - told me Burnham ought to respect the public's decision 10 years ago, not "pat them on their head" as if they gave the wrong answer and should have "another go".

And she said she was "aghast" at what he was doing, dangling the possibility of rejoining the EU, warning it would absorb huge amounts of government effort.

"The hours that have to be put in, it's across the whole of government," she said. "It's not just prime ministerial time, [it's] cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations."

But while some on his own side are very keen to get on with a campaign to rejoin the EU - and the foreign secretary tells me this option is on the table - May is not the only voice urging caution.

Earlier this month David Cameron also said starting a conversation about rejoining would be "long and painful".

And former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair has told the Sunday Times this weekend that Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.

News.title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
News.content:
The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did.

"That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.

Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.

The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.

Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent.

"Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina.

"And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.

When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025.

He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.

After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.

The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.

He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.

News.title: Verstappen wins extraordinary Las Vegas Grand Prix as Ferraris collide
News.content:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an extraordinary Las Vegas Grand Prix that featured 34 lead changes in a non-stop battle at the front.

The leading group of 10 cars were tied together for the vast majority of the race as the lead constantly changed hands between Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers George Russell and Kimi Antonelli.

But Verstappen was the one constant, always seeming a step ahead of his rivals as he debated electrical energy deployment strategy with his team.

And in the final laps Mercedes' challenge unravelled as first Russell made a mistake and crashed trying to pass Antonelli, and the Italian lost out to the two McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri going into the final lap.

The world champion dropped to fifth going on to the Strip on the last lap but was able to reclaim the place from Alpine's Pierre Gasly at the end of the long straight.

And there was more drama at Ferrari as Charles Leclerc earned a 10-second penalty for tipping Lewis Hamilton into a spin.

Earlier, Hamilton had been given a 10-second penalty of his own for passing Norris off the track in a fight for position that also involved Leclerc.

It was a grand prix more reminiscent of American oval racing than Formula 1, and it depended on unique circumstances revolving around the Las Vegas circuit and energy-starved hybrid engines this year.

But there was no questioning the showbiz value in the city that prides itself as the entertainment capital of the world.

The key stories of an engrossing race were:

News.title: Catherine talks openly about how cancer changed her in documentary on BBC
News.content:
The Princess of Wales has spoken about how "cancer does change you," in a forthcoming documentary called Heal to be shown on the BBC.

"It changes your body, it changes you physically - but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you," says Catherine in the first glimpses from the documentary, which features her private thoughts on her illness and recovery.

The highly personal film, to be screened on BBC One on 29 November, will see Catherine share her experiences of cancer, saying: "Healing is a journey."

It includes new footage of her completing the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year, which involved climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland and Wales over a day.

"It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone," says Catherine's voice-over, accompanied by images of other cancer patients and the princess hugging her own family, including Prince William.

"It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," she says, once again reflecting the sense of change from her cancer experience.

News.title: BBC apologises for 'any offence caused' by Strictly noise disruption
News.content:
The BBC has apologised "for any offence caused" after lewd audio was heard during the live broadcast of Strictly Come Dancing.

A recording of sex noises appeared to be playing from the audience in Blackpool's Tower Ballroom as judge Motsi Mabuse gave feedback early in Saturday's episode. She paused before joking: "It's not me."

At the end of the programme, presenter Emma Willis apologised to viewers "if you heard any audio disruptions". A BBC spokesperson also issued an apology and said it was "investigating how this happened".

Lancashire police said it was assessing whether any criminal offences may have taken place, after receiving a formal complaint and a mobile phone being seized.

The moment was streamed on social media by content creator Daniel Jarvis, whose videos include pranks. He appeared to place a phone call before the audio began playing in the ballroom, and suggested he was trying to target judge Craig Revel Horwood for his "bullying".

Jarvis has previously claimed he was responsible for sex noises disrupting Match of the Day in 2023.

Willis told viewers: "Before we see the judges' leaderboard, we'd like to apologise if you heard any audio disruptions earlier in tonight's show and for any offence caused."

A BBC spokesperson said in a statement: "We apologise to any viewers offended during the live broadcast of Strictly this evening.

"We are investigating how this happened."

An edit will be made to the programme available on BBC iPlayer.

A spokesperson for Lancashire Constabulary said: "We are aware of an incident that took place during the filming of Strictly Come Dancing in Blackpool.

"We have been in contact with the event organisers, and a formal complaint has been made to us.

"A mobile phone has been seized and we are now looking into the matter to see if any criminal offences have taken place."

News.title: Employers are being asked to give interview feedback - here's what applicants want
News.content:
Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?

So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.

It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.

Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".

The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?

Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.

But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".

He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."

News.title: The real people finding their work copied and stolen by AI characters
News.content:
Is this real or AI? It is a question increasingly asked underneath social media videos, and often difficult to tell.

But there is a new trend when it comes to digital manipulation. Across social media, AI-generated characters are appearing in videos that look remarkably similar to those posted by real people.

From musicians to dancers and comedians, content creators are finding their performances cloned by these characters that are designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualised.

Experts call the practice "reskinning" and say it is made possible by cheap, easy-to-use AI tools. People can discover their work has been copied by seeing a video of a character making the same joke or doing the same dance, even with the same background. Sometimes the AI version has millions more views than the original.

Some of the accounts identified by BBC Verify appear to be using these AI-generated videos to get views and likes, and to eventually make money. Others appear to be experimenting with AI to make people laugh or simply for the attention that comes with going viral. But the practice has angered content creators who say their original work is being stolen.

News.title: Why Nicola Coughlan's new drama might leave viewers uncomfortable
News.content:
Filming the series without a script meant the actors were fully immersed in their characters, making them real not just for viewers but for themselves too.

"I'm not playing myself, but there's far less, let's say 'character' here than anything else I've ever done because a lot of this is about just reacting," Coughlan says.

She and Cole would film long takes, some lasting about an hour and often with heated exchanges, which might need to be shot multiple times.

Coughlan describes I Am Helen as "the most challenging thing in terms of material that I've ever worked on", adding for the first time in a role she needed counselling.

"You literally would be physically and mentally quite exhausted," she says.

"There were times that I said to Dominic [Savage] if he wanted to do a third take for example - and I've never said this before on set - but I actually don't think I have that in me because you hit a wall.

"It's a lot to keep going."

Cole agrees that "it was tough".

"When you're given that freedom, things happen and I think you can get some really interesting and also quite shocking stuff," he says.

For him, that came when he damaged a fridge on set with a punch.

But it's that authenticity of emotion which, while difficult for the actors, is what Coughlan thinks makes the series so engaging.

"When people watch the 'I Ams', they feel quite truthful," she says.

"I think that's a big reason as to why, to be honest."

News.title: Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'
News.content:
Former Prime Minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham he should "move on" from Brexit, telling the BBC she is "aghast" the prime minister could be considering rejoining the EU.

At the Brussels summit this week the PM said he wanted to "brainstorm" options for the future relationship between Britain and the trading bloc.

In an exclusive interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, said: "Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

May claimed Burnham "wants to pat people on the head" by suggesting "remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you. So have another go and come out with the right answer."

May, who was prime minister between 2016 and 2019 urged Burnham to "just get on with" today's challenges rather than re-opening the conversation around being in the European Union.

Before becoming PM she had campaigned to stay in the EU, but when in No 10 she presided over three years of tortuous negotiations.

The deal she concluded was rejected by MPs. She was forced to quit and was replaced by Boris Johnson in 2019.

Telling Burnham to "move on", she said: "What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it's across the whole of government.

"It's not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you're getting out what you want.

"And that's one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit.

"When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I'm afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

Warning against another vote, May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people, sort of patting them on the head.

"He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you? So have another go and come out with the right answer.

"Or what he thinks is the right answer. But as I say, let's just get on with making sure the UK is as strong economically, in security terms, and in terms of opportunities for people as it can be."

Speaking to the BBC back in 2023, she said the UK "would have been better off if MPs had backed her deal to leave the European Union".

Her deal had included the prospect of a vote on holding a second referendum, and a vote on a temporary customs union, as well as promises on workers' rights and environmental protection.

May claimed her plan was thwarted by "hardline" Brexit-supporting MPs and those who wanted to remain in the EU.

News.title: UK should only rejoin EU if it innovates on technology, Blair warns
News.content:
Former prime minister Sir Tony Blair has said Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.

Speaking to The Sunday Times, external, Sir Tony said: "I was painted as saying Britain should just go back and rejoin - I'm not saying that - it's heavily conditioned."

Sir Tony was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, and told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."

But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.

Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.

He said: "The problem if we go back and join Europe is that; I can't say that the technology revolution is the single biggest thing, and then if Europe moves in the wrong direction on technology innovation, which they might do and presently probably are doing, that it's a good idea for Britain to rejoin. That's what's changed in this last ten years."

He argued Britain should have an ambition to reform the EU.

But he added that we have to be "prepared to walk away from that negotiation" and need to make our own economy and tech sector strong.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham this week agreed what he called a "win-win" deal with the EU.

The agreement covered British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also announced that the trading bloc and the UK are launching a digital partnership, including areas like artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology.

The EU and Britain "have enormous potential to innovate together", she added.

News.title: From pit-stops to go-to destinations: The transformation of service stations
News.content:
Service stations have been a fixture on the nation's motorway network for more than six decades, but while they may once have been just a place to go when needing a break on a long drive, could it be that these roadside retreats have now evolved into destinations in their own right?

Next to the motorway near Rotherham, where traffic seems to be forever thundering by, is a covered square, surrounded by what at first appears to be sandy-coloured stone buildings - and there is a general air of calm.

But this is not one of many pretty rural villages that dot the Yorkshire countryside - this is actually the service station which was recently named in survey as the UK's favourite.

While it is only mid-morning, the Welcome Break site's concourse is already bustling.

A father, juggling a tray of coffee and his small child, heads straight upstairs to the soft play area.

Outside the main building, there is a doggy exercise area and even a gym for HGV drivers.

In the recent Transport Focus survey, 123 service stations were ranked, but it was this place, which opened in January 2025, which came top with a 99% satisfaction rating. A number of operators opted out of taking part in the watchdog's annual review, although 37,000 visitors shared their views.

It is a long way from when drivers pulling in for a refuel and refresh may have picked their stop by a simple little symbol on a physical map, with no idea what the site may look like.

News.title: Village vote 'sent powerful message', say politicians
News.content:
No-one was surprised by the outcome of the poll which saw 257 people vote for the village ''to become an independent self-governing Crown dependency'' and just 16 vote against the idea. One ballot was spoiled.

The result has no legal basis, but there were warnings from local politicians for ministers not to ignore the result.

"It sends a powerful message that it is a completely unsuitable site.

"I hope just for once that the government will actually listen to local people," said Tim Passmore the Conservative Police and Crime Commissioner for Suffolk.

"That is what Andy Burnham said he would do, now it's time for action."

Terry Jermy is the Labour MP for Thetford, which is just two miles away from the base.

He said: "The people of Barnham have done a really good job in raising awareness of the issue and demonstrating the strength of feeling against these plans.

"The message to the government is that this MoD site is not suitable."

While Michael Hadwen, the Reform UK leader of Suffolk County council, said: "This is a clear demonstration of democracy at work.

"Barnham has said loud and clear that that the government cannot impose this base upon them and the government should start to listen because when things like this start to get ignored that's when society starts to collapse."

The estimated turnout of around 70% was lower than campaigners had been hoping for.

When a similar referendum was held in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington 89% of locals took part.

The chair of the residents association in Barnham said some people had decided not to vote after seeing the government ignore the result in Piddington and give planning permission for a nearby military base to be used for asylum seekers.

News.title: M42 near Birmingham Airport reopens after crash
News.content:
A stretch of the M42 near Birmingham Airport has reopened after a serious crash.

Drivers faced long delays on Saturday afternoon after the northbound carriageway was closed between junctions 5A and 6 following a collision involving a lorry and a van, which resulted in a vehicle fire.

Motorists caught in standstill traffic described seeing a "huge fire" after the crash, while West Midlands Police urged motorists to avoid the area.

National Highways said all lanes reopened on Sunday from 04:50 GMT and there were no further delays.

News.title: Man charged with attempted murder after Bradford councillor stabbed
News.content:
A man has appeared in court charged with attempted murder after a Bradford councillor was seriously injured in a stabbing.

Councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:00 GMT on Thursday on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to nearby Manse Street, according to West Yorkshire Police.

Arfan Ali, 32, of Thornbury Avenue, is also charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place. At Leeds Magistrates' Court earlier, he was remanded into custody until he appears at Bradford Crown Court on 21 December.

Councillor Ali remains in hospital in a serious but stable condition, police said.

Councillor Ali is a Your Bradford Independent Group representative for Bradford Moor ward and was first elected in May.

He works as a community development manager at charity The Leap, and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.

Speaking after Thursday's incident, his family thanked police, paramedics and members of the public who "courageously provided first aid and assistance at the scene" and asked people to "keep him and his family in your duas [prayers]".

News.title: Rare Titanic items sell for record-breaking sums
News.content:
Rare items belonging to passengers of the Titanic have been sold at auction for record-breaking sums.

The highest selling artefacts were a pocket watch from third-class passenger Mary Mangan, which fetched Â£250,000, and a diamond ring worn by famous passenger Lady Duff Gordon, which was bought for Â£140,000.

Another item was a detailed, water-stained letter recovered from the body of its writer, first-class passenger Ramon Artagaveytia Gomez, which was auctioned for Â£80,000.

Auctioneer Andrew Aldridge from Henry Aldridge and Son in Devizes, Wiltshire, said the "epic sale" was evidence of the lasting global interest in the tragic story.

News.title: Man dies putting up shopping centre festive lights
News.content:
A man in his 40s has died after an incident involving the installation of Christmas lights at Brent Cross Shopping Centre in north-west London.

Emergency services were called to the centre in Prince Charles Drive, Hendon, shortly after 05:00 GMT on Wednesday. The man, who had been carrying out work at the shopping centre, was taken to hospital but died the following day, the Metropolitan Police said.

A spokesperson for the shopping centre said they were "deeply saddened by the passing of a contractor who was undertaking overnight works earlier this week".

An investigation into the circumstances of his death had been launched and the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) has been informed.

The shopping centre closed for the day following the incident.

Its spokesperson said checks and consultation had been carried out with the relevant authorities before it was reopened on Thursday.

"Our thoughts and sincere condolences are with their family, friends and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time," they added.

David Pinto-Duschinsky, MP for Hendon, said he was "incredibly sad" to hear the man had died.

"My heart and my deepest condolences go out to his family and friends," he wrote on social media.

"May his memory be a blessing."

A spokesperson for Barnet Council said: "Our thoughts and wishes are with those affected by this tragic accident.

"The police have primacy until they formally handover the case.

"As the local authority with responsibility for health and safety in Brent Cross shopping centre, Barnet Council will launch an investigation into the accident."

HSE has been approached for comment.

When is Black Friday 2026?

Black Friday officially falls on Friday 27 November 2026, but you can already shop hundreds of early deals. Some of the strongest offers can appear well before the main event, so I'd recommend checking historical prices before deciding whether to buy now or hold out. Lucky for you, this is something myself and IndyBest’s shopping experts usually flag in our guides – so make sure to browse our descriptions in full before heading to the checkout.

When does Black Friday end?

Cyber Monday (30 November) marks the unofficial end of Black Friday each year, although there's technically no forced cut-off for retailers. Some will pull their discounts at 11:59pm that evening, while others will keep the offers running into early December.

When is Cyber Monday?

Cyber Monday is on 30 November 2026. It was originally created to encourage shoppers to buy online, but is now just an extension of Black Friday, giving you a final chance to save before Christmas.

There’s also Travel Tuesday, which takes place on the day after Cyber Monday and focuses on deals for flights, hotels and package holidays, and Small Business Saturday, which encourages shoppers to support independent retailers instead of the big chains.

How can I tell if a Black Friday deal is genuine?

The easiest way is to check a product’s price history. If it’s been the same price for weeks before Black Friday, or the discount is only a few pounds, it probably isn’t as impressive as it looks. Make sure to write a list of everything you want and need, noting down the current price so you can check the discount in November. I also recommend comparing prices across multiple retailers. Just because something has a big percentage off doesn’t automatically make it a good deal. Having covered sales for more than a decade, I’ve written a detailed guide to my top shopping tips for Black Friday.

News.title: Cop31 climate talks ‘on brink of collapse’ over fossil fuels row
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Negotiators are in a race to save climate talks at Cop31 from breaking down entirely as the conference in Turkey stretches into its second day of extended talks on Sunday.

Delegates are poring over the third draft of a proposed deal to tackle climate change, which is seen by some as not ambitious enough, largely because of its its failure to directly mention fossil fuels.

Instead, the text includes language referring to a previous COP, at which governments agreed to transition away from oil, gas, and coal.

If approved, the current deal would acknowledge for the first time that global warming is on course to exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that countries had sought to preserve, while calling for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse the ⁠overshoot.

"From ⁠what we can see, there is a large majority consensus... there is compromise on the horizon," COP31 President Murat Kurum said ​ahead of ⁠the plenary session which could try to approve the ‌deal. The session was repeatedly delayed by last-minute shuttle diplomacy.

open image in gallery COP31 President Murat Kurum speaks to media outside the plenary hall at the UN Climate Change Conference ( Reuters )

Other delegations at the venue, where catering outlets and exhibits have already been dismantled, were less sure.

Observers to the closed-door talks said Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producer nations had pushed hard in negotiations for keeping fossil ‌fuels out of the text, and carbon removal in.

"It seems like we ‌are negotiating with the Saudis," said Tuvalu's climate minister, Maina Talia.

A representative for the Saudi delegation declined to comment.

open image in gallery Delegates have failed to reach an agreement and are into overtime at the conference ( Reuters )

Speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the ongoing talks, several delegations raised the prospect of leaving without a deal.

Jennifer Morgan, former German climate minister and a senior fellow at The Fletcher School at Tufts University, said: "After ⁠the presidency ignored the views of 150 countries and tabled a very weak text, negotiations are on the brink."

Environmental group 350.org said it was disappointed by the draft's failure to mention fossil fuels explicitly, as well as its encouragement of carbon-removal technologies.

"Carbon capture is one of the biggest scams of the overshoot era, and our leaders are on the verge of falling for it," said Sara Shaw, the group's campaigns and networks director, referring to the practice of trapping carbon dioxide before it reaches the atmosphere.

Critics say the technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and that including them in a deal opens the door to continued oil and gas development.

The ‌new draft text followed intensive consultations between Australia, which is leading the talks, Turkey, which is hosting the meeting, and nearly ​200 delegations from many of the world's richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations.

The presidency gave delegations several hours to ‌raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled ⁠later on Sunday to begin approving it.

Australia's task, supported by Turkey, has been to find a deal that balances the ⁠needs of nations most vulnerable to climate change with those whose economies depend on either the production or consumption of fossil fuels.

This year's COP is the first since the ‌UN's environmental body confirmed that the rise in ​global temperature was set to blow past 1.5 degrees, a threshold ‌all countries agreed over a decade ago to try not to ​exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify.

News.title: Shirley Ballas fights back tears after Dani Dyer makes heartbreaking Strictly admission
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing judge Shirley Ballas fought back tears during Saturday’s legendary Blackpool show after contestant Dani Dyer revealed how she had struggled with her confidence.

The former Love Island winner explained how her lack of confidence left her feeling like she wasn’t good enough to be on the show.

After Dyer performed with her Strictly professional partner Nikita Kuzmin, and scored 35 out of 40, the head judge became emotional.

Ballas told Dyer: Your posture from week one is absolutely remarkable. you could be a poster at Wembley. You’re like a tiger.”

She added: “I am getting quite emotional, you are a different woman, it is really remarkable to watch.”

News.title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in Palm Springs ceremony
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Miley Cyrus has tied the knot with Maxx Morando in California, according to reports.

The ceremony is said to have taken place at a Palm Springs resort once owned by Frank Sinatra.

Guests were asked to wear all black, with the bride the only attendee in white.

The private occasion was attended by the singer's father, Billy Rae Cyrus, and his partner Liz Hurley, according to reports.

Before her relationship with Morando, Cyrus was married to actor Liam Hemsworth.

She had also reportedly dated pop star Nick Jonas and singer Cody Simpson.

Cyrus and Hemsworth wed in 2018, months after a California wildfire destroyed their Malibu home.

open image in gallery Miley Cyrus on stage with Dolly Parton ( AFP/Getty Images )

The couple split the following summer, and their divorce was finalised in January 2020.

Cyrus found fame playing a high school student with a pop star alter-ego on Hannah Montana.

Her godmother, Dolly Parton, appeared on the TV show as her Aunt Dolly.

Since Hannah Montana ended, Cyrus has built a successful music career, winning three Grammy Awards and one Brit Award.

Her hit songs include Wrecking Ball, Flowers and Party In The USA.

She has scored three number one singles and two number one albums in the UK, according to the Official Charts Company.

Cyrus has performed a number of duets with Parton over the years, among them a cover of Wrecking Ball for the country singer's 2023 album Rockstar.
