Strictly Come Dancing’s Blackpool Week ran into trouble when the police were called after sexual noises interrupted the live broadcast.

The BBC dance show returned to the northwest coast for its annual Tower Ballroom special, which is where the “disturbance” occurred.

The judges were in the process of giving feedback to Delta Goodrem and her partner Kai Widdrington, back from illness last week, when they were interrupted by sexual noises.

Delivering her verdict at the time, Motsi Mabuse appeared to be distracted by the sounds coming from behind her and paused before saying: “It’s not me.”

The incident was later acknowledged by presenter Emma Willis who issued an apology to viewers. “Before we see the judges’ leaderboard, we’d like to apologise if you heard any audio disruptions earlier in tonight’s show and for any offence caused,” she said.

A BBC spokesperson said: “We apologise to any viewers offended during the live broadcast of Strictly this evening. We are investigating how this happened.”

The pornographic sounds appear to have been the doing of YouTuber Daniel Jarvis, who had seemingly snuck a burner phone into the studio.

The serial prankster, who previously claimed to be responsible for a similar Match of the Day incident in 2023, filmed himself live as he watched the show and rang the phone, setting off its explicit ringtone.

He had been intending to target Craig Revel Horwood for his “bullying”, said Jarvis.

A spokesperson for Lancashire police said: “We are aware of an incident that took place during the filming of Strictly Come Dancing in Blackpool. “We have been in contact with the event organisers, and a formal complaint has been made to us.

“A mobile phone has been seized and we are now looking into the matter to see if any criminal offences have taken place.”

An edit will be made to the programme available on iPlayer.

The interruption occured when Motsi Mabuse was delivering her verdict to Delta Goodrem and Kai Widdrington ( BBC )

It was certainly an eventful week for the eight remaining celebrities who brought their A-game. Goodrem opened the show with Widdrington, who was making a return after being forced to miss last week’s live show due to illness. The duo set the bar high with their quickstep, but it wasn’t quite enough to finish top of the leaderboard. That honour went to three stars who all scored 39: John Nellis, Tabby Stoecker and Cach Mercer.

Just seven points separated the leading stars from the lowest scorers – Jaime Winstone and Carlos Gu, and Graeme Hall and Lauren Oakley – who landed 32 marks each.

Emotions were running high with Dani Dyer bringing Shirley Ballas to tears after a powerful Couple’s Choice routine dedicated to her grandfather, who she revealed is “not very well at the moment”.

Last night would have been the final performance for one of the couples, who will be sent home following the dance-off. The results show kicks off at 7.10pm on BBC One on Sunday (22 November).

News.title: Government intervention ‘a drop in the ocean’ ahead of energy price cap rise
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Government intervention on soaring household energy bills will be a “drop in the ocean” for many people who “don’t have the money to cope” with yet another price hike, charities have warned.

Experts at Cornwall Insight have predicted Ofgem’s energy price cap, which will be announced next week, will rise by 26% to £2,166 from January 1, which could see a typical household bill jump by more than £400 per year.

The hike, which will leave the cap at its highest level in four years, comes as households are already grappling with sky high energy costs.

It has left charities and campaigners “deeply concerned”, confronting a reality that “lives are in danger” if people cannot heat their homes.

The UK Government announced a £100 household energy payment for up to 20 million households, which Citizens Advice said will cover “less than two weeks’ worth” of energy usage for most this winter.

The charity estimates that £100 represents just two weeks of energy for the majority of households based on usage data from 2025 and applying the predicted increase from Cornwall Insights.

A spokesperson for Citizens Advice said: “This £100 that the Government has announced; for someone in a lot of debt, who can’t afford their bills, it’s not going to touch the sides.

“It’s a drop in the ocean, however you want to put it.

“The average person’s energy debt is in the hundreds, if not thousands of pounds.

“I’m not really sure what, if any, impact it will have on the average consumer who is in debt.

“Not to sound morbid, but we will see cold-related deaths.

“The threat is quite real, people are literally at risk of dying.

“And failing that, it’s acute illness, hospital admissions, other general burdens on the NHS and social care.”

The charity added that it is “bracing for a wave” of people seeking emergency help, estimating a rise of at least one fifth compared with last winter.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the Government has taken “immediate action” on energy bills, including the £100 energy payment and the move to temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which reduces costs by about £45 a year.

The Chancellor also announced in his autumn Budget that gas standing charges will be scrapped in England, Scotland and Wales.

Age UK has said that while the “limited support” from the Government is welcome, it is “dwarfed” by the scale of the energy price hike.

The charity’s director Caroline Abrahams said: “Age UK is deeply concerned that this winter could be one of the toughest in recent years for older people,

“We know that many will be terrified about how they will manage if the cap announced by Ofgem on Wednesday is as high as estimated.

“The fact is that they simply just don’t have the money to cope with another big energy price rise.”

She added that “no-one should have to choose between keeping warm and paying for other essentials” and called on the Government to introduce an emergency support package.

Wholesale energy prices have reduced in recent weeks on hopes of a resolution to the Middle East conflict, but not soon enough to prevent the January bill shock.

Fuel poverty campaigners said that households are being left to absorb a crisis they did not cause, “while the energy industry banks billions in profit”.

Simon Francis, co-ordinator of the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: “Behind the bills are people heating a single room, wearing coats indoors, skipping hot meals and watching damp and mould spread across their walls.

“For older people, disabled people and those living with long-term illness, a cold home is far more than uncomfortable.

“It makes them sicker, puts pressure on the NHS and even means their lives are in danger.”

Mr Francis also criticised the Government’s choice to tie the £100 payment to council tax bands, which he said would miss many that needed it most.

He added that ministers need to help households “get off gas for good” so that a crisis like this cannot happen again.

Ofgem will announce the quarterly price cap level for January to March on November 25.

News.title: Iran airs footage of underground ‘missile city’ with launcher capable of firing two missiles at once
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Iran unveiled a new missile launcher at an underground facility, touting what it says is its continued capability to strike if the war with the United States accelerates once more.

Iranian state television aired footage from an underground missile facility where the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard unveiled a new launcher it said was capable of firing two liquid-fuelled missiles.

The launchers appear to be an advance over a dual launcher that Iran previously used that fired two solid-fuel missiles at a time. Liquid fuel is more efficient and gives operators some capability to adjust the missiles’ speed and trajectory.

The Fars news agency posted a video on X of IRGC commanders visiting what it described as an “underground missile city.”

Commuters travel past a billboard depicting a launched missile and a logo that reads in Farsi: "The sky is a place for our pride and loyalty," in Valiy-Asr Square in Tehran on 17 November 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

The location of the missile site was not revealed, but the broadcast aimed to tout Iran’s missile capabilities and counter past US claims to have destroyed the missile programme, amid fears that the war with the US could heat up once again.

During the unveiling of the launchers, Brig Gen Seyyed Majid Mousavi, commander of the Guard’s Aerospace Force, boasted that Iran’s “capabilities have expanded significantly,” adding, “We have integrated ‘surprises’ and highly effective assets into our combat structure.”

At least three oil tankers were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint.

The British military’s maritime security centre said in online postings that two tankers were struck separately by projectiles early Saturday while exiting the Persian Gulf through the strait.

One was hit in the stern, the other in the engine room, and there were no reports of casualties, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center reported.

There was no immediate comment from Iran on the centre’s report.

The Iranian Navy said in a statement carried in state media that a tanker hit a naval mine east of the strait before noon and caught fire. State media also said the military carried out its most “intense and varied” operations yet in the strait overnight to stop vessels, aimed at foiling the US military’s efforts to escort shipping through the narrows.

Iranian forces have been attacking shipping through the strait in a campaign aimed at hiking global energy prices to pressure the United States, which has imposed a crippling blockade on Iranian ports.

News.title: Superb Verstappen wins 50-lap thriller in Las Vegas after Russell crashes
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix, coming to you from very early on a Sunday morning (if you are in the eastern hemisphere) and very late on a Sunday night (if you are in the western hemisphere).

It is a strange race in a strange place, but this is now the fourth edition of the race and it looks to be here to stay for all its strangeness. It does present the teams with problems and problems are there to be solved or negotiated as well as can be in F1. That is the name of the game.

In qualifying yesterday the world champion, Kimi Antonelli, did that expertly, sneaking in at the end to finish fastest. He does, however, take a five-place grid penalty, so will be starting in sixth. Taking first place on the grid will be the in-form Max Verstappen, followed by George Russell, who could do with a strong finish to the season.

Russell seemed miffed about missing out on pole position, particularly with how Mercedes managed the qualifying situation, particularly with how the tow was managed. Antonelli was always going to take a grid penalty, so why give him the tow, was Russell’s reasoning.

In any case, Russell has a good chance to take his third victory this season. At least on paper. Russell’s qualifying has probably been his strongest suit this season, but race days have let him down. Let us not forget that Lando Norris, who won last time out in Brazil, starts third.

There could be a bit of aggro on the first lap, given Russell and Verstappen’s “disagreement” yesterday, but let’s see. It may end up being a clean race.

It all starts in about an hour and we will be here for all the updates and reaction from the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix.

News.title: Wales ‘frustrated’ after being brought back down to earth by Wallabies
News.content:
Wales have a spring in their step coming into their game tonight as they host Australia at the Principality Stadium. Wales pulled off one of their best wins in recent memory last weekend, ending an over 70-year with for a victory over New Zealand. Despite pulling off that shock victory, Wales sit down in fifth in the northern hemisphere standings coming into this final round of fixtures. In all likelihood, they can only improve one spot. They have made four changes from the historic win over the All Blacks, with the likes of Josh Adams and Aaron Wainwright coming in.

“We were all immensely proud to make history last week,” Wales head coach Steve Tandy said. “There is a new opportunity and challenge for us against Australia and we are looking to back up our performance this weekend. It is our last home game of this competition. The support that fans give to the players and staff has been incredible and we cannot wait to get back out at Principality Stadium.

“We made nearly 350 tackles, the ball in play time was one of the highest in Test rugby in the last three years and we have got competition. The plan was always to freshen up and we are likely to do similar for the week after, because we need to find out about players. We have fresh and hungry players coming in, which will add the energy that we need at the weekend. The training environment is getting more competitive in certain positions we have the ability to put people in and feel confident about performance.”

News.title: Whiff of arrogance as Arsenal unexpectedly implode
News.content:
Speaking to Sky Sports, the Arsenal boss said: “My feeling is that we lost two points today. I think we were exceptional in the first half. At every level. Our intensity, the clarity that we have, how to attack the jumps of Newcastle every time they wanted to go man-to-man, the composure that we have, the way we use our relationship to break their press. And it should have been 2-0, 3-0 or 4-0 up, clear.

“But it wasn’t. And when it wasn’t, then we expected in the second half that we have to again raise the level because the opponent is going to have a reaction. And the opponent did have a reaction and we were very below the level that is required to stretch the gap in a game like this in this stadium. And then we gave them belief.

“And I say we give them belief because we give them a goal, we give them a throw-in that we just give them the ball. We have no structure to control the opposite winger. We concede a goal and it’s game on. And from that it became a very chaotic game. Every set-piece, we know that they are exceptional at it and we concede from a set piece.

“And then you have to react. And then we went back to the team that the exceptional team that we were in the first half again for another 25 minutes and we scored a great goal. We create infinity of openings to create and score the third goal, but we lack some time or to be precise, to make that count.”

News.title: ‘Remarkable’ Ireland deliver perfect riposte to Erasmus mind games
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Ireland vs South Africa from the Nations Championship in Dublin, with both teams harbouring hopes of finishing the day at the top of their respective tables.

Ireland and South Africa have both won four of their five games in the group phase of this year’s inaugural Nations Championship, and come into their last match before next weekend’s finals still in contention for the overall title.

Andy Farrell’s men begin the afternoon in third in the Northern Hemisphere table, but level on points with second-placed England, who are currently hosting New Zealand, and just one point behind leaders France, who take on Argentina this evening.

The reigning world champions, meanwhile, are guaranteed to at least remain in second in the Southern Hemisphere table, but are just one point behind the All Blacks at the top of the group, so will be hoping for a favour from Steve Borthwick’s men at Twickenham.

The Springboks will be without head coach Rassie Erasmus for today’s contest in the Irish capital, with the 54-year-old facing a six-match ban because of his criticism of officials following his team’s narrow defeat by France last weekend, including asking whether they were “match-fixing”.

“He’s been hands-on with our team, and we’re in a good space,” assistant coach Mzwandile Stick said of Erasmus on Friday. “Irrespective of what has happened, we love him, we appreciate him, and no one is going to break us. I can tell you that for sure.”

In the same press conference, Erasmus predicted that Sam Prendergast would be cleared to play after being cited for a hip-drop tackle against Fiji. The Ireland fly-half escaped punishment from the independent panel and starts for Farrell’s side this afternoon.

News.title: Alonso heckled as Chelsea are humiliated by Leeds
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to coverage from the Premier League as domestic football returns after an international break.

We have five matches to bring you, including Chelsea vs Leeds, Aston Villa vs Sunderland and Tottenham vs Ipswich.

Xabi Alonso said his Chelsea side needs to learn to deal with the absence of Joao Pedro as the Blues struggle for goals in the absence of their injured striker.

The Brazilian has not played since the 2-0 win over Everton on October 17 and will be unavailable again today.

Without a focal point in the number nine position, Chelsea’s goal output has been dramatically reduced and they have dropped to fifth and having suffered two defeats in their last three games.

“(We need) the whole team for that,” said Alonso. “It’s not just the strikers that can score. We can score from set-pieces, from defenders, from midfielders.

“It’s teamwork. For sure Joao is an important player but we need to deal with this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying.

“We need to deal with it. It’s not that I’m going to look for one explanation. I think that there are more explanations for one defeat than missing just one player.”

Tottenham will not have their manager, Roberto De Zerbi, on the touchline after receiving three yellow cards this season.

Gary O’Neil is targeting a “special” result at Tottenham, but promised Ipswich will not make any drastic changes after a four-match winless run.

Ipswich lost 2-1 at home to Bournemouth before the two-week break, which followed draws with Hull and Nottingham Forest along with a narrow defeat at Manchester City, but O’Neil is happy with his new-look group.

“There won’t be any drastic changes. The odd personnel change, (but) I don’t think it’s going to be a big shift for us,” O’Neil told a press conference.

“It’s a very well-balanced squad. There’s going to be no massive uplifts or downgrades when we have to change players within this group.”

Aston Villa will have Johan Manzambi available for the visit of Sunderland.

The midfielder did not feature for Switzerland during the recent international break because of a calf injury but he has trained with the rest of the squad and can feature today.

Villa can also call on right-back Aaron Wan-Bissaka after a muscle injury ruled him out for six matches. His return is timely as Matty Cash is unavailable.

Cash was suspended for Villa’s 4-4 draw with Manchester United before the international break but suffered a concussion while away with Poland.

News.title: England obliterate All Blacks in record win
News.content:
A nearly perfect half for England was ruined just two minutes before half-time when Ben Earl gave up a penalty from the restart, immediately after scoring the home side’s third try. New Zealand kicked to the corner and Ethan de Groot plunged over to give the All Blacks a lifeline they scarcely deserve.

Until that point, this was as dominant a half against top-tier opposition that we have ever seen from Steve Borthwick’s team. Much like they did against Australia, England have strangled the life out of New Zealand and have enjoyed a preposterous 78 per cent territory.

They have also repeatedly cut New Zealand open in midfield. The interplay between Fin Smith, Seb Atkinson and the regal George Furbank has been sumptuous to watch. England have struggled to break New Zealand down in the red zone but still have three tries to show for their efforts. Smith’s cute little poke through was grounded by Henry Slade after five minutes and then scrum half Jack van Poortvliet did his best Superman impression by diving over the top of a ruck for England’s second try.

Earl also went route one, picking off the back of a scrum and through Cam Roigard’s tackle to put England in dreamland. Not every department has functioned perfectly. New Zealand have been on top of the scrum and have stopped the English maul in its tracks, but the All Blacks have been dominated physically. When was the last time we said that about an England team?

The De Groot try has taken the wind out of England’s sails a little but a similar setback took place in the Australia game just before half-time and Borthwick’s team responded with an emphatic second-half performance.

England need to see this out too, otherwise they’ll be kicking themselves all the way through to the World Cup.

News.title: England lose to ‘Australia B team’ in thriller
News.content:
England’s white-ball tour of Australia continues as a five-match T20 series between kicks off in Melbourne at the iconic Melbourne Cricket Ground, with the sandpapergate saga rumbling on. The first part of the tour went England’s way, as they came from 1-0 down to win the ODI series 2-1, following wins in Adelaide and Hobart. All of that action on the field has taken place whilst there has been plenty of “he said, she said” as some, like Cameron Bancroft, David Warner and Usman Khawaja say that everyone knew about the use of sandpaper whilst Pat Cummins has categorically denied that.

The last time these sides met in a T20 series back in September 2024, the three-match series ended in a 1-1 draw, with the final match abandoned. England won the last series played down under in October 2022, claiming a 2-0 series victory. Therefore, England are unbeaten in their past three bilateral mens’s T20I series against Australia. England are currently top of the ICC T20 rankings, with Australia third.

England were last in T20 action back in September, when they beat Sri Lanka 3-0. They have won all but two completed T20Is in 2026, with their last defeat coming in the World Cup semi-finals against India in March. They have decided to rest a number of the seamers who played in the ODI series including Jofra Archer and Gus Atkinson, whilst Josh Tongue is out injured. With those seamers absent, it will likely present opportunities for Henry Crocombe and Eddie Jack. Jacob Bethell remains out with a knee injury that he is still struggling with whilst Jos Buttler continues to recover from an hamstring injury.

Australia bombed out of the T20 World Cup in the group stages earlier this year, the first time that has happened since 2009. They did though win their most recent T20 series, beating Bangladesh 3-0 in June. Australia’s fast-bowling trio of Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood have all been rested for England’s white-ball tour, something that was planned long before the 2018 sandpapergate was reignited. Not only are that trio not involved but the likes of Nathan Ellis and Xavier Bartlett will also not play, therefore it will be a relatively inexperienced bowling attack for the hosts.

They will give a debut to wicketkeeper Sam Harper, who was named player of the tournament in the most recent edition of the Big Bash with the Melbourne Stars, with Josh Inglis being rested ahead of Australia’s upcoming busy Test schedule. Inglis is not the only player to sit out this series having played in the ODIs, with the likes of Travis Head, Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green and Cooper Connolly also not participating.

Play from the MCG gets under way from 8.15am GMT.

News.title: Anthropic plunges as Wall Street suffers AI sell-off
News.content:
Anthropic’s share price slump triggered a sharp sell-off on Wall Street with tech stocks closing down more than 5pc.

More than $163bn was wiped off the value of the AI giant on Friday, just a day after it touched a $2tn valuation on its stock market debut.

The decline prompted a wider flight from AI shares, with the tech-focused Nasdaq 100 down 5.6pc. It means the index has now erased all its gains year to date.

The S&P 500 fell 3.7pc at close, putting it on course for its worst week since Donald Trump’s ‘liberation day’ tariffs last year, and into correction territory.

Anthropic has endured a hugely volatile introduction to public markets, surging as much as 39pc on the Nasdaq on Thursday, before closing the day 17pc higher.

However, it fell by as much as 14pc to $83.16 on Friday, just above where it started trading on Thursday.

It started the day at $97, less than 24 hours after it hit a high of $115.

The latest sell-off has fuelled fears that the company’s record-breaking float, which raised $87bn, is not enough to dispel lingering concerns over the AI bubble.

It comes after a series of threats to the investment boom.

That includes anti-data centre Democrats taking control of Congress, the downfall of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and tighter export controls on chips to China.

The Philadelphia semiconductor index, a grouping of the major US chip companies, dropped by as much as 9pc on Friday.

AI-linked companies dragged the Nasdaq lower, with the likes of semiconductor maker ARM losing 14pc.

CoreWeave also weighed on the Nasdaq, with its shares down 12pc.

European shares were also on track for their worst week since March amid investor concern over an AI bubble.

In a day of volatile swings on Wall Street, Nvidia also slipped behind Google parent Alphabet to become the fourth-most valuable US company.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “It’s been another hectic and negative week and one where even positive news is struggling to help the market stabilise.”

Pressure on stocks also rose after Donald Trump on Friday threatened to ban technology companies from building data centres outside of the US.

In a White House press conference, Mr Trump warned there would be “tremendous penalties” on US companies that tried to build data centres in foreign countries.

He said: “We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen.”

He added: “We’re going to fight very hard for the data centres because we’re not going to let China [overtake us].”

The ban threat will raise questions for AI developers who are spending hundreds of billions of pounds building data facilities in the UK, Europe and across Asia.

It is not clear whether Mr Trump’s ban would apply to all data centre developers or just the most advanced facilities.

The sell-off came as Anthropic’s approach to copyright was slammed by news publishers, who said the company lacks “a basic moral compass”.

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents titles including The Telegraph, The Times and The Guardian, attacked the company for its policy on journalism.

Anthropic told investors it could not guarantee it would adhere to measures that prevented journalism from being used to train AI models.

The Claude maker said it took steps to abide by paywalls but that this “may not always be successful”.

Sports.title: Verstappen wins wild Las Vegas GP as Ferraris collide again
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen produced a remarkable drive to win a wild Las Vegas Grand Prix that saw him withstand extreme pressure from George Russell and Kimi Antonelli before a late Mercedes collapse.

Pole-sitter Verstappen retained the lead at the start but the enormous power of a slipstream on the long straights of the Las Vegas Strip Circuit made it impossible for the Dutchman to pull clear, and resulted in 34 changes of the lead and well over 300 total overtakes in the 50-lap race.

First Russell, and then later newly crowned world champion Antonelli were each able to pass Verstappen on multiple occasions but the Red Bull driver calmly retook the lead within a few corners every time, expertly managing the deployment of his power.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell hits the barrier after a lock-up when trying to overtake team-mate Kimi Antonelli at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, much to the delight of rival Max Verstappen.

Russell, trying to pass his team-mate for second with three laps remaining, ran into a barrier after overshooting a corner and dropped down the order, before Antonelli made an error with his deployment at the start of the final lap that allowed Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri to snatch a double podium for McLaren.

"That was crazy. Really, really surreal and something I've never seen before in F1 myself," Verstappen said.

"I think we had it [deployment] set up well and it was a crazy amount of fighting, and the slipstream was so big that it was just impossible to drive off, and it was just crazy how many people were following."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton spins after contact with Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc, which led to a 10-second penalty for the latter at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

There was more unwanted drama for Ferrari as team-mates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collided again as they battled for sixth with 12 laps remaining, with the latter given a 10-second penalty by the stewards for causing the incident.

Pierre Gasly took fifth ahead of his team-mate Franco Colapinto to secure a major points haul for Alpine, with Hamilton recovering to seventh, having served a 10-second penalty himself earlier in the race for overtaking Norris off track.

Carlos Sainz snatched eighth from Russell on the run to the finish line to equal Williams' best result of the season, while Leclerc claimed the final point in 10th.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Red Bulla's Isack Hadjar was running in third place but was forced to pit after losing his front wing at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The result all but secures second in the drivers' standings for Verstappen, who made it four wins in six races to pull 37 points clear of third-placed Hamilton with two rounds to go in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

McLaren's late gains enabled them to close within nine points of Red Bull in the battle for third in the constructors' standings, with Verstappen's team-mate Isack Hadjar unfortunate to finish outside the points after a front-wing failure - moments after a Safety Car stoppage that had bunched the field - dropped him from third to last.

Las Vegas GP Result: Top 10 1) Max Verstappen, Red Bull



2) Lando Norris, McLaren



3) Oscar Piastri, McLaren



4) Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes



5) Pierre Gasly, Alpine



6) Franco Colapinto, Alpine



7) Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari



8) Carlos Sainz, Williams



9) George Russell, Mercedes



10) Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

Verstappen has last laugh in Russell battle

Despite Antonelli and Mercedes having already closed out this year's championships, there was plenty of tension on the grid as Verstappen and Russell lined up on the front row following a renewal of a long-term spat between the pair earlier in the weekend.

Following a collision between the pair in final practice that resulted in Verstappen being given a warning by the stewards, Russell launched a scathing criticism of the Dutchman, echoing comments he made almost exactly two years ago as he said someone needed to "stand up" to the Red Bull driver.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The start of the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Despite those words, there was plenty of respect on show between the pair on track as they battled for much of the race after Verstappen had made a strong start to retain the lead.

Russell, who was already under constant pressure from Hadjar and then Norris, adjusted his deployment strategy to repeatedly find a way past Verstappen in the final sector. However, he could never find a way to keep the Red Bull behind him through the opening corners of the following lap.

The only real pause in the frantic action came on lap 19 when Cadillac's Sergio Perez and Haas' Rafael Camara collided as the former attempted an overtake.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell tussles with Max Verstappen and Isack Hadajr at the start of the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The damage left Perez stranded on track, triggering the Safety Car. Its deployment was extended when Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad, who was running fifth at the time, spun and also came to a stop on the circuit.

When the race resumed at the end of lap 25, Russell continued to put Verstappen under pressure, retaking the lead several times. He even reclaimed first place after briefly dropping behind Norris.

Russell made his final move into the lead at the end of lap 37, but Verstappen quickly reclaimed the position. For the first time in the race, Russell then dropped behind team-mate Antonelli, who had fought back from a five-place grid penalty despite securing pole position in qualifying.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes' George Russell insists he's got no regrets despite locking up and hitting the barrier late in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Russell was tyring to mount one last push for victory on lap 48, but his attempt to go up the inside of Antonelli at Turn 5 came unstuck as he locked up and nudged into the barrier.

Having seen the incident in his mirrors, Verstappen immediately came on team radio - apparently delighted at his rival's error - saying: "Haha. Well done! My god…"

Verstappen had already demonstrated his awareness midway through the race, opening discussions with his team over the radio about adjusting their deployment strategy to ensure Mercedes could not beat him in a drag race to the line on the final lap.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Max Verstappen had a choice few words for long-time foe George Russell after winning the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Ultimately, such tactics weren't necessary as Antonelli, by lifting off the throttle, triggered a loss in deployment that allowed both McLarens to overtake him and gave Verstappen a relatively stress-free final lap.

The four-time world champion wasn't finished taking a dig at Russell. Asked about the Brit during the post-race press conference, Verstappen added: "It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and saw what was happening. I was like, 'Fantastic, my day is only getting better.'"

"And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete."

Leclerc penalised for 'unacceptable' collision with Hamilton

With Antonelli and Mercedes dominating this year's championships, much of F1's drama in recent weeks has been provided by the repeated battles between Ferrari team-mates Hamilton and Leclerc.

Hamilton was left furious following the Mexico City Grand Prix at the start of the month when Leclerc launched an ambitious attempt to take the lead from him on the opening lap, resulting in a clash that cost the team a likely one-two and gifted Verstappen victory.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari team-mates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc react after they crashed into one another at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Both drivers said the situation had been resolved following talks in Brazil the following week, but that didn't appear to be the case on Saturday night in Las Vegas.

Starting from 9th and 10th after a dismal qualifying, the pair made minor contact at the start, but far worse was to come.

Hamilton had driven impressively to fight his way back through the field after serving a 10-second penalty for going off track while passing Norris. He was ahead of Leclerc in the battle for sixth and pushing to retake the position from the McLaren when the pair came together.

Seeing Hamilton fail to get past Norris, Leclerc attempted to capitalise, making an ambitious move up the inside at Turn 7.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari Team Principal has branded Charles Leclerc's driving as 'unacceptable' after his collided with Lewis Hamilton during the Las Vegas GP.

The result was a collision that spun Hamilton and saw him drop back through the field, with the stewards deciding Leclerc was to blame as he had come from too far behind his team-mate, which meant Hamilton had no obligation to leave space on the inside.

Hamilton was measured in his comments both on the radio and after the race, but Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur summoned Leclerc to speak to him immediately after the race before later telling Sky Sports that the Monegasque had committed an "unacceptable" mistake.

While the latest episode of the Verstappen-Russell beef will perhaps be the biggest talking point ahead of Thursday's media day at the Qatar Grand Prix, a new chapter of Ferrari's internal battle and Vasseur's inability to control the situation will be met with similar anticipation.

Sports.title: 'He's so far below my level' - Verstappen taunts Russell over Las Vegas GP error
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen says George Russell is "so far below my level" in a scathing response to the Mercedes driver after winning the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Verstappen claimed his fourth win of the season after a stunning defensive drive while Russell crashed in the latter stages and finished ninth, having battled Verstappen for the win earlier.

The pair collided in final practice on Saturday with Verstappen warned for "driving erratically" in the incident but Russell criticised the Red Bull driver.

"There's nothing in the rules to say you cannot overtake someone who is starting a lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over and he does this week in, week out with many drivers and everybody accepts it," he told Sky Italy.

"I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody's got to stand up to that guy."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell hits the barrier after a lock-up when trying to overtake team-mate Kimi Antonelli at the Las Vegas Grand Prix, much to the delight of rival Max Verstappen

Verstappen was asked about the comments in the post-race press conference following his third Las Vegas Grand Prix victory and hit back at Russell.

He said: "The thing is, he speaks a lot next to the track. And honestly, for me, it doesn't really bother me because he's so far below my level that it doesn't really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that. So, it doesn't bother me.

"And today, karma is a b****. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening [when Russell crashed]. I was like, 'fantastic, my day is only getting better.'

"And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete."

Sports.title: Harrison: The animosity Fury and AJ have is genuine
Sports.content:
Audley Harrison has backed Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury to deliver when they fight on December 11 in Cardiff.

Harrison was one half of an all-British heavyweight grudge match when he boxed David Haye in a 2010 event that was much hyped but ultimately disappointed.

Harrison though doesn't think Fury and Joshua have left their fight too late.

"'Politricks' has always been there in boxing, always unfortunately messing up boxing," Harrison told Sky Sports.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Frank Warren hints at a trilogy fight between Tyson Fury and Oleksandr Usyk and discusses Moses Itauma's future with a fight in early 2027 expected to be confirmed.

"I will be sitting on the edge of my seat for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. They're not in their primes but there's still enough there and the animosity that they have is genuine. So it's a fight definitely I want to see. While it's a little late, I can't argue with that.

"It's not going to be them in their primes but it's going to be good enough. We need to see it for sure."

He added: "Look at Mike Tyson-Lennox Lewis, everyone was complaining for that fight, that fight was like five years too late in many people's eyes.

"I was there in Memphis, it was a great fight, great atmosphere, exactly what we wanted.

"Lennox banged him out but the fight was so exciting."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Anthony Joshua has made the bold prediction that he will knockout Tyson Fury in a round. Watch back at his previous explosive first round KOs.

Harrison preceded Joshua as an Olympic super-heavyweight gold medallist for Great Britain. But he did not scale the heights Joshua achieved in the professional ranks. Joshua has twice been a unified heavyweight world champion and has made a habit of selling out stadium shows in London and Cardiff.

"All of these guys came from nowhere. AJ went to the Olympics not as the favourite, same as Deontay Wilder, and they punched their way to glory," Harrison said.

"When Joshua turned pro he was raw as hell, you've got to give him credit he was able to go through.

"When he lost to [Andy] Ruiz they crucified him because he was meant to win, but he was still raw. He's always been really disciplined, he's strong and he's always come into the ring ready.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Barry Hearn says he was pleased with the 'respect' shown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua at their press conference.

"Technically and tactically he's been off in some fights, obviously with [Oleksandr] Usyk, obviously with [Daniel] Dubois. But came back in the [Wladimir] Klitschko fight. When you look at his career, you've got to take your hat off. He wasn't perfect, but he's not supposed to be."

Harrison added: "He's still got the power, he's still got the punch but he doesn't have the punch resistance now.

"We're seeing that with Joshua, we're seeing that with Fury. We haven't seen that with Usyk yet. I haven't seen him start to flounder yet in terms of punch resistance.

"To be fair to AJ and Tyson Fury, they've both had a legendary career, when you look at what they've done, not just the money they've made, if you look at their legacy."

Sports.title: 'Completely unacceptable! - Vasseur slams Leclerc for Hamilton collision
Sports.content:
Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur blamed Charles Leclerc for a "completely unacceptable" collision with team-mate Lewis Hamilton in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The Ferrari drivers made contact when battling over sixth place with 12 laps remaining in a breathless, frenzied race in which the team were attempting to recover from a poor qualifying when both drivers were knocked out in Q2.

Hamilton was spun around in the Turn Seven-collision, dropping to 10th in the order. Leclerc was found to be at fault by race stewards, who imposed a 10-second penalty on him.

That was applied to Leclerc's final race time and dropped him to 10th place in the final classification, with Hamilton ending up seventh.

Two weeks after speaking to both drivers to remind them of their responsibilities to the team after a squabble on track in Mexico had cost them a likely win, Vasseur was left unimpressed. He also revealed they had asked Leclerc not to overtake Hamilton given they did not want the drivers fighting amongst themselves and leave them vulnerable to slip-streaming rivals.

"Clearly, it's unacceptable," Vasseur told Sky Italy.

"A little bit the same message as Mexico because you have to think about the team, about the people working in Maranello. About all the stakeholders, the sponsors and so on.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari Team Principal has branded Charles Leclerc's driving as 'unacceptable' after his collided with Lewis Hamilton during the Las Vegas GP.

"We told Charles not to overtake, because in a race like this, you have to focus on your own race rather than risk being overtaken by others. Charles clearly made a mistake, and it has cost the team dearly. What happened today [Sunday] is completely unacceptable.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari team-mates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc react after they crashed into one another at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

"Honestly, I am more than upset because that message was clear after Mexico.

"We had a chat all together in Brazil. Today we passed the message to think about the team when they were racing together and the outcome is this one. It's mega frustrating for all of us."

'I'm penalised so it has to be my mistake' - Leclerc frustrated but accepts decision

In their report confirming the decision to penalise Leclerc, the stewards said the Monegasque had started his move on Hamilton from "a considerable distance behind" in the sister Ferrari, Hamilton's car, and had "not earned the right to the corner" by the apex.

They therefore found him to be "wholly to blame".

On Leclerc's cool-down lap back to the pits at the end of the race, Vasseur told him on Ferrari team radio: "Charles, I want to see you just after the race, before everything"

While stopping short of any apology in his post-race interview, instead saying he was "embarrassed for the team", a visibly-frustrated Leclerc said he accepted the stewards' decision.

"I have been penalised so, as a result, I guess the majority and the stewards thought that it was my mistake. I'll accept that," Leclerc told Sky Sports F1.

"I'm not going to say much more. At the end of the day, I'm penalised so it has to be my mistake."

Asked if Ferrari now needed to impose stricter rules, Leclerc said: "Well, I just feel quite embarrassed for the team in general. We'll review."

Sports.title: France reach Nations Championship final with bonus-point Argentina win
Sports.content:
France book South Africa rematch in Nations Championship final with bonus-point victory over Argentina

Antoine Dupont was back at scrum-half and helped France to a big win

France reached the Nations Championship final after beating Argentina 45-17 with seven tries on Saturday.

England's 37-12 win against New Zealand left France needing a bonus-point victory to make the November 29 final against South Africa, who topped the southern hemisphere group despite losing to Ireland.

Already leading 21-10, Emilien Gailleton got France's fourth try for the bonus point in the 64th minute against 14 men, and moments later the yellow card for Pumas prop Mayco Vivas was upgraded to red.

France finished with three more tries. Lock Tyler Duguid charged through following an attacking lineout, centre Kalvin Gourgues showed stunning pace from near halfway to make the left corner, and Louis Bielle-Biarrey completed the rout with his 31st try in 30 tests.

France beat the Springboks 21-19 last week in Paris

In the first half lock Mickaël Guillard and try-scoring hooker Peato Mauvaka crossed for France. Returning fly-half Matthieu Jalibert cleverly set up silky centre Gourgues shortly after the break for the first of his two tries.

Argentina led briefly at 10-7 for 10 minutes thanks to a converted try from centre Justo Piccardo and a penalty from fly-half Tomas Albornoz.

Jalibert's faster than expected recovery from a torn thigh allowed captain Antoine Dupont to resume at scrum-half after wearing the No 10 jersey a week ago against South Africa.

Dupont showed his class at the end with a kick down the left flank for Bielle-Biarrey's try.

Gourdes nailed five conversions as a makeshift kicker on the night.

Tributes were held before the game for Federico Martín Aramburú, the former Argentina player who died four years ago after being fatally shot in Paris.

Sports.title: César Azpilicueta: ‘At Chelsea a draw was a catastrophe – if you can’t perform, you’re out’
Sports.content:
César Azpilicueta looks well. César Azpilicueta always looks well – “ah, Captain Handsome,” one Chelsea fan says when told who’s turning up – but today especially, smiling in the sunshine. Strolling in, he eases into an easier chair, golf course spreading out beyond the terrace, west of Madrid, and orders a detox almost as green. It is nearly 20 years since he played his first game and a few months since he played his last, training kit replaced by bermudas, loafers and a polo, a picture of relaxation. So what’s it like not being a footballer? “Well, different,” he says. Then he laughs, which he does a lot.

It is not a laugh-your-head-off laugh, more a chuckle, a giggle, as if amused at everything he did. And for all the self-deprecation, the lack of triumphalism, he did everything. Now, at 37, it’s not the same, although there remains much to do, Azpilicueta as understated and quietly busy as ever: “square,” he calls himself. He’s completed an MBA, a sports directorship diploma and there are media offers, a life to live. Matches to play still: against his kids the needle is never far away, he says. And although he hasn’t found a seven-a-side team yet he will.

“I get up, take them to school, go to the gym. I do pilates some days. I walk the dogs, play golf, then it’s after-school activities. I read, try to learn new things. I haven’t yet thought: ‘I’m bored,’” Azpilicueta says, although you wonder how long that will last. “Over the last 12 months I could see it. The summer before I already ‘hit the post’ with retirement. It’s natural: a day comes … if only I could play for ever but it is what it is and you have to keep evolving. I’m enjoying it.”

Don’t get the wrong idea. “In terms of controlling your time, playing every three days, always waiting on the next message: ‘Meet at …,’ it’s a release. But it’s not a liberation because you’re delighted to pull your boots on. An important part of your life ends; you kick a ball almost from the moment you walk, live your passion. Even last season – when there were days everything hurt, when you think: ‘How can I get injured like that?’ – I would make demands of myself, my teammates. I always liked that.

“I never thought I’d be a professional. I couldn’t tell you the moment I thought: ‘I’m a footballer,’” Azpilicueta continues, but he can tell you the score on his debut, for Osasuna in 2007. “One-nil win, Getafe.” Celta de Vigo were the last opponents: a 1-0 loss in May for Sevilla. Between those, more than 800 matches, 508 for Chelsea. Only five players have played more for Chelsea; no foreigner has.

View image in fullscreen César Azpilicueta returns to Stamford Bridge for October’s match against Tottenham. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters

“I don’t think anyone who saw me back then could explain how I played 11 years at Chelsea … and nor could I,” Azpilicueta says, and there’s that laugh again.

It’s a long time since he stood before his new teammates and sang an Estopa track. He arrived in London with a labrador and a sausage dog; he left a legend and the captain, with three kids and every trophy, a European and world champion.

Asked to define his career in a word, Azpilicueta goes for: constancia. Perseverance, consistency, commitment. He talks about the cruciate tear with Marseille aged 19 as a lesson, something that “changed my perspective and made me value discipline, preparation … Out of something negative I grew.” About always adapting, always overcoming, becoming what managers need you to be. There’s a laugh at the little lies – of course I’ve played on the left, boss – and the hours spent alone practising, convincing coaches or teammates to stay behind with him and go over it again and again.

“I arrived at Chelsea late in the market [in 2012],” Azpilicueta says. “My representative said: ‘We’ve spoken to Michael Emenalo, the sporting director, and they’re signing younger players.’ Oscar, Eden Hazard, Victor Moses, Marko Marin, Paulo Ferreira. I was 22. Doubts? Pfff … Olympique needed the money. Chelsea had just won the Champions League and I …”

That laugh. “I hadn’t played for Spain. What did Emenalo see in me? It’s hard to work it out. Also, what you are and what you become is different. You think: ‘What’s it going to be like?’ Another country, another pace, but Juan Mata was there, Fernando Torres, Oriol [Romeu]. Doctor [Paco] Biosca, Ivan the physio. Petr Cech spoke Spanish. Hazard and I spoke French together. I could [communicate] with the Brazilians. But it wasn’t just them. I integrated fast, tried to speak English.

double quotation mark I don’t think anyone who saw me back then could explain how I played 11 years at Chelsea … and nor could I

“Not long after arriving there was this audience with fans. Fernando, Juan, Oriol and I. A Q&A. One said: ‘Look, your name is very difficult. Can we just call you Dave?’ Juan translated. I said: ‘Yeah, sure,’ thinking that they meant for the evening. And it stuck. Going down the street: ‘Hey, Dave!’ There was the occasional ‘Dave’ in the dressing room but mostly it was fans. I felt the affection.

“You go with an open mind and bit by bit carve yourself a place. Every time a new coach comes you think: ‘Now what? Will I fit?’ I started as a winger in Pamplona. At Chelsea I played right-back, left-back, a line of three which I hadn’t played in my life … lots of systems, lots of coaches.”

Twelve coaches, in fact. Azpilicueta played under all of them. ““You arrive at a historic club like Chelsea and just try to stay as long as you can. That machine makes demands of you every three days. What I really noticed was a hunger to win: either you have that culture or … forget it. At Chelsea a draw was a catastrophe. You see teammates come and go. The reality is the reality. On the pitch, you have to do it. It’s hard? Yes. But you can’t be sunk by a bad game. If you win: very good, done, next. If you can’t perform, you’re out … You have to manage that pressure.

View image in fullscreen ‘Dave’ Azpilicueta took to life in England quickly after his move to Chelsea in 2012. Photograph: Gerry Penny/EPA

“I’ve had plenty of unpleasant days. I remember a 6-0 loss Manchester City.” So then what? “For me, the first thing would be watch the video. Look at the data. But know that’s not everything. Sleep, get up, turn it round. Get into to training first. And it’s not just about you; some days it’s about lifting up teammates too.”

Preparation, he says, was fundamental. “I analysed everything. I want to know if when the winger receives, he turns left. I needed that. Football’s not mathematical – ‘this equals that’ – but that information helps you have more control, feel readier. I don’t know if I was more [serious] than others, but I was very cuadriculado, square. Others hardly did anything and were fine.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That sounds like Eden Hazard. Azpilicueta laughs. “He was more … more … relaxed. Not everyone has to be the same. I was very square, I prepared differently, I was like a robot.”

Besides, Hazard was the best; it is his name, not Lionel Messi or Ronaldo’s, that comes up when Azpilicueta is asked his toughest opponent. “I was fortunate to train with Eden. He didn’t train 100%, but he forced you to. I had to kick him sometimes, haha! Playing together, he would say: ‘Give me the ball.’ I would say: ‘Stay there, I’ll defend for you.’”

Azpilicueta defended them all. “The first time I was captain was an FA Cup semi-final against Tottenham [in 2017],” he recalls. “We arrived late, no one said anything. [Gary] Cahill, the captain, was injured. We walk in and, pam, the armband’s in my place. Steve Holland says: ‘Let’s go to the referees meeting.’ ‘Oh, OK’ … and that was it. I liked it. I don’t think you change much; you have your own personality. You don’t have to score two because you’re captain. Besides, that was a one-off until later. But you do feel a little extra responsibility.”

View image in fullscreen ‘He didn’t train at 100%, but he forced you to,’ Azpilicueta says of Eden Hazard. Photograph: Andrew Fosker/BPI/Shutterstock

New players found Azpilicueta waiting for them, leadership through empathy and example. “Quite a few stayed at my house,” he says. But if there is a portrait of his leadership perhaps it is him paying for the bus, covering petrol for the first team and youth team, when Chelsea’s assets were frozen after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. And his reaction to that being put to him now. “Nah,” he says. “Well. No. All of us. I didn’t do anything anyone else didn’t. We did it together, which is how things should be done.

“There a feeling of: ‘We have this issue, we’re going to sort this out,’” Azpilicueta adds, fist hitting the desk. “That situation was strange. We had won the Club World Cup, been with [Roman Abramovich] there and suddenly … it was the uncertainty: players, staff. Many people work for Chelsea, depend on that.”

Underlying it all is the same basic principle, Azpilicueta says: “People. There are so many day-to-day who make it work. And sure, we’re good at football but what really fulfils you is see people there with their families all together when you win, when you lift the Champions League.”

View image in fullscreen Azpilicueta lifts the Champions League as Chelsea captain in 2021. Photograph: Carl Recine/Reuters

Have you got a photo of you lifting that cup? “At home? No. A friend gave me a very nice one framed but it’s half hidden. I don’t much like showing it off.” If someone came to your house could they tell a footballer lives there? “No.”

Twenty years on, a lifetime later, a footballer doesn’t. So now what? “I don’t know,” Azpilicueta says, laughing. “Maybe I’ll be here, playing off a better handicap. But I like football, being involved. I’ve done some co-commentating. I have the MBA, the diploma. Not because I necessarily want to be a sporting director tomorrow, but because it interests me, because it’s nice to learn. I enjoyed the classes, meeting people, doing course work.”

The practical experience is even better. “The last few contracts I negotiated myself. I’ve had various agents help over the years but a time came with Chelsea when I thought: ‘What for?’ I sit down with Marina [Granovskaia], then with Behdad [Eghbali] and Todd [Boehly]. As captain I had spoken to them about so many issues that when it came to my own I thought: ‘I can do this alone.’ I might have got a better deal, who knows, but I was comfortable that way. I was never looking for anything, I was happy, my family was happy, I felt loved and valued and that was it. I just wanted to go in to work every day.”

Sports.title: Raya injured but Madueke rescues point for Arsenal in seesaw Newcastle draw
Sports.content:
If Mikel Arteta was delighted to see the back of Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s head coach, the bad news is that another similarly awkward technical area adversary has been installed at St James’ Park.

Arsenal’s manager never seemed to relish trips to face Howe’s old team and he certainly did not enjoy this latest trip to Tyneside, where Matthias Jaissle’s initially overwhelmed team fought back commendably to earn a point courtesy of a stellar second-half performance. At half-time the crowd had felt close to turning against Jaissle but he held his nerve and, thanks to a triple substitution and subtle tactical rejig suggested he is no mug after all.

It left Arsenal – who lost their outstanding goalkeeper David Raya to a potentially significant second-half shoulder injury – still top of the Premier League, six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City, and Arteta with a face like thunder.

View image in fullscreen David Raya is helped off the pitch with a shoulder injury. Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA

Just last week Bruno Guimarães claimed he was “beloved” by Newcastle fans but the club’s former captain turned Arsenal midfielder found himself serenaded by a soundtrack of boos of the sort usually reserved for Sunderland players. Newcastle’s problem is that, despite spending about £275m this summer, they have struggled to replace last season’s departed star trio – Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon.

That reality perhaps left Howe’s successor – who arrived just before the start of the season – making a not so subtle point with his team sheet here. Of Jaissle’s starting XI only the goalkeeper, Lukas Hornicek, the right-back Amar Dedic and the midfielder Sean Steur were close-season signings.

The other five new faces were either benched (Nico González and Matias Fernandez-Pardo) or did not make the 20-man matchday squad (Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Touré). Admittedly Ewen Jaouen is injured but, given Bamba and Toure cost a combined £78.5m, their omission represented quite a statement. Ditto the decision to bench González and Fernandez-Pardo and their individual £50m plus price tag.

Meanwhile the jury remains out on Hornicek. The Czech international has made some excellent saves this season but, initially here, his kicking proved pretty much uniformly poor and he was fortunate to be reprieved after hesitating too long as the impressive Kai Havertz closed in.

Jaissle’s frustration with his goalkeeper proved well apparent as Arsenal took increasing control of a first half that saw Newcastle’s lone striker, William Osula, isolated and even their normally imperious England left-back Lewis Hall given a thorough work out by Noni Madueke.

Much to Arteta’s chagrin, Lewis Miley, preferred to González in the midfield holding role, endeavoured to slow the tempo but the red tide could only be stemmed for so long.

When Havertz dispossessed Hall after the latter miscontrolled a long ball, he cut inside and slid a highly intelligent, beautifully calibrated, pass across to the on-rushing Eberechi Eze. Without breaking stride, Eze exhibited perfect balance and unleashed a gorgeous first-time shot that arrowed, inexorably, past Hornicek.

Quick Guide Newcastle 2-2 Arsenal: key facts Show • Arsenal ended a 21-game run of Premier League games without a draw (W18 D3) since a 2-2 draw with Wolves back in February. • Since the start of last season, all five of Newcastle’s Premier League draws at St James’ Park have been a 2-2 scoreline. • Eberechi Eze’s opener for Arsenal (pictured) was his first Premier League goal since April, which also put the Gunners 1-0 ahead against Newcastle. Opta Photograph: Lee Smith/REUTERS Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

As the home fans fell eerily silent, Arteta and his staff celebrated a goal sufficiently special to rebuke suggestions that his side are all about efficiency at the expense of artistry these days.

With Declan Rice always available to reinforce his defence and smother any flickering home attack it proved a struggle to recall Newcastle making a meaningful attacking touch inside Arsenal’s box. Fans stationed near the home dugouts told Jaissle what they thought of it all.

Arsenal’s pressing was initially so good that Newcastle were left almost incapable of playing short passes and, instead found themselves reduced to aimless long balls. With Rice and Martin Ødegaard apparently operating on a different midfield planet an equaliser felt like a distant dream.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Yet that seemingly ambitious vision was something Harvey Barnes proved fully capable of buying into. When, early in the second half, Ødegaard made an uncharacteristic error, his heavy touch sliced the ball in Osula’s direction and the Dane played it into Barnes’s path.

All that remained was for the left winger to take a single, steadying, touch before an assured finish left the hitherto redundant David Raya picking his shot out of the net.

Jaissle’s second-half introduction of Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga – all at Newcastle last season – at the expense of Dedic, Steur and Jacob Murphy was paying dividends. Suddenly, almost astonishingly, Arsenal were the team in danger of being pressed into submission.

The home side were closing their guests down far higher up the pitch and had morphed into an infinitely more menacing team. Soon, they were ahead when a Hall corner was headed down by Dan Burn, allowing Malick Thiaw to stab the ball beyond Raya.

View image in fullscreen Malick Thiaw roars his approval after giving Newcastle a second-half lead. Photograph: Harvey Murphy/Danehouse/Getty Images

Shortly afterwards Arsenal’s goalkeeper was helped off the pitch in evident pain after sustaining a nasty left shoulder injury during an ostensibly benign collision with Osula. On came Kepa Arrizabalaga in a triple substitution also featuring Guimarães’s exit.

Madueke though was still around and he reminded everyone of his presence by meeting the counterattacking Ødegaard’s fine pass, dummying two defenders and watching his slightly deflected shot evade Hornicek’s grasp.

No matter; Jaissle had done enough to win plenty of hearts and minds. Not least the chair, Yasir al-Rumayyan, over from Riyadh to watch his first match of the season and reportedly “take the club’s temperature”.

Sports.title: Robins ‘aims for the stars’ as Stoke dream of Premier League return
Sports.content:
There have been false dawns before. Plenty of them. This time last year, with Christmas on the near horizon, Stoke sat second in the Championship table and were beginning to wonder whether they might allow themselves to dream. So hopeless was their subsequent run that by the onset of spring they were forced to consider a potential relegation fight.

Experience has taught the benefit of pragmatism, so no one will be getting ahead of themselves just yet. But this weekend was supposed to be the big test for Mark Robins’s team and few considered they would pass it quite so resoundingly.

Facing a Birmingham side who arrived top of the table and with firmly held Premier League ambitions, Stoke dominated for an hour, the hitherto goal-shy George Hirst earning a well-deserved lead to send a bumper crowd into raptures. The hand-wringing that then followed Luca Bombino’s sending-off with half an hour remaining made the victory that followed all the sweeter. The 10 men of Stoke were superb. It was no surprise that it took considerable time to convince those in the stands to depart for home after the final whistle.

You see, it is not just that Stoke are second in the table, kept off top spot by goal difference. It is not even that they are undoubtedly the Championship’s form side, with just one defeat in their past 13 games. It is the whole feeling around the place; the resilience Robins has developed, and the belief that they can take on the big guns and beat them.

“We are a work in progress, but today was that step in quality against different opponents. A step up in class,” said Robins. “I thought we were really, really good. The intensity, bravery and the intent that we showed was everything that we asked for.

“And, on the back of that, you’ve got the support that are absolutely right behind us. They trust the players. That is a really good feeling. It’s a great feeling for the players. It’s a heady mix, really.”

Eight years have passed since Stoke were last in the top flight; eight years spent as the Championship equivalent of a sea sponge, doing the bare minimum to survive and letting defeats wash over them while remaining resolutely attached to the rocks of the bottom half of the table. During that time they have ended every campaign no higher than 14th and no lower than 18th. Now, something altogether different is afoot. And this may well be the win that convinces supporters to trust their upbeat instincts.

View image in fullscreen Mark Robins’s Stoke have lost just once in their past 13 Championship matches. Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PA

There was an unavoidable fact heading into Saturday’s game. Stoke’s four defeats this season had all come when tasked with opponents fighting at the top end of the table in Swansea, Southampton, Wolves and Middlesbrough. They had shown themselves capable against much of the division, but a failure to deliver against another Championship heavyweight would have raised legitimate questions about their realistic aspirations.

The three August defeats at the start of the campaign preceded the departure of their best player, Sorba Thomas. His replacement, Jack McGlynn, has been an inspired signing. That this victory came without the talismanic figure of Ethan Galbraith, who was absent through illness, is considerable.

As well as switching to a three-man defence following those season-opening losses, a key factor in their upturn has been the restoration of a touch of old-school Stoke; a physicality that was frequently evident on a cold Saturday afternoon.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Bobby Madley, the referee, did not always take kindly to such an approach – to the indignation of the home crowd, who frequently made their feelings clear – but there was no complaint over Bombino’s sending-off for a second yellow after a rash challenge that left him head in hands before the card had even been shown. Tears followed on his slow trudge towards the tunnel, but he need not have worried, with Birmingham barely threatening thereafter.

Given just five points separate the top eight in the Championship table, it would come as no great shock to see Stoke drop off at some point. They do not have the financial benefit of recent Premier League parachute payments or big-spending owners, they are not prolific goalscorers, and a look at their expected goals and expected points tallies shows them firmly in the bottom half of the table. But they are finding ways to win and if McGlynn has a habit of scoring from unexpectedly long distances, perhaps it is because he is good at it.

Before this weekend, Robins had revealed that a top-eight finish was the pre-season target. “You aim for the stars and hopefully you land trying to grab hold of one,” he had said, rather poetically.

If promotion is a “P” they dare not yet speak of, another one – playoffs – is becoming an increasingly realistic proposition. No more sticking to a rock. Swim free and prosper.

Sports.title: Coventry edge thriller to keep Crystal Palace bottom and ruin Thomas Frank’s start
Sports.content:
New manager, new formation, familiar defensive failings. Twice Crystal Palace equalised. They seemed to have stabilised after half-time. But sometimes the rot is so deep-rooted that the new manager bounce manifests as nothing more than it not looking quite as shambolic as it did before. Thomas Frank started with a defeat that means Palace remain bottom of the table having lost five league games in a row.

Yet for much of the second half, there had been reasons for Palace optimism. They seemed to have settled better after a ludicrous first half in which neither side looked at all capable of defending. But a triple substitution by Frank Lampard with 20 minutes to go shifted the game back in Coventry’s favour. With five minutes remaining, a long throw arced into the box. Brandon Thomas-Asante headed it goalwards. Dean Henderson got in the way but the ball bounced off him, hit Dwight McNeil and ricocheted in. “We came through with spirit,” Lampard said. “There was good play and a big impact from the subs. It’s a good sign for the squad.”

Sometimes football is simply a bit daft, a series of events linked by very little discernible pattern – and that’s how it was before the break. Perhaps that’s just what happens when two of the three teams with the lowest possession stats in the league meet up; they can’t both not have the ball and so at least one side ends up having to do something they’re not used to. The second half was rather less frenetic and rather more coherent, as Palace’s full-backs played more conservatively.

View image in fullscreen Thomas Frank shows his frustration during his first game in charge at Crystal Palace. Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty Images

“There are more positives than negatives from the game,” said Frank. “Offensively we looked like a threat. The effort and mentality I was extremely happy with. Defensively we conceded the first goal in a situation we 100% should have defended better, then an individual mistake. We’ll keep working on it, keep reinforcing the message in terms of what we want to do.”

In itself, playing without the ball is not a problem; absorbing pressure and striking on the break is a perfectly legitimate tactic and Lampard’s side have done it well at times this season. Palace are a slightly different case, given the obvious disconnect between their possession figure and Pierre Sage’s insistence he wanted to defend by holding the ball. That disparity, the sense that Palace’s players were unable to play as he wanted them to play, was probably the strongest argument in favour of cutting their losses quickly.

View image in fullscreen Tatsuhiro Sakamoto restores Coventry’s lead with their second goal. Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/Reuters

Frank abandoned the back three that had been the default not merely under Sage but also under Oliver Glasner, preferring a 4-3-2-1 with Anan Khalaili returning at right-back. It’s fair to say the Israel international is rather better going forward than at defending; playing at full-back rather than wing-back looked a real struggle for him – although he may feel there was mitigation in the way he was repeatedly left exposed. It took just five minutes for Coventry to open Palace up on that flank, three players converging on Yann Gboho as he backheeled a return pass to Jack Rudoni, who swept it across the box for Taiwo Awoniyi to stroke in.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Quick Guide Coventry 3-2 Crystal Palace: key facts Show • Coventry have won four of their last seven Premier League games (L3), with no side scoring more goals in the competition since the beginning of October (12, level with Bournemouth). • Crystal Palace have conceded 27 goals in the Premier League this season; only in 1927-28 in the Third Division South have they conceded as many or more after 11 games in a league campaign (28). • Only Brighton (6) have scored more goals from outside the box than Coventry City (4) in the Premier League this season, with 31% of the Sky Blues’ goals this term being scored from distance (4/13) – only Spurs (33% - 4/12) have a higher such share. • In what was his 115th Premier League game as a manager, Frank Lampard (pictured) has been booked for the first time, while he also didn’t receive a single yellow card in any of his last 31 Premier League games as a player. Opta Photograph: Hannah McKay/REUTERS Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

It soon became clear, though, that this was never a game of only one goal. It was startlingly, thrillingly, almost disconcertingly open, with chances at either end. Yéremy Pino levelled, thrashing in after Jørgen Strand Larsen had laid off Daichi Kamada’s overhit cross with an outstretched heel. Then Khalaili missed his tackle, allowing Rudoni to surge forward and square for Tatsuhiro Sakamoto who, from just outside the box, lashed the bouncing ball into the top corner. Palace’s second equaliser was the result of a complete defensive breakdown. Pino’s initial cross was blocked and when he dinked in a second attempt, the only player even close to marking Strand Larsen was his teammate Kamada.

Coventry’s threat had seemed diminished in the second half, partly as Palace looked less skittish and partly because Awoniyi aggravated an ankle injury and was unable to continue after the break. But those late substitutions gave them new impetus and, after a very silly first half, the game was won with a pretty silly goal.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi at center of red-card controversy as Inter Miami face early MLS playoff exit
Sports.content:
Columbus Crew coach Laurent Courtois said Lionel Messi should have been sent off after throwing a ball into an opponent’s face as Inter Miami crashed to a 3-0 defeat in the MLS Cup playoffs on Saturday.

Messi’s frustration boiled over on the stroke of half-time when he hurled a throw-in into the face of Columbus forward Gonzalo Tapia, with 10-man Miami trailing 1-0 at the time.

Messi and Tapia were both shown yellow cards for the incident by referee Allen Chapman, but Courtois said afterwards that the Argentina superstar should have been given a red card.

“Everybody knows that he deserved more than a yellow card,” Courtois said at a post-game press conference when asked about the incident. “It’s just really sad.”

Chapman later defended his decision to show Messi only a yellow card.

“The force used was negligible and the offense did not reach the level of violent conduct,” Chapman told a pool reporter.

Miami had already been reduced to 10 men when the incident occurred and were trailing 1-0 after an early penalty from the Chile international Tapia.

The reigning MLS champions went on to suffer a 3-0 defeat, with Taha Habroune doubling Columbus’s lead shortly after half-time before Tapia added his second at Miami’s Nu Stadium.
