Outside, a large screen and several framed photographs depicted images of Reeves and his loved ones as well as his boxing gloves.

The images carried captions such as 'brother', 'son', 'nephew', 'uncle' and 'pride of Limerick'.

Attendees included Mayor of Limerick John Horan as well as Defence Forces colleagues including the General Officer Commanding 1 Brigade, Brigadier General Caimin Keogh and Officer Commanding 12th Infantry Battalion, Lieutenant Colonel Ian Harrington.

Reeves was placed in a medically-induced coma and had emergency surgery after a junior welterweight fight in Dublin on August 1.

He had won 16 of his 18 bouts after turning professional in 2018, with several of his fights in Canada and Colombia.

The hearse is pictured carrying the coffin of boxer Lee Reeves arriving at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, for his funeral with full military honours, on Friday

Family members stand behind as soldiers from the Irish Defence Forces place the coffin of boxer and serving soldier Reeves on an adapted gun carriage at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, on Friday

Reeves' August clash with final opponent Gary Cully saw the 31-year-old knocked down twice in the 10th round

He was also a contestant on BBC reality show, Survivor, in 2023.

Defence Forces head chaplain Fr Paschal Hanrahan said Reeves showed physical courage in the boxing ring but also moral, courage and integrity in his mental health advocacy.

'We hold in our prayers today his colleagues serving overseas at this time with the 128th Infantry Battalion in Unifil, along with their chaplain Fr Piotr, who I know are gathered at this very moment in prayer for Lee.

'With all the agility and dexterity of a professional boxer, Lee moves seamlessly from being a model to being a role model in the Defence Forces.

'And those who served with him in Sarsfield Barracks saw our Defence Forces values in the way that he lived.'

He added: 'They saw his respect in the way he treated people, his loyalty in the way he stood by his comrades, and his selflessness in the time he gave to those who needed encouragement.'

Reeves, who was nicknamed 'El Champo', had won 16 of his 18 professional bouts since turning professional in 2018, and had been challenging Cully for the vacant BUI Celtic light-welterweight title.

He had been knocked down twice in the 10th round against Cully before being taken out of the ring, and in his tribute message for his opponent, Cully admitted that he was still in shock at how their match had ended.

Members of the Irish Defence Forces walked in procession alongside the coffin of boxer and soldier Reeves on an adapted gun carriage at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, on Friday

'I still remember the stadium days when I used to watch Lee in the nationals, the weight above me, and (I would) always be impressed by his fights and his flashy gear,' Cully wrote.

'What a character and a gent. It's never been nothing but love between us champ, can't really believe I'm writing this but RIP brother.'

Sports.title: 'It's amazing that Scotland now has TWO world champions'... Meet the Kilmarnock kid who idolises Prince Naseem Hamed and is part of the Scottish boxing boom with Willy Hutchinson
Sports.content:
'It's amazing that Scotland now has TWO world champions'... Meet the Kilmarnock kid who idolises Prince Naseem Hamed and is part of the Scottish boxing boom with Willy Hutchinson

Only last month, the mutterings were about where Scottish boxing goes from here, three years after Tartan Tornado Josh Taylor was toppled and with doubts mounting about the health of the sport’s grass roots.

Three weeks on, seemingly from nowhere, the nation has not one but two new world champions.

Willy Hutchinson claimed the WBC light heavyweight belt in a tussle with Joshua Buatsi earlier this month in the full glare of the television cameras. But slipping beneath the radar were the achievements of Aaron Sarwar, who was anointed the under-19 world flyweight champion in Montenegro on October 27.

Both men sobbed in the ring and fell to their knees as the simple raising of a referee’s hand detonated identical emotional explosions in them – sudden vindication of years of grinding roadwork, gruelling gymwork and grafting ringwork.

With beautiful symmetry, the only other Scot to have won a world amateur title was Hutchinson himself, in Russia in 2016. Now his ascent to the top of the pro game has lit the path for Sarwar to follow. And if there are still mutterings, they are that this kid from Kilmarnock could be the real deal.

Compared with big-ticket bouts, youth boxing’s short contests can appear cagey and sterile – but it’s hard to peel your eyes off Sarwar’s compelling repertoire of shots, defence, switches and occasional showboating.

Kilmarnock fighter Aaron Sarwar with his trophy for winning the Under-19 world championship

Those who know him best say his most remarkable asset is an iron psyche that, even at such a tender age, has created a machine-like drive to reach whatever peak is placed in front of him.

Having become a world junior karate champion and double black belt by the age of 11, the ring became his home during the Covid-19 pandemic as he looked for a fresh challenge.

Speaking to Daily Mail Sport, Sarwar insists he has already set off on a mission for another Montenegro moment.

He said: ‘People ask me about that feeling. It’s indescribable. I wish I could go back and relive that ten, 15 seconds of getting my hand raised because I don’t think anything will come close to it again.

‘But I’ll be chasing it. I want to make my mum and dad proud again. I watch [the video of] it every day. I get goosebumps every time.

‘I’d spoken to Willy before, but we met at a boxing show this week and had a good chat about what’s next for us.

Sarwar admits he still struggles to describe the euphoria he felt on being crowned the winner

‘It’s amazing that in the space of two weeks, Scotland’s got two new world champions. It’s crazy.’

Sarwar turned to boxing when lockdown meant karate was reduced to online seminars. He stumbled across a basic gym with punchbags behind the shop from where he’d buy lunch on school breaks – and from there he joined the local club.

The 18-year-old was back to his roots this week at the Northwest ABC in Onthank, the estate made infamous by the BBC Scotland fly-on-the-wall documentary The Scheme.

Hitting our screens in 2010, the series won a Bafta award but also stood accused of creating a ‘poverty safari’ for the chattering classes and creating dubious celebrities out of light-fingered drug addict Marvin Baird and his dog Bullet.

Northwest ABC was feted and funded for being a beacon among the anti-social behaviour, even receiving a personal visit from Justice Secretary Kenny MacAskill. Now Graeme Marshall’s committed coaching team has helped create a new poster boy for The Scheme.

Down at the club, they are proud of their prodigy, but the mood is more about hope than hype. They remorselessly tease Sarwar about his fussy fringe and point out, to rein in expectations, that he’s still so young he’s yet to even fight without a headguard.

Sarwar bumped into his fellow world title holder Willy Hutchinson during a boxing show

But Marshall – who Sarwar refers to as akin to a second father – is in no doubt about their boy’s freakish potential.

He said: ‘When he asked to come to the club after lockdown, it was Aaron himself who called up, which was unusual for a 12-year-old.

‘We knew straight away there was a talent there — he’s fast and strong and dedicated. After a few months, we entered him for the Scottish championships. It was his first fight, but he went and won the tournament.

‘Second season, he won the GB championships. I took him all over to fight. In Sweden, he stopped the Swedish champion, and when you see him beating Irish boys in Ireland, you know you’re dealing with something special.

‘He’ll turn professional at some point; it’s every young boy’s dream. And there’s no reason why he can’t go on and match what Willy Hutchinson’s done and become a world champion.’

The calls have started coming from managers testing the water about going pro – as Hutchinson did immediately after winning amateur gold – and McBookie are already offering odds of 8/1 that he goes right to the top.

Hutchinson brought Scottish boxing out of the doldrums with his defeat of Joshua Buatsi

But, for now at least, Sarwar – who ditched his engineering college course to concentrate on the sport – remains focused on fighting for Scotland at the 2030 Commonwealth Games in India.

He said: ‘I’ve got all the time in the world. I’ve opened myself a lot of doors now. I’ll speak to my coaches and mum and dad about what they think is best for me. But I know what I can achieve off the back of this now.

‘For karate, I was dedicated and hard-working but I didn’t have that same passion. Boxing, it’s all I do. I’ve left all my education to box full time. It’s all my eggs in one basket so there’s no choice, I have to do it. It’s boxing or nothing.’

Sarwar names his inspiration as Prince Naseem Hamed, the flamboyant featherweight world champion from the 1990s, for ‘his style, his flashiness, his power’. He added: ‘I’ve got that flashy side too, but if they get serious, I’ll stand toe to toe. I can box, I can fight, I can do it all.’

Despite training solely with Boxing Scotland now, Sarwar can’t keep away from his home club. He added: ‘I try to carry myself well all the time and inspire the young ones to come to the gym and train that bit harder, and it’s good to be around the coaches all the time.

Sarwar is in no rush to turn professional and is eyeing the 2030 Commonwealth Games in India

‘The support they’ve given me over the years has been second to none, I can’t thank them enough. There’ll be no way I can ever repay them the sacrifices they’ve made [for me].’

Meanwhile, in the ring at the Northwest, a small boy’s fists are a deadly blur, thwacking the pads held out by his coach with awesome efficiency. To misquote Muhammad Ali, he has the legs of a sparrow but the sting of a bee.

Aidan Sarwar – 12 years old – is already part of the Scotland set-up.

It was a Glasgow music hall crowd that first memorably coined the heckle, ‘Oh no, there’s two of them’ when English comedian Bernie Winters joined his brother Mike on stage. Boxers across the land may soon empathise.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua becomes a father for the second time: Boxing star welcomes baby girl in secret with mother of his son - but won't meet her until after his fight with Tyson Fury on December 11
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua has revealed he is a father again, welcoming a new baby girl into the world with Nicole Osbourne.

Former heavyweight world champion Joshua, who is gearing up to fight long-term rival Tyson Fury at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, already has a son with Osbourne called JJ, aged 11.

Now JJ is a big brother, with Joshua deliberately not finding out the sex of his newborn during pregnancy. His daughter is yet to be named but was born on November 14, weighing 5.5lb.

Joshua is yet to meet his daughter as he is in Marbella preparing for his long-awaited showdown with Fury in the early hours of December 12, but will meet and hold his newborn after the fight. In the meantime, there have been FaceTime calls with Osbourne to see their daughter.

'It's been amazing, a big blessing, and I can't believe I'm a girl dad. I didn't want to find the sex out during the pregnancy,' the 37-year-old told The Sun.

'I love boys but as soon as I found out we had a little girl I said, "No more Fifa, no more motorbiking, no more PlayStation!".

Anthony Joshua has announced that he is a father again, welcoming a baby girl into the world

The ex-heavyweight world champion already has a son called JJ who is now 11 (duo in 2021)

'I'm going to do it all, so you might see me with some eyeshadow on, some nail polish on, drinking some tea in a doll's playhouse and just trying to do the right thing by her, you know? I will change nappies, I've gotta go through all that stinky bum time again!

'Now I've got a daughter, I will get an insight and a bit more understanding of what it means to be a woman, and how I can be supportive.

'My daughter will give me a first-hand experience of the power of a woman - I've spoken to all the women in my family, and it's amazing the amount of support that women give each other.'

Joshua, who almost lost his life in a devastating car crash in Nigeria that killed two of his best friends last year, said the ordeal has taught him not to take life for granted.

'This past year has been incredibly tough, I realised how precious life is, and how short it can be. I’m just going to live my life by duty, and even having a baby girl was part of my duty. I wanted to bring life in, it was a conscious decision, 100 per cent. If something happened to me, I didn’t want JJ to be out here alone,' he added.

The wholesome news comes less than a year after Joshua was devastated by the loss of his best friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele last December, after the trio were involved in a car crash near Lagos.

Joshua has been deeply affected by the death of his friends and surviving the fatal crash himself, with the accident coming just ten days after he took down YouTuber-turned-boxing star Jake Paul.

Upon his return to the ring in late July with his fight against Kristian Prenga, Joshua broke down during his post-fight interview as he credited Ayodele and Ghami for getting him through a tough first round.

The 37-year-old is preparing to fight long-term British rival Tyson Fury in Cardiff next month

'I don't want to talk about it anymore,' Joshua had said quietly as he let out his emotions.

Earlier in the evening he had stepped into the ring wearing his friends' names on pennants pinned to his chest and had admitted before the fight that he had spent months suppressing the pain of their loss.

Joshua was being driven along one of Nigeria's deadliest roads in December when his SUV crashed into a stationary truck on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway.

He is thought to have narrowly escaped major injury or worse after having switched to sit behind the driver in the back seat on the left-hand side of the car.

Joshua was admitted to hospital with 'minor injuries' after being pulled from the wreckage of the crash.

In February, Joshua added the names of 'LATZ' and 'SINA' to the tattoo outline of Africa he sports on his bicep.

Sports.title: Tragic boxer's heartbroken final opponent pays tribute to 31-year-old rival in emotional Instagram statement after Irish fighter lost his life following three-month coma
Sports.content:
Tragic boxer's heartbroken final opponent pays tribute to 31-year-old rival in emotional Instagram statement after Irish fighter lost his life following three-month coma

The final opponent of boxer Lee Reeves has paid an emotional tribute following the death of the man he shared a ring with in August.

Gary Cully, 30, knocked Reeves down in the bout and his fellow Irishman was in a coma for three months before tragically losing his life on Monday.

The 31-year-old Reeves, who was nicknamed 'El Champo', had been challenging Cully for the vacant BUI Celtic light-welterweight title and was sent to the canvas twice in the tenth round before being taken out of the ring on a stretcher and rushed to hospital.

Cully shared his shock and grief at Reeves's death on Instagram, writing: 'We shared the ring back in August but we been going back for years.

'I still remember the stadium days when I used to watch Lee in the nationals the weight above me and always be impressed by his fights and his flashy gear myself and Luke Thomas used to plague him to spit us out an MC when we were staying in Dublin on training camp and they’d always be fire.

'What a character and a gent. It’s never been nothing love between us champ can’t really believe I’m writing this but RIP brother.'

Lee Reeves died on Monday having been in a coma for three months after fighting Gary Cully

The 31-year-old (right) was knocked down twice in the 10th round and Cully (left) shared an emotional tribute

Cully shared a number of pictures from their fight and also screenshots of messages between them from the last few years.

In one, Reeves wrote: 'Take a bow son! Fantastic win well done champ!' Cully replied: 'Thank you bro, congrats on your two also.'

Limerick-born Reeves spent time away from the ring as a competitor on BBC reality show Survivor in 2023, and served as an ambassador for Limerick Treaty Suicide Prevention group.

The fighter, the oldest of four siblings, lost his mother Cathy to suicide in 2015.

Reeves had initially been declared as in a critical but stable condition in hospital when he was placed into a medically-induced coma.

But the grim news was announced on Monday by his friend and coach Jonathan O'Brien, who paid tribute to Reeves in a poignant statement on social media.

'Goodbye son, sleep tight, you fought so hard till the end,' O'Brien wrote. 'We love you so much, rest in peace with your mam and brother waiting at the heavenly gates.

'Look over your sisters and your father, give them the strength to get through this. We love you Lee.'

'Limerick is a very dark place tonight with the loss of Lee Reeves. Lee was not just a boxer that excelled in his career - he was a mental health advocate who highlighted mental health and how it can affect young people,' Limerick City councillor and Reeves' family friend Catherine Slattery said in her tribute.

Cully shared screenshots of messages between him and Reeves over the years

Reeves (second from right) was described as a 'character and a gent' by his last opponent Cully (centre)

'Lee was a very proud Limerick man, he loved Limerick and its people and any chance he got to promote Limerick, he took it.

'Lee loved his family. He was very proud of his dad, Tony, and he adored his sisters and his nieces and nephews and they, in return, adored him.

'Lee had great faith in God and the only (consolation) is that Lee's mam and brother are embracing him in their arms in heaven.

'The loss of Lee will be felt in Limerick for a long time to come and I am heartbroken for Lee that he lost his fight.

'Rest in peace El Champ - you will be missed by us all.'

Queensberry also shared a statement after news broke, writing: 'Everyone at Queensberry is devastated to learn of the passing of Lee Reeves.

'Lee was an immensely talented boxer, as well as a true role model and inspiration to his community.

'Our deepest condolences go to Lee's family, friends and all those who loved him. We ask that their privacy be respected at this incredibly difficult time. Rest in peace, Lee.'

Sports.title: Boxer Lee Reeves dies, aged 31, after three months in a coma - having been knocked out in the ring
Sports.content:
Boxer Lee Reeves dies, aged 31, after three months in a coma - having been knocked out in the ring

Boxer Lee Reeves has died at the age of 31 after spending three months in a coma following his final fight in August.

The Irish southpaw had been carried out of the ring on a stretcher following his defeat to his countryman Gary Cully and immediately taken to hospital.

There, his promoters Queensberry announced that the fighter was in a 'critical but stable' condition before he underwent surgery.

Reeves was then placed in a medically induced coma, and passed away on Monday surrounded by his family.

The tragic news was announced by his friend and coach Jonathan O'Brien, who paid tribute to Reeves' unerring fight in a poignant statement on social media.

'Goodbye son, sleep tight, you fought so hard till the end,' O'Brien wrote. 'We love you so much, rest in peace with your mam and brother waiting at the heavenly gates.

Limerick fighter Lee Reeves has died after spending three months in a coma, his friends and family have shared (Source: Instagram/Lee Reeves)

Reeves' August clash with final opponent Gary Cully saw the 31-year-old knocked down twice in the 10th round

'Look over your sisters and your father, give them the strength to get through this. We love you Lee.'

Reeves, who was nicknamed 'El Champo', had won 16 of his 18 professional bouts since turning professional in 2018, and had been challenging Cully for the vacant BUI Celtic light-welterweight title.

He had been knocked down twice in the 10th round against Cully before being taken out of the ring, and in his tribute message for his opponent, Cully admitted that he was still in shock at how their match had ended.

'I still remember the stadium days when I used to watch Lee in the nationals, the weight above me, and (I would) always be impressed by his fights and his flashy gear,' Cully wrote.

'What a character and a gent. It's never been nothing but love between us champ, can't really believe I'm writing this but RIP brother.'

Limerick-born Reeves spent time away from the ring as a competitor on BBC reality show Survivor in 2023, and served as an ambassador for Limerick Treaty Suicide Prevention group.

The fighter, the oldest of four siblings, lost his mother Cathy to suicide in 2015.

'Limerick is a very dark place tonight with the loss of Lee Reeves. Lee was not just a boxer that excelled in his career - he was a mental health advocate who highlighted mental health and how it can affect young people,' Limerick City councillor and Reeves' family friend Catherine Slattery said in her tribute.

'Lee was a very proud Limerick man, he loved Limerick and its people and any chance he got to promote Limerick, he took it.

His final opponent, Gary Cully (centre). paid an emotional tribute to Reeves (second right)

'Lee loved his family. He was very proud of his dad, Tony, and he adored his sisters and his nieces and nephews and they, in return, adored him.

'Lee had great faith in God and the only (consolation) is that Lee's mam and brother are embracing him in their arms in heaven.

'The loss of Lee will be felt in Limerick for a long time to come and I am heartbroken for Lee that he lost his fight.

'Rest in peace El Champ - you will be missed by us all.'

Queensberry also shared a statement after news broke, writing: 'Everyone at Queensberry is devastated to learn of the passing of Lee Reeves.

'Lee was an immensely talented boxer, as well as a true role model and inspiration to his community.

'Our deepest condolences go to Lee's family, friends and all those who loved him. We ask that their privacy be respected at this incredibly difficult time.

'Rest in peace, Lee.'

Sports.title: Chris Eubank Jr in talks to fight Kell Brook in first bout since Conor Benn loss - with 'Special K' to come out of retirement
Sports.content:
Chris Eubank Jr is in talks to fight Kell Brook in his return to the ring.

Brook, 40, has not fought since beating Amir Khan in 2022, but has emerged as a potential option to fight Eubank in his first fight since losing to Conor Benn late last year.

According to Elliott Amoakoh, the executive director of Eubank Jr's management team, Nova Sport LLC, any agreement is still a way away.

He told Sky Sports: 'Talks are ongoing but the date, purse and location are yet to be confirmed.'

Ben Shalom, however, who has represented both fighters in the past, told talkSPORT: 'It's a fight that we have been trying to make for a couple of months.

'They have pretty much agreed terms on both sides, there is just some final bits to go. It is one of the biggest fights in British boxing. I think you are right on February and in Manchester.'

Chris Eubank Jr (pictured) is in talks with Kell Brook to face off in his return to the ring

Brook (pictured) hasn't fought since 2022 and retired after beating long-term rival Amir Khan

Brook retired after beating long-time rival Khan in Manchester, having been linked with a fight with Eubank in the aftermath.

Brook has seemed almost certain to return to the ring, having revealed his return fight would be 'announced soon'.

He retired with 40 wins from 43 fights, and is a former International Boxing Federation welterweight champion.

Having debuted as a professional in 2004, he didn't lose until September 2016, when he was stopped in the fifth round by Gennady Golovkin.

Eubank Jr, meanwhile, had faced questions over retirement following his defeat by Benn but has refused to call it quits on his 15-year career.

He had claimed to have major fights scheduled for 2026, but has taken a whole year out of action.

Sports.title: English boxer, 18, banned from World Championships after extraordinary sex test mix-up: 'Broken' teenager reveals how his dream was shattered after team forgot to prove he was a man
Sports.content:
English boxer, 18, banned from World Championships after extraordinary sex test mix-up: 'Broken' teenager reveals how his dream was shattered after team forgot to prove he was a man

A teenage English boxer has said they have been left 'broken' after being denied the chance to compete at the World Championships due to officials failing to organise a sex verification test to prove he is male.

George Francis, 18, had been due to represent England at the Under-19 World Championships in Budva, Montenegro last month.

Francis was withdrawn from competition on the eve of the event after an administration error by England Boxing, with the governing body having failed to arrange the necessary sex verification test.

'They got me in a room and told me that I couldn't box because they didn't know if I was a boy or a girl, basically,' Francis told the BBC.

'The explanation was that they couldn't provide a blood sample for me in time. Everyone else was able to provide a blood sample, but they just forgot me.

'Somehow I wasn't on the system.

George Francis, 18, missed out on competing at the Under-19 World Championships after England Boxing failed to arrange a necessary sex verification test. Source: Instagram/georgefrancis_07

'It was the worst news I've ever had in my life.

'I wouldn't wish it on anyone, to be honest. I was just broken. They were speaking to me and I couldn't even really hear. I was devastated.

'I couldn't really talk. I literally couldn't feel anything. There was a hole left there.'

Francis's situation, first reported by The Times, followed the mandatory introduction of sex verification tests by the sport's governing body World Boxing.

World Boxing announced the move last year, with genetic sex testing initially introduced for female competitors aged 18 and above. The governing body stated the move was due to a 'duty of care to deliver safety and competitiveness fairness'.

It followed controversy at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, where boxers Imane Khelif and Lin Yu-ting won gold.

Khelif and Lin had been disqualified from the previous year's World Championships, with boxing's former governing body – the International Boxing Association – claiming the pair had failed sex eligibility tests.

Earlier this year, Lin was cleared to compete in women's events following a review of her sex eligibility.

World Boxing's mandatory tests were extended to include male boxers earlier this year.

Francis had been required to undergo a test due to turning 18 four days before travelling to the World Championships.

Francis, a multiple national champion, had been required to undergo a mandatory test after turning 18 days before the World Championships. Source: Instagram/georgefrancis_07

World Boxing introduced sex testing last year amid the controversy surrounding Algerian boxer Imane Khelif's participation at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games

The multiple national and GB champion has claimed he is considering turning professional following the mix-up.

England Boxing reportedly contacted Francis's father to apologise for the 'administrative oversight', with the governing body stressing it will 'strengthen processes' to avoid a repeat incident.

'We maintained open communication with George and his family throughout, despite this, a resolution was not possible,' an England Boxing statement read.

'George remained a valued member of the England team, including representing the squad as flag bearer.

'England Boxing has no greater priority than the health and wellbeing of athletes on its performance pathway and are committed to learning from this experience and strengthening our processes to prevent a recurrence.'

World Boxing's policy requires boxers to undergo a once-in-a-lifetime PCR (polymerase chain reaction) test to determine their sex and their eligibility to compete in either the male or female category.

The PCR test is a laboratory technique used to detect specific genetic material, in this case the SRY gene, which reveals the presence of the Y chromosome that is an indicator of male biological sex.

A dozen boxers, representing five nations, were last year blocked from competing at the World Championships in Liverpool because deadlines for their sex tests were missed.

Under World Boxing rules, national federations are responsible for testing and will be required to confirm the sex of their athletes when entering them into World Boxing competitions

Sports.title: Viddal Riley opens up on why he stuck with his dad instead of moving to Las Vegas to train with a Mayweather as he eyes fighting Oleksandr Usyk
Sports.content:
Derrick Riley almost never speaks publicly. Ahead of his son's European title defence against Seydi Coupe at Wembley on Saturday, father and son sat down together to talk about trust, tough love, Joe and Enzo Calzaghe, and why Oleksandr Usyk returning to cruiserweight is 'a little bit greedy'.

But to understand where Viddal is going, you first have to understand the man in his corner.

Derrick Riley has been watching his son get punched since he was a little boy. He still can't put into words what it does to him.

'It's strange,' he exclusively tells Daily Mail Sport. 'I've been doing it for a long time. But you have to try and separate it. You have to shut off the emotion and the sentiment. If you let that sentiment in, I think that's a bad thing. That's your boy in there. He's getting hit and he's getting hurt. I would say it's not easy, and some people can't separate it.'

It's rare to hear Derrick say anything at all. He stays out of the spotlight, and he leaves the talking to his son. Sitting beside Viddal days before the biggest night of his career, when the unbeaten Londoner headlines OVO Arena Wembley against Frenchman Coupe, you quickly see how their relationship works.

'Only my dad would be able to speak to me the way he does,' Viddal says. 'But it comes from a place of genuine care. It's not a job. Someone can only care so much when it's a job. It's like being an employee at a company and having your own business. It's a completely different mentality. This is my business, so he cares and I care.'

WATCH THE EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW ON THE DAILY MAIL BOXING YOUTUBE CHANNEL

Derrick Riley (R), the father and trainer of son Viddal Riley (L), almost never speaks publicly

Viddal is set to take on Seydi Coupe at Wembley on Saturday evening, headlining the event

Derrick added: 'Part of caring too is the fact it's the same brain you've got now that you're going to need after boxing. You can't go to the shop and buy a new one, so you need to protect it. That's why it's difficult to separate the two.'

Viddal grins and says: 'It's the same brain I need for the grandkids.'

The partnership was not always a given. At 21, Viddal went looking for something of his own.

'I was at a stage where I was trying to find some independence. That's the truth,' he says. 'I was presented with the opportunity to go to Vegas, train with a Mayweather and work with Jeff Mayweather. I was thinking, "Yeah, I'm doing this my way. I'm doing things differently."

'But the truth is, I knew my ceiling was getting lower. And I knew the only person who could push that ceiling higher, and continue to do so, was my dad.

'So when I came back to the UK, I said, "Dad, can you train me?" He was like, "Nah, I'm alright. I'm not doing it." And I was like, "Nah, I need you to do it, because that's the only way this dream we've been talking about is going to be fulfilled."

Derrick's refusal was not stubbornness. It was self-preservation.

When asked why he initially said no, Derrick admitted: 'I know what the game is about. I know what boxing involves, and I thought to myself, do I want that in my life? It's a good question when you're in your 50s. I've lived life. There are no rose-coloured glasses. I know what boxing is. But I had to think about it.'

Derrick Riley has been watching his son get punched since Viddal was a little boy

The irony was that he was already qualified for the job. 'By this point I already had a British Boxing Board of Control licence, because I was in the corner with Viddal in Dubai,' he laughs. 'So, funnily enough, I already had the licence.

'He looked at me with those puppy-dog eyes, and I thought, you know what? We've got to do this. But I did say to him, "It's not going to be easy, son. We're going to have to do this properly. You're going to get no ranking belts, no intercontinental belt, nothing like that. You're going to have to do it the old-school way, with the British, Commonwealth, European, and it's going to be hard." And we've done it, man.'

The record backs him up. Viddal is 14-0 with seven knockouts. He won the European title in April with a wide points win over the vastly experienced Pole Mateusz Masternak at The O2, a fight that also served as an IBF world title eliminator. Saturday is his first defence, and it's a mandatory one against a challenger who is also unbeaten in 14.

For a template of what father and son can achieve together, Derrick points to Wales.

'I appreciate Enzo [Calzaghe] more now than I did before,' he says. 'I've always appreciated him, but I appreciate him even more now because I'm doing it myself. People have no idea what it takes, and for him to do what he did with Joe was absolutely amazing. I take my hat off to him.

'Don't get me wrong, I had a boxing background. I wasn't great, I wasn't pulling up trees, but I had a boxing background. Enzo had no boxing background whatsoever, yet he managed to do what he did with Joe. That is amazing.

'It's funny. During the fight with Bernard Hopkins, I think Enzo was saying something to Joe, and Joe gave Enzo a look. I know that look. I give Viddal that same look.'

Viddal and his father have become a force to be reckoned with but they've faced criticism

Joe Calzaghe has described his own brief split from his father, and how he came back because he realised he wanted those highs to be shared with Enzo. Viddal sees the same story in his own.

'We relate to that story because we were severely doubted,' he says. 'It wasn't celebrated. The partnership is only now starting to get some recognition, with people acknowledging that it works. It wasn't like that at the beginning.

'It's been suggested to me that my dad shouldn't train me and that there are people better suited to the job. That's what we walked into. It wasn't accepted as, "Oh yeah, this is a nice family dynamic, let's get it going." It was challenged. The aim was to separate us.

'When we're up against it, we just keep proving ourselves, time and time again. That's what I take from Enzo and Joe. It wasn't celebrated either. They had to keep doing what they were doing, and he turned his son into a 46-0 fighter and one of the best to have ever done it.'

Fathers who train their sons are often accused of living through them. John Fury, so often more visible than Tyson, is the obvious example. Derrick, a former boxer himself, rejects the comparison.

'I don't live vicariously through Viddal. I don't want that,' he says. 'I'm not hogging the camera. It's not about me. It's about Viddal. He asked me to help him, and I'll help him.'

Viddal is just as clear about who he fights for. 'I do it primarily, first and foremost, for me,' he says. 'And very quickly after that, it's for everyone around me that's put work into me achieving it, because it couldn't be done by myself.

Derrick has said he resonates with Enzo (pictured right) and Joe Calzaghe (pictured left)

'When I became British champion, it made me give my dad the belt. We sat down at home for years watching people pick up the Lonsdale belt and hold the Lonsdale belt. So I heard the announcement, "British champion", and I'm like, "Dad, hold this." That's something he's always deserved.'

By rights, Viddal should already have fought for a world title. When Jai Opetaia was stripped of the IBF belt after signing with Zuffa Boxing, the Masternak win put Viddal in line for a shot at the vacant title against New Zealand's David Nyika. Then Opetaia sued the IBF, the governing body held off sanctioning the fight, and Viddal was left waiting.

At the same time, the division has been turned upside down. Opetaia is moving up to heavyweight to face Deontay Wilder on the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua card in Cardiff on December 11. David Benavidez holds the WBA and WBO belts and faces WBC champion Michal Cieslak next month. And now Oleksandr Usyk wants to come back down.

'As I have been saying, it's messy, but I'm trying to get in the mess,' Viddal says. 'I don't want to be on the outskirts of that mess. I'm trying to be in it.

'Right now, I'm just on the outside of the door. I can hear the music in the club, I can hear the bassline. I know there's a vibe in there. I've been seeing the people getting in the door, walking past me. I want to get in there. And Coupe this weekend is another step towards that.'

The most famous person trying to get through that door is Usyk. The Ukrainian became undisputed at cruiserweight, moved up to become undisputed twice at heavyweight, and his team says he now plans to return to 200lbs to chase Benavidez and become undisputed at cruiserweight again. He hasn't fought at the weight since knocking out Tony Bellew in November 2018, and he turns 40 in January.

Viddal admires him. But he isn't convinced.

'It's a bit greedy. It's a little bit greedy,' he says. 'He's completed the level here. He's gone up, he's completed it there, and I think he's just needing that challenge. He's a guy you can tell lives for challenge. All he does is take challenges. "If I'm fighting for a world title, I'm going to go to your country and I'll beat you there." He's that character. That's what makes him a GOAT. That's what makes him a legend.

Viddal has said Oleksandr Usyk is 'greedy' for returning to the cruiserweight division

'But it's dangerous too. Forty years old, dropping all that weight. He hasn't been a cruiserweight since 2018. If I'm in his circle, I'm saying, "Bro, you ain't got to do this. Why? There's no need to." It's not going to be financial. It's just that craving for a challenge.'

Regardless, Viddal is happy with where he is at.

'What I like is that if I'd done this interview four or five years ago, everyone would have asked me, "Do you want to fight Tommy Fury or Jake Paul?" he says. 'Now people ask me, "Would I fight Usyk?"

'Clearly, I'm doing something right.'

Sports.title: Vasseur furious with "unprofessional" Ferrari clash and demands fresh talks after Las Vegas GP
Sports.content:
Ferrari team boss Fred Vasseur says Charles Leclerc's contact with Lewis Hamilton in the Las Vegas Grand Prix was "unacceptable" and showed "lack of respect for the team", with the Formula 1 team set for fresh crisis talks just three weeks after their spat in Mexico.

Vasseur had to hold talks with both Leclerc and Hamilton for their costly Mexico skirmish and will do so again after his two cars tangled on the streets of Las Vegas on lap 38, with Leclerc to blame for leaving his front wing dangling on the inside of Hamilton, sending the Briton into a spin.

Leclerc received a 10-second penalty for the collision, while Hamilton dropped to 10th and eventually crossed the line in eighth. Leclerc was classified in 10th place after the penalty had been added to his race time.

Coming so soon after Mexico, the thought of his drivers tangling again and the prospect of fresh talks to clear the air had worn thin on Vasseur.

"Charles, I want to see you at the end of the race, before anything else," Vasseur said on the team radio during the cooldown lap.

When asked what that discussion was like, Vasseur tellingly replied: "It was not a discussion. I spoke.

"I think he apologised, he understood, but the result is there. You make a mistake, you say: 'My mistake, I'm sorry'. But you [still] made a mistake."

Frederic Vasseur, Ferrari Photo by: Alex Pantling / LAT Images via Getty Images

He added: "It's unacceptable. It's a lack of respect for the team, for the sponsors, the same speech as after Mexico. I think we had a clear discussion in Sao Paulo. Today it wasn't professional. I think it's probably the escalation of tension."

Following complaints from Hamilton, Ferrari had already been in touch with Leclerc about the aggressive way he was squeezing the Briton. Las Vegas' oval-like slipstreaming race required a degree of trust and teamwork for drivers to move through the pack of cars, as not racing each other was not an option either. The race became a painful reminder that trust between Leclerc and Hamilton is absent.

"We passed the message to Charles during the race to think about the team when he was fighting in the right way, but you can't freeze the position on this kind of race, because you are in the slipstream," Vasseur explained. "If you slow down, the guy who is behind you is overtaking you. And all the other teams were able to overtake each other 20 times during the race. You can't imagine the frustration for me, but more important for all the guys at home."

When asked if it's now time for tougher guidelines or rules, he said: "It's not a matter of rules. What can you do differently, except that you have to respect your team-mates. In this kind of race, you have to overtake the car in front of you. You can't stay behind. It's completely unmanageable. You just have to do it with respect when it's your team-mate, to take less risks. They just have to act in a professional way."

Having just had this very talk between Mexico and Brazil, it is not entirely clear what Vasseur can now do differently, a thought which has left the Frenchman feeling powerless.

"That's why I want to once again have a discussion tomorrow," he added. "And also, to try to digest the situation. I think it's not the right place to discuss with them two minutes after the race. I saw Charles a bit down. And I told him what I have to say. I've got to discuss it with him tomorrow."

Sports.title: Verstappen hits back after Russell criticism: “He’s so far below my level”
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen has hit back at George Russell’s Friday comments by winning Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix – and delivering scathing remarks afterwards.

The pair were involved in an incident in Free Practice 3, with Verstappen breaching what Russell deemed to be a gentlemen’s agreement by overtaking him ahead of a flying lap. The Briton moved to get back ahead but Verstappen unsuccessfully attempted to close the door and the duo eventually had a small collision.

The shenanigans led stewards to officially warn Verstappen for moving under braking, while Russell unabashedly blamed his rival on Sky Sport Italy: “He does this week in, week out with many drivers and everybody accepts it, and I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody's got to stand up to that guy.”

Twenty-four hours later, Verstappen held off both Mercedes for victory in an eventful race as they traded the lead throughout the contest. Russell crashed as he locked up when diving down the inside of team-mate Kimi Antonelli for second place on lap 48 of 50, ending up ninth – and in Verstappen’s eyes, this speaks volumes.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Jordan McKean / Formula 1 / Getty Images

Asked if Russell’s words had been on his mind when they were racing one another for the lead, Verstappen retorted: “It's not like it's a success today.

“I mean, the thing is, he speaks a lot next to the track. And honestly, for me, it doesn't really matter because he's so far below my level that it doesn't really make any sense for me anyway, to try and challenge that, so it doesn't bother me.

“And today karma is a bitch. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening. So I was like, ‘Fantastic! My day is only getting better.’

“And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete.”

Verstappen may not care about the runner-up spot in the championship, but his victory and Russell’s downfall mean he now has a 40-point advantage over the Mercedes driver, with just two rounds remaining – only Lewis Hamilton is closer, albeit still 37 points adrift.

Sports.title: “My mistake was to lift” – Why Antonelli lost power in Las Vegas GP victory battle
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli has explained the quirky “mistake” that cost him a shot at Formula 1 victory in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The fastest driver in qualifying, Antonelli was sixth on the grid owing to a five-place drop for an engine change and was the only top-10 starter on mediums rather than softs, which contributed to a further two-position drop on lap one.

The new world champion recovered to fourth by lap 17 and went on to challenge polesitter Max Verstappen and Mercedes team-mate George Russell in the second half of the race, emerging as the Red Bull’s main rival late on.

Antonelli and Verstappen traded the lead repeatedly as ‘yo-yo’ racing returned, with the Italian 0.001s ahead on the finish line on lap 43 of 50, which was a major concern for his rival.

Attempting to be in the optimal position to overtake the Red Bull on the final lap, Antonelli refrained from attacking Verstappen at the end of the penultimate tour, but ended up losing out to both McLarens and finishing just fourth.

“Basically I lifted off before Turn 14 to keep overtake [mode] and stay behind Max to give myself the best shot for the win,” the Mercedes driver explained. “However, the lift triggered something in the system so I exited the corner at zero battery. So I lost it all.”

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Manuel Eletto

Pressed on the issue by Autosport, he added: “My mistake was to lift, actually. That triggered the issue, so I couldn't charge any energy. So already by the end of the straight you're quite low on energy. So because I couldn't harvest anything, then I see that I'm zero.

“Basically the system wasn't ready for that and my mistake was to lift off, reapply a bit of throttle to keep a little bit of speed, and that triggered the system, and that meant that in the straight I lost almost two seconds.”

When it was suggested to him that Mercedes was losing out to Red Bull on straights – despite the W17’s top speed in the race being 320.6km/h, compared to the RB22’s 314.3km/h – Antonelli clarified: “No no, we were able to keep up.

“Obviously, we had a lower downforce level this weekend and it was a bit more difficult in the corners, but definitely it was helping us in all the straights. It was clear where Red Bull was deploying more, but we had something in the pocket for that last lap, but I couldn't even try.”

As for the ‘yo-yo’ style of racing, unlike some of his peers, Antonelli appreciated it.

“I mean, it was a bit stressful at times because it was impossible to pull away and there were so many different speeds in all kinds of straights so you had to be very strategic,” the Italian admitted. “But other than that, I think it was a fun race, and it was a shame not to be able to fight all the way to the end [because of] something out of my control.”

Sports.title: F1 Las Vegas GP: Verstappen wins thriller as Russell hits the wall late on
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen won a wild Las Vegas Grand Prix, holding off both Mercedes drivers as Formula 1’s ‘yo-yo’ racing returned – with no Silver Arrow on the eventual podium.

With qualifying pacesetter Andrea Kimi Antonelli taking a five-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation, Max Verstappen inherited pole position and retained the lead from George Russell at the start with an unchanged top five: Lando Norris, Isack Hadjar and Arvid Lindblad followed – though Hadjar swiftly found a way past the McLaren on lap one.

The only top-10 driver starting on mediums, Antonelli lost two spots to the Alpines at lights out, finding himself eighth ahead of the Ferraris, who were out in Q2 – though Franco Colapinto would soon collapse from seventh to 10th, then out of the points-paying positions.

Verstappen couldn’t break away from Russell, and the Briton briefly snatched the lead away on lap two before the Dutchman immediately responded. Russell couldn’t attack the leader again and was instead overtaken by the sister Red Bull car. Further back, Lindblad overtook Norris and Russell in quick succession, even though he could not hold the Mercedes off.

Meanwhile, Hadjar was pressuring Verstappen for the lead but had to deal with Russell’s attacks. “We need to not lose time as a team,” the Frenchman was told. “Can he stop defending?” he inquired as to his team-mate’s driving. Hadjar briefly took the lead soon after, though he dropped to third moments later.

On lap 10, the top 10 cars still lay within four seconds. Russell momentarily retook the lead again as Pierre Gasly fought to third, though he couldn’t hold off Hadjar for long. There were no changes among the top four for a moment, but Norris’ collapse continued as he ended up outside the top 10.

Russell took the lead back on laps 14 and 18, but this was again Turn 14 moves with Verstappen sweeping back past on the start/finish straight. The second time, Hadjar snuck by in second.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Jim Watson / AFP via Getty Images

New world champion Antonelli climbed to fourth on lap 17, recovering from eighth on lap one. Meanwhile, the Ferraris were battling both their rivals and among themselves for seventh place. Charles Leclerc called on his team-mate to “be careful with this squeezing”, Lewis Hamilton said the sister car should “back the fuck off” – and copped a 10-second penalty for leaving the track and gaining an advantage after a move on Norris.

The safety car was called into action on lap 19 as Sergio Perez spun Rafael Camara around and broke his front suspension; nearly all cars pitted straightaway – Red Bull’s double-stack allowing Russell to sneak back into second – but not Hamilton, due to the seven-time world champion’s track position ahead of his team-mate and his 10-second penalty. In order not to delay the sister car in the pits, he changed tyres on the following lap and emerged back out in 14th.

Meanwhile, sixth-placed Lindblad had an odd spin in safety-car conditions and retired from the race, promoting Norris back to sixth ahead of Leclerc and Gabriel Bortoleto.

The green flag was waved on lap 26, and Hadjar’s front wing broke on its own. The Red Bull driver pitted, with Gasly inheriting third before losing out to a resurgent Norris on lap 31. Meanwhile, Hamilton needed just one lap to fight his way back into the top 10.

Russell retook the lead then – again ever so briefly – but his incessant attempts to surpass Verstappen brought Norris into play, with the Briton now challenging – and temporarily overtaking – the leader.

Russell recovered second place, and finally found a way past Verstappen into Turn 1 on lap 37, rather than Turn 14, but he still couldn’t hold on to the lead. Antonelli, the only driver on soft tyres in the top 10, even took second place away from his team-mate on lap 38 and briefly passed Verstappen for the lead one lap later.

At the same time, further down the field, Leclerc and Hamilton clashed as they battled each other for sixth, with the latter being spun around and ending up down to 10th. Leclerc dropped down to himself eighth and copped a 10-second penalty.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Manuel Eletto

So far, Verstappen had proved to be only temporarily assailable, but the Red Bull driver was worrying about the end of the race. “You guys have to look at the deployment of the final lap because they’ve figured it out, that they can stay ahead of me until the line, so we need to see what we need to do for the final lap only,” he said on team radio.

Antonelli and Verstappen traded the lead again and again, with Antonelli 0.001s ahead on the finish line on lap 43, vindicating the Dutchman’s aforementioned concern. However, Red Bull let its driver know that there was no better deployment strategy available for the final lap.

On lap 48, Russell attempted to overtake Antonelli for second place but locked up and hit the wall, collapsing down to ninth, seemingly letting the top two drivers fight it out for the win… but Antonelli lost ground at the end of lap 49 and dropped behind the McLarens.

Verstappen therefore triumphed from pole ahead of Norris, who had started third but dropped to 11th before driving to the runner-up spot, and Piastri, who was 15th on the grid and fought to a podium finish.

Antonelli saved fourth ahead of Alpine duo Gasly and Colapinto, while the Ferraris of Hamilton and Leclerc were a disappointing seventh and 10th respectively, separated by Carlos Sainz and Russell.

Hadjar couldn’t do better than 14th after his front wing broke, right ahead of Lawson, who was supposed to be seventh on the grid but had to start from the pitlane due to a fuel leak and never recovered.

Alex Albon, who was supposed to start from 14th, encountered a brake overheating issue despite 12C weather and couldn’t take part in the race.

Sports.title: Antonelli and Russell set for Mercedes talks over Las Vegas GP qualifying mix-up
Sports.content:
George Russell and Kimi Antonelli will discuss the fallout from Formula 1’s Las Vegas Grand Prix qualifying “offline” following confusion over team orders and track position.

Traffic played a significant role in qualifying on Friday night with drivers reluctant to go first, considering the advantage of a tow is huge around the low-downforce street circuit.

There was the added complexity of five drivers taking a grid penalty, so their primary role was to help their team-mate like Haas’ Oliver Bearman giving Rafael Camara a tow in Q1.

Antonelli was another one of those, taking a five-place drop for a new engine, so the plan was to give Russell the slipstream in the fight for pole but it quickly unravelled.

That was because the Mercedes duo got caught in a pack with both Alpine and Racing Bulls cars ahead of the final lap, at times going three-wide despite trying to find space.

Antonelli eventually backed off at Turn 5 while Russell reluctantly went first of the pack and the 2026 world champion was fastest in qualifying with his team-mate 0.331s off in third.

So when asked afterwards if he was hoping for assistance from Antonelli, Russell replied: “It's still important, if you've got a grid penalty, to start as high up the order as possible.

“But we'll take it offline and we can talk about it. I think tomorrow is going to be very close between everybody, similar to Monza - it'll be very challenging to pull away from the pack.

“I would have liked to have been on pole, but I think anywhere in the top seven positions and you're in the fight.”

The situation caused Mercedes boss Toto Wolff to express disbelief at how Antonelli was quickest, particularly because Russell didn’t receive his request of leaving the pits second.

“It's very high risk,” added Russell, who will share the front row with Red Bull’s Max Verstappen due to Antonelli’s penalty.

“Kimi got the pole, but if he started the lap a second later, he wouldn't have got the lap in.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images

“It's very difficult to orchestrate because everybody's going for it, and also the fact that half the cars were doing prep laps and half the cars were not also made it difficult.

“If you could choose, you would be at the back of a pack of nine cars with around a three-second gap, if you could perfectly choose.

“But that's what everyone's chasing, so it's kind of like Monza 2019."

Although Antonelli eventually backing off gave him the space needed to set his fastest lap, a 1m33.893s, it could have cost him as he only just crossed the line in time to start his final tour.

“As George said, we will talk about it because we've been sent out at the front in qualifying always,” said Antonelli.

“About Turn 5, it was fully on me. Like I said, we were three-wide, first of all, and I just said, "You know what? I'm just going to back off’."

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“It was tricky because, first of all, I almost missed the flag. Yes, I did get a big tow, but I was also so close that getting around the corner was actually difficult with the dirty air and so on.

“We're already on a lower-downforce package, so you do feel even more the loss when following.

“But overall, it was just one of those times where you think you're screwed, but actually it works out.

“On Turn 5, I just decided to back off. I didn't really know how tight I was with the timing. I probably would have done it differently, but in hindsight, it still worked out.”

Sports.title: Verstappen reveals mysterious Red Bull F1 car issue that cannot be fixed in Las Vegas
Sports.content:
Thanks to Kimi Antonelli 's grid penalty, Max Verstappen will start Formula 1's Las Vegas Grand Prix from pole position, but that is not necessarily a reason for the Dutch driver to be satisfied.

Yes, Red Bull has made significant progress with its power unit on energy-poor circuits and, following the balance problems during free practice, the team also managed to make effective set-up changes, but the feeling behind the wheel was still not what Verstappen believes it should be.

"Already since Brazil I have some weird issues in the car and that continued this weekend. I'm just trying to get my head around how to deal with that for the remainder of the weekend," Verstappen said.

"That didn't make things easy in FP3, but I think in qualifying we managed to make it work."

When Verstappen was asked during the press conference whether he could elaborate on those "weird issues", he responded firmly: "No."

Nevertheless, the subject naturally came up again during his subsequent Dutch media session in the paddock. Verstappen was still unable to go into detail, but did shed a little more light on the situation.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Jordan McKean / Formula 1 / Getty Images

"It's not a balance problem, I can tell you that. There's simply something wrong with the car, but we can't fix it right now," the Red Bull driver said, when asked about the issue by Autosport.

"We know where the problem is coming from, but we can't solve it. It's now the second weekend in a row that it's been like this, but I can't say too much about it."

On the face of it, the issue appeared to emerge during the race in Brazil. After all, Verstappen reported that the car felt very different during the second and third stints compared to the opening stint, but the Dutchman clarified that the problem had actually been troubling him for longer.

"It suddenly appeared in Brazil, yes, but that was already before the race. I had problems there throughout the entire weekend," he said.

The four-time world champion clarified that it is different from the 'car degradation' he complained about at circuits including Monza. Back then, the car would deteriorate over the course of a session, whereas this time the issue is more fundamental. According to Verstappen, it is mainly related to the feeling through the steering wheel.

"It's something completely different from car degradation, but the feeling is simply not how I want it to be," he said. "I can't say much more about it, because otherwise I'll start explaining things that I don't want to give away."

Following the introduction of Red Bull's Baku upgrade, Verstappen said he had gained more confidence in the car and could therefore attack the corners more aggressively, but that has become more difficult because of this issue.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty Images

He added: "In certain places that's less the case now, yes. It doesn't matter what type of corner it is, either. The problem is simply there everywhere. I just have to try to adapt, but that's not easy."

Finally, Verstappen made it clear that team-mate Isack Hadjar is not experiencing the same problem: "No, apparently it's only on my side. It's not dangerous, but it's just not pleasant for me to drive. We just have to try to solve it. It had been working well for a very long time, but suddenly it wasn't in Brazil, and it isn't here either."

Sports.title: Verstappen responds to Russell after Las Vegas GP practice clash over 'gentleman's agreement'
Sports.content:
During the final practice session for the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix, Max Verstappen and George Russell crossed paths once again. The Dutchman overtook the Mercedes driver, but then slowed down in front of him and, according to the stewards, changed direction several times.

Russell subsequently went down the inside of the four-time world champion, leading to contact between the two at Turn 14. It earned both rivals a trip to the stewards, although they ultimately dealt with the incident by issuing a warning to Verstappen. Unlike a reprimand, a warning carries no consequences at all.

When Verstappen was asked about the incident during the press conference after qualifying, the Dutchman had little interest in discussing it. Asked what had happened, he simply replied: "Nothing. Nothing happened."

Russell, however, subsequently launched an attack on the Red Bull driver in the media pen. Speaking to Sky Sports Italy, Russell said: "I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

Verstappen was largely unmoved. When Autosport asked him about the clash during the Dutch media session that followed in the Las Vegas paddock, he replied: "I don't even want to waste my time on that. It's not worth it to me at all."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Jim Watson / AFP via Getty Images

When it was pointed out that the stewards had referred in the FIA document to a gentlemen's agreement during preparation laps, under which drivers are expected to maintain their positions and avoid interfering with one another before starting a flying lap, Verstappen responded: "I've never seen such an agreement in my life."

The stewards also made clear that they had attached little weight to the gentlemen's agreement mentioned by Russell in reaching their decision, instead focusing on the actions of both drivers.

"The Stewards noted these explanations but considered that such informal understandings were of limited relevance to the assessment of the incident. The decisive considerations were the actual movements of both cars and their relative positions."

It is particularly notable that the two drivers will share the front row of the grid in Vegas on Saturday night following Kimi Antonelli's grid penalty, but Verstappen insists the clash has not given him any extra motivation to keep Russell behind: "No, that's definitely not where I get my motivation from."

Sports.title: Floor damage, deployment down to Hamilton's Las Vegas GP Q2 exit
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton put Ferrari's Q2 exit in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix down to energy deployment and floor damage, as the seven-time Formula 1 world champion felt he'd rallied from difficulties with overall tyre grip.

The Briton struggled throughout FP3 under braking, as the front tyres proved particularly lock-up prone and resulted in Hamilton enduring multiple excursions into the run-off.

Hamilton landed in Q2 despite suffering floor damage in the opening stage of qualifying, but neither he nor Charles Leclerc were able to make their way into the top-10 shootout for pole.

Hamilton appeared generally happy with his runs in Q2, which demonstrated few of the lock-ups characteristic of his lead-up to qualifying, but the Ferrari power unit's energy deployment seemed to hit its maximum sooner than the Mercedes and Red Bull-powered cars and inhibited straightline speed and performance.

Ferrari has been down on power versus those two manufacturers, and the long acceleration zone along the Strip exposed this deficit throughout the session.

"We lost a piece of the floor on the first or second lap of Q1 and the car balance shifted, and we lost I think it was like three or four tenths of downforce we lost," Hamilton stated.

"And then after that we were struggling more so with sliding, but it was basically from the get-go.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

"And then my last lap was really good at the end, but I did the best I could with what I had. But then we lost something like six tenths just on deployment. So I think with that we would have been in Q3, but otherwise I was happy with my lap.

"We knew long straights and stuff was going to be challenging. The gap seems to be a little bit more than I anticipated in a straight line. It's not insignificant. It's a big chunk on the straights."

There had been a pervading sense that Ferrari would struggle in the low-temperature conditions in Las Vegas, as the team has struggled throughout 2026 to maintain tyre temperature through a qualifying lap.

Hamilton agreed that the car was difficult to work with amid frequent sliding through the low-speed corners, especially after losing a chunk of floor, and only hopes that Ferrari can move forward in the Saturday night race as it aims to lock out second in the constructors' championship.

"Just grip-wise, it just didn't feel like we had a ton of grip. We were struggling to get the tyres working and we were just kind of nowhere," he added.

"These tyres have been very, very difficult this year to get working, even on hot surfaces. So it's definitely been difficult. I don't have any expectations [for the race]. Just trying to see if I can move forward."

Sports.title: Hadjar given 10-second penalty for holding up Safety Car queue behind Verstappen | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The stewards have handed Isack Hadjar a 10-second time penalty for driving unnecessarily slowly during the Safety Car period.

Hadjar was running second behind team mate Max Verstappen when the Safety Car was deployed. The stewards ruled he reduced his speed excessively, delaying the queue of cars behind him as they were unable to pass. doing so would have reduced the chance of both Red Bull drivers losing positions when they pitted.

The stewards decided Hadjar deliberately slowed down after Red Bull gave him the repeated instruction “five seconds”. At one point Hadjar’s speed fell to less than 100kph below Verstappen’s.

A Mercedes representative attended the post-race hearing. George Russell was the first driver in the queue behind Hadjar.

“While driving on the straight between turns 13 and 14 under Safety Car conditions, the driver of car six [Hadjar] received repeated instructions from his team stating ‘five seconds, five seconds, five seconds’,” the stewards noted.

“Following these instructions, car six significantly reduced its speed, at one point travelling approximately 100 km/h slower than car three, which was ahead of it.

The stewards determined that this significant reduction in speed was deliberate and intended to create a gap to the car ahead and was not made for safety reasons, thereby allowing the team to perform a double-stack pit stop without car six losing time waiting behind its teammate in the pit lane. Furthermore, this manoeuvre directly impacted the cars following car six, which were forced to reduce their speed accordingly and could not overtake car six due to the restrictions applicable under Safety Car conditions.

“The stewards considered that car six was driving unnecessarily slowly for tactical reasons and that such conduct constituted a breach of the applicable regulations. In reaching their decision, the Stewards also took into account the precedent involving car four (Norris) at the 2023 Canadian Grand Prix, where a penalty was imposed for similar conduct.

“The Stewards imposed a 10 seconds time penalty which is consistent with the 2026 F1 Penalty Guidelines.”

Sports.title: Perez handed five-place grid penalty for Qatar Grand Prix for Camara collision | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Sergio Perez will go into the penultimate round of the championship with a five-place grid penalty.

The stewards held the Cadillac driver responsible for his collision with Rafael Camara during the Las Vegas Grand Prix. The Safety Car was deployed after the pair made contact at turn 14.

“Car 11 [Perez] attempted to overtake car 51 [Camara] on the inside, on the left-hand side, approaching turn 14,” the stewards noted.

“At no point during the manoeuvre was the front axle of car 11 at least alongside the mirror of car 51. The two cars collided at the entry to turn 14, resulting in car 11 retiring from the race.

“Applying the Driving Standards Guidelines, the Stewards determined that Car 11 had not earned the right to the corner and was wholly to blame for the collision.

“The stewards therefore imposed a 10-second time penalty. As Car 11 retired from the race and could not serve the penalty, it was converted into a five-place grid penalty at the driver’s next race.”

Perez said he gained so much on Camara in the straight before they collided that the Haas driver wasn’t aware he was there. “I just spoke to Camara and he said he didn’t see me,” said Perez.

“It’s a bit weird: you exit turn 12 one second behind, which is a massive distance, and then you are halfway down the straight alongside.

“Unfortunately he didn’t see me, so I was alongside him and when I saw that he basically did the corner as if I wasn’t there and when I tried to avoid it, it was just too late.”

Sports.title: “He’s so far below my level”: Russell’s mistake in Las Vegas GP delights Verstappen | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen said it was “honestly fantastic” to see George Russell make a mistake in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The pair clashed during practice on Thursday at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit . The stsewrads issued Verstappen a formal warning for “braking earlier than expected and changed direction under braking.”

Russell criticised Verstappen afterwards. “I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else,” he said. “Somebody’s got to stand up to that guy.”

Verstappen won today’s Las Vegas Grand Prix after scrapping with Russell in the opening stages. Russell finished ninth after skidding into a barrier while trying to pass Andrea Kimi Antonelli.

After his victory, Verstappen was reminded about Russell’s comments. “The thing is, he speaks a lot next to the track,” said Verstappen, “and honestly, for me, it doesn’t really bother me because he’s so far below my level that it doesn’t really make any sense for me anyway to try and challenge that, so it doesn’t bother me.”

The race winner spotted Russell’s mistake and was amused. “It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening.

“So I was like, fantastic. My day is only getting better. And of course, when I then crossed the line in first, my day was complete.”

Sports.title: “I thought I was doing something right”: Why power loss ended Antonelli’s win hopes | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli explained the sudden loss of power which ended his chances of fighting for victory in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The Mercedes driver slowed abruptly as he tried to attack race leader Max Verstappen as they began the final lap.

Antonelli explained he was trying to remain within the one-second zone behind Verstappen so he would be able to use the more power Overtake Mode. However when he lifted his throttle briefly the system responded by reducing the amount of power he could use.

“Because I wanted to keep the Overtake Mode, I lifted off and reapplied some throttle to keep a little bit of speed,” Antonelli told Sky. “That messed up the whole battery harvesting and I see at the chicane that I had zero.

“So I lost more than a second going into turn one and not only I couldn’t stay close to Max and give myself a good shot for the win but I got smoked by the two McLarens as well and lost the podium.”

Antonelli said he though he was using the power unit in the correct way to maximise his chances of being able to attack Verstappen at the end of the race.

“Probably it was a mistake on my side,” he said, “but in the moment it’s also very difficult because I thought I was doing something right to stay behind and keep the Overtake [Mode] but it turned out it compromised the race.”

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff confirmed Antonelli’s loss of energy was caused by his lift on the throttle.

“He wanted to stay behind Max, lifted the throttle and that depleted the battery and so at the final lap he had no energy anymore,” said Wolff. “He lifted, he thought it was better to stay behind, but if you lift there and then reapply, the battery is gone.”

Sports.title: Leclerc’s collision with Hamilton was “completely unacceptable”, fumes Vasseur | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur is deeply unhappy about the collision between his two drivers in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

Charles Leclerc received a 10-second time penalty for knocking Lewis Hamilton into a spin at turn seven. In a race which saw frequent position swaps between drivers, the collision between the Ferrari drivers was one of few incidents.

It comes after a series of clashes between the pair. Vasseur spoke to both drivers about their hard racing in Mexico, where both went off on the first lap and ultimately lost victory to Max Verstappen.

“Clearly it’s unacceptable, first,” Vasseur told Sky. “It’s a little bit the same message as Mexico because that you have to think about the team, about the people working in Maranello, about all the stakeholders, the sponsors and so on.”

Earlier in the race Hamilton urged the team to tell Leclerc to back off when racing him. Vasseur said the team warned Leclerc to take care when fighting with his team mate.

“We passed the message to Charles to not overtake because in this kind of race […] you have to overtake the cars in front of you or you are passed by the others. It means that you have to do your race.

“Charles did clearly a mistake, it’s penalising the team a lot, and it’s completely unacceptable. Honestly, we are more than upset because that message was clear after Mexico.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“We had the chat together, all together in Brazil. Today we passed the message to think about the team when they were racing together and the outcome is this one. It’s mega-frustrating for all of us.”

Leclerc accepted the blame for the incident. “At the end of the day, I guess we have stewards that are trying to do the best, trying to understand who is at fault whenever there is a clash, and today I was considered to be at fault and I took a 10 seconds penalty, I’m not going to argue that,” he said.

However he said he felt the move was on when he tried to pass Hamilton. “I will look back at it. It felt like I had plenty of space in the inside of turn seven because of the fight with Lewis and McLaren in front.

“I thought that it was definitely safe to be on the inside there. Unfortunately I don’t think Lewis with the angle of his car saw me in the mirrors and the gap that was once there at the apex was not so much there, but not to blame Lewis, I think he didn’t see me.”

Leclerc admitted he “feels very bad for the team again” following his latest clash with Hamilton.

“We’ve had discussions and I think the discussions have gone very well, but today I don’t think it’s similar to Mexico where we probably over-drove both of us and kind of went over the limit, there it was maybe more for racing incident but it’s still not acceptable to have a clash between cars and again I’ll accept the blame for whatever comes with this incident because at the end I took the penalty but I’ll look back at it and analyse it.”

Sports.title: Stewards explains Leclerc’s penalty for hitting Hamilton | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The stewards have explained why they penalised Charles Leclerc for colliding with his team mate.

Leclerc was given a 10-second time penalty for knocking Lewis Hamilton into a spin at turn seven.

Both Ferrari drivers received 10-second time penalties during the race. Leclerc’s was added to his time at the end of the race, while Hamilton served his during his pit stop. Hamilton was penalised for going off the track while passing Lando Norris.

Stewards’ verdict on Leclerc’s collision with Hamilton

Car 16 attempted to overtake Car 44 on the inside at Turn 7. The Stewards noted that Car 16 initiated the overtaking manoeuvre from a considerable distance behind Car 44, attempting to position his car on the inside. In assessing the incident, the Stewards also took into account the FIA Driving Standards Guidelines, in particular the criteria applicable to overtaking manoeuvres on the inside of a corner. The Stewards determined that the front axle of Car 16 was not at least alongside the mirror of Car 44 at the apex of the corner. The Stewards therefore determined that Car 16 had not earned the right to the corner at Turn 7 and was wholly to blame for the resulting collision. Accordingly, the Stewards imposed a 10-second time penalty

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Stewards’ verdict on Hamilton cutting turn seven while racing Norris

Car 1 (NOR) attempted to overtake Car 44 (HAM) on the left-hand side approaching Turn 7. At the apex, the front axle of Car 1 was at least alongside of the mirror of Car 44. Applying the Driving Standards Guidelines, the Stewards determined that Car 1 was entitled to the corner. Car 44 remained alongside Car 1 and subsequently crossed the white line on the right-hand side, leaving the track. By doing so, Car 44 avoided a potential collision but maintained its position ahead of Car 1. By leaving the track while defending, Car 44 therefore is considered as having gained a lasting advantage. Car 44 did not concede the position to Car 1, as he should have done. The Stewards therefore determined that Car 44 had left the track and gained a lasting advantage.
