“Through every season, one thing never changed: loyalty. trust. Love that stayed when it was easy, and stayed when it wasn’t. Almost 5. Still mine. Still my favourite mystery. And still the most real thing I’ve ever known. Here’s to forever, mon coeur,” Iyke said.

Backstory

While Iyke kept details of his marriage private, including information about any children he shares with his wife, he previously discussed aspects of his personal life during an interview with BBC News Pidgin.

PREMIUM TIMES reported earlier in April that the actor reflected on the experiences that shaped his life, calling the birth of his son his greatest source of happiness.

He said becoming a father changed his life, while the death of his mother remained the most heartbreaking experience he had faced.

However, he avoided giving a definite answer about his marriage then, describing his stance as “extremely middle”.

“When my boy looked at me, I came in one day, my boy, I was showing my boy some things about what I was going to create and everything.

“And he looked at me for one second; I’m like, why is he staring at me like that? He said, Papa, you’re a genius. I’m not a crying man, as you all know, but I went to the bathroom like something was wrong and I had a quiet cry,” he said in the interview.

This newspaper earlier reported that Iyke confirmed he had three children. His first son was born in 2015 to his Lithuanian ex-partner, while his other son, JJ, turned seven in February 2025.

Iyke was known for his roles in films such as “A Better Place”, “Between Kings and Queens”, “The Set Up 2”, “Different Strokes”, “No Fury”, “The High Class”, and “The Generals”, among others.

World.title: EPL: Iwobi makes Fulham history as Awoniyi scores before injury in Coventry win
World.content:
Alex Iwobi made history for Fulham on Saturday, becoming the first African player to record 100 Premier League starts for the London club. At the same time, compatriot Taiwo Awoniyi scored for Coventry City before an injury cut short his involvement in their victory over Crystal Palace.

Iwobi achieved the milestone in Fulham’s 1-1 draw against Manchester City, further underlining his importance to the club since joining from Everton in the summer of 2023.

The 30-year-old midfielder was named in the starting line-up and delivered another committed performance before being substituted in the 70th minute, with Antonee Robinson taking his place. He was also booked in the first half.

According to the Premier League, the appearance made Iwobi the first African to reach 100 starts for Fulham in the competition.

The former Arsenal academy graduate has established himself as one of Fulham’s dependable players, with his versatility, work rate and ability to operate in different midfield and attacking positions contributing to his regular place in the team.

He has made 122 Premier League appearances for the club, scoring 20 goals and providing 12 assists since his arrival at Craven Cottage.

Meanwhile, Awoniyi endured a bittersweet afternoon at the Coventry Building Society Arena, scoring in the opening five minutes of Coventry’s 3-2 victory over Crystal Palace before suffering an ankle injury shortly after returning to the pitch for the second half.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Super Eagles striker opened the scoring by connecting with Jack Rudoni’s pass after Yann Gboho’s backheel helped create the opportunity. However, the 29-year-old went down while jogging onto the pitch for the restart, pointed to his ankle and requested to be substituted.

Manager Frank Lampard brought on Sidiki Cherif, with the incident causing a brief delay to the start of the second half. The extent of Awoniyi’s injury was not immediately known, leaving Coventry and the national team awaiting further assessment.

Rudoni inspires Coventry comeback

Despite Awoniyi’s withdrawal, Coventry secured their fourth league victory of the season in an entertaining contest in which Palace twice came from behind to level.

Yeremy Pino equalised for the visitors in the 13th minute before Tatsuhiro Sakamoto restored Coventry’s lead shortly after the half-hour mark with a left-footed strike from 20 yards, following another assist from Rudoni.

Palace drew level again in first-half stoppage time when Pino set up Jorgen Strand Larsen, who headed home to make it 2-2.

Coventry eventually secured the win five minutes from time after Palace failed to deal with Milan van Ewijk’s long throw. Substitute Brandon Thomas-Asante’s header was saved by Dean Henderson, but the rebound deflected off Dwight McNeil and into the net for an own goal.

The victory moved Coventry three points clear of the relegation zone, while Palace suffered their fifth consecutive league defeat and remained bottom of the table.

Awoniyi’s goal was his second since joining Coventry in August, having scored once in his first eight league appearances. He had recently returned from international duty, playing 61 minutes in Nigeria’s goalless draw against Tanzania on Tuesday.

His early goal offered Coventry a boost, but the injury overshadowed his contribution, leaving his availability for subsequent matches uncertain.

World.title: CAF records $31.2 million profit as Motsepe’s reforms drive financial turnaround
World.content:
The Confederation of African Football (CAF) has reported a significant financial recovery under President Patrice Motsepe, with its latest annual financial statements showing a return to profitability, stronger reserves, and an improved cash position.

The figures, presented at the 48th CAF Ordinary General Assembly in Abuja, Nigeria, on 21 November 2026, highlight the progress the continental football governing body has made after years of financial difficulties.

CAF disclosed a net profit of $31.2 million, while total revenue climbed to $284 million, up more than 200 per cent.

The organisation’s financial reserves have also moved from a deficit of $16.8 million to a positive balance of $14.4 million. Its cash position stood at $118.8 million at the end of the financial year in June 2026.

The latest figures represent a major shift from the financial situation CAF faced five years ago, when the organisation was reportedly burdened with debts exceeding $100 million.

A turnaround programme introduced under Motsepe’s leadership in 2021 has been credited with putting CAF on a path towards financial independence and long-term sustainability.

Beyond returning to profitability, the improved financial position has allowed CAF to increase its investment in football development across the continent, with greater financial support for its member associations, zonal unions, clubs and competitions.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

CAF increases financial support to member associations by 250%

One of the major objectives of Motsepe’s administration has been to provide greater financial assistance to CAF’s 54 member associations, to improve football development structures and expand opportunities across Africa.

Since 2021, the annual financial allocation to each member association has increased by 250 per cent, rising from $200,000 to $700,000. The latest adjustment came into effect in July 2026.

The new allocation takes CAF to 70 per cent of its stated target of providing $1 million annually to each member association.

The increased funding is expected to support grassroots football development, strengthen administrative and governance structures, and create more opportunities for youth and women’s football.

CAF has also raised its annual allocation to each of its six zonal unions by 80 per cent, from $500,000 in 2021 to $900,000 in 2026.

African club football receives $48 million investment

CAF’s financial recovery has also translated into increased investment in club competitions, with total funding for clubs rising by 153 per cent over the last five years.

The figure has grown from $19 million in 2021 to $48 million in 2026, reflecting a significant increase in the financial rewards available to clubs competing in CAF’s interclub tournaments.

Winners of the CAF Champions League now receive $6 million, compared with $2.5 million in 2021.

Similarly, the champions of the CAF Confederation Cup are now rewarded with $4 million, up from $1.25 million five years ago.

The overall prize money for the Champions League has increased to $19.6 million, while the Confederation Cup now has a total prize fund of $11.9 million.

CAF has also improved its solidarity payments to clubs eliminated during the preliminary rounds of its interclub competitions, doubling the amount from $50,000 to $100,000 per club.

The increased financial incentives are part of efforts to improve the competitiveness and sustainability of African club football, while providing more resources for teams participating in continental competitions.

AFCON and WAFCON prize money reach new heights

CAF’s revenue growth has also created room for a significant increase in prize money across its flagship national team competitions.

The winners of the CAF Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025 received a record $10 million, twice the $5 million awarded to the champions of the 2021 edition.

The overall prize money for the men’s tournament also rose by more than 40 per cent, increasing from $24.8 million in 2021 to $35 million for the 2025 competition.

Women’s football has also benefited from the financial changes, with CAF substantially increasing the rewards available at the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations.

The winners of the CAF Women’s Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2026 received $2 million, representing a 900 per cent increase from the $200,000 awarded to the champions in 2021.

The overall prize fund for the women’s competition also increased from $975,000 in 2021 to $5.8 million in 2026.

The tournament has also expanded from 12 to 16 participating national teams, allowing more countries to compete at the continental level.

CAF moves to strengthen financial accountability

Beyond the improved figures, the 48th Ordinary General Assembly also highlighted efforts to address longstanding concerns surrounding CAF’s financial reporting and governance.

The organisation disclosed that it had tackled a decade-long backlog in timely financial reporting, with two sets of accounts presented in 2026 as part of its efforts to improve transparency, accountability and financial management.

The progress marks another important part of the reforms introduced under Motsepe, as CAF seeks to establish a more transparent and sustainable financial structure.

With a return to profitability, stronger reserves and increased investment across its competitions and member associations, CAF believes it is now in a stronger position to support the continued growth of African football.

World.title: How my wife was taken away from Government House – Kano governor
World.content:
Kano State Governor Abba Yusuf has said his wife left Government House and later filed for divorce in an Abuja court.

In an interview with BBC Hausa, which aired Sunday morning, Governor Yusuf detailed his rift with his wife, Zainab Kwankwaso, a niece of former Kano State governor and vice-presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Rabiu Kwankwaso.

On 16 November, Governor Yusuf said, while addressing pensioners at the Government House in Kano, that he had divorced Zainab after the court filing.

This followed a Daily Nigerian newspaper report that Zainab had filed for divorce.

The issue generated controversy given the relationship between the governor and Zainab’s guardian, Mr Kwankwaso, who was Governor Yusuf’s political godfather.

What caused the crisis?

“What is your explanation regarding the remarks you made about your family?” the BBC asked the governor.

“This kind of family matter is very difficult,” Governor Yusuf said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“This woman, Zainab, is the daughter of his (Kwankwaso’s) elder brother. He previously married her off to someone, though that marriage did not last long. After that, God brought us together, and I married her. We got married about 20 years ago, and we have children.

“Many things happened, to the point where her belongings were packed and she was taken away from my house, and through it all, I remained patient and did not speak out,” the governor stated

The governor added that he had even assured their children that Zainab would return home.

“Suddenly, he (Mr Kwankwaso) made her drag me to court—a court in Abuja, not even in Kano,” the governor said.

“It is an unpleasant situation,” he added.

He stated that although he would not tell the world the exact manner in which his wife was taken from his house, he has evidence and detailed information on how the incident occurred.

According to him, this should not have become a subject of public controversy, as such domestic matters are not uncommon.

When asked why he chose to speak about the matter publicly, Governor Yusuf replied, “I am not the one who politicised it. If this was done to you, how would you feel?

“To have your wife’s belongings packed without your knowledge, for her to be taken away and kept elsewhere without your knowledge, taken to someone else’s house without your knowledge, and then suddenly you hear that she is the one who has sued you in court,” Governor Yusuf narrated.

The governor said the matter was still being looked into and that a resolution may be reached.

Who is Zainab Musa Kwankwaso?

Zainab is the daughter of Mr Kwankwaso’s late elder brother, Dahiru Kwankwaso, who died in an accident on the Kano-Kaduna expressway in 1985.

Zainab grew up in Mr Kwankwaso’s household until he gave her out in marriage – first to an unidentified person, then to Governor Yusuf.

She married the future governor in 2006. Their marriage lasted 20 years, and they have six children together.

Strain reportedly entered the marriage following the feud between Governor Yusuf and Mr Kwankwaso.

For over two decades, Mr Yusuf was one of Mr Kwankwaso’s closest allies and a central figure in the Kwankwasiyya political movement.

He served as Mr Kwankwaso’s personal assistant and later as Commissioner for Works during his second term as governor (2011–2015).

In January, Governor Yusuf broke ranks with Mr Kwankwaso and defected from the NNPP to the APC, citing the need to align Kano State with the federal government.

Mr Kwankwaso also defected from the NNPP to the African Democratic Congress (ADC), before joining the New Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and emerging as running mate to the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi.

World.title: Troops storm kidnappers’ hideout in Kogi, recover rifles
World.content:
The Nigerian Army says its troops have dislodged suspected kidnappers from a hideout in Okehi Local Government Area of Kogi State, recovering two AK-47 rifles and ammunition.

The operation was conducted in the early hours of Saturday, 21 November, following intelligence about the activities of suspected kidnappers in the Osara, Gada and Ohakiti forest areas of the local government.

In a statement issued on Saturday, the Acting Director of Army Public Relations, Appolonia Anele, said troops deployed from Patrol Base Kabba, working with other security personnel, raided the identified hideouts.

She said the soldiers encountered about six armed men at an abandoned settlement and engaged them, forcing them to flee.

A subsequent search of the area led to the recovery of two AK-47 rifles, three magazines and 65 rounds of 7.62mm special ammunition.

Ms Anele said other items recovered included bags, torchlights, food supplies and a power bank believed to have been used by the fleeing suspects.

She said the operation was aimed at dismantling criminal hideouts and curbing kidnappings along the Kabba-Okene Road and surrounding communities.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Related security operations

The operation comes days after a joint security team rescued 15 kidnapped victims from Magaru Forest in Kakun-Kabba, Kogi State.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the victims were rescued in the early hours of 18 November after police personnel, soldiers and local security groups engaged the kidnappers in a gun battle.

The Police Public Relations Officer in Kogi State, Saliu Afusat, said the rescued victims included children and teenagers.

She added that two other female victims had escaped from their abductors during the initial encounter.

The police said no arrests had been made and that investigations were ongoing to track down the fleeing suspects.

In another operation, the army said it arrested a suspected ammunition supplier, Umaru Muhammad, on 17 November, after recovering 300 rounds of 7.62 x 39mm ammunition allegedly concealed in a sack of beans.

The ammunition was reportedly intended for two individuals in Gori Village, Lokoja Local Government Area.

PREMIUM TIMES also earlier reported that soldiers killed three suspected kidnappers and recovered four AK-47 rifles during an operation around Edimogbo and Obele forests in Igalamela/Odolu Local Government Area.

The army said it would sustain intelligence-led operations with other security agencies to dismantle criminal hideouts and improve security along vulnerable routes in Kogi State. It urged residents to provide credible information to support the operations.

World.title: First-Class degree not enough to make excellent teacher – TRCN
World.content:
The Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) says possessing a first-class degree does not automatically make an individual an excellent teacher.

Dr. Ronke Soyombo, Registrar/Chief Executive of TRCN, stated this in an interview with Newsmen on Sunday in Abuja.

Soyombo stressed the importance of professional competence adding that effective teaching required more than academic qualifications.

The registrar explained that teachers must demonstrate competence in five critical areas assessed through the Council’s professional qualifying examination.

She identified the areas as basic mathematics, foundational literacy, digital literacy, pedagogy, and safeguarding and child protection.

According to her, teachers must possess a sound understanding of basic mathematical concepts to effectively support children’s learning and development.

She described foundational literacy as equally important, noting that strong literacy skills enabled teachers to support learning across other subject areas.

The registrar said teachers must also understand today’s children, particularly those belonging to the Alpha Generation, and the technological environment in which they operate.

She identified digital literacy as the third major area of assessment, describing it as compulsory for teachers seeking to engage effectively with contemporary learners.

To illustrate the challenge, Soyombo recalled visiting an examination centre where she encountered an elderly teacher struggling with a computer mouse.

“I remember visiting an examination centre recently and meeting an elderly teacher who held a computer mouse and asked me, ‘Madam, what am I going to do with this?’” she said.

She said the encounter highlighted the extent of digital literacy challenges confronting some teachers and raised concerns about their preparedness for modern classrooms.

“How can teachers effectively engage children in today’s classrooms if they are not comfortable with basic technology?” she asked.

Soyombo, however, acknowledged the challenges and disclosed that several training programmes were being implemented to improve teachers’ digital competence.

On pedagogy, she said possessing excellent academic qualifications did not automatically translate into the ability to teach effectively.

“Having a first-class degree does not automatically make someone an excellent teacher,” she said.

She explained that academic qualifications alone could not guarantee that a teacher understood how to apply appropriate instructional methods to address different learning needs.

According to her, classrooms comprise learners with varying abilities, including average pupils, children requiring additional support, and gifted and talented learners.

She stressed that teachers must possess the pedagogical skills to effectively reach all categories of learners and ensure inclusive classroom experiences.

“This is why pedagogy is a critical component of our examination.

“Without sound pedagogical skills, a person cannot be considered a fully competent teacher,” she said.

The registrar identified safeguarding and child protection as the fifth critical area, emphasising the need to guarantee every child’s safety within the school environment.

She said teachers must understand safeguarding principles, child protection requirements and their professional responsibilities towards learners.

Soyombo said one positive development was the growing awareness among teachers that preparing for the TRCN examination involved more than simply passing a test.

She urged candidates preparing for the next examination scheduled for May, 2027, to explore the Council’s online resources and apply the knowledge gained in their classrooms.

“There is no point preparing for the next TRCN examination in May, 2027 without exploring the available resources and ensuring that the knowledge acquired improves children’s learning outcomes,” she said.

She emphasised that professional development should translate into measurable improvements in teaching quality and children’s educational experiences.

According to her, every agency within the education sector must remain conscious of the learning outcomes it seeks to achieve.

“For the education system to progress, every agency must remain conscious of the learning outcomes we want to achieve,” she said.

Soyombo maintained that improving professional standards was essential to the credibility and relevance of the Council, insisting that its mandate must produce tangible improvements

World.title: Fire destroys goods worth millions in Yobe market
World.content:
…Traders count losses as inferno razes shops in Potiskum

By Maryam Abdul-aziz Usman

A midnight fire outbreak has destroyed several shops and goods worth millions of naira at the Potiskum Central Market in Yobe State, leaving traders counting their losses.

The fire, which reportedly started at about 2:00 a.m. on Sunday, November 22, 2026, initially affected the section of the market occupied by traditional medicine dealers before spreading to adjoining shops.

The outbreak reportedly caught traders and residents around the market unawares, as the flames spread rapidly through the affected section, making it difficult to salvage goods and other valuables.

Following the incident, traders and residents rushed to the scene in an attempt to rescue merchandise and prevent the fire from spreading to other parts of the market.

However, several shops and their contents had already been destroyed before effective intervention could be mounted.

The arrival of fire service personnel helped contain the inferno and prevent it from spreading to other densely populated sections of the market, thereby averting further destruction.

An eyewitness commended the firefighters for their timely intervention, saying their arrival helped prevent the fire from engulfing the entire market.

Although no casualties had been reported as of the time of filing this report, the destruction of goods and property has left affected traders facing significant financial losses.

The exact number of shops destroyed and the total value of merchandise lost were yet to be ascertained.

The Yobe State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA) is expected to assess the affected section to determine the extent of the damage, document the losses suffered by traders and establish the circumstances surrounding the outbreak.

The incident has renewed concerns over fire safety in commercial markets, particularly those with closely packed shops and large quantities of combustible materials.

For the affected traders, the immediate challenge is how to recover from the losses and rebuild their businesses following the destruction of their merchandise.

World.title: Omo-Agege backs Obi, not Tinubu, says aide
World.content:
...Says APC circulating seven-month-old video to misrepresent senator’s position

Senator Ovie Omo-Agege has reaffirmed his support for Peter Obi as the Nigerian Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate for the 2027 general election, dismissing a video circulating on social media in which he expressed support for President Bola Tinubu.

Omo-Agege’s position was contained in a statement issued on Saturday by his Special Adviser on Strategy and Communications, Godwin Anaughe, who accused the Delta State chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) and some officials of the state government of circulating an old video to misrepresent the senator’s political position.

The statement said the video, recorded in April 2026 at the Federal Polytechnic, Orogun, when Omo-Agege was still a member of the APC, showed him expressing support for Tinubu.

However, Anaughe described the circulation of the footage as misleading, arguing that it predated the senator’s defection from the APC to the NDC in May 2026.

According to the statement, Omo-Agege subsequently endorsed Obi at the NDC nomination convention on May 30, 2026, where he seconded the former Anambra State governor’s nomination as the party’s presidential candidate.

It added that the senator also declared his support for Obi during an appearance on Arise Television on June 3, 2026, describing him as his preferred presidential candidate for 2027.

The aide maintained that Omo-Agege had consistently expressed the same position since joining the NDC.

“For the record: Senator Omo-Agege is not endorsing President Tinubu for re-election. He is not going back to the APC. He is the NDC Senatorial candidate for Delta Central, and he stands solidly with Deltans and Nigerians in their resolve to make Peter Obi President in 2027,” the statement said.

Anaughe argued that a video recorded while Omo-Agege was still in the APC could not be used to establish his current political allegiance.

He accused those circulating the footage of deliberately ignoring the date it was recorded, insisting that the senator’s subsequent public declarations provided a clearer account of his present political position.

The statement also challenged the APC to focus on defending its performance in government rather than circulating old political footage.

It cited rising food prices, unemployment and declining public confidence as issues Nigerians expected political parties to address.

“If the APC wants to talk, it should talk about its record, not its video library,” Anaughe said.

He added that Omo-Agege remained focused on the 2027 elections and his support for what he described as a new Nigeria where opportunities would not depend on personal connections. The statement concluded with the slogan, “A New Nigeria Is Possible.”

World.title: Full list: FG announces 19 international job vacancies [How to apply]
World.content:
The Federal Government, FG has announced 19 international job vacancies for qualified Nigerians at the African Space Agency and the General Secretariat of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).

The vacancies, announced by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, comprise five positions at the African Space Agency headquarters in Cairo, Egypt, and 14 positions at the OIC headquarters in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

The ministry disclosed this in two separate vacancy announcements dated Friday, November 20, 2026, signed by its spokesperson, Oluwafemi Adeniyi, and shared on its official Facebook page on Saturday.

According to the ministry, the African Space Agency is recruiting for five positions, with application deadlines of November 25 and December 10, 2026.

The positions include Director, Corporate Services (D-1); Director-General, African Space Agency (D-2); Head of Legal Affairs (Grade P-5); Senior Finance Officer (P3); and Senior Human Resources Officer (P3).

The ministry said interested and qualified Nigerians should visit the agency’s official website at https://africanspaceagency.org for details of the eligibility requirements and application procedures.

For the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, the ministry announced 14 vacancies across its departments and specialised units.

The positions include Director-General of Political Affairs; Director, Administration Department; Director, Information Department; Director, Conference Department; Director, Muslim Communities and Minorities; Director, African Affairs; and Director, European Affairs and International Organisations.

Others are Head of Human Resources (PP2); Professional Officer, Human Resources (PP2); Professional Officers, Administration Department (P2); Director, Peace, Security and Mediation Unit; Chief of HRC Office – IUT; Registrar – IUT; and Deputy Internal Auditor – IUT.

The ministry said the application deadlines for the OIC positions range from November 29 to December 24, 2026.

It urged interested and qualified Nigerians to visit the organisation’s official vacancy portal at https://www.oic-oci.org/en/vacancies for information on the specific requirements, application procedures and deadlines for each position.

How to apply

Interested Nigerians can apply through the following official platforms:

African Space Agency: Visit https://africanspaceagency.org, navigate to the recruitment or careers section, and check the available positions, eligibility criteria and application instructions. Organisation of Islamic Cooperation: Visit https://www.oic-oci.org/en/vacancies, select the relevant vacancy and follow the stated application procedure.

Applicants are advised to review the requirements for their preferred positions and submit their applications before the respective deadlines.

Vanguard News

World.title: APC cancels Cross River campaign kick-off
World.content:
…Directs National Assembly, Assembly candidates to continue ward-to-ward campaigns

By Ike Uchechukwu, CALABAR

The All Progressives Congress (APC) in Cross River State has cancelled its statewide campaign kick-off scheduled for Thursday, November 26, throwing its campaign timetable for the National Assembly and State House of Assembly elections into temporary uncertainty.

The cancellation was announced in a statement issued on Saturday by the Director-General of the Cross River State APC Campaign Council, Prof. Stephen Odey, from the campaign secretariat at 42 Murtala Muhammed Highway, Calabar.

The statement said the campaign itinerary, which had earlier been released, had been cancelled, adding that a new date would be announced in due course.

The Campaign Council, however, did not disclose the reason for the cancellation.

It apologised for any inconvenience the decision might have caused party leaders, stakeholders, candidates, supporters and members of the public.

Despite the cancellation, the council directed APC candidates contesting the National Assembly and State House of Assembly elections to continue their grassroots campaign activities.

It urged them to proceed with their respective ward-to-ward campaigns, visits, consultations, engagements with stakeholders and other approved campaign activities.

The directive suggests that the party intends to sustain grassroots mobilisation while arrangements are being made for a fresh date for the statewide campaign programme.

Odey thanked party members and the general public for their understanding and cooperation, assuring them that further information would be communicated in due course.

World.title: Dickson mourns victims of Bayelsa boat mishap, seeks safety measures
World.content:
Former Governor of Bayelsa State, Senator Henry Seriake Dickson, has commiserated with the families and friends of victims of the boat mishap along the Ayama/Oweikorogha waterways in Southern Ijaw Local Government Area of the state.

Dickson, who disclosed this in a post on his X platform on Sunday, described the incident as unfortunate and expressed sadness over the loss of lives.

He also extended his condolences to the Bayelsa State Government and the people of the state over the tragedy.

The senator said he deliberately scaled down his engagements on Saturday as a mark of respect for those who lost their lives in the incident.

According to him, he reduced the number of visitors he attended to and cancelled some previously scheduled visits to reflect on the tragedy.

Dickson commended the relevant emergency response agencies and other individuals involved in the rescue operation for their swift response, urging them to sustain their efforts until the operation was successfully concluded.

He also called for stricter enforcement of maritime safety regulations and increased public awareness to prevent similar incidents.

The former governor stressed the need for continuous safety education for marine operators, security personnel and residents of Bayelsa State.

He further urged traditional institutions and the media to support efforts aimed at promoting maritime safety and ensuring compliance with relevant regulations.

Dickson reiterated his condolences to the bereaved families, praying that God would grant the deceased eternal rest and give their loved ones the strength to bear the loss.

World.title: Tinubu reiterates commitment to uninterrupted academic calendars
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has reiterated his administration’s commitment to strengthening public tertiary institutions through infrastructure interventions, student financing and policies supporting uninterrupted academic calendars.

Tinubu said this during the grand finale of the 37th Convocation ceremony of the Federal University of Technology, Akure (FUTA) on Saturday in Akure.

The ceremony featured conferment of postgraduate degrees on 1,173 graduands and the decoration of the scholars as Professors Emeriti.

The President, represented by Prof. Olatunde Ajagbonna of the National Universities Commission (NUC), said his administration recognised universities as vital to scientific, technological and economic progress.

“My administration recognises the critical role of universities in national development and has continued to support our tertiary institutions through interventions in infrastructure, equipment, research facilities, laboratories, lecture theatres and student accommodation.

“In furtherance of our commitment to student welfare, the Federal Government is also supporting the construction of 1,500-capacity hostel at FUTA in partnership with private sector organisations.

“In the education sector, I remain committed to ensuring that no Nigerian student is denied access to tertiary education on account of financial difficulties.

“The commitment informed the establishment of Nigerian Education Loan Fund(NELFUND) by my government, which provides financial assistance to eligible students in public tertiary institutions, including support for their upkeep,” he said.

Tinubu noted that economic reforms had yielded growth above four per cent in 2026 across oil and non-oil sectors, urging judicious use of federal interventions.

He urged the private sector and development partners to collaborate with FUTA in engineering, agriculture, healthcare, artificial intelligence and information technology to drive innovation and job creation.

In his goodwill message, Gov. Lucky Aiyedatiwa of Ondo State, represented by Commissioner for Education, Science and Technology, Prof. Igbekele Ajibefun, congratulated the graduands and commended the vice-chancellor’s leadership.

Aiyedatiwa said the state government would continue to partner with and support FUTA in achieving its aspirations and advancing human capital development.

Earlier, FUTA Vice-Chancellor, Prof. Adenike Oladiji, said the event marked the fourth and final convocation of her tenure as the eighth substantive vice-chancellor since May 2022.

Oladiji said the university sustained a stable academic calendar and achieved NUC accreditation for its College of Health Sciences.

She said FUTA had no abandoned projects, reporting 21 completed projects and 24 ongoing projects, alongside agricultural expansion, a 5,000-layer poultry revamp and a revitalised feed-mill.

Giving a breakdown of the 1,173 postgraduate graduands, Oladiji said 641 received Master’s degree and 225 bagged Postgraduate Diploma.

She added that 173 earned Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) degree, 131 graduated from the School of Professional Development, and three received Master of Philosophy (M.Phil) degree.

She announced that Prof. Felix Akinyosoye and Prof. Thomas Ofuya would be decorated as Professors Emeriti.

Prof. Akinyosoye was decorated as Professor Emeritus of Microbiology, Food Fermentation and Zymology, while Prof. Ofuya was decorated as Professor Emeritus of Crop Entomology.

Also speaking, Pro-Chancellor and Chairman of the Governing Council, Dr Olugbenga Awe, congratulated the graduands and the two decorated Professors Emeriti.

Awe urged the graduands to approach their future with intellectual humility and apply their knowledge to improve institutions and solve societal challenges.

World.title: Photos: Police take over Fountain of Life Church amid leadership crisis
World.content:
…As trustees, Jimmy Odukoya trade court actions, church postpones thanksgiving service

There was a heavy presence of police personnel at the headquarters of The Fountain of Life Church, Ilupeju, Lagos, on Sunday, as the leadership crisis rocking the church deepened, leaving worshippers uncertain about who would preside over the regular Sunday service.

The security presence came amid a bitter dispute between Senior Pastor Jimmy Odukoya and a group of church trustees over his continued leadership of the ministry founded by his late father, Pastor Taiwo Odukoya.

The disagreement has escalated into a legal battle, with both sides seeking judicial intervention over the control and administration of the church.

On Friday, Odukoya approached the Federal High Court in Lagos, challenging his reported removal as senior pastor and questioning the legality of decisions taken by some members of the church’s Board of Trustees.

The suit, instituted by Odukoya alongside the Incorporated Trustees of The Fountain of Life Church, named his sister, Tolu Odukoya, and seven other church leaders as respondents.

The respondents include Pastor Rotimi Okpaise, Pastor Tobi Enuha, Pastor Gbenga Onabanjo, Pastor Fred Ohiani, Pastor Akin Osinbajo, Biodun Balogun and Biodun Awosika.

In the court action, Odukoya is challenging the validity of meetings held by some trustees on January 22, February 28 and November 16, 2026, as well as the decisions allegedly taken at those meetings.

He is also asking the court to determine whether the trustees could remove him as senior pastor without following the procedures stipulated in the church’s constitution.

How the crisis started

The leadership dispute became public on November 17 when a group identifying itself as members of the church’s Board of Trustees announced that Odukoya was no longer recognised as the senior pastor, with immediate effect.

The trustees reportedly based their decision on a review of the church’s constitution and recorded succession instructions allegedly left by its late founder, Taiwo Odukoya, before his death in 2023.

They maintained that the decision was intended to give effect to the founder’s wishes and ensure compliance with the church’s governing provisions.

The group subsequently named Pastor Rotimi Okpaise as interim spiritual and administrative leader pending consultations and the establishment of a substantive leadership structure.

However, the announcement immediately generated a counter-reaction from the church, which rejected the purported removal and described it as constitutionally invalid.

In a statement issued after the announcement, the church maintained that Jimmy Odukoya remained its duly appointed senior pastor and chairman of the Board of Trustees.

It argued that his appointment in September 2023 was unanimously approved by the recognised board and that no constitutionally valid decision had been taken to remove him.

The disagreement also extended to the control of the church’s communication channels, with the trustees alleging that individuals acting on Odukoya’s behalf had taken control of its official social media accounts without authorisation.

Court restrains Odukoya

The dispute took another turn on Wednesday, November 18, when the Lagos State High Court granted interim orders restraining Odukoya from holding himself out as the Senior Pastor and Spiritual Head of the church.

Justice O.O. Adewunmi-Oshin made the orders following an application by the Incorporated Trustees of The Fountain of Life Church.

The court also restrained Odukoya, whether acting personally or through proxies, from interfering with, disrupting or obstructing the church’s governance, administration and activities.

The orders were made ex parte, meaning they were granted before Odukoya had an opportunity to respond to the application.

However, the court preserved his right to challenge the orders or respond to the substantive claims.

The court did not order the closure of the church, suspend its worship services or appoint a replacement for Odukoya. The matter was adjourned until December 1 for mention.

Thanksgiving service postponed

Amid the unfolding dispute, the church announced the postponement of its much-anticipated 2026 Thanksgiving Service, which had been scheduled for Sunday, November 22.

In a notice published on its official social media platforms on Thursday, November 19, the church said a new date would be communicated in due course.

The postponement generated further uncertainty among members, particularly as reports circulated that police officers had sealed the church premises and directed workers to vacate the facility.

However, the church subsequently dismissed reports that its premises had been sealed.

In a message shared on its official social media account on Friday, it declared: “Don’t believe the noise; church is not sealed. See you in church on Sunday.”

It also announced that its regular Sunday service would hold at 9am, inviting members to attend physically or participate online.

Despite the clarification, a visit to the church premises on Sunday revealed a notable presence of security operatives, while access and activities at the facility appeared restricted.

Worshippers were nevertheless seen arriving and being ushered into the main auditorium for the regular service.

As of the time of filing this report, it was unclear who would lead the congregation or preside over the service.

Vanguard Newspaper

World.title: When Will an Igbo Be Elected President?
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

One subject that may be of interest in ‘Winning Formula’ — my book on the 2023 presidential election, which goes on general sale from Monday, November 23 — is the pathway for an Igbo to become president. The Nigerian federation was originally built on the tripod of Hausa-Fulani, Igbo and Yoruba, with each ethnic classification dominant in the Northern, Eastern and Western regions respectively. Among hundreds of ethnic groups, the Big Three are estimated to constitute roughly two-thirds of the Nigerian population. In the Fourth Republic, the Yoruba and the Hausa-Fulani have each produced two presidents. The Igbo have not produced a vice-president, much less a president.

Why have the Igbo not produced an executive president, despite bids by heavyweight politicians such as Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe, Dr Alex Ekwueme, Dim Chukwuemeka Ojukwu and Mr Peter Obi? The answer you get depends on who is responding. One frequent answer is that it is because of the unsuccessful secession bid by the Igbo in 1967 which led to a three-year Civil War. The belief is that the Igbo are yet to be fully trusted with holding the apex political position in the land. Some other analysts would argue that the competition for the No 1 position is very complicated; any power bloc that is going to win the race must be able to build a winning coalition across the political constructs.

Azikiwe, elected by parliament as ceremonial president in 1963 under the parliamentary system, made a strong bid for executive presidency in 1979 but came third behind Alhaji Shehu Shagari and Chief Obafemi Awolowo. He tried again in 1983 and came thirdagain. Ekwueme, vice-president from 1979 to 1983, sought the presidential ticket of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in 1999 and 2003 without success. Dr Ogbonnaya Onu, by a special arrangement, was nominated the presidential candidate of the All Peoples Party (APP) in 1999 with the caveat that he would step down for the flagbearer of the Alliance for Democracy (AD) under a joint candidature deal by the smaller parties.

Ojukwu, who led the Biafran secession bid, twice contested the presidential election as candidate of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA) but did not get significant votes. Obi, however, put up a strong challenge in 2023, shaking the established politicalorder. He came third, though he insists he won. He is making a second bid in 2027 with a stronger running mate in Dr Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso this time and is hoping to break the jinx. I did not appraise his chances in my book, but his candidacy means that once again, we are poised for a three-horse race, assuming Alhaji Atiku Abubakar would be on the ballot. We always had two-horse races from 1999 until Obi entered the fray in 2023.

It is the contention of many that there is a conspiracy to keep the Igbo from having the presidency. This remains a suspicion, a very strong one. However, there was also a time it was believed that no southerner would be elected president of Nigeria. I grew up hearing about a powerful “Kaduna Mafia” that determined who would be president. Shagari winning in 1979 and 1983 was provided as proof that no southerner would taste presidency. Chief MKO Abiola had been hoping to bid for the ticket of the ruling National Party of Nigeria (NPN) in 1983 but was told that there was no vacancy. This was at a time some thought a sitting president could be stoppedfrom seeking re-election.

Under President Ibrahim Babangida’s transition programme in 1992, the leading presidential candidates were northerners. Gen Shehu Musa Yar’Adua had won the Social Democratic Party (SDP) ticket while Alhaji Umaru Shinkafi and Mallam Adamu Ciroma of the National Republican Convention (NRC) were to face a runoff when Babangida cancelled the primaries and ordered a fresh one in his unending chop-and-change drama. If the election had gone ahead, it would have been an all-north affair. The conspiracy theory still had a life though after Abiola defeated Alhaji Bashir Tofa of the NRC in 1993. The annulment was cited as further proof that southerners were not welcome to Aso Rock.

After northerners had ruled Nigeria for roughly 35 out of 39 years from 1960 to 1999, Gen Olusegun Obasanjo was elected president. His election in 1999 demonstrated that the presumed ethnicitybarrier was not insurmountable. The speculation then was that Obasanjo was a figurehead meant to hold power in trust for just one term before returning it to its “rightful owners” in 2003, but he asserted himself. Power rotation between the north and the south became a convention. Therefore, even if there is a scheme to keep the Igbo out of power, it can be undone. Rather than dwell on the conspiracy theories, though, ‘Winning Formula’ examines the practical pathways for the Igbo.

From 1999 to 2007, the informal tripod arrangement was respected. The Yoruba produced the president, the Hausa-Fulani the vice-president, and the Igbo the senate president. When presidency went to the north in 2007, an Igbo would have been vice-president under normal temperature and humidity. But the Niger Delta had started campaigning for resource control and the oil-producing region ended up getting the vice-presidency as a political solution to theiragitation. This, I would say, effectively displaced the Igbo from the power equation in the tripod tradition. Naturally, an Igbo would have been vice-president in 2007 if the tripod arrangement had not been disrupted.

Hypothetically, an Igbo would have automatically assumed power when Alhaji Umaru Musa Yar’Adua died in May 2010. By default, the jinx would have been broken. It could be further assumed that an Igbo would have ruled Nigeria from 2011 to 2015, as a result. In my book, I take a look at the voting patterns in our presidential elections since 1999 and make some critical observations. For one, the Igbo path to the presidency does not look like something to be accomplished through an alliance with minorities and religious groups, as Obi worked very hard to achieve in 2023. As I have noted, the biggest voting blocs are the tripod. Votes from the otherblocs are best for consolidation purposes.

Judging by the electoral behaviour of Nigerian voters, I identifythree possible pathways for an Igbo to be elected president. One, there is the all-important “two out of three” formula. That is, all winners of presidential elections since 1999 have always won substantial votes in at least two of the tripod blocs. No one has been elected president without the “two out of three” pattern. Therefore, the Igbo could have a warm handshake with the Hausa-Fulani. This means the current Yoruba/Hausa-Fulani alliance will have to give way at some point. With the Yoruba having twice held the No. 1 position in the Fourth Republic, a good case can truly be made for an Igbo/Hausa-Fulani handshake.

Two, there could be a repeat of President Goodluck Jonathan’sroute of 2011: getting the bulk of the Yoruba and Igbo votes (“two out of three”) as a gesture of southern solidarity — andconsolidating with the votes of the northern and/or southern minorities. That was how Jonathan was able to defeat a strong Hausa-Fulani candidate, Gen Muhammadu Buhari, in 2011. If anIgbo candidate is able to put together a similar coalition, chances of winning will be very high, in view of the recurring patterns among Nigeria’s voting blocs. But will the Yoruba throw their weight behind an Igbo candidate? That is very tricky. I would say anything is possible in politics, no matter how unlikely.

Three, there can be a consensus among the leading parties to cede or zone their presidential tickets to the south-east. Heads or tails, an Igbo will become president. This is not unheard of: in 1999, thisunderstanding produced Yoruba candidates in the AD/APP alliance and the PDP. It was achieved through a combination of political bargaining, party arrangements and the national reaction to the June 12 crisis. The logic is that a similar arrangement could be agreed to heal the wounds of the Civil War. The only difference is that there is yet no unanimity of opinion over the events leading to the war and who should take the blame. But it’s not a problem beyond what good politics can resolve.

All said and done, the lesson is that the presidency is neither the birthright of any ethnic group nor a prize that will be awarded simply because one group has waited long enough. It is won through political calculation, compromise and coalition-building. The Yoruba mainstream used to treat the Hausa-Fulani as “enemies”. But three Yoruba men — Abiola, Obasanjo and Tinubu — won presidential elections by aligning with the same “enemies”.That is how “two out of three” — the central thesis of my book — works. If an Igbo is to be elected president, the missing piece is not necessarily a qualified candidate. It is forming a winning national coalition. That is the formula.

AND FOUR OTHER THINGS…

FOUNTAIN OF STRIFE

The crisis that has engulfed the Fountain of Life Church is nothing but an unmitigated embarrassment to Christendom. Murmurs and rumours of internal strife since the death of Pastor Taiwo Odukoya, the founder, have now come out in the open, with Pastor Jimmy Odukoya, his son and successor as senior pastor, and members of the board of trustees fully engaged in an open war. The face-off has now shifted to the courts. This crisis is not exactly the legacy we would expect from the lineage of Pastors Taiwo and Bimbo Odukoya who gave their all to the gospel. I can only hope that Nigerian churches with a similar “ownership” structure are going to learn from this succession crisis. Shame.

SORE SOULS

The US on Wednesday commended the Nigerian military for rescuing 125 kidnap victims and dismantling terrorist camps during operations, as well as the recovery of weapons and clearance of explosive devices. For those who were excited that President Donald Trump was coming to abduct President Bola Tinubu and try him for “Christian genocide”, this was bad news. Comments under the X post by the US Bureau of African Affairs were filled with bitterness. Many commenters sounded quite sad that the US was commending our progress. My point remains: we can hate Tinubu and still be happy for Nigeria when things are going right. Tinubu will leave one day. Nigeria remains. Think.

GUNSHOT GAMES

Mr Tunji Disu, the inspector-general of police (IGP), has just repeated what I have been hearing since circa 1996: that hospitals are not prohibited from treating bullet-wound victims. Under military rule, when Nigeria was in the grip of armed robbers, hospitals were allowed to treat bullet-wound victims but with the caveat that they would report to the police. Hospitals quickly took that as an excuse not to treat victims at all. The authorities have repeatedly clarified that hospitals are not prohibited from treating gunshot victims. There is even the Compulsory Treatment and Care for Victims of Gunshots Act, 2017. I implore Disu not to relent. Most importantly, wilful violators must face the law. Simple.

NO COMMENT

When the US bombed Islamic State militants in the Sokoto bushes on Christmas Day last year, we saw many unexploded devices and doubted the success of the mission. President Trump celebrated the air strikes and even added his usual drama: “They (US military) were going to do it earlier. And I said, ‘nope, let’s give a Christmas present.’” The Wall Street Journal has now reported, citing a US official, that expired Tomahawk missiles were used in the strikes. Separately, Hung Cao, Trump’s nominee for navy secretary, admitted at his confirmation hearing that the navy had “recoded” expired munitions for use in Iran. He compared the practice to eating expired bread. Hahahaha…

World.title: 2027: As Fear of Defeat Fuels Political Violence
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

With the widespread attacks sponsored against political opponents by some political leaders who fear they might lose the 2027 elections, Ejiofor Alike writes that the retired General Abdulsalami Abubakar-led National Peace Committee should call political actors to order to save Nigeria’s democracy

President Bola Tinubu received a dose of the political violence spreading across the country ahead of the 2027 general election when his motorcade was attacked on Friday, November 13, 2026, at a mosque in Garki District, Abuja, shortly after the President observed Jumu’ah prayers.

According to the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Police Command’s spokesperson, Josephine Adeh, as the president’s convoy was leaving the area, some individuals attacked the convoy with stones and other dangerous objects, damaging several vehicles and causing injuries to some security operatives.

However, Adeh disclosed that the 78 suspects arrested over the incident were to be released following the President’s extension of clemency to them.

The police statement was the first official acknowledgment of the attack on Tinubu’s convoy.

The video of the incident, which went viral, captured some of the youths chanting “Ba ma yi, ba ma so,” an Hausa expression meaning “we don’t want you; we don’t support you.”

Few hours after the attack, President Tinubu issued a statement, condemning what he described as the rising cases of violence at political events across the country, warning that all political parties and candidates must enjoy equal protection and the freedom to campaign anywhere in the country without harassment or fear.

Before the attack on the president, the opposition parties and their leaders were the main targets of attacks.

Reacting to Tinubu’s statement in a post on X, the presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC), Omoyele Sowore questioned why Tinubu did not condemn previous incidents of political violence.

Following the widespread attacks on opposition parties and their leaders, the National Leader of the NDC, Senator Seriake Dickson, had recently called on the National Peace Committee (NPC) led by a former military Head of State, General Abdulsalami Abubakar (rtd.), the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and security agencies to convene an all-party summit to address rising political violence ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Dickson warned that the increasing attacks on NDC members, candidates and supporters could undermine the credibility and peaceful conduct of the elections if urgent steps were not taken to contain the situation.

The National Peace Committee had earlier raised concerns over rising political tensions and warned President Tinubu, Atiku, Obi, and other political actors against inflammatory statements and incitement ahead of the 2027 polls.

The committee had also raised the alarm over 60 election-related incidents recorded across the country within one month.

Worried by the spread of violence, a chieftain of The Alternative and a key promoter of President Tinubu’s re-election bid, Segun Showunmi, had urged the National Security Adviser (NSA), Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, to establish clear boundaries for political conduct and ensure that individuals who threaten national security are held accountable, irrespective of their political affiliations.

Showunmi, who made the appeal in an open letter to Ribadu, warned that inflammatory political statements, ethnic and religious insinuations, threats and the manipulation of sensitive national issues for political advantage could worsen Nigeria’s security challenges.

He warned that political status, public office or proximity to powerful interests should not be treated as immunity from the consequences of unlawful conduct.

Political analysts believe Sowunmi’s letter to Ribadu was timely following the increasing attempts by some political actors to exploit the country’s ethnic fault lines for electoral gain.

The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Mr. Festus Keyamo, was recently accused of attempting to exploit ethnic insinuations, and manipulation of the sensitive issue of secession for political advantage against Obi.

This followed an accusation by the minister that Obi and the members of NDC, sang the old National Anthem at the recent town hall meeting held by the party in Lagos.

Keyamo, in his verified Twitter (X) account, said that by refusing to sing the new national anthem, Obi and his group might be planning to break away from Nigeria.

But Obi’s supporters argued that both old and new national anthems pay allegiance to Nigeria.

Reacting in a post on her X, a chieftain of the NDC, Aisha Yesufu, accused the ruling APC government of attempting to use the secession narrative to discredit Obi.

Yesufu dismissed Keyamo’s narrative, insisting that the attempt to portray the NDC or its supporters as separatists would not change the political mood ahead of the 2027 elections

Former President Goodluck Jonathan had also issued a stern warning to Nigerian political actors and citizens, cautioning that weaponising ethnic rivalry and political intolerance would pose a severe threat to the country’s survival.

Speaking on November 17, 2026, at a high-level peace and security conference hosted by the Goodluck Jonathan Foundation in Abuja, the former leader stressed that politicians must refrain from exploiting ethnic fault lines for electoral gain, noting that democratic stability relied on shared national unity.

He warned that undermining national cohesion for political ambition would pose a severe danger to the country’s existence.

But in its reaction to the nationwide violence, the APC Presidential Campaign Council accused the ADC and the NDC of sponsoring violence and deploying young Nigerians to disrupt its campaign activities.

The council alleged that the opposition parties were using hoodlums, artificial intelligence-generated images, deepfakes, fake news and sponsored protests to create tension, manipulate public opinion and discredit President Tinubu and the APC.

In a press statement issued last Tuesday, and signed by its spokesperson, Mr. Dele Alake, the council recalled that it had warned Nigerians ahead of the flag-off of its presidential campaign rally in Kaduna on October 24 about alleged plans by opposition elements to introduce violence and disharmony into the campaigns.

It claimed that the alleged plots were beginning to unfold, accusing the ADC and NDC of sponsoring groups of hoodlums to disrupt APC rallies with cudgels and banners while chanting “Bamaiyi” in an attempt to portray widespread public discontent against the president.

The council cited the recent incident at an Abuja Mosque, where it alleged that some of the sponsored thugs pelted the presidential motorcade with stones.

The APC campaign council also expressed concern over alleged attacks and threats against its members and supporters in the South-east, claiming that some had been labelled ‘saboteurs’ for refusing to support Obi.

The council maintained that no political party or candidate should be denied access to the democratic space in any part of the country.

On its part, the Senate recently called on INEC to disqualify any political candidate whose supporters are found to have instigated or participated in electoral violence, irrespective of party affiliation.

The upper chamber also urged state governors to stop denying opposition parties access to public facilities, hotels and stadia under their control for political activities.

Electoral violence and political impunity contributed largely to the collapse of civilian administrations in the past.

To save the current democracy from collapse, the Abdulsalami-led committee and other elder statesmen should caution political actors.

World.title: Use the Senator Kawu’s Blunt Truth to the APC
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

A senator on the platform of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Suleiman Kawu, last week told his party the truth when he acknowledged that economic hardship associated with President Bola Tinubu’s reforms was creating resentment among voters in northern Nigeria, warning that the ruling party must reconnect with ordinary citizens ahead of the 2027 elections.

Kawu, who is seeking re-election to represent Kano South Senatorial District in the forthcoming election, said the party must acknowledge the suffering of Nigerians and explain the intended benefits of the administration’s policies rather than rely on campaign rallies and political displays.

Kawu in a television interview, admitted that the economic consequences of the reforms had created challenges for the ruling party, particularly in its efforts to persuade voters to support Tinubu’s re-election. He said he had urged the party’s leadership and campaign council to demonstrate empathy and responsiveness to citizens in view of the prevailing economic realities.

His comments came as political parties intensified mobilisation ahead of the January 16, 2027 presidential and National Assembly elections.

Opposition parties have accused the leaders of the APC of going about their campaign as if the feelings of Nigerians do not matter to them.

They accused senior members of the party of dancing and throwing jabs at opposition political parties without telling Nigerians what they have done to justify a fresh mandate.

Currently, a large number of Nigerians are hungry and facing economic hardship. There are no good roads for them to travel on, no reliable electricity, no good hospitals, many do not have jobs, fuel is still high and above all many are still dying due to the insecurity ravaging the country.

The senator’s admission is a challenge for the APC as it seeks another presidential mandate, persuades Nigerians to support economic reforms whose intended long-term benefits have yet to translate into sufficient relief for many households.

World.title: Jonathan: Nigeria Needs Honest, Visionary Leaders to Restore Global Respect
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

•Condemns money-driven politics, primitive wealth accumulation

•Says democracy has standards, calls for investment in the younger generation

Ndubuisi Francis in Abuja

Former President Goodluck Jonathan has called for purposeful, honest and visionary political leadership to rebuild Nigeria’s battered international image and restore the respect the country once commanded globally

Delivering the keynote address at the third edition of the annual The Paul Alaje Colloquium (TPACOLLOQUIUM), with the theme, “The Brand Nigeria”, in Abuja yesterday, he said the country needs leaders who are deliberate about national development rather than personal wealth accumulation.

Jonathan recalled Nigeria’s towering global image, especially in the 1960s and 70s.

He lamented that the quality of politics currently practised in Nigeria was undermining democracy and threatening the country’s progress.

“Some of what goes on in our political space does not represent democracy. The brand of politics we are playing will set us backwards. Democracy has standards,” he said.

The former president urged political leaders to emulate the late Chief Obafemi Awolowo, whose clear vision and commitment to compulsory education transformed the old Western Region.

According to him, Awolowo’s education policy produced remarkable results, with the South-West at one point having more professors than the rest of Nigeria combined.

He challenged present-day leaders to abandon primitive accumulation of wealth and invest in the younger generation, stressing that leadership should be measured by the legacy left behind.

“Why will you stomach what you are supposed to invest in the younger generation at a time you know your time on earth is really not much?” he asked.

The former president criticised politicians who lacked knowledge of their parties’ manifestos, noting that many of the documents were prepared by hired consultants without any meaningful commitment from the candidates.

He noted that a nation’s brand was its identity, reputation and standing among the comity of nations.

Jonathan recalled that Nigeria once enjoyed considerable international respect and influence but regretted that its reputation had suffered significant setbacks.

He identified insecurity, corruption, economic difficulties, unemployment, political instability and negative perceptions of public institutions as factors damaging the country’s image.

The former president particularly expressed concern over the limited international mobility associated with the Nigerian passport, which exposes citizens to considerable visa restrictions and difficulties travelling abroad.

However, he cautioned against equating the country’s challenges with the character of its people, maintaining that millions of Nigerians remained honest, industrious, talented and respected internationally.

He attributed the deterioration of Nigeria’s national identity partly to the erosion of societal values, where wealth was celebrated without questions about its source. At the same time, honesty, hard work and integrity received insufficient recognition.

Other factors, he said, included corruption, abuse of public office, impunity, weakened public institutions, and insecurity, which had created doubts about the state’s ability to guarantee the safety of lives and property.

To reverse the trend, Jonathan called for stronger leadership and governance, insisting that public office must be treated as a position of trust.

He said merit, competence, transparency, accountability and the rule of law must become the guiding principles of public administration.

He also advocated reforms in political recruitment, stronger internal party democracy, credible elections, and a political culture that rewards ideas, character, and competence rather than money, patronage, and sectional interests.

Jonathan also regretted that the country’s image had suffered considerable setbacks, even as individual Nigerians continued to excel internationally.

He said, “Today, we must honestly acknowledge that the image of our country has suffered considerable setbacks. Although Nigerians continue to excel internationally, our national reputation is increasingly overshadowed by insecurity, corruption, economic difficulties, unemployment, political instability and negative perceptions of our institutions.

“One particularly troubling reflection is the limited international mobility associated with the Nigerian passport. Its relatively weak global standing, compared with many other countries, means our citizens face considerable visa restrictions and difficulties travelling internationally. This should concern us.

“A passport is more than a travel document; it is a symbol of national identity, and the confidence other countries place in the nation that issues it. Yet, we must distinguish between the country’s challenges and the character of its people. Millions of Nigerians remain honest, industrious, talented and highly respected across the world.

“Our problem is not a shortage of human potential. It is our failure to translate that potential consistently into effective institutions, responsible leadership and national progress.”

Jonathan reminisced about the good old days, saying, “There was a time when Nigeria commanded considerable respect and influence internationally. We were regarded as a promising African nation with enormous potential and a strong sense of continental responsibility. Nigeria was frequently mentioned among the emerging economies alongside countries such as Brazil and Malaysia, with the potential to become a major global power.

“We had confidence in our institutions, national ambition and the capacity to influence events beyond our borders. We played leading roles in the liberation of Southern Africa and the struggle against apartheid.

“Our military earned international recognition through peacekeeping operations in Liberia and Sierra Leone. Our diplomacy carried considerable weight in Africa and beyond. Our athletes, footballers, academics, doctors, engineers, entrepreneurs and professionals represented the country with distinction.

“Our literature, music, films and creative arts projected our identity to the world. Specifically, our athletes and footballers, including Dick Tiger, Kanu Nwankwo and Austin Jay-Jay Okocha, became global ambassadors whose achievements brought honour to our country.

“Our professionals- doctors, engineers, academics and scientists- also earned international respect. Today, Afrobeats and Nollywood continue to project Nigeria’s cultural identity to international audiences.”

He argued that a strong national brand would attract investment, tourism, international partnerships and opportunities for its citizens, adding that it would also inspire patriotism at home and respect abroad.

He noted that despite the motley negative tendencies undermining Nigeria’s image, all hope was not lost, arguing that Nigeria must be willing to learn from countries that have achieved remarkable transformations, including India, South Korea, Malaysia and Singapore.

“The lesson is not that Nigeria must become Singapore. It is that national transformation requires purposeful leadership, institutional discipline and long-term commitment to the public good.

“Restoring the Nigeria brand requires more than slogans and publicity campaigns. It requires a national commitment to changing the realities that shape our reputation.

“First, we must restore integrity, discipline, hard work and patriotism as fundamental national values. Our homes, schools, religious institutions and communities must teach young Nigerians that genuine success must be achieved through honest and productive means.

“Second, we must strengthen leadership and governance. Public office must be regarded as a position of trust. Merit, competence, transparency, accountability and the rule of law must guide public administration.

“We must reform our political and leadership recruitment processes. We must strengthen internal party democracy, electoral credibility, and a more inclusive political culture and reward ideas, character, and competence rather than money, patronage, and sectional interests.

“Third, we must build a secure and productive economy that creates employment, encourages enterprise and improves the living conditions of our people. Education, healthcare, agriculture, manufacturing, technology and infrastructure must receive sustained attention.

“Fourth, we must invest in our cultural, sporting and professional assets. Afrobeats, Nollywood, our literature, fashion, football and other sporting achievements demonstrate the power of Nigerian creativity. We must support these industries and use them more effectively for cultural diplomacy and economic development.

The Convener of the colloquium, Dr. Paul Alaje, noted that Nigeria has never lacked conferences, reports, development plans or diagnoses of its challenges.

According to him, what Nigerians must now demand was implementation.

He noted that productivity must be a central national development priority, rewarding efficiency, innovation, value addition, and competitiveness.

Alaje also called for rebuilding institutional trust through transparency, accountability, consistency, and effective public service.

World.title: FG’s Reforms Push Combined Tax Expenses of 30 Listed Firms up 72% to N4.6tn in Nine Months
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

•Combined profit after tax up 19% to N8.06tn

Kayode Tokede

Thirty companies listed on the Nigerian Exchange Limited (NGX) reported combined tax expenses of an estimated N4.6 trillion in the first nine months of 2026, up 72 per cent from N2.68 trillion in the corresponding period of 2025, following the federal government’s tax reforms.

However, despite the rising tax expenses, the 30 firms posted a combined profit after tax of N8.06 trillion, up 19 per cent from N6.77 trillion in the first nine months of 2025.

The companies are subject to taxes administered by the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS), state internal revenue services and other revenue authorities in the jurisdictions where they operate, including markets across sub-Saharan Africa and Asia.

The firms reviewed by THISDAY operate in several sectors of the Nigerian economy, including banking, cement manufacturing, fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) and telecommunications.

The firms include: FCMB Group Plc, United Bank for Africa Plc, Jaiz Bank Plc, Sterling Financial Holdings Company Plc, Zenith Bank Plc, Guaranty Trust Holding Company (GTCO), First Holdco Plc, Stanbic IBTC Holdings Plc, Access Holdings Plc and Wema Bank Plc.

Others are: Dangote Cement Plc, HBM Nigeria Plc, BUA Cement Plc, BUA Foods Plc, MTN Nigeria Communications Plc, Nestle Nigeria Plc, Cadbury Nigeria Plc, Seplat Energy Plc, Aradel Holdings Plc, and Total Energies Marketing Company Plc.

Also on the list are: Okomu Oil Palm Plc, Presco Plc, Transcorp Power Plc, Transcorp Hotel Plc, Geregu Power Plc, NASCON Allied Industries Plc, Nigerian Breweries Plc and Conoil Plc.

Seplat Energy Plc reported the highest tax expense among the 30 companies, followed by Aradel Holdings Plc, MTN Nigeria Communications Plc and Dangote Cement Plc.

In its unaudited results for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, Seplat Energy reported tax expenses of N987.15 billion, up 34.8 per cent from N732.35 billion in the corresponding period of 2025.

The group said it had applied the provisions of the Nigeria Tax Act 2025, which took effect in January 2026 and consolidated the education tax, the NASENI levy and the Police Trust Fund levy into a development levy.

“In accordance with IAS 34: Interim Financial Reporting, income tax expense for the interim period has been determined using the estimated weighted average annual effective income tax rate expected for the full financial year.

“This estimate is reviewed at each interim reporting date and adjusted, where necessary, to reflect changes in the expected annual tax rate.”

Seplat attributed N929.9 billion of its nine-month income tax expense to its oil segment, up from N695.9 billion a year earlier. The gas segment accounted for N57.2 billion, up from N36.4 billion. For the third quarter alone, the oil segment recorded N396.2 billion, compared with N342.4 billion in the corresponding quarter of 2025, while the gas segment recorded N26 billion, up from N21.6 billion.

Aradel Holdings reported tax expenses of N721.41 billion for the first nine months of 2026, up from N55.6 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. MTN Nigeria’s tax expenses rose by nearly 68 per cent to N630.47 billion from N376.3 billion.

MTN Nigeria was the most profitable of the 30 firms, posting a profit after tax of N1.17 trillion, up 55.3 per cent from N750.19 billion in the first nine months of 2025.

Dangote Cement reported an income tax expense of N497.71 billion, up 67.2 per cent from N297.7 billion in the corresponding period of 2025.

The 11 banks in the review accounted for 26.9 per cent of aggregate tax expenses in the first nine months of 2026, compared with 30.7 per cent in the corresponding period of 2025.

Guaranty Trust Holding Company Plc (GTCO) recorded the highest tax expense among the 11 banks, reporting N265.3 billion, up 31.9 per cent from N201.16 billion a year earlier.

GTCO said its company income tax rose to N283.1 billion in the first nine months of 2026 from N201.12 billion in the corresponding period of 2025.

Its under-provision for prior years increased to N18.3 billion from N10.1 billion, while the amount relating to the origination of temporary differences rose to N36.07 billion from N10.06 billion a year earlier.

GTCO’s profit after tax fell by 12.2 per cent to N614.57 billion from N699.64 billion in the first nine months of 2025.

Nigeria’s standard corporate income tax rate remains at 30 per cent. Under the tax reforms, companies within scope are subject to a four per cent development levy on assessable profits. The levy replaces several federal levies, so its effect on each company’s tax bill depends in part on what the company previously paid.

The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and related legislation, which took effect on January 1, 2026, affect the tax costs, cash flow, dividend capacity, investment decisions and compliance expenses of NGX-listed companies. The reforms could also affect share prices.

The impact will vary by company, depending on profitability, sector, available tax incentives, capital expenditure, financing structure and how each company adapts to the new rules.
