But in the four months since he became prime minister, Burnham has staked out a more bullish position on Europe, appearing willing to revisit the politically charged Brexit debate and take on the right-wing parties that fiercely oppose reversing 2016’s referendum result and reestablishing closer ties with Europe.

Last month, he even said he’d like to see Britain rejoin the bloc in his lifetime but ruled that out in this parliament, alongside crossing his party’s “red lines” from their 2024 manifesto of returning to the single market or customs union, or restoring freedom of movement.

Nonetheless, he committed to beginning talks with the EU “about options for our long-term relationship” after Friday’s summit without providing further details or timeline.

Burnham, center, and Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey, right, attend the EU-UK summit on Friday. Hannah McKay/Reuters

The cost of Brexit

Economists broadly agree that leaving the EU stymied the UK’s economic growth potential – with estimates ranging from 2% to as much as 8% of foregone output. So as the government scrabbles for levers to kickstart economic growth, the EU, as Britain’s biggest trading partner and neighbor, has become part of the conversation.

Following Labour’s election in 2024 under Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, it promised to “make Brexit work.” Starmer’s strategy was to reboot the UK-EU relationship by negotiating limited deals and aligning some regulations to ease trade frictions.

But Starmer’s technocratic, cautious approach – on Europe and other policy areas – led in large part to his party ousting him this summer. The more confident, media-savvy Burnham emerged in his place.

The deal is expected to ease trade frictions for food products. Carl Court/Getty Images

Friday’s summit was largely a product of Starmer’s approach, originally scheduled for earlier this year but delayed when his premiership imploded.

Nick Thomas-Symonds, a member of parliament who served as Europe minister under Starmer, told CNN the deal was “90% there” when Burnham’s team took over.

Even after the summit, sticking points remain, including whether tuition fees for EU students studying at UK universities will be aligned with those of their British counterparts. European Council President António Costa shied away from directly answering a question about whether the deals announced today are contingent on the UK agreeing to lower tuition fees for European students.

A joint EU-UK statement released Friday said the parties would work toward a “supplementing agreement” on tuition fees, with negotiations expected to conclude within six months.

The youth scheme, which will allow 100,000 young people from the EU and the UK respectively to live for up to three years for work, studies or traveling, is expected to be available no later than January 2030, the statement said.

A limited ‘reset’?

Burnham’s rhetoric on Europe has been more forceful, but his actual approach hasn’t changed “an iota” from Starmer’s, said Anand Menon, a professor at King’s College London and director of the think-tank UK in a Changing Europe, in comments to CNN ahead of the summit.

“The only difference is how we talk about the future, and Burnham saying we might consider rejoining,” he said. “The more people talk about rejoining, the more obviously complicated an undertaking it becomes. I don’t know where Burnham goes on this.”

Further changes in the UK-EU relationship are unlikely, Menon added, unless the government compromises on its “red lines.”

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is pictured with the President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen earlier this month. Stefan Rousseau/Reuters

His assessment echoes that of the EU’s former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier, who warned earlier this month that the UK cannot “cherry pick” certain elements of the single market.

For his part, Thomas-Symonds pointed to more cooperation on immigration, stronger military ties and aligning regulations in other sectors as ways to deepen ties with the EU without breaking party promises. “Obviously, these bigger points are ones that we’re looking at in the next manifesto,” he said.

Even Burnham himself acknowledged that Friday’s agreement is “probably the limit of what we can achieve in this parliament.”

‘Lessons of the past’

Burnham’s ambitious rhetoric has shifted the political conversation, however. Two campaign groups – both with ties to the original “Vote Leave” campaign – either launched or rebranded this week with the express purpose of opposing any attempts to rejoin the EU.

Conservative opposition leader Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, accused Burnham of having “not learnt the lessons of the past,” arguing that “the problems this country faces today have nothing to do with being in or out of the EU.” Brexit architect Nigel Farage, who leads the hard-right Reform UK party, said that Burnham “has no mandate” to negotiate closer ties with Brussels.

Notwithstanding the Euroskeptic right flank, who are unlikely ever to vote for Labour, the politics of promising to rejoin the EU might actually be favorable for Burnham, noted Morgan Jones, deputy director of Persuasion UK, an organization that researches public opinion.

Polling suggests that if “there were an option to rejoin on 2016 terms tomorrow, it would be resoundingly popular,” she told CNN, saying that it also appeals to the different voters Labour would need to win a parliamentary majority.

But the same cannot be said of the process of actually doing so, she added. “We found that people were put off by the prospect of budget contributions or any threat of joining the Euro and also simply by the process itself – there is significant voter exhaustion on this topic,” she said, citing research Persuasion conducted with a pro-EU think tank.

‘A lot of trauma’

Until now, the “reset” has yielded few tangible outcomes aside from an agreement for Britain to rejoin the Erasmus student exchange program next year, at a much higher cost than before.

Burnham says these agreements could add up to 0.5% of GDP to the British economy and remove bureaucratic hurdles for food exporters.

But Europe Minister Hamish Falconer conceded to the BBC that their implementation would compel the UK to accept EU regulations on products without being able to shape them.

It echoes the old trade-off – sovereignty versus frictionless trade – which underpinned the fractious years-long Brexit debate, the legacy of which hangs over whatever Burnham’s government decides to do next and Europe’s own moves.

Indeed, the bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said last week that the EU had suffered “a lot of trauma” from Britain’s departure before warning that any future negotiations “will not be that easy.”

World.title: Finland warns Ukraine war ‘spilling over’ after Baltic Sea drone strike on Russian cargo ship
World.content:
Helsinki Reuters —

A Russian cargo ship with links to the military was hit by drones and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday in what Finland said was likely an attack by Ukraine, and the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters.

The 16-member crew of the Sparta II evacuated onto lifeboats, then to a nearby Russian ship, and is on its way back to Russia, Finnish Border Guard Commander Ilja Iljin told public broadcaster Yle late on Saturday.

Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwest Leningrad region this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of the Baltic region, leading to fears that the war was affecting NATO territory.

“It is likely that Ukraine … is behind (the attack),” Finnish armed forces spokesperson Aki-Mauri Huhtinen told a press conference, adding it was not clear why the vessel had been targeted.

The ship, bound for Russian exclave Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland island, Finland’s Defence Forces said, corroborating an earlier account by Russian officials.

The blaze was ongoing late on Saturday and Finland is leading the rescue operation as the ship is at anchor in its waters, although Russian vessels may eventually tow the wreckage home, Finnish authorities said.

A Russian helicopter was suspected of briefly violating Finnish airspace during the rescue operation, said Mikko Simola, commander of the Gulf of Finland Coast Guard.

‘War is spilling over’

Helsinki said it had introduced temporary aviation and maritime restrictions in the eastern Gulf of Finland to protect civilians and allow authorities to operate if drones needed to be intercepted.

“The war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas. Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said on X.

Swedish combat aircraft, operating under Finnish command, took part in safeguarding Finland’s and NATO’s territorial integrity following the incident, Sweden’s Defence Minister Pal Jonson said.

Director of Communications of the Defence Forces, Colonel Aki-Mauri Huhtinen, center, speaks during a press conference by the Finnish Border Guard, in Helsinki, on November 21, regarding the damaged Russian cargo vessel in the Gulf of Finland. Mikko Stig/Lehtikuva/Reuters

Finland and Sweden are NATO’s newest member states, joining the military alliance in 2023 and 2024, respectively, in response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

“The consequences of fighting Russia’s aggression have reached the Baltic Sea. Another signal for the aggressor to stop. But nothing will stop us from supporting Ukraine,” Estonia’s Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote on X.

Estonia sent a navy vessel to assist in the rescue operation, including firefighting and pollution response, its government said.

Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Russia’s embassy in Helsinki did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The vessel is subject to US sanctions and is linked to Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika, according to the US Treasury Department.

Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry, according to the company’s website.

“At the moment, there is no confirmed information about what cargo is on board, but it cannot be ruled out that there is military materiel on board,” Iljin of the Finnish Border Guard said.

Russia says drones shot down over Leningrad region

Leningrad region Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said on Telegram that a cargo vessel had been attacked by two drones in international waters about 3 nautical miles from Russia’s border.

Drozdenko also said 80 drones had been shot down over the Leningrad region overnight.

Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks on the Leningrad region.

Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said the incident posed no threat to supplies to the region.

Kaliningrad, which lies between Poland and Lithuania, has periodically been a flashpoint between Russia and NATO and the European Union.

Russia has previously described attacks on its commercial vessels outside its territorial waters as acts of terrorism and maritime piracy.

The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to LSEG data.

The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia that extends east to St Petersburg. Gogland lies in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

World.title: If not Vance or Rubio, then who? GOP 2028 questions mount
World.content:
Social media caricatures him as the man of many jobs. He’s been depicted as the Verizon Guy, the governor of Greenland and Manchester United’s next manager.

But, in the parlance of Oval Office couch memes: Is “Marco Rubio realizing” that a new role now beckons — as a 2028 presidential candidate?

CNN reported Thursday that some Republicans are quietly thinking about how to nudge President Donald Trump’s secretary of everything into the race. Many see him as the best hope of heading off another savage voter verdict on Trump’s presidency in two years’ time.

New Rubio buzz followed the clumsy bid by presumed front-runner JD Vance to distance himself from the Iran war on the morning after the midterm elections.

Rubio insists he won’t talk 2028. But he’s also not repeating his earlier line about not running if Vance does. And his steadying presence piped in from Manila about recent tech meltdowns made him look like a rare adult in the Trump room.

Speculation about the secretary of state and national security adviser — who also had spells as the acting head of the National Archives and acting USAID administrator — opens an intriguing chapter of the next presidential race, in which both parties will have open tickets.

But Rubio — and anyone else who fancies the GOP nomination — has some hard thinking to do.

Amid the wreckage of the midterms, a GOP hopeful might well wonder whether 2032 would be a better bet. It’s early, but Democrats are in the box seat because voters seem unlikely to be looking for a third term of Trumpism.

Rubio is potentially intriguing. He’s managed to maintain a distinct political identity even inside the Trump maelstrom. This might equip him for the next GOP nominee’s most difficult mission: looking like someone new while running in Trump’s shadow. And Rubio has shown chameleon qualities by shedding his past as a traditional conservative hawk to enter Trump’s “America First” inner circle.

Still, it’s a reach to think his Teflon act can survive association with Trump’s wild foreign policy and his deeply unpopular Iran war. If he became the Republican nominee, how would he answer Democratic accusations of complicity in policies like ICE’s street raids against undocumented migrants? And what would he say about Trump’s latest cozying up to his “friend” Vladimir Putin on Thursday?

Rubio is also a willing member of an administration that permitted the world’s richest man Elon Musk, to desecrate USAID and deprive some of its poorest people of medical treatment and humanitarian supplies. Some independent observers warn this may lead to millions of deaths.

Rubio also ran foreign policy while Trump threatened the sovereignty of Canada, one of America’s closest friends, and insulted America’s allies over their sacrifices in its post-9/11 wars.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance attend a meeting at the White House on October 7, 2025. Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

Vance’s path looks increasingly difficult

But if Rubio’s path looks daunting, Vance’s looks worse.

His post-election critique of the Iran war might have appealed to members of the anti-war MAGA base who feel let down by Trump’s repudiation of his vow to fight no more foreign wars. But his social media post was maladroit, underscoring his own relative inexperience as a political campaigner: His Ohio Senate race in 2022 represented the only race he’s so far run in his own right.

And Vance’s decision to embrace a Republican attack ad highlighting alleged child abuse suffered by Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton, which was widely regarded as the vilest such spot in recent memory, also raised questions about his political acumen.

A presidential campaign is a relentless and exhausting two-year examination in which a candidate is always on and can’t afford mistakes. Vance made two big ones within the space of a few weeks, damaging his political stock.

Still, the post of vice president does have advantages for an aspiring candidate. Air Force Two, official motorcades and a White House-level Secret Service detail convey the aura of the presidency and help voters see the veep in the top job.

But history is daunting. Being a heartbeat away from the presidency and winning the job has proven all but impossible. When George H.W. Bush won the presidential election in 1988, he was the first sitting vice president to do so in 150 years.

And Republicans like Rubio and Vance must ask themselves a key question: Where is their coalition? It’s not just a race to be Trump’s heir.

“Trump’s base of support is uniquely un-inheritable,” Rick Tyler, the former spokesperson for Sen. Ted Cruz’s presidential campaign, said on CNN News Central Thursday. “So this idea … ‘Who is he going to give his base to?’ That’s not going to happen because Trump’s base is like fangirls. I mean, they’re just there for him. They’re for nobody else.”

Rubio, with the experience of running his own campaign in 2016 and with the respect of various factions of the GOP, may have more unifying potential than Vance. There’s a chance that in a general election his profile might attract swing voters, especially if Democrats nominate a progressive candidate.

Rubio’s dilemma in separating himself from Trump would pale in comparison to Vance’s similar problem. As vice president, Vance would need Trump’s blessing, but would also be forced to run away from the president to create his own political lane. That would be tough at any time. With the quick-to-take-offense Trump in office, it might be impossible.

“The vice presidency is an unusual position,” Al Gore, who understands Vance’s position given his own unsuccessful 2000 bid to succeed President Bill Clinton, told CNN’s Dana Bash on Thursday. “And whatever power or influence a vice president has is almost entirely dependent on that which is granted by the president. The vice president has to work closely with the president. If that relationship is not good, then that’s going to be a difficult situation for JD Vance.”

This could open a lane for rivals outside the administration.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks at the National Building Museum in Washington, DC, on June 3, 2025. Nathan Howard/Reuters/File

Rubio and Vance wouldn’t have the field to themselves

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, for example, has a demonstrable conservative record. His two terms were Trump-flavored. But he’d have the advantage of distance, having never served in the Cabinet.

If Republicans crave a unifier, then Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, Utah Gov. Spencer Cox or former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin might work. And Sarah Huckabee Sanders could claim to be a Trump loyalist, as his first-term press secretary, but she’s sat out the mayhem of his second term while serving as Arkansas governor.

But DeSantis would need to up his game after some awkward moments in his first presidential run in 2024. And the others are untested on the national stage.

The 2028 nomination might look like a poisoned chalice now. But voters are in a volatile mood, and they’re yet to trust Democrats despite the massive anti-Trump vote in the midterms. And politics is so unpredictable that the nomination of a major party is always worth having.

In presidential politics, timing is everything. If Rubio thinks his moment is at hand, he’d have to resign his posts fairly soon, since trying to run the world and a presidential bid are incompatible.

Just maybe there’s an opening for a political athlete like Rubio, who has one foot on Trump’s half of the field and another in traditional GOP territory, with the nous to reinvent his party and engineer a positive pivot away from Trump’s dystopia.

In Athens last month, Rubio seemed to test such a straddle, reviving the soaring, aspirational rhetoric that had him pegged as a potential president before Trump crashed the party. He backed the unapologetic use of American power but urged the reinvigoration of US alliances. He positioned the US as the steward of Western civilization dating back to Ancient Greece while lauding “individuality and relentless ambition, daring exploration and invention.”

Was that a signal? Maybe, since everyone’s suddenly talking about Rubio — including his boss.

“How hot is Marco, right? Is Marco doing a great job? He’s been fantastic,” Trump said while addressing Southeast Asian leaders in Manila this week.

Trump’s dire approval ratings mean his praise could be a blessing or a curse.

But at least he didn’t praise Rubio’s “ass.”

This headline has been updated.

World.title: Egypt signs agreement to bring 100 idle oil wells back into production
World.content:
Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawy on Friday witnessed the signing of a framework agreement between the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation (EGPC) and the global company Weatherford.

The agreement aims to implement a program to bring approximately 100 idle oil wells back into production over the next 18 months—across both onshore and offshore production areas nationwide—thereby supporting efforts to increase domestic output.

The program utilizes AI systems to analyze data from the idle wells, assessing the potential for resuming production and identifying the most suitable technology for each specific well.

These technologies enable well intervention operations to be carried out without the need for drilling rigs – which saves time and costs – enhances operational efficiency, and accelerates the return of these wells to production in a cost-effective manner.

Following the deal, Badawy said that the deployment of AI technologies opens new horizons for increasing production from available resources—a key objective within the ministry’s five-year plan to boost oil and gas output through the end of the 2029/2030 fiscal year.

This effort complements ongoing exploration, prospecting, and field development activities.

The minister noted that there are opportunities to resume production from wells that are currently idle due to technical challenges or aging infrastructure.

Through rigorous technical assessment and the application of appropriate technologies, these wells can be brought back into production.

The ministry is thereby accelerating collaboration with specialized international companies to facilitate the transfer of expertise and implement cutting-edge technological solutions tailored to Egypt’s oil and gas fields.

World.title: Almost all of Anthropic’s employees are now millionaires
World.content:
New York —

Anthropic’s stock market debut turned the vast majority of the young startup’s staff into overnight millionaires — some many times over.

The company’s headcount stood at 5,300 as of September this year, according to regulatory filings. After Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, about 600 employees entered the rarefied “centi-millionaire” club, with equity holdings valued north of $100 million, according to data from Hill.com, which tracks private-company shares.

As many as 2,800 staffers, known internally as “Ants,” have holdings valued above $10 million. And about 5,100 — 96% of the staff — are sitting on equity north of $1 million.

“What’s most surprising here is how quickly this this happened,” Andrew Benson, Hill’s founder and CEO, told CNN on Thursday, noting Anthropic has seen very little attrition. “It’s been pretty clear for some time that Anthropic is a rocket ship, and so it definitely discouraged people from leaving because they knew what the opportunity cost of that would be.”

It’s not unusual for Silicon Valley startups, which are typically light on cash, to pay their staff with a combination of salary and stock. The promise of a future acquisition or initial public offering tends to keep workers motivated to work hard and stick it out until payday.

But few startups have grown as big or as quickly as Anthropic. The company, founded in 2021, had fewer than 1,000 employees at the end of 2024.

As with most tech startups, Benson noted, “being early is more important, in terms of a financial outcome, than being senior … You could be very low on the totem pole, and if you joined in 2023 or 2024, you’re likely to have a significantly better outcome than a senior person who joined earlier this year.”

SpaceX, by contrast, spent more than two decades as a private company before its blockbuster IPO in June. That debut minted around 4,400 millionaires, out of a staff of 22,000.

Anthropic’s IPO is also unique for allowing non-founder insiders to cash out on Day One of trading. In most IPOs, staff are subject to a “lockup” period — typically three to six months — during which they can’t sell their shares. But Anthropic’s listing included a complex, staggered lockup schedule that allowed non-founder insiders to cash out up to 10% of their shares as soon as the stock began trading. (It’s not known how many insiders may have taken advantage of the opportunity Thursday.)

And unlike SpaceX, which has employees spread across Texas, California and Florida, Anthropic is uniquely concentrated in San Francisco, a city whose entire economy has been reshaped by sudden surges of tech wealth.

A rash of newly minted millionaires could soon amplify pressure on San Francisco’s housing market, where home prices are already rising at their fastest pace in years.

The typical home there sold for $1.7 million in October, up nearly 19% from a year earlier, according to Redfin. By contrast, the national median home price was roughly flat over the same period, at $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors.

World.title: Nayib Bukele promised Haiti a ‘triumph.’ Are his forces delivering?
World.content:
Gun-toting robots trotting down a dark alley. The blaze of a helicopter-launched rocket. A gang boss’s mansion crumbling in the sunshine.

Thousands of Salvadoran troops landed in Haiti last month to combat gangs overrunning the Caribbean nation. While it’s too early to tell if they’re succeeding, the personal involvement of popular Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele has stirred rare hope on the island – and avid interest across Latin America.

What’s the difference between the newly arrived Salvadorans and all the other fighting forces in Haiti’s crowded security landscape? “They’re really good at making videos,” one local security source said.

Most of what we know about the Salvadoran force has come in glimpses from Bukele’s social media accounts. The deal governing their presence has not been made public, but the 45-year-old president is effectively drumming up support with promises in Creole to root out the gangs as he has done in El Salvador, combined with explosive footage and online banter.

“For the first time, I felt like someone had listened to me,” said Sophia Fecu, describing the moment she saw a video posted by Bukele that showed helicopters attacking gang leader Lanmo Sanjou’s house on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince. “I felt like my voice had finally been heard.”

Days earlier, Fecu, a Haitian entrepreneur and writer, had posted a picture of the notorious gang clubhouse on X and tagged Bukele. “I just felt that it wasn’t right for these criminals to be living so comfortably while the rest of the population was forced to flee their homes and communities,” she said from the US, where she now lives. “I honestly didn’t expect him to respond.”

But he did. Bukele answered on X asking for the location of the house, sparking a flurry of responses. Three days later, he posted an update: Video of helicopters blasting apart the building’s blue-tiled facade, shadowy figures of suspected gang members fleeing the compound on foot.

It’s hard to imagine other forces in Haiti crowdsourcing coordinates for a well-known gang headquarters. But Haitian police, a secretive task force involving a private military contractor led by Erik Prince, and the multinational Gang Suppression Force have been busy, too: Police announced on Thursday that they had killed 34 gang members in a major operation in the Port-au-Prince neighborhood of Martissant. The GSF, still building its force, said its operations are entering a “new phase” of pressure and is also posting more videos of soldiers at work. But no one boasts the same reach as Bukele.

Some friction was inevitable. Security sources in Haiti complain about a lack of cooperation and credit-sharing with the Salvadorans and point out that fighting videos don’t show the difficult reality of working in Haiti, like finding parts to repair helicopters damaged by gang fire.

Last week, Salvadoran troops reportedly fired perilously close to GSF troops. On another occasion, they sparked tensions after trying to enter a GSF outpost without notice, sources said. On Friday, two soldiers died and two others were wounded in an incident handling explosive material, according to the Salvadoran army.

Still, there is hope for a deeper eventual collaboration once the new force finds its footing. And Bukele will need it. He has raised expectations in an exhausted nation, and now he must deliver. His troops are far from home and facing a gang alliance that knows the terrain better, can replace fallen soldiers with forced conscripts, and shares information and resources across Port-au-Prince.

“Imagine if the police, task force, GSF and Salvadorans were all working together, with their combined ground and air forces — that would be amazing,” a security source said wistfully.

World.title: Venezuela a ‘compliant security partner,’ Hegseth says as he announces military deal with Caracas
World.content:
The United States has signed a new agreement to reestablish military ties with Venezuela more than 10 months after toppling its leader in a military raid, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced during his first trip to the South American nation on Wednesday.

“Venezuela has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner,” Hegseth said outside the US Embassy in Caracas.

The Pentagon chief described the deal as “historic,” saying it would allow American and Venezuelan forces to train together and share intelligence, defense equipment and other capabilities.

He insisted that the partnership would not be “cosmetic” and would require defense and security reforms in Venezuela to modernize its military and eliminate “persistent threats” to both nations.

Venezuela interim President Delcy Rodriguez and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth meet at Miraflores Palace in Caracas, Venezuela, on November 18. Miraflores Palace/Handout/Reuters

The timeline and scope of the deal remain unclear.

The Defense Department has not responded to questions about the agreement or Hegseth’s trip, nor did it provide a daily schedule for the secretary on the day of his visit.

Hegseth appeared to have signed the agreement earlier at the Venezuelan presidential palace with Defense Minister Gustavo Gonzalez Lopez, according to footage broadcast on state TV.

In a televised meeting with Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodriguez, Hegseth said the US looks forward to deepening their defense cooperation “to ensure the Venezuelan people are not threatened by foreign actors or narco-terrorists or criminals and that they are safe and secure inside sovereign borders.”

Rodriguez said their renewed “technical-military cooperation” is meant to confront common threats and make the region safer.

Both Hegseth and Rodriguez underscored their countries’ remarkable turn in relations since the US captured Venezuela’s authoritarian leader Nicolas Maduro on January 3.

“The weight of this moment does not escape me,” Hegseth said outside the embassy. “Just one year ago, my presence here, our presence here would have been deemed impossible.”

Rodriguez said, “We have turned very difficult and very harsh moments for our people … into an extraordinary space for cooperation and the mutual benefit of our countries.”

Since Maduro’s capture, the US has been working with the acting Venezuelan government on the country’s democratic transition and political reconciliation.

Rodriguez has met just about every demand from Washington, including releasing hundreds of political prisoners and making it easier for US companies to invest in the country.

Wednesday’s military deal is the latest effort by the Trump administration to bolster security cooperation with Latin American countries with the aim of combating what it calls “designated terrorist organizations” in the region.

Hegseth traveled to Colombia later on Wednesday and was expected to discuss security ties and deliver military equipment, according to the Colombian defense minister.

That visit comes amid a New York Times report that said Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella this week rejected a US plan for joint anti-crime operations on Colombian soil. The president later denied that claim.

A source from Colombia’s Ministry of Defense told CNN that while the government supports increased military cooperation and the intelligence sharing to combat drug cartels and terrorist organizations, it cannot greenlight operations involving foreign forces on the ground, as this requires legislative authorization.

Hegseth is also expected to travel to Ecuador and Honduras as part of a tour of Latin America.

World.title: As COP31 Debates Ocean Protection, Liberia Offers 15 Offshore Blocks
World.content:
An offshore oil platform at sea. Photo: Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority

Summary

Liberia is offering 15 offshore petroleum blocks to investors while pledging to expand marine conservation and protect coastal livelihoods.

Fishing communities face existing pressures from coastal erosion, declining catches and industrial fishing, while residents of West Point say they have not been directly consulted about the offshore oil and gas plans.

With plans for two marine protected areas and four co-managed fisheries areas, questions remain about their locations, potential overlap with petroleum blocks, environmental safeguards and how the government will protect coastal communities.

By Aria Deemie

As world leaders negotiate stronger commitments to protect the oceans at COP31 in Türkiye, Liberia is offering 15 offshore petroleum blocks to investors while pledging to expand marine conservation and protect coastal livelihoods.



The Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority launched its 2026 Offshore Direct Negotiation Licensing Round in October, offering 12 blocks in the Liberia Basin and three in the Harper Basin. Interested companies have until April 15, 2027, to submit letters of intent. The round is intended to attract exploration investment, with the government promoting the country’s offshore petroleum potential to international investors. The LPRA licensing invitation provides details of the blocks and application process.

“The oceans are central to their chances of survival,” Australia’s Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said at a COP31 presser, referring to countries and communities whose existence is threatened by rising ocean temperatures and other climate impacts. “We’ve said this would be the implementation COP, the COP of implementation and acceleration.”

For Liberia, the negotiations carry implications beyond climate diplomacy. Its offshore licensing plans are unfolding alongside commitments in its 2035 Nationally Determined Contribution, or NDC 3.0, to establish two marine protected areas and four co-managed fisheries areas by 2035. The country also depends on marine ecosystems for food, employment and income, particularly in coastal communities where fishing and fish processing support household livelihoods.

The potential environmental risks of offshore exploration concern Bruna Campos, an oil and gas campaigner at the Center for International Environmental Law. She said activities associated with oil exploration and production can affect marine life through several pathways, including seismic surveys, drilling waste and accidental spills.

Seismic surveys use powerful sound waves to map geological structures beneath the seabed. Campos said the noise can disturb marine mammals such as whales and dolphins, while other impacts can affect smaller organisms that form the foundation of marine food chains.

One of those groups is zooplankton, tiny drifting animals and larvae that provide food for fish and other marine species. Campos said disruption to these organisms could affect the wider food web.

“So if you’re having a reduction in zooplankton, you’re basically having a reduction on all the fish,” she said.



Drilling can also introduce muds and chemicals into the marine environment, while a blowout or other major accident could release oil into surrounding waters. Campos referred to the Deepwater Horizon disaster in the Gulf of Mexico as an example of the risks associated with offshore exploration. The drilling rig exploded while BP was completing an exploratory well, killing 11 workers. Oil continued leaking from the well for 87 days, releasing millions of barrels into the sea.

Liberia has a history of offshore exploration, but the International Tanker Owners Pollution Federation reported in its Liberia country profile that there did not appear to have been any major oil spills in Liberian waters. The profile is dated October 2008, however, and does not provide a record of incidents covering the years since then.

Campos said marine ecosystems cannot be treated as isolated spaces when assessing risks.

“We don’t think that there is a possibility of safeguarding by not doing it in a specific area or not doing it, because basically, the impact will be felt everywhere,” she said. “In the marine environment there are no borders.”

Liberia’s NDC 3.0 also commits the country to identifying endangered and vulnerable fish species and mapping areas important to their protection by 2028. It calls for increased research into climate-related pressures on fisheries and stronger management systems for fishing communities.

However, publicly available information does not establish where the two planned marine protected areas will be located or whether their proposed boundaries overlap with any of the 15 offshore blocks.

The government has not publicly provided a map showing how the licensing areas relate to planned conservation zones and important fishing grounds.

A 2022 assessment by the International Union for Conservation of Nature identified Margibi Mangrove, Cestos-Senkwehn and Grand Kru-River Gee as potential marine protected areas in Liberia, although the government has not said which two locations it plans to designate.

For people whose livelihoods depend on the sea, the stakes are immediate. In West Point, one of Monrovia’s largest coastal communities, fishing and fish processing remain important sources of income, while erosion continues to threaten homes, landing areas and other infrastructure.

Seaweed and other debris along the shoreline in West Point, Monrovia. Residents say coastal conditions and declining fish catches are adding to the challenges facing fishing communities.

A 2025 environmental and social impact assessment for the Green Climate Fund-supported Monrovia Metropolitan Climate Resilience Project identifies possible restrictions on fishermen’s access to landing sites and beaches, as well as disruption to women engaged in fish processing and trade, as risks that could arise during construction of the coastal defense structure. The assessment says the project design includes protected areas for fishing boats to launch and land.

Thomas Tweh, a West Point community leader, estimated that 92 percent of the community depends on fishing, with the remaining 8 percent relying on other activities such as petty trade and support from friends and relatives.

Fishermen in West Point, Monrovia. Fishing remains an important source of food and income for residents of the coastal community.



“Today the fishing community is experiencing a bigger challenge because of less quantity of catch due to climate change and other ocean related forces,” Tweh said. He said lower catches reduce income and worsen food insecurity among fishing households.

On the proposed offshore petroleum activities, Tweh said residents had not been adequately informed or consulted. He described the plans as new to the community and said there had been “no direct benefits, no community engagement at the moment.”

He wants the government to consider assistance for coastal communities if offshore operations affect fishing activities and income. He said a special financial support package should be designed for communities whose livelihoods depend on the coast.

The pressures facing fishing communities extend beyond Monrovia. Liberia’s national disaster risk reduction strategy identifies coastal erosion hotspots in several counties, including Grand Cape Mount, Grand Bassa, Margibi, Grand Kru, Rivercess, Sinoe and Maryland. Vulnerable communities listed in Maryland include Harper, Fish Town, Rock Town and Middle Tow.

A 2025 study published in npj Ocean Sustainability examined pressures on small-scale fishing communities along Liberia’s coastline. Based on 337 interviews with fishers, fishmongers and cold-storage employees across all coastal counties, alongside fisheries data from 2004 to 2019, it documented competition between small-scale fishers and distant-water industrial trawling fleets.

Of the fishmongers interviewed, 95 percent reported declining fish availability in their communities, while 96 percent said market prices had increased. Although the study focused on industrial fishing rather than offshore oil and gas, its findings highlight the pressures already facing coastal livelihoods and the need to manage competing demands on Liberia’s marine resources.

A separate report by the Environmental Justice Foundation, published in September 2025, mapped 73 fish landing sites and public fish-smoking facilities across Grand Cape Mount, Margibi, Grand Bassa and Grand Kru counties. It identified coastal erosion, mangrove destruction and insecure land rights as threats to fishing communities. The report said erosion was already destroying landing sites in Robertsport, Buchanan and Marshall, increasing costs for fishers and threatening important infrastructure.

In Maryland County, three communities in Harper District, Fish Town, Worteken and Kablakeh, signed a conservation agreement in June 2025 to protect mangroves and promote sustainable fishing, with support from Conservation International-Liberia.

Experiences elsewhere in Africa offer cautionary examples. In Ghana, an October 2026 investigation by The Fourth Estate reported that the country’s first marine protected area overlaps with existing offshore oil blocks. Petroleum and fisheries regulators discussed the overlap after the protected area was declared, while its management plan and zoning remained unfinished.

In Senegal, Greenpeace Africa reported in September 2026 that coastal communities were organizing against the effects of expanding oil, gas and mining projects on fishing grounds and local livelihoods. In Saint-Louis, residents raised concerns about access to fishing grounds and offshore incidents linked to the Grand Tortue Ahmeyim gas project. Communities in Djiffer also raised concerns about the proximity of the Sangomar oil field and the effects of offshore operations.

In Nigeria’s Ogoniland, a United Nations Environment Programme assessment documented extensive pollution after decades of oil operations, including damage to mangroves and fish habitats.

Liberia’s own coastal protection efforts are also under discussion at COP31. Speaking during a side event at Liberia’s pavilion, Public Works Minister Roland L. Giddings called for greater use of locally available rocks and boulders to protect vulnerable sections of the coastline. He questioned why Liberia would allow foreign companies to extract rocks locally and then sell them back to the country for coastal protection.

“We have rocks in Liberia!” Giddings said. “Our coastline will be eroding and we’re just sitting and the rocks are there and foreigners come here, mine them and then sell them to us?”

He pointed to Cape Coast in Ghana as an example of a place where boulders have been used for coastal protection. His comments focused on local solutions to erosion; he did not announce a funded or approved plan for the proposed works.

Liberia has also received international support for marine conservation through the Blue Ocean Program, funded by Sweden and implemented by Conservation International-Liberia. The program began in December 2019 and is scheduled to end on December 31, 2026.

According to the Liberia Development Dashboard, program results reported for 2023 and 2024 include microloans that supported 506 women to expand their businesses and livelihoods, as well as a revolving fund maintained by the Grandcess Fishing Cooperative that supported 45 women. The program also supported training for 30 professionals in mangrove restoration at the University of Liberia.

Its other work has included support for marine and coastal governance, community stewardship and the development of a national blue economy framework. Its scheduled end makes the question of how these gains will be sustained important as Liberia pursues new investment in its marine environment.

At COP31, African negotiators have continued to emphasize the need for climate finance, technology transfer and capacity building to help countries implement their climate commitments. Civil society representatives have also called for stronger action to move away from fossil fuels and protect vulnerable communities.

As COP31 negotiations entered their final stages on November 19, Mohamed Adow, founder and director of Power Shift Africa, a Nairobi-based climate and energy think tank, criticized revisions to the proposed final agreement that removed references to fossil fuels and weakened commitments on adaptation finance. Speaking to journalists in Antalya, he warned that the summit risked becoming a “ghost COP” if the revised text remained unchanged. “This new text has gone backwards from the one released earlier in the week. If this version of the text remains, it will be a ghost COP. The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here,” he said, according to Power Shift Africa’s COP31 daily coverage.

The Environmental Protection Agency’s Executive Director, Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo, was contacted through WhatsApp about the offshore licensing round, environmental safeguards and the relationship between petroleum development and Liberia’s marine conservation commitments. He said he was occupied with COP31 activities and would revert, but had not provided substantive answers by the time of publication.

The Director General of the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority, J. Cyrus Saygbe Sr., was also contacted for comment on fisheries protection and the potential implications for fishing communities but had not responded by publication.

The communications team of the Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority was contacted by email with a request for comment from its Director General, Marilyn T. Logan, on the licensing round, environmental assessments, safeguards and the relationship between the offshore blocks and planned marine conservation areas. No response had been received by publication.

As COP31 negotiations continue, Liberia faces the task of turning its ocean and climate commitments into protections that can be measured and enforced. That means identifying conservation areas, assessing environmental risks, making information about offshore activities accessible and ensuring that coastal communities are consulted before decisions affecting their livelihoods are made.

For communities whose food and income depend on the sea, the outcome will be measured not only by the investment attracted offshore, but also by whether the waters and fisheries they depend on remain protected.

This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership, a journalism fellowship organized by Internews’ Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

World.title: Liberia Speaker Koon Caught in Nigeria Hotel Dispute as ‘Wife’, Partner Allegedly Clash
World.content:
Viral Audio Captures Heated Exchange Involving Speaker, Cecelia Kpor Koon and Macdella Cooper; Office Yet to Comment

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Monrovia – Reports from Nigeria indicate that Macdella Cooper, a presidential political adviser to President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, was allegedly slapped by Madam Cecelia Kpor Koon during a confrontation at a hotel in Nigeria.



Cooper is publicly identified as the partner of House Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon. However, the relationship has been at the center of a growing dispute involving Cecelia Kpor Koon, who maintains that she is married to the Speaker.

Speaker Koon has repeatedly rejected her claim, insisting that Cecelia Kpor Koon is his biological sister and that they are related by blood, not marriage. Members of his family have also maintained that the two are siblings.

A viral audio recording circulating on social media appears to capture a heated exchange involving Speaker Koon, Cooper and Cecelia Kpor Koon. In the recording, the Speaker can be heard attempting to calm the two women during the argument.

At one point, he is heard addressing Cecelia, saying: “Stop, Cecelia. Is that why you came to the hotel?”



He is also heard telling Cooper that Cecelia Kpor Koon is his sister. Cooper, apparently responding to the explanation, is heard saying: “Is that why she hit me? Leave me. Don’t hold me.”

While the recording captures what appears to be a tense confrontation, FrontPage Africa has not independently verified its authenticity or established the circumstances that led to the alleged physical assault.

The Office of the Speaker has yet to issue an official statement addressing the reported incident in Nigeria or the circulating audio.

FrontPage Africa contacted Vehzelee Sumo, spokesperson for Speaker Koon, for clarification. However, calls to his phone went unanswered, and he had not responded to text messages and WhatsApp inquiries at the time of publication.

Meanwhile, sources familiar with the dispute suggest that the confrontation may be connected to longstanding tensions surrounding the relationship between Speaker Koon and Cecelia Kpor Koon. The sources claim that Cecelia has been asking the Speaker to sign divorce papers, a request he has allegedly refused.

However, the circumstances surrounding the alleged marriage and divorce remain disputed.

While Speaker Koon maintains that Cecelia is his biological sister, she insists that they were legally married in the United States. Neither claim has been independently established in connection with the reported incident.

The dispute became more publicly pronounced after Speaker Koon and Cooper announced their relationship on social media, drawing renewed attention to the competing claims surrounding the Speaker’s personal relationships.

For now, questions remain about what triggered the reported confrontation in Nigeria, whether a physical assault occurred as alleged, and the circumstances surrounding the relationship dispute.

The Speaker’s Office has yet to publicly address the allegations.

World.title: CDC Sets December 11–13 Extraordinary Congress, Names Koijee Convention Chairman
World.content:
The opposition Congress for Democratic Change has scheduled an extraordinary congress for December 11–13 in Smell No Taste, Margibi County, to address leadership vacancies, internal democracy, and the party’s strategic direction, following its 2026 Martyrs’ Day celebrations in Grand Cape Mount County./Jefferson Koijee, Secretary General, CDC.

MONROVIA — The opposition Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) has announced plans to hold an Extraordinary Congress from December 11 to 13, 2026, in Smell No Taste, Margibi County, as the party moves to address leadership vacancies and chart its political direction ahead of future electoral contests.

The announcement, issued by the party’s National Executive Committee, also names several committees and officers who will oversee preparations, elections, constitutional review, and communication for the gathering.

Former Monrovia Mayor Jefferson Tamba Koijee has been named Chairman of the Convention Committee, with Dr. Elizabeth Gaye Kamara serving as Co-Chairman and Samuel Jacobs as Secretary.



According to the official announcement, the three-day gathering will provide a platform for delegates to examine critical internal party issues, including leadership vacancies, internal democracy, electoral preparedness, membership and representation.

Delegates are also expected to consider proposals relating to the party’s policies, manifesto, and constitution.

The announcement comes less than two weeks after the CDC concluded its 2026 Martyrs’ Day celebrations in Kinjor, Grand Cape Mount County, held from November 4 to 7.

The event brought together senior party officials, former government officials, lawmakers, and partisans to commemorate CDC members and other Liberians who lost their lives during political struggles and confrontations with state security forces.



The upcoming extraordinary congress is expected to provide an important opportunity for the opposition party to review its internal structures and determine its strategic priorities.

Committees Constituted

In addition to the Convention Committee, the National Executive Committee has constituted an Elections Committee headed by Ronald Kerkula Menscole, with C. Mike Doryon as Co-Chairman and Gaiyeizohn Aba Davis as Secretary.

Other members of the Elections Committee include Sriya Musu Momolu, David B. Saylae Sr., Gertrude Williams, Raymond Kosigba Roberts, Ben Believe Togbah, and Joshua Karr.

The party has also established an Extraordinary Congress Communication Team comprising Abu Sheriff, Eric Perviist, Michael Tarr, Shanti Kromah, and Lisa Kollie.

Meanwhile, Thompson Jabber has been appointed Chairperson of the Constitutional Review Committee, with Alexander V. Saydee Sr. serving as Co-Chairman and Cllr. K. Jarlateh Sayon as Secretary.

Other members are Cllr. James N. Kummeh, Eddie Tarawali, Atty. Jefferson Chesson, Mamesie Kabba, Atty. Garmondeh Clinton, Cllr. Henry Wokolo, Cllr. Yancy K. Horton Sr., and Cllr. Garrison Yealue.

Prof. Wilson Tarpeh and Cllr. Ndubuisi Nwabudike will serve as Senior Advisors to the committee.

Further Arrangements Pending

The National Executive Committee said additional announcements concerning the confirmed venue, possible additional committees, and other arrangements for the extraordinary congress would be made through the Convention Committee.

The announcement was issued under the authority of the CDC National Executive Committee and signed by Koijee in his capacity as Convention Chairman.

The December gathering comes at a significant moment for the opposition party, which is expected to use the extraordinary congress to address organizational questions, review its governing framework, and establish priorities for its next phase of political engagement.

World.title: How a $54 Million Deal Nearly Handed Liberia’s Identity Registry to an Austrian Firm Without a Bid
World.content:
MONROVIA – Rick Scott got to the registration center in Red Light before dawn. He had left his job, paid the $5 fee and joined a line hundreds of people long. By evening, he went home with no ID card. It was his fourth try that week.

By Rodney D. Sieh

“I leave my job in the morning and come to find an identification card because it’s a government mandate,” the 54-year-old businessman told New Narratives earlier this year. “Some of us are not feeling well, but we are forced to come here.”



For Liberians outside Monrovia, it is worse. In many counties there is a single enrollment center. A resident of Foya can pay for transport to enroll, go home, then pay again to come back for the card.

The card is not optional. Under an April 2025 executive order, Liberians need it to bank, buy a SIM card, see a doctor, enroll in school and deal

with immigration. Many have been turned away from those services before they could even get one.

This is the problem the government said OeSD would fix. When President Joseph Nyuma Boakai sent the Legislature a $54.7 million concession to rebuild Liberia’s national identity system, it came with his approval. It also came with an operator already picked. Nobody had bid for the job.



Now a House joint committee has recommended that the deal be thrown out entirely. In a report dated Nov. 18, 2026, the Joint Committee on Investment and Concessions and on Ways, Means, Finance and Budget said it found “over 40 distinct defects” in the agreement between the government and OeSD International GmbH. The Austrian firm’s Vienna-registered contracting entity, the report says, has share capital of just 35,000 euros.

The committee said several of the defects were “statutory violations that occurred prior to execution.” Ratification by the Legislature, it said, could not cure them. Several sources familiar with the deal told FrontPageAfrica the President was badly misled by aides who pushed it.

One source, closed to the process to FPA on condition of anonymity that the deal “was going to take the NIR to the cleaners.” Among the most glaring items: a $19.82 million data center the country does not need, because LIBTELCO already has one.

The committee’s case against the agreement comes down to three things: there was no bidding, Liberians’ biometric data was left unprotected and the registry’s own legal mandate was signed away.

A deal sealed before the rules were followed

Liberia already has a national biometric platform. In April 2017, after an open tender among 19 firms, the government paid Techno Brain $5.9 million to build and maintain it. The National Identification Registry (NIR), the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation (NASSCORP) and the National Elections Commission (NEC) still use it.

The OeSD deal would have scrapped that system. The committee report and earlier reporting, including leaked procurement documents first published by FrontPageAfrica in August 2025, show how it took shape:

* Dec. 18, 2024: The government signs a non-binding memorandum of understanding with OeSD International GmbH.

* Feb. 9–14, 2025: Liberian officials travel to Austria on a due-diligence trip paid for by OeSD, the company they were supposed to be vetting.

* May 2025: The Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC) refuses a request to sole-source the contract.

* May 30, 2025: The NIR signs an undisclosed contract with OeSD anyway.

* June 23, 2025: The government suspends the issuance of national biometric ID cards.

* July 5, 2025: A presidential memo to a new steering committee chaired by National Security Advisor Samuel Kofi Woods says OeSD has already been selected and orders that the process be “upheld.

* July 7, 2025: Two days later, the PPCC formally rejects restricted bidding and orders open international competitive bidding and a formal concession plan. The committee says that order “was never followed.”

* April 30, 2026: The concession agreement is signed.

* July 15, 2026: The President approves it and sends it to the Legislature.

* Oct. 15, 2026: The House refers it to the joint committee, which holds hearings on Oct. 28, Nov. 4 and Nov. 11.

The July 2025 memo treated as settled a choice the procurement regulator was about to reject. Woods told The Liberian Investigator at the time that he had not advised the President on the ID contract.

NIR Executive Director Andrew Peters has defended the deal. In September, he told FrontPageAfrica that OeSD would finance about $54.7 million under a build-operate-transfer arrangement to ease the burden on a cash-strapped government. He said Liberian identity data would remain “a national asset under the authority and control of the Republic of Liberia.”

The committee’s reading of the contract is very different.

‘Shall be void’: no bidding, no certificate

The committee’s first and heaviest finding is that the deal was never competed. In its words, the agreement is “legally void.” Under Regulation 57(4) of the PPCC’s amended 2026 regulations, any concession procured without a Certificate of Concession “shall be void.” The committee said the OeSD agreement cites none.

The Executive also went around the PPCC’s July 2025 order for open international bidding. Instead, the deal was handled as an unsolicited proposal. Lawmakers said that route was closed on two counts:

* Regulation 69(9) bars unsolicited proposals when the government makes substantial financial contributions or when the service is contestable.

* Regulation 69(18) requires competitive bidding whenever rival proposals arrive before PPCC approval.

There were rival proposals. MWETANA and Dynamic Global Technologies came forward in September 2025, Lake Piso Solutions on Sept. 29, 2025, and MRT on April 3, 2026. Each submitted an expression of interest, an objection to sole-sourcing or an alternative proposal before the contract was signed.

The committee also found that no summary of the deal’s main terms was published two weeks before signing. Required stakeholder forums in the 15 county seats were never held.

Liberian tech firms: ‘Bad for Liberia’

Liberia’s own technology sector told lawmakers the same thing. Members of the Liberia Information Technology Consortium (LITCON) testified before the joint committee that the concession duplicated systems Liberia already has and was bad for the country.

Top of their list was the data center. The contract charges $19.82 million for a “Renewable License” data center. Yet the state-owned Liberia Telecommunications Corporation (LIBTELCO) already runs a Tier III facility where the system could be co-located, and the government is already obliged to provide Tier IV capacity. In other words, Liberia would pay nearly $20 million for something it already owns.

The committee reached the same conclusion. It also found that the deal would abandon the Techno Brain platform the NIR, NASSCORP and the NEC still use.

Local firms have been sounding the alarm for more than a year. In August 2025, eight Liberian-owned ICT companies wrote to National Security Advisor Woods.

They warned that the NIR was preparing to sole-source a foreign firm and that citizens’ biometric data could end up under foreign control, according to a report of the letter. Among the signers were MWETANA and DGT, two of the firms the committee says were later passed over. The companies noted that Liberia’s biometric ID system, launched in 2012, was built by Liberian experts. They asked that identity-document contracts be at least 75 percent Liberian-owned.

This week, PSI Liberia and its sister company, M Tosh Prints Media, demonstrated biometric equipment at the Capitol and questioned why qualified local firms were never given “an opportunity to compete.” Their representative, Varney Fahnbulleh, showed about $2 million worth of equipment and services, including 150 biometric enrollment kits. By

comparison, the concessionaire committed to 146 kits in its second year. He also said PPCC Executive Director Bodger Scott Johnson had told lawmakers that the President’s Jan. 30, 2026 letter did not ask for single-sourcing.

Who holds the keys to Liberians’ identities?

Every Liberian who enrolls hands over fingerprints and a photograph of their face. Unlike a password, those can never be changed. If they leak, they stay leaked for life. The NIR has said repeatedly that Liberians’ data would stay under Liberian control. The committee found nothing in the contract to guarantee it.

The agreement does not require that primary or backup data be hosted inside Liberia. It does not require hardware security modules, the devices that protect encryption keys. And it does not require the government to hold the root encryption keys to its own citizens’ biometric records.

Lawmakers said the contract allowed data to be transferred before the deal took effect. That breaks the 1,000-record limit on off-site data in Section 23(b) of the Data Protection Act. It also breaks electoral data laws, because the agencies whose data was involved had not consented.

The committee flagged three other risks:

* Base64 is not encryption. Biometric templates would be sent using Base64 encoding. That is a format for moving data, not a lock. Anyone who intercepts it can read it.

* ID by referral. Annex 2, Section 7.1 lets people enroll themselves by phone, including signing up “friends, family and colleagues.” That produces a “partially verified” National Identification Number (NIN) good for opening bank accounts and registering SIM cards before any fingerprints are taken. The committee called it an open door to “systemic identity fraud.”

* Paying twice for storage. The $19.82 million data center, flagged by LITCON, duplicates capacity Liberia already has.

A chapter on data

Protection that appeared in a January 2026 draft was deleted before the agreement was signed, the committee said. So were chapters on anti-corruption and state auditing.

Signing away the registry’s job

The third ground goes to what the NIR exists to do. Article 7.1 of the agreement gives OeSD the exclusive right to assign NINs. It also makes OeSD the only provider of ID cards and identity checks. Under Sections 3.1, 3.2(d) and 7.3 of the NIR Act of 2011, those powers belong to the NIR alone. The committee cited the Supreme Court’s Feb. 12, 2026 ruling in LAC v. LRA that a concession cannot override a statute.

Other clauses reached further:

A toll on daily life

Articles 7.3 and 12.1 would make paid OeSD verification mandatory for nearly every public and private service, from banking and SIM cards to permits and court business. The committee said that goes beyond the NIR Act, and that Executive Order 147 cannot legally expand it.

* Skipping the Legislature. Article 5.3 lets the two parties waive conditions precedent by mutual agreement. One of those conditions is legislative ratification. Lawmakers called the clause “ultra vires and unacceptable.”

* Liberia in a London courtroom. Article 31 sends disputes to UNCITRAL arbitration in London and waives Liberia’s sovereign immunity from enforcement. That would expose Liberian state assets abroad.

* Other agencies’ work. Appendix 4 lists work and residence permits among the concession’s requirements. Those belong to the Ministry of Labour and the Liberia Immigration Service.

* Few jobs for Liberians. The deal sets no measurable targets for Liberians in senior management or in the workforce over its 10-year life. It does not require any role for Liberian-owned IT firms.

* ⁠On money, the committee said it rebuilt the financial model from OeSD’s own Annex 5 tables. It found a lopsided structure that pushes costs and risks onto the Republic while guaranteeing the operator’s returns.

The document itself was a mess. The agreement was signed April 30, 2026, but Annexes 2 and 4 are dated May 4 and Annex 1 is dated May 5. The whole fee schedule and revenue split sit in those annexes. That leaves “no legal certainty that the economic terms were agreed upon at signing,” the committee said.

The text sent to lawmakers also contained duplicated pages, missing clauses from Article 3 and Article 12.2, broken cross-references and an unsigned template memorandum for Ecobank. It even got the NIR director’s name wrong, calling Andrew Peters “Peter Andrews.”

Back to the drawing board

The report was signed by members of both committees. They are led by Rep. Foday E. Fahnbulleh, chairman of Investment and Concessions, and Rep. P. Mike Jurry, chairman of Ways, Means, Finance and Budget. It now goes to the full House, which the committee urged to “reject and decline ratification” of the agreement “in its entirety.”

The committee also wants the House to give the Executive three directives:

1. Enforce the law. Restore the NIR’s statutory role as a service bureau, overseen by its Board of Registrars and the General Auditing Commission.

2. Bid it out. Follow the PPCC’s July 2025 order and the 2026 regulations. That means a valid Certificate of Concession, a value-for-money assessment, and weighing upgrades to the existing biometric system against competing bids.

3. Protect the data. Make any future vendor comply with the Personal Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2026, the Cybercrime Act of 2025 and the mandates of the NEC, the Liberia Revenue Authority, the Liberia Immigration Service and the Ministry of Health.

FrontPageAfrica sent detailed questions to NIR Executive Director Andrew Peters about the committee’s findings. He had not responded by press time.

None of that helps Rick Scott, or the traveler from Foya. ID card issuance has been suspended since June 2025. New Narratives reported that the program also stalled over about $1.7 million the government owed Techno Brain. Fewer than 15 percent of the population holds an official ID card, according to Biometric Update.

The question lawmakers are now asking is not whether Liberia needs a modern ID system. It is who decided that one Austrian company, contracting through a 35,000-euro Vienna entity, should build it, and why nobody else was allowed to try.

World.title: Liberia: Attorney General Summoned Over IB Atlantic IV Release Order; Crew Still Held Past Deadline
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Justice Ministry’s failure to obey a court order to release the vessel IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members has turned into a direct confrontation with the judiciary.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Criminal Court “A” has summoned Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. Betty Lamin-Blamo to answer allegations of contempt.



Assigned Circuit Judge D. Onesimus Banwon issued a writ of summons ordering Lamin-Blamo to appear before the court at the Temple of Justice on Friday, Nov. 20, at 9 a.m. She must show cause why she should not be held in contempt for disobeying the court’s order to release the ship and its crew.

As of Thursday, when the writ was issued, the vessel and all seven crew members were still in state custody. The court’s deadline had passed at 4 p.m. Wednesday.

The summons puts the country’s chief legal officer before a judge to account for the government’s failure to obey a court order. It comes in a case that has dragged on for nearly three months without a full public explanation of what the vessel was doing or the legal grounds for holding it.

‘Show cause’



The writ, dated Nov. 19 and issued under the authority of the First Judicial Circuit, Montserrado County, is explicit. It orders the attorney general to explain why she should not be held in contempt for disobeying the release order.

Assistant Clerk of Court Gideon A. Eshun issued the summons to Montserrado County Sheriff H. C. Sulonich or his deputy for service. The court told the sheriff to report back to the clerk’s office on how the summons was served.

The writ is not a finding of contempt. But it is a serious step. It requires the government’s top lawyer to answer personally for her ministry’s failure to comply.

It also raises a larger question: Can the government keep people and property in custody after a court has ordered their release, without going back to the court for permission?

Deadline passes, crew stays put

Judge Banwon had ordered the release of the IB Atlantic IV and its crew after their lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition challenging their detention. The ministry was given until 4 p.m. Wednesday to comply.

It did not. At about 5 p.m. Wednesday, FrontPageAfrica observed that the order had not been carried out. Lawyers for the seven crew members confirmed their clients were still being held.

By Thursday, nothing had changed. That left the court to take the extra step of summoning the attorney general.

Reached late Wednesday and asked why the release had not happened, Solicitor General Cllr. Abrahim Sillah gave no explanation.

“I will refer you to find out from the court, my brother,” Sillah told FrontPageAfrica.

His answer left the central question unaddressed: On what legal basis is the government still holding the ship and its crew after the court’s deadline expired?

Ministry ‘struggling’ for an explanation

Sources at the Justice Ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter, told FrontPageAfrica earlier that the ministry was struggling to come up with an explanation for the continued detention.

Part of the difficulty, the sources said, was the government’s own earlier public statements that it was investigating the vessel’s movements and how it came to be intercepted. No findings from that investigation have been made public. That left officials hard-pressed to justify holding the ship and crew in the face of a court order.

The sources said the ministry was considering releasing the vessel and crew early Thursday to comply with the order. That did not happen.

Lamin-Blamo is now expected to explain in court why the order was not obeyed on time, and to present whatever legal justification the government has for keeping the ship and crew in custody.

The ship that slipped away

The IB Atlantic IV is a 41-year-old, Comoros-flagged general cargo ship. It first drew attention this summer when it lingered off York Island in Tewor District, Grand Cape Mount County, alarming residents and fishermen.

Before that, the ship had already tried to get into Liberia. On July 13, a Liberian businessman, Kuiah, wrote to the Liberia Maritime Authority (LiMA) on behalf of a company called Madris Group of Companies Inc. He asked for docking rights and a dive team at the Freeport of Monrovia, describing the vessel as disabled and “in distress.” FrontPageAfrica later reported that Kuiah, a former deputy at Roberts International Airport who was dismissed, was the company’s sole owner. LiMA turned the request down. The ship was still in Sierra Leonean waters at the time and had not docked anywhere, yet it was already seeking a Liberian berth.

Once the vessel drifted onto the Liberian side of the maritime border, the order came to search and seize it. It kept moving. On Aug. 4, then-Armed Forces of Liberia Chief of Staff Maj. Gen. Davidson Forleh confirmed that security forces were in pursuit. He told FrontPageAfrica that the Coast Guard’s boats were not equipped to chase a ship far out to sea. With Nigerian help, the military tracked it off Rivercess County but could not board it.

Investigators also looked into reports that a smaller vessel had approached the IB Atlantic IV and tried to throw something aboard. The government said a Liberian fishing vessel had gone out to meet the ship, and the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority opened an inquiry.

The ship was finally seized by Ivorian authorities on Aug. 9. On Aug. 14, Information Minister Jerolinmek M. Piah confirmed the arrest and said Liberia was working with Côte d’Ivoire to bring it back. It returned under Liberian Coast Guard command on Aug. 27.

The chase unfolded amid a widening national drug-trafficking scandal, and speculation about contraband aboard ran high. But authorities have never publicly established that any narcotics were found on the vessel.

Its return was supposed to give the government a chance to investigate and give the public a full account. Instead, the ship and crew stayed in custody for nearly three months with no findings released. That drove the vessel’s management and crew to court.

Friday’s test

For the seven crew members, the case has meant months of uncertainty, held aboard a ship whose presence in Liberian waters is still unexplained.

The government is now being asked to answer for more than the vessel. It must also explain why it kept the ship and its crew in custody after a judge ordered them freed.

That answer is due Friday at 9 a.m., when Lamin-Blamo is expected to appear before Criminal Court “A” at the Temple of Justice.

World.title: Who Tried to Sell Liberia’s Identity?
World.content:
The $54.7 million national ID deal ignored the procurement regulator, shut out every competitor and stripped away the safeguards protecting Liberians’ biometric data. Rejecting it is not enough. The President must find out who tried to slip it past him, and hold them to account

A NATION’S IDENTITY is not a commodity. It is the record that says who belongs, who can vote, who can open a bank account, who can cross a border and come home. The National Identification Registry was created to keep that record in Liberian hands, under Liberian law.

THAT IS WHY the House joint committee’s report on the $54.7 million concession with OeSD International should alarm every Liberian. The committee found more than 40 defects in the agreement. Several, it said, were violations of the law committed before the deal was even signed. No vote of the Legislature can cure them.



STRIP AWAY THE technical language and the story is simple. In May 2025, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission refused a request to hand the contract to OeSD without competition. Then, on May 30, the NIR signed a contract with OeSD anyway. In July 2025, the PPCC ordered open international bidding and a formal concession plan. That order, the committee says, “was never followed.”

RIVAL FIRMS, INCLUDING Liberian ones, came forward. They were ignored. No Certificate of Concession was obtained, though the regulations say a concession without one “shall be void.” No summary of terms was published. No county consultations were held. Liberian officials even made their due-diligence trip to Austria at OeSD’s expense, vetting a company that was paying their way.

WHAT EMERGED WAS a contract that would have handed a private company the exclusive power to assign every Liberian’s national ID number. It would have made paid verification mandatory for banking, SIM cards, permits and the courts. It would have sent disputes to London and waived the Republic’s immunity over its assets abroad. It would have charged nearly $20 million for a data center Liberia does not need, when LIBTELCO already has one. And it would have done all this without requiring that Liberians’ fingerprints and faces be stored in Liberia, or that the government hold the keys to them.

THE CONTRACT EVEN contained a clause letting the parties waive legislative ratification. Chapters on data protection, anti-corruption and state auditing that appeared in a January 2026 draft were gone by the time it was signed.



THIS WAS NOT carelessness. Mistakes do not repeat themselves at every step, each time in the same direction. A process that ignores the regulator twice, shuts out every competitor and quietly deletes the safeguards is a process designed to avoid scrutiny.

PRESIDENT JOSEPH NYUMA Boakai approved this agreement and sent it to the Legislature in July. Sources tell this newspaper he was badly misled by those who brought it to him. We are prepared to believe that. A President cannot read every annex. He must rely on the people around him to tell him the truth.

BUT IF THE President was misled, then someone misled him. And the people who did so are still in place.

THE HOUSE SHOULD adopt the committee’s report and reject the deal in full. That is only the first step. Killing a bad contract does nothing to fix the process that produced it, or to stop the same people from trying again under a new name.

WE THEREFORE CALL on the President to act on three fronts.

FIRST, ORDER AN independent review of how this concession was put together. It should establish who decided to bypass the PPCC, who signed the May 2025 contract, who approved the OeSD-funded trip to Austria and who removed the safeguards from the January draft. The General Auditing Commission and the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission are equipped to do this work, and the findings should be made public.
