World.title: Get the 47+ best Advent calendars of the year before they sell out
World.content:
Traditionally, Advent calendars count down the days until Christmas. Some classic options have chocolate, caramels or other sweet treats hidden behind little doors, while others require you to turn on a light or check off a box leading up to the holiday. In recent years, however, Advent calendars have taken on a new life. Now, there’s an option for any holiday you celebrate, and they’re filled with coffee, wine, Legos, beauty products, pet treats and more.

If you plan on counting down to the holidays this year with an Advent calendar, you don’t have much time left to buy one: You need a 24-day option by Dec. 1 or a 12-day option by Dec. 13 to stay on track. Popular calendars are already selling out, so don’t dilly-dally. This is officially your last chance to get one for yourself or a loved one.

Below, I rounded up the best Advent calendars of 2026. I’ll frequently update this article throughout the next few weeks to share ones that are still available.

Want more from NBC Selected? 

Best Advent calendars overall

I’m loyal to Bonne Maman jam, and every year, I look forward to its Advent calendar, which is filled with new limited-edition spreads. There’s a mini glass jar hidden inside each of the 24 boxes, and the festively decorated calendar opens like a book, which lets me stand it up on a shelf, doubling as holiday decor. This year, you’ll get to try spreads like caramel with salted butter, strawberry with Madagascar vanilla and raspberry with dark chocolate. Don’t worry if you can’t finish every jar before the end of the season — the spreads will last through June 2027, according to Bonne Maman.

You can’t go wrong with a chocolate Advent calendar whether you’re buying it for yourself or gifting it to a loved one. It’s a classic for a reason, and getting to unwrap a new piece of chocolate every day is a small joy that anyone can appreciate. Lindt’s Advent calendar comes with 24 pieces of chocolate, including those shaped like mini bears, chocolate balls and chocolate neapolitans. For the first time this year, Lindt is adding an interactive element to its Advent calendar: From December 1 to 24, you can scan the QR code on the box to unlock the augmented reality experience, with new video drops daily.

“The hot Advent calendar with the five-year-olds who can’t get the Needoh calendar is the Squishmallow calendar, so that’s what I’m buying for my daughter this year,” says NBC Selected commerce editor Bethany Heitman. “As a mom, I appreciate that the smaller-sized stuffies will be easy to contain and don’t add a ton more clutter to our playroom, and my daughter will love seeing which cute character she gets each day.”

This Advent calendar comes with 24 itty bitty Squishmallows stuffies that are 2.5 inches tall. Your recipient gets to collect characters like Junie the Banana, James the Fox, Cam the Cat and Benny the Bigfoot decked out in their holiday apparel.

BETA We can help you find

Papier’s Advent calendar is as beautiful as it is useful. There’s 24 days worth of desk accessories inside, all of which are items you likely use every day at the office, home or school, like pens, journals, sticky tabs, highlighters, to-do notepads and stationary sets. Each item is individually wrapped in a paper box, which really makes it feel like you’re opening a gift every day. The Advent calendar, which folds open on the top and has three drawers, is designed to be a reusable organizer. Papier is also selling a 12-Day Advent Calendar for the first time this year.

There are 12 Voluspa mini coconut wax candles inside this Advent calendar, each of which comes in a decorative glass votive. You’ll collect candles in a few of the brand’s bestselling scents, like white cypress, forbidden fig and santal vanille, as well as some holiday-specific fragrances like Gingerbread Chalet. The Advent calendar comes with a gold-plated wick trimmer, too.

Anyone who thinks gifting candles is overdone clearly doesn’t know about Baobab Collection. These candles are not just things to make your space smell good: They also offer one-of-a-kind decor that will always be a conversation piece when you host. This 24-day Advent calendar is the ultimate gift — and it’s priced that way.

“You could keep half of the items for yourself and gift the other half to twelve people you love, and everyone would be so happy,” says NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans. “I don’t even celebrate Christmas and I want this because I am absolutely in love with this brand’s offerings. Everything it makes looks exquisite and luxe, and yes, the candles smell divine.” You get candles — some that are calendar exclusives — along with hand creams, shower gels and home sprays.

There’s a handful of candle Advent calendars out there, but Yankee Candle fans will only have eyes for this one. It comes with 12 1.3-ounce candles made from a soy wax blend, and the fragrances are all bestsellers like Pink Sands, Vanilla Cupcake, Sparkling Cinnamon, Spiced Pumpkin and Christmas Cookie.

Best chocolate and candy Advent calendars

Even Swedish candy makers are getting in on the Advent calendar game. Socketbit’s has drawers packed with tasty gummies, letting you sample some of the brand’s most beloved options, all of which NBC Selected commerce editor Mili Godio says are addicting. “I had a Swedish candy phase a few years ago and never looked back — at this point, I’ve tried several dozens of sweet and sour candies from countless brands,” she says. “Sockerbit quickly became one of my favorites. Its mixed candy is perfectly curated, and I specifically love the sour candies because they’re actually sour, unlike some brands that don’t even scrape the sour surface.”

Compartés’ Nutcracker and Winter Forest Advent calendars are back this year, plus the brand added a brand new one: the Enchanted Castle Advent calendar. There’s 24 chocolates inside, and each one has a different filling, like buttered croissant, espresso toffee, pistachio marzipan, cinnamon sugar donut and salted honeycomb. The calendar starts shipping on November 2.

There’s plenty of candy-filled Advent calendars to choose from if you or your loved one don’t eat chocolate. Sugarfina’s is packed with the brand’s gummies, like sugared cranberries, sour rainbow bears, heavenly sours and magic mangos, plus there’s caramel and cereal balls. You get four pieces of candy per drawer for 24 days. Sugarfina is also selling a 12-day Advent calendar this year, as well as a Peanuts themed one.

With this Advent calendar, you’ll get to snack on some of Dylan’s Candy Bar’s bestselling sweets leading up to the holidays, like cotton candy-flavored balls, blueberry candy sticks and fruit gummy stars. There are also seasonal candies inside, including green apple marshmallow Christmas trees, milk chocolate Santa’s helpers, gingerbread man lollipops and fruity gummy snowflakes.

Opening the See’s Candy Advent calendar is the best way to try a variety of the brand’s chocolates and confections. There’s about a pound of sweets hidden inside the box’s drawers, including dark chocolate peppermint patties, chocolate lollypops, dark chocolate marshmallow trees and milk chocolate almond caramels. The box is also decorated with a storybook scene that has 3D illustrations and foil accents, so it’s worth displaying at home.

Swedish candy company BonBon’s Advent calendar is filled with 24 individually-wrapped, numbered mini bags of candy — you eat them in order leading up to the holiday. Some of customers’ favorite sweets are included, in addition to 13 never-before-released candies.

Snack on a Ferrero confection each day leading up to the holidays with this calendar — you can save them for dessert, but I believe that chocolate compliments any meal (or activity). There are three types of treats inside: a hazelnut milk chocolate Ferrero Rocher, a creamy coconut Raddaello and a rich dark chocolate Rondnoir.

Best beauty Advent calendars

L’Occitane’s Advent calendar is filled with 24 of the brand’s bestselling skin, body, hand and hair care products, many of which come highly recommended by NBC Selected commerce editor Cory Fernandez. “I love just about everything from L’Occitane, and it’s not only because everything smells amazing,” he says. “The products are also effective — they don’t have a greasy residue and don’t dry my skin or hair. Also, the Advent calendar is great because everything is the perfect sample size.”

This holiday season, you’ll get to unbox L’Occitane’s hand creams, shower oil, exfoliating shower gel, fragrance and more, some of which are scented with the brand’s signature almond fragrance.

This is the ideal Advent calendar for the person who never leaves home without lip balm and has one in every bag they own. There’s 12 Burt’s Bees lip balms inside in flavors like sugar cookie, cinnamon apple crisp, vanilla bean and peppermint bark, the latter of which is exclusive to Amazon. The lip balms are all made with beeswax and vitamin E to soften and hydrate skin for up to 24 hours, according to the brand.

The Glow Recipe Advent calendar is filled with 12 skin care finds, including the brand’s watermelon glow products, like the niacinamide drops, BHA toner and moisturizers. It also comes with multiple toner pads, a cleanser, a lip treatment and other products to help brighten and hydrate the skin, which is key heading into the winter months.

Some of Charlotte Tilbury’s most beloved makeup and skin care products are hidden inside this treasure chest-shaped Advent calendar’s drawers. You get 15 items in total, four of which are full-size, including the Matte Revolution Lipstick and Hollywood Beauty Light Wand Highlighter in Pillow Talk, the Unreal Blush Healthy Glow Stick and a Lip Cheat Contour Duo. For the first time this year, the brand added two accessories to the calendar: a gua sha tool and a velvet makeup bag.

Expand your lineup of Laneige skin care beyond the Lip Sleeping Mask with the K-beauty brand’s Advent calendar, which is filled with 12 products in full and mini sizes. You get the lip mask, of course, as well as face masks to put on before bed, moisturizer, cleanser, serums and lip balms. Laneige says the products are formulated with ingredients like peptides, hyaluronic acid and ceramides to help hydrate, plump and nourish skin.

Ulta only put the absolute best of its offerings inside this 25 Days of Beauty Advent calendar, which comes with 31 products total. You’ll get nine full-size products, including a set of Glamnetic Press-On Nails, The Ordinary’s Multi-Active Delivery Essence and NYX Professional Makeup Butter Gloss. The rest of the skin care, hair care, nail care, makeup and fragrances are mini- and travel-size from brands like Amika, Morphe, Tarte, Osea and Peach & Lily.

You may pay $250 for Dermstore’s Advent calendar, but there’s $1,147 worth of skin care, hair care and makeup inside. You’ll get to try mini versions of products from brands like Korres, PCA Skin, Oribe and Dr. Dennis Gross, as well as numerous full-size items from Morccanoil, Paula’s Choice, Tarte and Elemis.

I’ve used Kiehl’s Ultra Facial Cream for years, but I haven’t ventured out and tested many of the brand’s other products — its Advent calendar is the perfect opportunity to do so. There’s 24 customer favorites inside, including three full-size items, three travel-size items and 18 minis. By the end of the month, you’ll open a full Kiehl’s skin care routine complete with cleansers, serums, treatments, moisturizers, eye creams, hair care and body care.

Best hair care Advent calendars

Kitsch’s 12-day Advent calendar helps you refresh your collection of hair care and styling products. You get full-size items, most notably the brand’s beloved silk pillowcase — I own about six of them and sleep on one every night to protect my curls. The Advent calendar also includes clips, scrunches, a bonnet, hair perfume and shampoo and conditioner bars. There’s also two dermaplaning products for your face: dermaplaners and oil.

The glitzy, glamorous hair accessories in Conair’s Advent calendar are exactly what you need to dress up any look, especially during the holiday season. It comes with 24 products, including bobby and hair pins, ponytail holders, claw clips and a scrunchie with a bow on it. You also get salon clips to help with skin care and makeup application, and a 2-in-1 mini boar slick back brush and taming wand.

Best nail Advent calendars

You get $316 worth of nail salon-quality products for $139 with this Advent calendar from Manucurist. It comes with 24 full-size products, like eight quick-drying polishes that have a gel-like finish and three polishes that can go on bare nails without needing a base or top coat. Nail and hand care essentials are also included, like a file, cuticle oil and cream, plus a jar of gold glitter.

Olive & June’s Advent calendar will upgrade your at-home manicures with 11 exclusive and previously sold out full-size nail polishes in a rainbow of shades. It also comes with two types of top coats: Sparkle Fairy Top Coat, which has an iridescent effect to it, and Long-Lasting Top Coat, which has a glossy finish.

If you prefer a gel mani but want to do it yourself without the UV or LED light, Dazzle Dry’s Advent calendar is calling your name. It comes with everything you need to prep, paint, finish and touch up your nails, and directions that tell you which order to use all the products in. You get two exclusive full-size nail polish shades, as well as two sparkly minis. The polish is quick-drying and lasts for up to two weeks, according to the brand.

Best wine and spirits Advent calendars

Each of VineBox’s Advent calendars comes with 3.4-ounce sampler bottles of wine from across the world, and you get an insert with tasting notes and food pairing recommendations, a limited-edition art print and access to sommelier-led virtual tasting videos. So you could essentially host your own wine tastings at home.

Vinebox sells three Advent calendars: the 12 Nights Velvet Collection, which comes with eight reds and four whites; the 12 Nights Vine Collection, which comes with six reds, one rosé and five distinctive wines; and the 24 Nights of Wine, which comes with all the wines in the Velvet and Vine collections.

The 12 canned wines in this Advent calendar come from small-batch female- and minority-led wineries, and they have zero grams of sugar, according to the brand. The cans are each equivalent to about one-third of a bottle, giving you about two glasses to share with someone or enjoy yourself. You get a mix of red, white, rosé and sparkling wines, plus a guide that provides links with in-depth information about each type. The calendar ships November 6.

In Good Taste releases numerous wine Advent calendars every year, and it just debuted a Wine Cocktail Advent Calendar for the first time. There are 24 ready-to-drink wine-based cocktails inside, including an espresso martini, piňa colada, mimosa, mojito and cosmopolitan. You get a 6-ounce serving of each one, as well as daily videos that pair with drinks so you can learn about tasting notes, food pairing suggestions and tips for garnishing.

Straightaway’s Advent calendar comes with 12 pre-made canned cocktails, so you don’t need to be a mixologist to enjoy a margarita, whisky sour, Manhattan or gimlet at home this holiday season. Just crack open an 3.4-ounce can, sip directly out of it or pour it into a glass and add ice. This is the third year the brand is selling an Advent calendar, and it added three brand-new beverages for 2026 customers.

Best coffee and tea Advent calendars

Instead of drinking the same type of coffee every morning, mix it up around the holidays with this Advent calendar. It comes with 24 K-Cups from brands like Caribou Coffee, Green Mountain Coffee Roasters, The Original Donut Shop and Peets, which you can pop into any compatible single-serve machine. In addition to standard, flavored and seasonal coffee pods, you also get hot cocoa and latte pods.

No coffee maker? No problem. Cometeer’s coffee concentrate pods come frozen, and to turn one into a cup of joe, you just melt it with hot water. You can also melt the coffee in its capsule by leaving it in the refrigerator or at room temperature, and pour it over iced water to make iced coffee, or over hot or cold milk to make a latte. Cometeer’s Advent calendar comes with 24 pods from a handful of roasters the brand works with, like Birch, Joe Coffee and Red Bay Coffee. There are rare blends, single-origin roasts and festive holiday varieties. You have to store the calendar in the freezer to keep the pods frozen throughout the month.

There’s 24 2-ounce packets of single-origin beans behind the doors of this Advent calendar, each of which makes about 24 ounces of pour-over coffee. You’ll get to try a new type of coffee every day from December 1 to Christmas Eve, so each one tastes a little different and you can learn about your preferences. In addition to the beans, you’ll get a custom 500-piece puzzle, access to Onyx’s web game and daily brew guides that share information about the coffee you’re drinking, recipes and stories from the Onyx team.

Tea Forte is known for its pyramid-shaped tea sachets, which lets the tea leaves unfurl and steep properly, making your beverage more flavorful and aromatic, according to the brand. There’s 24 sachets in this Advent calendar, including varieties like harvest apple spice, English breakfast, pumpkin spice and Belgian mint. Tea Forte also sells other Advent calendars that come with different types of tea: Winter Chalet (12 days), Warming Joy Herbal (24 days), Volaré (12 days) and Demoiselle (12 days).

This is the only Advent calendar on my list that’s filled with loose leaf tea rather than tea bags, giving you more control over how you make and enjoy it. The teas are packed in 10-gram tins, enough for a single cup, and come in flavors like blooming rose, turmeric chamomile, mint melody and original chai.

Restock your supply of Twinings tea with the brand’s Advent calendar, which covers the 24 days leading up to the holidays but is packed with double the amount of sachets — there are two behind every door, so you can sip one in the morning and keep one for your evening wind down. You get black green and herbal teas, including flavors like gingerbread joy, lemon and ginger, winter spice and lady grey.

Best food Advent calendars

There are 24 all-butter shortbread cookies inside Walker’s Advent calendar, which takes care of dessert (at least somewhat) prior to the holidays. They come in six different shapes and flavors, like shortbread fingers, rounds, hearts and stars, as well as chocolate chip and salted caramel square cookies.

As far as I’m concerned, Fishwife is responsible for making tinned fish a cool ingredient to snack on and add to meals, not something you ignore at the grocery store. The brand launched its first Advent calendar this year, which is filled with multiple cans of tinned fish, like smoked salmon, sardines, tuna and mussels. There’s also a handful of other surprises, like fish-shaped moisturizers from a collaboration with Bag Balm and a mini jar of hot sauce.

Baking cookies around the holidays is a tradition for many, and Williams Sonoma’s Advent calendar comes with lots of the supplies you need to whip up and package a batch. There’s 24 items inside, including cookie and biscuit cutters, piping bags, stencils, decorating tips, gift bags and spatulas.

Best Advent calendars for kids

After kids open all the doors of Magna-Tiles’ Advent calendar, they’ll be able to use the pieces to build a train that runs along a built-in track and create characters ready to board. It comes with exclusive figures you can mix and match the pieces of, as well as 10 decorated square blocks and three decorated triangle blocks.

The Miffy lover in your life will look forward to finding out what stickers they’ll get from this Advent calendar leading up to the holidays. It comes with 12 sticker sheets; the recipient can use them on notebooks, toys, their clothes and coloring book pages.

Your little scientist will have 24 days of hands-on activities to do in December with this Advent calendar. It comes with 13 kits for mini experiments and 11 specimens to study, like fossils and gemstones. And on Christmas Eve, they’ll get an extra special surprise: a sparkly piece of fool’s gold.

Kids will take extra pride in decorating their Christmas tree with the ornaments inside this Advent calendar, which they can make themselves. Each day, they’ll open a pack of materials and directions that teach them how to put together the final product. The ornaments they create all move: For example, the reindeer ornament flops forward, the polar bear ornament throws a snowball and the snowglobe ornament has falling flurries. KiwiCo says the calendar is best for kids age 5 and older.

Best Advent calendars for pets

If your dog could talk they might agree that the 24 treats packed inside Wufers’ Advent calendar are as tasty as they are beautifully decorated. They come in festive shapes and when you open the calendar, it starts playing “Jingle Bells.”

Bark’s Advent calendar is packed with 24 goodies for your dog. They’ll get 16 treats and eight plush toys, including those with squeakers, crinkle-textured fabric and strong hairs to prevent shredding.

Make playtime more exciting for your cat during the holidays with Chewy’s Frisco Advent calendar, which gives them 12 new toys to swat, kick, scratch and chase. They’ll get plush toys stuffed with silvervine and catnip, springs, plastic balls with bells, crinkle balls, feather teasers and more. There’s also a version for small dogs, which includes squeaky plush toys and several balls for them to play with.

The 24 dog treats that come in this Advent calendar are likely the fanciest ones your pup will ever be offered. They’re made in small batches with natural, human-grade ingredients, and come shaped like bones, truffles and macarons. The treats are decorated with festive “frosting” and “sprinkles,” too.

How I picked the best Advent calendars of 2026

To recommend the best Advent calendars, I researched highl -rated options across major categories like chocolate and candy, coffee and tea, food, wine and beauty. Every option on my final list comes from a brand we’ve previously covered or have personally tried. Some of the calendars were also sent to us as courtesy samples from brands or ones we bought with our own money.

To evaluate each one, I assessed its contents, price and packaging. Our list includes options that countdown the 12, 24 and 25 days before a holiday.

Why trust NBC Selected?

I’m a reporter at NBC Selected, where I’ve been writing gift guides for more than six years. I’ve specifically covered Advent calendars for the past four years. For this article, I compiled a list of the best Advent calendars of 2026, including highly-rated options, NBC Selected reader favorites and ones our team tested.

World.title: Kansas City Current capture first NWSL trophy
World.content:
The Kansas City Current made history Saturday, capturing their first NWSL Championship title in a thrilling 2-1 victory over the Washington Spirit in front of a D.C. crowd.

Kansas City's Vanessa DiBernardo broke the deadlock in the 54th minute with an "Olimpico," a rare goal scored directly from a corner kick without being touched by another player. Kansas City's Debinha scored in the 97th minute of stoppage time to extend the lead.

The Kansas City Current celebrate after winning the NWSL Championship over the Washington Spirit at Audi Field on Nov. 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Todd Olszewski / Getty Images

The Spirit's star forward Trinity Rodman pulled one back in the 98th minute, but it was too little too late.

The first half was physical, with fouls traded back and forth. Despite having less possession, Kansas City posed the greater offensive threat. The Spirit, meanwhile, struggled to capitalize on their time with the ball and recorded no shots on target in the first 45 minutes of the match.

Rodman took a hard hit from behind by Kansas City's Laney Rouse just five minutes into the match. Although she was able to continue playing, Rodman appeared bothered by her left arm and spent much of the first half stretching it before returning to play.

The Current, who were founded as an expansion franchise in 2021, were playing in their second ever championship game. Last season, their title hopes came to a stunning end when they were upset by bottom-seeded Gotham FC in the quarterfinals.

The Spirit found themselves in an all-too-familiar position Saturday night: on the losing end of a one-goal game in their third straight NWSL Championship appearance. They fell to the Orlando Pride in 2024, and Gotham FC in 2025.

Trinity Rodman of Washington Spirit looks dejected after the team's loss to the Kansas City Current in the NWSL Championship at Audi Field on Nov. 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Elsa/NWSL via Getty Images

The Spirit have reached the final five times but have claimed the title just once, in 2021, when they defeated the Chicago Red Stars 2-1 during Rodman's rookie season.

The Current have benefited from the addition of former Spirit attacking midfielder Croix Bethune earlier this year. The 25-year-old was drafted by Washington in 2024 and went on to earn Rookie of the Year honors before enjoying her best season yet with the Current.

The Current finished the regular season with a 16-9-5 record, while the Spirit went 17-4-9. The Current were the No. 4 seed heading into the playoffs, but defeated top-seeded Gotham FC in the semifinals.

Several women's pro sports leagues have seen rapid growth in recent years, and the NWSL is no exception.

NWSL Commissioner Jessica Berman told "CBS Mornings" this week that the surge of interest from new fans has been one of the league's biggest drivers over the past five years.

"If you look at women's sports over the past few years, the thing that has changed is that people are buying tickets. People are watching on TV and that is actually creating a business for us to grow," Berman said. "It is also the players, and they are the best in the world."

World.title: ICE officers arrest 2 passengers boarding flight in Seattle
World.content:
Masked immigration officers arrested two passengers on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, federal officials said, causing what Alaska Airlines called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Videos of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screamed that her daughter was being taken and she has a work permit.

Online flight data showed that Alaska Airlines Flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.

Alaska Airlines said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."

It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect."

In a statement provided to CBS News Saturday evening, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, the parent agency of ICE, said that ICE officers "conducted a targeted enforcement operation" on a Mexican national identified as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza who had "overstayed his visa."

During the arrest, a second passenger "hurled hot coffee" at the officers, the DHS spokesperson said in the statement. That second passenger, identified by DHS as Sofia Hernandez Mejia, is a Mexican national who had also been determined to have overstayed her visa, the spokesperson said.

Mejia was also subsequently arrested and will face federal charges of assaulting a federal officer, DHS said.

A DHS source told CBS News the two people arrested are a father and daughter.

Democratic Rep. Adam Smith of Washington said in an earlier statement that "masked ICE agents detained at least one passenger waiting to board an Alaska Airlines flight at Sea-Tac Airport. The masked agents forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge, taking them into custody."

The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. Videos showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases looked on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past. ICE sources told CBS News in July that the uptick in arrests stems from increased collaboration between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration.

On Thursday, a Princeton University student and Chinese national was detained by ICE at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., after attending a neuroscience conference, the school and her colleagues said.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, called the incident "just the latest example of ICE's deeply un-American tactics."

"ICE is completely and totally out of control," Ferguson said in a statement. "Like many Americans, I'm outraged by masked agents, who do not identify themselves, dragging people off jetways as they board a flight, creating chaos in our communities."

Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal of Washington said in a social media post that she was "disturbed by the reports of this detention at Sea-Tac," adding that her office was "working to gather more information on the situation."

DHS numbers obtained by CBS News last week found that ICE arrested 491,000 people in FY 2026, a record, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests, also a record. Administrative arrests are those in which alleged undocumented immigrants are arrested for civil violations rather than criminal charges.

In a "60 Minutes" interview earlier this month following the heavy losses suffered by Republicans in the midterm elections, President Trump appeared to acknowledge that his administration's immigration crackdown may have contributed to his party's poor showing.

"For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Mr. Trump told "60 Minutes." "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."

Of his deportation policies, the president said: "I think it was too tough. A lot of people would say that it's great, but a lot of people think it's too tough."

World.title: Athlete swims Strait of Hormuz to highlight Iran war's wildlife toll
World.content:
British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh has swum in the North Pole and Antarctica to draw attention to environmental causes. But battling freezing waters and extreme conditions hasn't prepared him for his latest challenge: swimming the Strait of Hormuz while tankers are attacked and blown up nearby.

Pugh, who is a United Nations Patron of the Oceans, spent three days this week swimming parts of the dangerous waterway to highlight how the war with Iran threatens the area's habitat and wildlife.

In this handout photo provided by the Lewis Pugh Foundation, British endurance swimmer and UNEP Patron of the Oceans Lewis Pugh dives into the Strait of Hormuz, off the Musandam Peninsula, Oman, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Lewis Pugh Foundation via AP

Wearing only swimming trunks, goggles and a cap bearing the U.N. logo, the athlete started from the Musandam Peninsula, on the southern tip of the strait, and ended by rounding the Cape of Hormuz, completing about 9.3 miles in total. Pugh is believed to be the first person to undertake a long-distance swim there since the war started.

The swimmer said that minutes after he entered the water on Monday, he heard two loud explosions that rocked the sea.

"I looked up and I could see that an oil tanker about four kilometers away had been hit," he told The Associated Press after he returned to London. "The explosion was so loud, two booms, and then fighter jets coming in. And at that moment I realized we have to get out of here right now."

Pugh, 56, managed to finish his feat after more stops and starts, including passing another vessel that sent fireballs into the sky after it was attacked.

"Most people, when they think about the Strait of Hormuz, they think of a shipping lane," he said. "But it is also one of the most beautiful places I have ever been … it's one of the treasure troves of the natural world."

"With all these ships being sunk, this area is under severe threat," he added. "It's going to take years, decades for this area to recover."

In this handout photo provided by the Lewis Pugh Foundation, British endurance swimmer and UNEP Patron of the Oceans Lewis Pugh dives into the Strait of Hormuz, off the Musandam Peninsula, Oman, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Lewis Pugh Foundation via AP

Iran has in recent weeks increased attacks on vessels that it claimed traveled along unauthorized routes in the strait as it seeks to impose its control on the crucial waterway, where a fifth of all oil traded passed through before the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Feb. 28.

Several tankers have also struck sea mines laid by Tehran, in some cases exploding and bursting into flames, among them one that was carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil last month.

Pugh warned of how oil leaking from the dozens of tankers damaged since February could create lasting problems for the region's animals, as well as its coastlines, coral reefs and mangrove forests.

He described seeing large numbers of dolphins following his boat as he sailed in, as well as turtles and ospreys. He also marveled at the hundreds of turtles he saw during a swim along the Omani coast before the war.

"When oil gets in there, when chemical pollution gets in there, it becomes very, very difficult to clean up that type of mess," he said. "It lasts for generations."

Pugh has had plenty of experience facing extreme temperatures and predators, including great white sharks. But swimming in a conflict zone presented entirely new dangers.

Lewis Pugh gestures as he looks at a map of the Strait of Hormuz before he swims in Plymouth Sound, off the coast of Devon, England, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Alastair Grant/AP Photo

To stay safe, the challenge was done in sections over three days, with a total of about 6½ hours of swimming. The athlete recalled seeing a gas carrier being struck as he returned to the harbor on the second day.

"I'll never ever forget going past that gas carrier, the smell of the chemicals and then the flames, they were literally like fireballs going up into the sky. Around the ship, the water was on fire," Pugh said.

"And to think of the impact which a casualty like this has on nature — it was very, very acute."

Pugh has spent much of the past 40 years swimming in places from Antarctica to the Red Sea and the English Channel to urge more action to protect marine environments from climate change, pollution and loss of biodiversity.

He was the first athlete to swim across the North Pole and complete a long-distance swim in every one of the world's oceans. In 2023, he swam all 315 miles of the Hudson River to highlight the importance of clean rivers.

His foundation says the challenges have helped secure official agreements to protect more than 1.35 million square miles of vulnerable ocean.

Some have dubbed Pugh's blend of epic swimming and political outreach as "Speedo diplomacy."

"Sport opens doors, it creates dialogue, it enables people to start thinking about these important issues," Pugh said.

"My message is very simple," he added. "We've got to stop the war. We've got to open the strait, and we've got to clean up the pollution."

World.title: Princeton student detained by ICE at Reagan Airport after conference
World.content:
A Princeton University student was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement this week at Ronald Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., after attending a neuroscience conference, the school and her colleagues said.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Ph.D. student, was detained on Thursday night following a presentation she gave at the Society for Neuroscience, her colleague wrote on X.

"News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community," Rodney Priestley, the dean of the Princeton graduate school, said in a statement. "The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support. We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton."

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement that Xie was taken into custody during a "targeted immigration enforcement operation" at Reagan Airport.

FILE -- Princeton University professor John Hopfield after receiving the Nobel Prize in physics in 2024. Graduate student Eva Xie asks Hopfield to sign a copy of one of his academic papers. Princeton University; Denise Applewhite

Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, according to DHS, which said she is a Chinese national. DHS said Xie had been required to depart the U.S. by Sept. 15, 2016.

"Xie will receive due process and remain in ICE custody pending her removal proceedings," DHS said in a statement. "Xie has NEVER held valid authorization to study in the United States. To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States."

Carlos Brody, of the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, wrote on X that Xie sent her lab mates a Slack message for help before she was detained. She's being held in Chantilly, Virginia, according to Brody.

"Her lawyers are working on her release," Brody wrote. "She's a brilliant neuroscientist, mentor, and friend. She went to a conference to present her work, and now she's in a detention center. She should be home."

Xie's attorney, Kerry Doyle, said in a statement that her "arrest and detention is without legal basis."

"They cannot arrest people without a warrant if they are not a flight risk or danger to the community," Doyle said. "She is neither. She's a star rising scientist with permission to be in the US and they grabbed her because she is easy pickings at an airport where TSA and ICE are sharing information and targeting unsuspecting travelers with authorization to be in the US."

World.title: Violence breaks out in Mexico after capture of drug kingpin wanted by FBI
World.content:
Mexico's military announced Saturday that it had captured a drug kingpin on the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Top 10 Most Wanted List. Violence broke out in the state of Sinaloa afterwards, rattling civilians.

Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, also known as "El Chapo Isidro," is allegedly the leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization, which the FBI described as a "heavily armed, major drug-trafficking organization" based in Sinaloa.

The cartel is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution and importation of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the U.S., according to the FBI, and has controlled drug production, transportation and distribution throughout Mexico.

Meza-Flores, his second-in-command "Germán" and cartel financial operator "José N" were all taken into custody during a raid in Sinaloa on Friday night, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said on X.

Elite military agents were able to find the targets and then arrive surreptitiously in the area, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. The agents set perimeters around a residence to prevent Meza-Flores from escaping, while also defending the area from reinforcements who could have interrupted the operation.

The arresting agents were attacked with gunfire and explosives, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. Seven attackers were killed during the operation. The agents entered the house and captured Meza-Flores, his two lieutenants, and five other suspected criminals. They also recovered drugs, cash, 10 firearms, a grenade launcher and other ammunition and weapons.

Meza-Flores and his lieutenants were flown to Mexico City and placed in custody of the Specialized Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime. The other five arrestees were taken into custody in Sinaloa, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. One of those arrested is a first cousin of Meza-Flores and a logistics operator for the cartel.

Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage marching a man who appeared to be Meza-Flores through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck.

Vehicles burn on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, Mexico, on Nov. 20, 2026, following an announcement by the interim government of the arrest of Beltrán-Leyva Cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro." Yohari Leon via Facebook/via Reuters.

The Mexican government said in an early Saturday report that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how the two countries coordinated. U.S. ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson said on X that "strategic intelligence sharing" between the U.S. and Mexico "helped make this operation possible."

In a social media post Saturday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that Meza-Flores had ben captured "in an operation by the Mexican government supported by a coordinated interagency effort that included" the U.S. Homeland Security Task Force.

Videos and photos from the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, where Meza-Flores was captured, show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, as well as burnt cars. The Mexican National Defense Secretariat said that four members of the Mexican Army's regular infantry forces "traveling to reinforce security" in the town have been killed.

Meza-Flores was indicted in 2012, then again in 2019. He faces multiple counts of drug-trafficking violations and the use and possession of a firearm. The FBI has described him as armed and dangerous. U.S. authorities had previously offered a reward of up to $5 million for information that led to Meza-Flores' arrest.

The high-profile capture comes as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from President Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.

A member of the Mexican Army stands guard outside the Special Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime (FEMDO) following the arrest and transfer of cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, 'El Chapo Isidro', in Mexico City, Mexico, on Nov. 21, 2026. Daniel Cardenas/Anadolu via Getty Images

The government has knocked out several cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Mexico's most powerful cartel leader, known as "El Mencho," who was killed in February. Similar to the capture of Meza Flores, the dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.

Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote in a post on X Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in the state of Sinaloa to protect civilians.

"These detentions are an important step in pacifying Sinaloa," he said.

World.title: Lock of George Washington's hair sells at auction for $4,000
World.content:
A lock of hair from America's founding father, George Washington, was sold at auction Saturday for $4,000, according to the South Carolina-based auction house Richmond Auctions.

The auction house said the lock of hair was obtained by famed collector John K. Lattimer, a descendant of John Gadsby, who had hosted the first U.S. president's final two birthday celebrations at his City Hotel and Tavern in Alexandria, Virginia, in 1798 and 1799.

A testament — posted with the framed lock of hair — on the auction house's website said that Gadsby, a resident of Alexandria, Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death at Mount Vernon in 1799.

The White House Historical Association said Gadsby leased and operated the City Hotel and Tavern in Alexandria and the Indian Queen in Baltimore. He ended his career operating the Franklin House and the National Hotel in Washington, D.C.

A framed lock of George Washington's hair, obtained by famed collector John K. Lattimer, from a descendant of John Gadsby who had hosted George Washington's final two birthday celebrations at his City Hotel and Tavern in Alexandria, Virginia, in 1798 and 1799, according to Richmond Auctions. Richmond Auctions

Gadsby was believed to have bought and sold enslaved people to work in his hotels, the association said, although records from that time were tenuous.

The granddaughter of Gadsby, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, said in a 1928 affidavit that he came into possession of Washington's lock of hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days ..."

She added Gadsby had the lock of hair framed and it hung "under General Washingtons portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life."

The auction house said the hair is framed in a 9-inch-by-2 1/2-inch round gold-gilded wood frame with a glass window. Details on the buyer were not provided by the auction house.

CBS News reached out to Richmond Auctions for more information.

Various artifacts of Washington have sold at auction throughout the years. In July, a letter from Washington requesting to raise the new Continental Army was sold for more than $109,000.

A letter written by Washington, dated Jan. 5, 1780, sold in 2024 for thousands of dollars. Briggs Auction in Pennsylvania said Washington was writing to Col. Stephen Moylan in Connecticut, who headed up the Fourth Continental Light Dragoons.

They were discussing commissions for different officer positions in the regiment.

World.title: Princess Kate reflects on healing in new documentary: "Cancer does change you"
World.content:
Britain's Catherine, Princess of Wales, opens up about finding hope and joy amid uncertainty in a new documentary exploring life since her cancer diagnosis in 2024.

"Heal" follows 44-year-old Catherine as she attempts the Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours.

The Princess of Wales said at the time she undertook the challenge in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, an organization connected to the hospital where she received her treatment. She was greeted by her husband Prince William, who is heir to the throne, and their children Princes George and Louis and Princess Charlotte, as well as her parents and brother after completing the climb.

In a trailer released Saturday by Prince William and Catherine's Kensington Palace office, the princess reflects on her cancer journey and speaks to others about their experiences.

Catherine, Princess of Wales, meets a cancer patient during a visit to The Royal Marsden NHS Foundation Trust on Sept. 11, 2026, in London, England. Ian Vogler / WPA Pool / Getty Images

Catherine announced in March 2024 that she had cancer and was undergoing chemotherapy following major abdominal surgery. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.

Catherine disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. At the time, she said in her post on Instagram that she remains focused on recovery: "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."

She has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.

In the trailer, Catherine says cancer changes people profoundly, and "healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty."

She adds that "it's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone" and "often, it is through pain that we realize there's a greater beauty that lies beyond that."

The film will premiere on the BBC in the United Kingdom on Nov. 29, before airing internationally on NBCUniversal in the United States on Nov. 30.

World.title: Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress
World.content:
Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress

toggle caption i Jacquelyn Martin/AP

NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order.

The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.

The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.

Sponsor Message

White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats.

Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."

Garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.

Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started."

In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."

Sponsor Message

Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.

The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses.

World.title: Google employees protest AI in schools policy
World.content:
Google employees protest AI in schools policy

More than 550 Google employees signed a petition to allow schools access to Search without AI. Parents and educators protested outside Google offices in 6 cities last week for the same ask.

Transcript

ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:

Parents and educators want Google to provide an AI-free version of the search engine for students. The backlash started after the company announced that they would not unbundle AI from their tools for education. Now some Google employees are joining in the push to provide AI-free access to students. NPR education reporter Sequoia Carrillo is following the story. She joins us now. Hey, Sequoia.

SEQUOIA CARRILLO, BYLINE: Hi.

SCHMITZ: So parents have mixed feelings, obviously, about using AI in the classroom. Why is Google taking such a firm stance on this?

CARRILLO: I think mixed feelings is actually kind of a nice read of the situation. I've pretty much only talked to very angry parents, and we have a lot of very angry legislators, too, at the state and at national levels. Why Google's taking such a firm stance? There's no clear answer. I mean, some will point you to the fact that Google's very heavily invested in AI, and they want schools to be just as invested in it.

And I actually spoke to some people who pointed me towards two court cases earlier this year. Google got those dismissed by arguing that AI Overview and their search function are one tool. And those dismissals might mean that breaking them up could potentially be legally difficult for them. And when I talk to Google, they would not give us comments. So who is to say right now?

SCHMITZ: That's really interesting. So it sounds like Google has sort of backed itself into a legal corner on this issue, and it sounds like Google's own employees are angry about this.

CARRILLO: Yes. So Google employees are now weighing in. A small percentage signed a petition to allow schools the option to use search without AI overview, and the union for Google employees says that they're worried that this could damage the company's reputation among students and teachers and end up with schools ultimately shutting out Google's products altogether. There is some merit to that. Earlier this month, we saw protests across the country outside of Google offices because of this exact stance.

SCHMITZ: So what are schools doing to prepare for this change?

CARRILLO: People are definitely finding workarounds, and if they haven't already found it, they're definitely working on it. They say something as simple as the Chrome extension might be able to help districts keep the search engine. Fairfax County, a very large, well-funded district in Northern Virginia, was actually already doing this. They're piloting a kind of ad-blocking-type tool for AI on their school devices that they developed.

SCHMITZ: OK. So if one school district in Virginia can do this, why is this an issue? Why doesn't everyone do this?

CARRILLO: It's a great question, but Fairfax County is a huge district, and they also are very well funded. We have a lot of small school districts in the country, and they are not able to develop their own Chrome extension in-house. And even if they could license it from someone else, they don't often have the staffing to keep up with the IT demand on something like that. A former Google for Education employee, Tracy Pizzo, now works with some of those districts to help them adapt to the AI landscape. And she said it might be time for something else.

TRACY PIZZO: Do I think that schools should be looking at where else they could go? Yes, I do. And I would encourage, at this moment, schools to say, we're not doing this.

CARRILLO: But of course, that takes time, and schools don't really have that right now. Like, school is in session, and the changes are already announced.

SCHMITZ: How likely is it that Google will end up backing down here?

CARRILLO: So some of the company's biggest fans - and I've spoken to a few of them, especially at the superintendent level - many that I spoke with feel like the company does listen to them and that this was just a failure in communication. Google said in the initial announcement of this on their blog that they will listen to feedback and evolve their approach to integrating AI in schools. But since the protests and this week's petition, and - there's really been no follow-up from them. So some of the company's critics think that this is an ultimatum, and they are throwing their weight around here.

SCHMITZ: So what's next?

CARRILLO: It's hard to tell. The change is supposed to roll out in the coming months, so we'll keep following it. For now, schools are definitely scrambling a bit as they head into the holidays.

SCHMITZ: That is NPR education reporter Sequoia Carrillo. Thanks so much for joining us.

CARRILLO: Thank you.

SCHMITZ: And a note - Google is a financial supporter of NPR.

World.title: Highlights and challenges from covering an historic month in South America
World.content:
Highlights and challenges from covering an historic month in South America

Transcript

ROB SCHMITZ, BYLINE: As an international correspondent, sometimes you're on hand to witness history in the making as NPR's Mike Shuster did in 1989 as East Germany was collapsing...

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

MIKE SHUSTER: The East German authorities took a giant hammer to the wall last night and simply knocked a bit of it down. With a large digging machine, the workmen smashed two 40-feet-wide holes in the wall to the cheers of crowds on both sides.

SCHMITZ: ...Or NPR's former Johannesburg bureau chief Ann Cooper, heard here reporting from South Africa in 1994 as Nelson Mandela was inaugurated as the country's first Black president.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

ANN COOPER: There was a lot of symbolism today of the reconciliation that Mandela preaches, and I think this - you know, the great variety of South African guests, you know, was a very potent symbol of that.

SCHMITZ: It's rare, though, that two historic events occur on your watch just weeks apart. Well, that was exactly what happened for NPR South America correspondent Carrie Kahn. Last month, she covered an historic election in Brazil, where President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva came from behind to win a runoff. And then Pope Leo XIV's first visit to Latin America as pope. So when we sat down for Reporter's Notebook, I asked her what covering these two big stories back to back was like.

CARRIE KAHN, BYLINE: It's been exhausting. But it's also incredibly amazing. You know, I just had this front seat to two very historic events on the continent. And to get to watch the mobilization just of millions in two very different public events, it was really - it was a career high point. Is that overstating it? But it really was. It was quite amazing. It was.

SCHMITZ: I mean, you've been covering Latin America for a long time.

KAHN: Yes. I don't want to date myself, but yes.

SCHMITZ: (Laughter).

KAHN: A couple decades.

SCHMITZ: That is a long time. I mean, let's talk about the papal visit. Here you are reporting on ALL THINGS CONSIDERED on the day that Leo arrived in Peru, a country that he called home for 20 years.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

KAHN: It's a huge party. This country is so happy the Pope is here.

UNIDENTIFIED GROUP: (Singing in non-English language).

SCHMITZ: That was obviously just a really celebratory mood there.

KAHN: It was. It was just amazing. There was a lot of bands and performers and local choral group all along Pope Leo's visit. There was a lot of waiting around, too, and so there were a lot of group celebrations breaking out. That was a group of young people that were singing in the streets. It was just wonderful. There was a lot of emotion in this visit.

And, you know, this trip came just weeks after he had a portion of his lung removed, you know, after being diagnosed with cancer. So the beginning was a little stiffer. You know, he was kind of standoffish, and you always wait for the pope to put out his hand before you touch the pope. But then they were hugging, and it was just - it was emotional all around. And, you know, it really - it was just surprising, all the emotions...

SCHMITZ: Oh.

KAHN: ...And the tears. This was this very plain, simple man.

SCHMITZ: Sure.

KAHN: And he just touched a lot of hearts with his simplicity and his very simple message. It was that everybody needs to work for the common good, the bien comun, the good of everyone. You know, as his mentor Francis preached, too, you know, individualism, vanity and hypertechnology is not what humanity needs now. It needs community and civility. And I think that really touched a lot of people in these troubling times.

SCHMITZ: You covered Pope Francis' trip to Mexico in 2016. How did this visit compare?

KAHN: It was just really different. It was a different time then.

SCHMITZ: Right.

KAHN: We hadn't seen so much polarization. And, you know, Francis was warmly welcomed to Mexico, but he's from a more liberal wing of the church, of Mexico's church. It was and still is very conservative. So it just felt different.

SCHMITZ: Got it.

KAHN: It was - you know, he wasn't as warmly embraced in Mexico as Leo was welcomed in Peru. And I think people, Catholic or not, during Leo's trip really just wanted to feel hopeful.

SCHMITZ: So I want to turn here to Brazil's election, and here you are again on October 4, when the first round had just finished.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

KAHN: Lula will have to find a way to close the gap in this runoff. He's not going to really be able to win over the 8% of voters who went for the other candidates. They were far-right and right, and their voters will fall in line with Bolsonaro, not with Lula.

SCHMITZ: So, Carrie , I mean, you can hear in your reporting here that Lula was facing long odds. And in fact, no one in modern Brazilian history had come back to win a second round after coming in second place in the first round. In the three weeks that followed, was it easy to see where this was going?

KAHN: OK, I would totally be lying if I told you that I perceived this changing landscape or a huge political shift. I did not.

(LAUGHTER)

KAHN: I wasn't making any predictions.

SCHMITZ: Thank you for being so...

KAHN: Well, actually...

SCHMITZ: ...Honest with me, Carrie.

KAHN: (Laughter) I just - I actually - you know, I thought Bolsonaro had it, you know, on election night. Where was I? I was in Brasilia at Bolsonaro's headquarters, waiting for him to come out...

SCHMITZ: Yeah.

KAHN: ...You know, with the hundreds of other reporters. It wasn't just me, but - that were waiting for him to give his victory speech.

SCHMITZ: I want to ask you a question just about covering South America as NPR's correspondent there. You know, when I was NPR's Shanghai correspondent - I was in charge of covering China - I would have this map of China, and I'd put pins in different parts of China that I went to or reported from just to make sure that I was covering the entire country of China because it's such a diverse country when you actually zoom in.

You are covering an entire continent. What is your approach to make sure that you're covering the stories that our audience needs to hear without trying to cover, you know, every story out there?

KAHN: I guess maybe I have to go get some pins.

(LAUGHTER)

KAHN: That's a good tip.

SCHMITZ: (Laughter).

KAHN: See if I'm really covering all over the place.

SCHMITZ: (Laughter).

KAHN: You know, it's tough. It's daunting. The continent is huge. I can travel a full day by plane and still be in Brazil. It's amazing.

SCHMITZ: That's incredible.

KAHN: It is. It's huge. I...

SCHMITZ: A full day...

KAHN: Yeah.

SCHMITZ: ...Just to stay in the same country.

KAHN: To get to the Amazon, you have to take...

SCHMITZ: Wow.

KAHN: You have to take, like, two or three planes, and they don't fly all the time, and it's costly, and it's time-consuming.

SCHMITZ: Right.

KAHN: I don't know. I always have to think about, will this story interest Americans? Under Trump - Trump 1 and Trump 2 - we do spend a lot of time, you know, covering what he is doing in Latin America. And, you know, in the second term, his administration has flexed so much U.S. power in the region that we're not - we haven't seen in decades.

SCHMITZ: Absolutely.

KAHN: So it's all new. And so that kind of pushes the agenda a lot, you know, from seizing Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela and the U.S. now pretty much running the country. And now I can get visas to go in there. You couldn't get visas before. It was very difficult.

SCHMITZ: Yeah, that - what a change.

KAHN: Yeah. There's rising gang violence and organized crime infiltrations all over the continent, so there's plenty to cover. And as you know, you know, you just work with a lot of amazing local journalists throughout the continent, in every country.

SCHMITZ: Right.

KAHN: I just had a great time with a journalist in Uruguay that I've never worked with before and my regular producer in Peru. And we spent a lot of time brainstorming some stories that we could work on in the future, so there's no shortage in the continent.

SCHMITZ: So, Carrie, you've been covering Latin America and beyond, and I'm just curious. Do you ever get homesick?

KAHN: Homesick - wait, where's home?

(LAUGHTER)

SCHMITZ: I knew you would say that.

KAHN: Of course. I don't know. I haven't lived in the U.S. for 20 years. I guess I do. For the U.S. - I'm from Northern California. Well, actually I grew up in Southern California, but I lived a lot of my life in Northern California. My kids are there, so yes, I would love to go back. My home is also in Mexico, where I have a lot of family. I don't know. I feel very comfortable in Latin America, and it feels like home.

SCHMITZ: That is NPR South America correspondent Carrie Kahn. Carrie, thank you so much.

KAHN: You're welcome.

World.title: Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
World.content:
Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America

The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.

On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.

The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a blood cancer that they claim is linked to glyphosate, which is the main ingredient in Roundup.

Under the settlement in circuit court, people affected could receive anywhere from $10,000 to $165,000 in compensation, depending on whether their work in agriculture or other occupations exposed them to higher levels of glyphosate, the age when they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other factors.

Sponsor Message

In a statement , the CEO of Bayer, Bill Anderson, called the settlement a "decisive milestone" that will "mitigate the risks" of pending and future litigation.

The presiding judge, Timothy Boyer, said it was "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bayer, the German company that now owns Monsanto, finding that it could be shielded from lawsuits filed in state courts over claims that it failed to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate.

Roundup is the most widely used weed-killer in the world.

The attorney representing the plaintiffs, Christopher Seeger, said in a statement that "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice."

The latest settlement comes in addition to a previous one in which Bayer agreed to pay between about $10 billion and $11 billion to settle more than 100,000 claims related to Roundup.

More than a decade ago, the World Health Organization's cancer agency concluded that glyphosate is probably carcinogenic to humans. Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns as recently as this year.

But Bayer has steadfastly denied that its product causes cancer.

The Environmental Protection Agency has also concluded it "did not identify risks of concern from glyphosate uses, including for cancer," though the agency is currently conducting a review of the evidence related to human health after facing intense pressure from advocates and some scientists.

Sponsor Message

Concerns about the safety of glyphosate has been an animating issue for supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and his Make America Healthy Again agenda.

However, the Trump administration has taken steps to support the herbicide-maker, siding with Bayer in the Supreme Court case and issuing an executive order to promote domestic production of glyphosate.

Several years ago, the company removed glyphosate from its U.S. products used in residential settings, although it's still in use in the agricultural industry.

World.title: Storms expected on both coasts threatens Thanksgiving travel
World.content:
Storms expected on both coasts threatens Thanksgiving travel

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images North America

Before worrying about the temperature of the turkey, travelers could face a different type of uncertainty next week. This time, it's the weather — and it's affecting both U.S. coasts.

"I know there's a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday, but I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential," said San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie on X Friday. He said the city is preparing this weekend for extreme high tides and rain that could hit the area Monday afternoon through Wednesday.

Sponsor Message

Over the past week, cities in California saw mudslides, waterspouts and flooding while Florida also saw coastal flooding and inundated streets. A new set of storms are expected to hit both sides of the country early next week, just as travelers head into the holiday week.

It's already been a wet fall in large swaths of the country, thanks in part to a Super El Niño, a natural climate pattern that shifts weather around the world. Devastating flooding in the Southwest U.S. left multiple people dead and hundreds stranded, and California and the Pacific Northwest have seen high sea level and multiple strong atmospheric rivers.

Atmospheric rivers are here to stay

"Take this weekend: get yourself ready," Lurie, the San Francisco mayor, said after a call with the National Weather Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Rain and snow, in higher elevations, is possible over parts of the northwest and northern California on Saturday, according to the NWS.

The West Coast is forecasted to see an atmospheric river, a narrow band of water vapor pushed by the wind, on Monday. Another is expected for the Pacific Northwest later in the week, according to the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes. Atmospheric rivers hang over an area and dump precipitation. They can cause months worth of rain in just a few days.

Sponsor Message

The center expects two to four inches of precipitation over northern California and southern Oregon through Wednesday.

Coastal flood advisories are also in effect through Monday morning in the Bay Area, the NWS said. This comes on top of historic high tides, known as King tides.

Travel troubles could persist after Thanksgiving

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images North America

A storm that started in Florida Friday will move north to the Mid-Atlantic and into the Northeast by Sunday evening, according to the NWS.

Some of the heaviest rain could be seen on the coast of the Carolinas through Sunday morning. Then, heavy rain is expected to move up the coast, said Dan Hoffman, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Baltimore, Md.

Hoffman said during a busy travel week, even with the weather not expected to bring flooding or strong winds, it "doesn't usually take too much to cause things to start to have delays."

As for New England, Andrew Loconto, a meteorologist at the NWS in Norton, Mass., said the storm this weekend is not forecasted to be as big as another storm hitting the region after Thanksgiving. "That could be more impacts for people coming back home," Loconto said, pointing to another highly anticipated day across the U.S. — Black Friday.

World.title: Cartel leader captured in northern Mexico in a bloody firefight that left 11 dead
World.content:
Cartel leader captured in northern Mexico in a bloody firefight that left 11 dead

toggle caption i Claudia Rosel/AP

GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — Heavy gunfire, helicopters and burning trucks marked Mexico's Sinaloa state Saturday after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," in an operation that left at least 11 people dead.

Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after the firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized.

toggle caption i U.S. Department of State via AP

Mexico's Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed.

The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.

Sponsor Message

Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.

He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.

Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.

As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.

Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violenceThe capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city.

Sponsor Message

Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.

"The fighting was happening all over Guasave," said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. "It spread throughout the city."

Mexican authorities said that they used "stealth and surprise" to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him.

Video shared by Mexico's Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities.

Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case.

"Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets.

Terror in SinaloaGuasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.

"Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press.

She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.

Sponsor Message

An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. He lamented the deaths of the four soldiers killed in the operation.

Burned-out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday.

"The aftermath of last night's war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down," Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico.

Guasave residents remained "very afraid" because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said.

Capture prompts celebration and warningsMeza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.

The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities.

"Results like these don't happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together," U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. "We will continue the hunt."

Mexican Security Secretary García Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."

Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho," who was killed by the military in February.

Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.
