The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.

Sponsor Message

"What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don't dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."

World.title: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
World.content:
Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules

toggle caption i Efrem Lukatsky/AP

GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."

After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.

Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.

Sponsor Message

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.

Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan, 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.

Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.

Algorithms making life-and-death decisions

"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."

No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.

Sponsor Message

On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.

Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.

A "nothing burger"

The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.

A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.

"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."

There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.

"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."

Sponsor Message

But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.

Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

World.title: Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
World.content:
Federal jury convicts man of starting the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles

toggle caption i Etienne Laurent/AP

LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.

Sponsor Message

With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.

Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.

"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.

Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.

Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren't presented as evidence during the trial.

Sponsor Message

Juror says Rinderknecht's own testimony pointed to a guilty verdict

toggle caption i U.S. Attorney's Office/AP

Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.

"It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said. "After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he's guilty."

Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a "lack of information" presented to the jury about the technical review.

In the end, it was Rinderknecht's own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.

"Stating that he was up on the hill, didn't smell a fire, didn't see fireworks … no one else was on the hill that night," Cameron said.

Prosecutors say Rinderknecht had been 'mad at everything'

During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did.

Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.

Sponsor Message

They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

"He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"

These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.

They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked.

Defense argues fire's origin is unproven

Haney cast doubt on the government's case, saying the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was publicly accessible until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.

The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.

Prosecutors attacked the fire investigator during cross examination and at one point accused him of perjury, alleging he did not disclose all records related to the case. The judge ultimately rejected prosecutors' request to strike his testimony.

Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.

He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act."

Sponsor Message

Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.

In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

World.title: Quebecor CEO defends Telus bid, cites falling wireless prices and Canada's sovereignty
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebecor Inc. CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau is defending his company's $31-billion bid to buy Telus Corp. amid concerns over competition in Canada's telecom sector, arguing the cost of wireless plans is dropping and non-Canadian companies are trying to expand.

"Telecom assets are strategic for our country — we all know this. And then therefore, we need to make sure that we're going to be on the same footing," Péladeau said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live airing Sunday morning.

The Montreal-based telecom, media and entertainment company said on Monday that it submitted a non-binding proposal to Telus in June to serve as a basis for negotiations and that the Vancouver-based corporation is currently reviewing an enhanced proposal submitted by Quebecor earlier this month.

Quebecor's move comes three years after the federal government approved Rogers Communications' acquisition of Shaw Communications on the condition that Freedom Mobile be sold to Quebecor to preserve a four-player market.

Péladeau told CBC chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that his company has been servicing Freedom Mobile and the Canadian market "pretty efficiently, and our results talk by themselves. We look forward to being able to continue to do the same with the Telus assets."

WATCH | What Quebecor's Telus bid means for your phone bill: Quebecor's $31B bid to buy Telus: What it means for your phone bill | Duration closed caption 4:07 Quebecor has launched a massive $31-billion bid to take over Telus, a move that would crown it Canada’s largest telecom company — and potentially shrink the wireless market back down to three major players in B.C. The CBC’s Lien Yeung breaks down why Telus is pushing back and what this blockbuster merger could mean for your monthly phone bill.

Asked how a merger of this size would help with Canadians' wireless costs, Péladeau said prices continue to fall after his company acquired Freedom Mobile.

"Our earnings are growing, our free cash flow is growing," he said. "Why would you change a successful strategy?"

According to Canada's annual telecom report , consumer prices for cellular services declined in recent years but ticked back up in 2025. Canada still had some of the highest wireless prices compared with other developed countries.

Quebecor is currently Canada's fourth-largest telecom company. With its $14.77-billion market capitalization and Telus's $21.72-billion market cap, the potential deal would make Quebecor larger than Rogers or Bell by that metric.

Péladeau also framed the proposed bid as a way of protecting Canada's sovereignty, noting Elon Musk's satellite internet provider Starlink services parts of the Canadian market and is likely hungry to expand its operations.

"[Starlink's] business model is the world, like Netflix's business model was the world," Péladeau said, adding that Netflix "destroyed a Canadian industry" despite not having a licence with the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC).

Quebecor is currently Canada's fourth-largest telecom company, with a $14.77-billion market capitalization. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

Telus says it has formed a special committee to review the offer and determine the value of the potential deal. So far, the committee has discovered a number of "significant risks," John Manley, the chair of Telus's board of directors, said in a statement on Monday issued by the company.

Telus also takes issue with how the Quebecor proposal values the company.

Manley said Telus would continue to engage with Quebecor, the government and regulatory authorities about those concerns while exploring alternatives.

The federal perspective so far

In its news release on Monday, Quebecor acknowledged that Canada's Competition Bureau — along with other authorities, such as the CRTC and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada — will need to approve the deal.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said more competition, lower prices and better service would be key to any decision regarding the telecom sector.

WATCH | NDP Leader Avi Lewis calls on Competition Bureau to block Telus sale: 'This is the last thing we need': NDP asks feds to block Quebecor's Telus bid | Duration closed caption 10:03 NDP Leader Avi Lewis joins Power & Politics after Montreal-based telecommunications company Quebecor announces its $31-billion bid to acquire competitor Telus. Critics of the potential deal are calling on the federal Competition Bureau to block the sale, saying it will increase costs for consumers and trigger layoffs.

Carney declined to comment directly on Quebecor's proposal but said that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly situation can lead to more competition with fewer players. He didn't elaborate further.

Péladeau said he doesn't think anyone would disagree with Carney's comments, noting that even if there are three Canadian companies, there will still be other competition, like Starlink.

On Friday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party has not yet seen the proposal but would study it and base its judgment on the principle of lowering prices for consumers.

Poilievre also criticized Carney's comments, saying he has never seen "any economist anywhere in the world say that oligarchies ultimately bring prices down.... Once again, Mr. Carney favours the corporate power brokers over the consumers."

NDP Leader Avi Lewis has called on the Competition Bureau to cancel the sale, saying it will increase costs for consumers and trigger layoffs.

"We already pay some of the highest cellphone prices in the world," he said. "I just think it's so obvious to the vast majority of people who are suffering under this cost-of-living crisis that this is just yet another thing where the big boys just ... swallow up another company."

World.title: Will Canadian workers refuse to handle Israeli goods? Why unions increasingly say they should
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A movement to cut off Israeli goods is spreading across Canada's unions and workers are preparing for potential battles with their employers.

The Canadian Labour Congress (CLC), which represents more than three million workers, passed a resolution last month declaring trade, services and relationships with Israel to be "hot cargo" and calling for workers to refuse to handle weapons and military equipment destined for Israel. The CLC also resolved to cut ties with the Histadrut, Israel's largest trade union organization.

The moved followed similar resolutions passed by numerous local and provincial labour groups over the past year, including the Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador labour federations.

Next week, the B.C. Federation of Labour will vote on a resolution that would "support affiliate locals and unions in refusing to engage with" Israeli goods and specifically ask the B.C. government to stop importing and selling Israeli wines.

A BCFL spokesperson said in an email that the union does not comment on resolutions before delegates have had a chance to debate them.

The movement to isolate Israel with economic pressure is growing as its deadly strikes on Gaza continue after a ceasefire deal was signed more than a year ago. Gaza health authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, while Israeli officials say five Israeli soldiers have been killed.

"I think the vast majority of union activists have come to see that this is a situation where people of conscience, and workers of conscience, need to do what they can to oppose Israeli crimes and our complicity in them," said Kevin Levangie, a member of the Labour for Palestine steering committee that pushed for the resolutions across Canada.

A report by the UN 's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian ‌Territory including East Jerusalem and Israel stated last month that Israel has continued to commit genocide since the ceasefire. Israel dismissed the charge as part of a "misinformation campaign."

Israel is facing accusations of genocide before the International Court of Justice, while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is wanted on an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Gaza.

Union says Palestinian workers made request

Levangie, a member of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers Atlantic in Halifax, says the Canadian government is not doing enough to stop the flow of weapons to Israel, or the import of products manufactured in illegal settlements in Palestinian territories, so it "falls on Canadian workers" to ensure they are complying with their obligations under international law.

Levangie visited the West Bank as part of a union delegation in September and October, where he met with Palestinian groups, including trade unions, who have asked unions in the West to take on this work.

"We're honouring a request that was made by Palestinian workers," he said.

"In that way, it's very similar to the South African context of the 80s and 90s, where South African trade unions, South African civil society organizations, were asking for us to isolate apartheid South Africa until the freedom struggle was won."

Kevin Levangie, a member of the Labour for Palestine steering committee, says workers want to comply with international law. (Submitted by Kevin Levangie)

Canadian dockworkers, postal workers and retail workers joined international campaigns declaring South African goods as hot cargo in the 1980s to pressure the country's government into ending apartheid.

Canadian workers also took hot cargo actions to protest Argentina's human rights abuses and suppression of trade unions in 1979 and joined a trade union boycott of Indonesia in 1999 to protest the country's military occupation of East Timor.

Canadian unions have not acted on the CLC resolution, though workers in other countries have taken action.

Italian workers staged a day-long general strike last month, blocking roads, causing rail delays and cancellations and disrupting airports to protest Israel intercepting an aid flotilla that was carrying food to Gaza.

Canada's unions did not participate in a global day of strike on Oct. 30, which saw efforts to disrupt weapons transfers to Israel as part of a broader anti-war protest at 113 ports across 22 countries.

Critic says Israel singled out

The CLC's resolution has created tension within the labour movement, according to Kim Kazur, labour consultant and adviser with the Canadian Jewish Labour Committee advocacy group.

A retired Ontario Public Service Employees Union member, Kazur says she feels unions are unfairly singling out Israel on the world stage and the resolutions are a way to "hide behind" what she views as "Jew hate."

Kazur says unions should "stay in our lanes" and not contribute to "divisive political ideology," adding workers could end up putting themselves at risk of being fired.

"The idea of a union encouraging its members to do some type of disobedience is not OK," she said.

Levangie denied accusations of hate and noted Labour for Palestine regularly collaborates with advocacy group Independent Jewish Voices in its organizing work.

"We in Labour for Palestine are strongly opposed to antisemitism and all other forms of hate," he said.

Advocates say they want to end Canada's involvement in manufacturing F-35 parts that could end up on Israeli jets. (Amir Cohen/Reuters)

Workers could face discipline

Levangie acknowledges a concern about discipline or retaliation by employers if workers refuse to handle certain goods — from components of F-35 fighter jets that are manufactured in Canada, to oranges shipped from Israel to Canadian grocery stores — but says the declaration of hot cargo is the labour movement's "greatest power."

The tactic is often used in the context of labour disputes, says Andrew Stevens, an associate professor at the University of Regina's school of business.

The BCFL issued a hot cargo edict on Nov. 2 — in solidarity with striking Trigon employees with the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 523 — ordering workers not to handle Trigon coal and petroleum products.

Moving to concrete action can be complicated, however, especially on a heated political issue.

"If an individual worker engages in this, I think people are going to see it as insubordination, which means that they could be subject to discipline up to and including termination of employment," Stevens said.

If two or more workers deliberately refuse orders to unload goods or procure services, he says that would be deemed an illegal strike.

WATCH | CBC investigates allegations against Israel: Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? | Duration 4:10 CBC’s visual investigations team uncovers new satellite imagery that shows the IDF removing rubble from sites in Gaza that it bombed, which experts and human rights advocates warn risks destroying evidence of alleged war crimes. Families in Gaza interviewed by CBC say this activity prevents them from retrieving the bodies of loved ones trapped under the rubble.

Stevens says workers will need strong support from their unions and labour organizations if they plan to carry out the CLC's resolution on the ground.

"Its strength is really going to be premised on the support from the unions themselves," he said.

CBC News has reached out to the CLC for comment but has not heard back.

World.title: How the Alberta government could fill a new pipeline with royalties paid in oil
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of the biggest challenges facing Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s ambitions to develop and build a large oil export pipeline to the West Coast is having oil companies sign long-term contracts to actually use the proposed project.

If that hurdle becomes too big to overcome, the Alberta government could turn to a relatively unknown policy that allows the energy royalties it receives to be paid in oil — and then use that oil to service the pipeline.

Companies have to pay a royalty to the provincial government for any oil and natural gas produced in Alberta. These monthly royalties add billions of dollars in revenue to provincial coffers each year.

But some industry experts say the provincial government could instead use the "royalty-in-kind" policy to collect enough oil to fill the proposed Pacific Link pipeline, which would transport oil from the Edmonton area to a port near Vancouver.

"If there needs to be more barrels that are diverted and are sent on the Pacific Link when constructed, for sure the Crown could elect to take more and more of its royalty in bitumen and physically allocate it to the Pacific Link," said Grant Sprague, a former deputy energy minister in Alberta.

For now, Smith is focused on encouraging the largest oil companies in the province to ramp up oil production, which is why the premier unveiled a new incentive program last week focused on promoting the construction of new oilsands facilities.

A view of Suncor's Base Plant oilsands mine. Suncor is one of the companies considering whether to proceed with expanding production in the oilsands. (Kyle Bakx/CBC)

More production is the ideal way of filling the Pacific Link pipeline, said Sprague, since the royalty-in-kind program would not help Alberta’s overall goal of increasing oil exports.

"It's a diversion. It's never additive. And I think the real goal has got to be to have sufficient production to fill — maybe not fill, but to service all of the existing pipelines," said Sprague.

"… Short answer: it's not a panacea."

Financial repercussions

Requiring companies to pay royalties in oil could also come at a financial cost for producers.

Oil companies have long-term contracts on other export pipelines to ship a certain amount of oil. If a producer would not have as much oil to fill their space on the pipelines, they would still have to pay for the amount of pipeline capacity they are signed up for.

That would result in oil producers paying for shipping on "air barrels."

Former Suncor chief executive Mark Little said he's "very certain" the Alberta government is considering the option to take payment in barrels of oil — and companies would feel the squeeze if it went ahead.

"It's a hit on the company's financial performance unless they expand," Little said.

"I think we're going to see some capital get invested just because they're either going to go willingly or get somewhat forced."

Alberta could access enough oil to fill the million-barrels-per-day Pacific Link pipeline by using the royalties-in-kind program, said a government official, speaking on background. However, the official said, it is not the government’s intent to do so, since it is confident the oilpatch will increase production.

The Pacific Link project faces other challenges, including legal challenges filed by three First Nations in Alberta in an attempt to overturn the federal government’s designation of the pipeline as a project in the national interest.

The designation allows the federal government to fast-track and consolidate the approval process for the pipeline under the Building Canada Act.

'If they want to acquire some barrels, just go buy them'

Foregoing royalty payments in cash could also blow a hole in Alberta's budget. Other ramifications include souring the investment climate at a time when Alberta is trying to attract tens of billions of dollars to grow its energy sector and double oil production.

"If you're trying to attract new investment to increase growth, threatening people ain't the way to do it," said Richard Masson, former chief executive of the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission, the province’s commercial oil and gas agency that runs the royalty-in-kind program.

"Royalties-in-kind is just a mechanism that complicates life, creates uncertainty and doesn't create an extra barrel to ship," he said.

Richard Masson, former chief executive of the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission, does not think using the royalty-in-kind program is a good idea for the province. (Justin Pennell/CBC)

If the provincial government needs oil to fill its pipeline, it’s much easier to purchase barrels on the open market, he said.

"Alberta gets its royalties in cash every month at the market price. If they want to acquire some barrels, just go buy them," said Masson. "Easy-peasy."

The Alberta government has said one of the reasons for having the royalties-in-kind program is to have "more control over the province’s resources, allowing for the expansion of egress and market access."

WATCH | How Alberta is encouraging new oilsands growth: Alberta announces royalty program as part of plan to double oilsands production | Duration closed caption 2:25 The Alberta government is introducing a royalty incentive program, the Oil Sands Growth Program, that it says will help the province meet its 2035 goal of doubling current oilsands production by easing the capital investment needed to kick-start new developments.

Some large oilpatch companies have been reluctant to build new oil production facilities because of a lack of support from shareholders. Despite lucrative oil prices, many investors would rather oil companies continue to produce hefty profits, as opposed to spending billions of dollars to invest in new projects.

The chances of the provincial government using the policy are relatively small, considering the financial harm it could cause some oil companies — but it does provide a pathway for the proposed pipeline to proceed even if oil companies don’t sign contracts committing to use it.

At the same time, the policy gives the provincial government an important tool to motivate the oilpatch to invest in pumping out more crude, even though it would complicate its relationship with Alberta's largest industry.

"There's this really interesting tension that I've never seen before," said Little, the former Suncor CEO.

World.title: Why the U.S. midterms might have ended JD Vance's presidential hopes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

JD Vance's presidential ambitions for 2028 could be among the most significant political casualties of the Democratic blue wave in this month's U.S. midterm elections.

His chances of becoming the Republican candidat e in two years may have suffered a more recent blow, as reports suggest U.S. President Donald Trump has begun to sour on his vice-president.

"Despite years of work to keep his feet glued to Trump’s MAGA coattails, [Vance] is probably losing any semblance of hope that he’ll get to be a GOP frontrunner in 2028," New York Intelligencer staff editor Chas Danner wrote in an article under the headline "JD Vance’s presidential dream is being snuffed out."

"At the beginning of the year, Vance was widely seen as the GOP’s presumptive 2028 nominee. He may end the year as the presumptive also-ran, if that."

Over at the conservative magazine National Review, senior writer Noah Rothman also weighed in on what he views as Vance's diminishing political fortunes, saying, "Those who invested in JD Vance ’s political stock ... may be looking to offload their holdings."

Vance hasn’t publicly said if he will run for president in 2028, but before the midterms, he was considered a front-runner, with perhaps the highest name recognition of any potential candidate.

However, since the midterms, Vance's aspirations "have suffered, because he's Donald Trump's vice-president," said Michael Traugott, a research professor emeritus at the University of Michigan's Center for Political Studies, in an interv iew with CBC News.

Exit polls suggested Republicans lost the election over issues relating to inflation and the cost of living, government corruption and the war in Iran.

"The problem is that the vice-president can't separ ate himself very easily from the administration's policies," Traugott said.

Donors express concern about Vance

According to the Wall Street Journal, after the Democrats' success in taking the House of Representatives and Senate in the midterms, some Republican donors began making calls to senior party members a nd expressing concerns that they couldn't back Vance, because he's too tied to an unpopular administration.

There are reports that Trump has grown frustrated with Vance's position on Iran. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

This illustrates the challenge Vance faces: Do Republican primary voters want a candidate who has broader support among the general public but isn't directly connected to the president, or will they only support someone who has Trump's endorsement?

"There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring,” Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist, told Reuters.

Trump hasn’t endorsed Vance or anyone else. Reports have also emerged recently that Vance himself is not so sure about a run, particularly in the wake of the Republicans' disastrous showing in the midterms.

In Republican primaries, Trump still commands a lot of votes and a lot of respect, Martin Cohen, a political science professor with James Madison University, told CBC News.

"I would definitely think that the front-runner would be the candidate with Trump's endorsement, if he does give one," he said.

Vance blamed Iran war for midterm losses

That means Vance will have to get his boss's approval, as well as the support of the MAGA base, while "trying to distance himself a little bit, at least," Cohen said.

Vance's attempt to distance himself from the administration may have already begun, with possible consequences.

Following the midterms, Vance, in a lengthy post on X, levelled much of the blame for Republican losses on the war in Iran.

"If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance wrote. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest."

WATCH | JD Vance blames Iran war for midterms. Is he really blaming Trump?: JD Vance blames Iran war for midterms. Is he really blaming Trump? | Duration 1:12 U.S. Vice-President JD Vance blamed deep Republican losses in the midterm elections on the Iran war, in a lengthy online post on Wednesday. U.S. President Donald Trump also acknowledged the impact of the Iran war, suggesting voters were frustrated by high gas prices caused by the conflict.

Vance, who according to reports has for a while privately expressed reservations about the war, has simultaneously argued that there's "no daylight" between him and the president on Iran.

In response to the X post, Trump agreed Iran may have been a factor in the midterm losses. But he also insisted that invading Iran was the right policy decision.

Trump told reporters that Vance's post should have added, "'If you had it to do again, would you do it again?' The answer is yes."

Soon after the X post, the vice-president, who had been leading negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, was taken off the file.

Posting on Truth Social, Trump said his administration no l onger needed a deal with Iran and that he wanted Vance to focus "his complete and total attention" on alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states.

Abe Greenwald, the executive editor of Commentary magazine, called Trump's sidelining of Vance a " remarkably skillful work of public humiliation."

Karen Beckwith, a political science professor with Ohio-based Case Western Reserve University, said in an email to CBC News that Trump's removal of Vance from any responsibility for negotiating or interacting with Iranian counterparts "undermines Vance as a potential presidential nominee in 2028."

Meanwhile, Fox News host Brian Kilmeade lashed out at Vance after his interview with Kilmeade's colleague Laura Ingraham, in which Vance said there were some who want the Iran war to go on indefinitely.

Kilmeade rejected that assertion, calling it "another straw man" argument from Vance, while adding that "he never should have been vice-president."

Trump reportedly frustrated with Vance

Beckwith said this could leave Vance without any substantive achievements on which to campaign for the 2028 nomination — unlike potential opponents like Secretary of State Marco Rubio or Republican governors and senators.

While Trump may have soured on Vance, he reportedly has been praising U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

Asked about his social media post about Iran at a news conference on Friday, Vance, flanked by both Trump and Rubio, said the president makes the decision, that the president has said he would attack Iran again and that it's his job to support the president.

Vance's comments followed a New York Times report earlier this week that Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how Vance has framed his assessment of what went wrong in Iran, complaining to aides and allies that Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran.

Accordi ng to the Times, Trump has instead been praising Rubio, a strong supporter of the U.S. war against Iran, as a potential presidential candidate.

While past polls have shown Vance as the leading Republican candidate for 2028, a recent poll from Emerson College had Rubio as the top choice.

Presidents in recent history, dating back to Ronald Reagan, have all publicly endorsed their vice-presidents who sought to be their party's candidate for the presidency. That includes Joe Biden's endorsement of Kamala Harris in 2024, despite Biden having been pressured by members of his own party to not run for second term.

"I don't think that Donald Trump is g oing to be shy about endorsing somebody," Traugott said. "Ordinarily, we would think the vice-president would have an advantage ... so the fact that he may be souring on this relationship is very important. Even if they were to say that [Trump] was remaining neutral, that would be a slap in the face of that."

Yet some political observers are cautious about writing Vance's political obituary just yet. Republican strategist Mark Bedn ar told CBC News that V ance has developed good connections to a large donor base within the Republican party over the past couple years.

Meanwhile, Republican strategist Barrett Marson told CBC News that Trump may have actually done Vance a favour by taking him off the Iran file.

"That is an absolute blessing. The less one has to do with this immensely unpopular war, the better you are off politically."

Marson added that there's still a lot of time before 2028, meaning things could improve to Vance's benefit. For example, gas prices could come down significantly, interest rates for homes could drop and voters could start to view the economy in positive terms.

"Two years is just an eternity," Marson said. "Especially in Donald Trump's America."

World.title: WhatsApp is a 'lifeline' for refugees. Advocates fear it could be severed in fight over federal bill
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Raymond Gukiina came to Canada in 2022 as a refugee, he used WhatsApp to stay in touch with his family back home in Uganda.

But Gukiina also turned to the popular messaging app to help other refugees and asylum seekers who were struggling to find safe places to live amid a housing crisis in Toronto.

"We opened up a WhatsApp group that had mostly refugees that were sent out of the shelters or living on the streets ... to share information" about shelter beds and other services, the 26-year-old said.

Gukiina, now executive director of the National Network for Immigrants and Refugees-Canada, a non-profit that grew out of the WhatsApp group, said the platform remains key for newcomers to get support in their new communities and maintain ties to loved ones abroad.

But a recent Senate committee hearing has fuelled concerns that a lawful access bill being advanced by the federal government could affect messaging services such as WhatsApp and cut vulnerable people off from the platform they rely on.

Raymond Gukiina says WhatsApp is a key tool for refugees and other newcomers to Canada. (Submitted by Raymond Gukiina)

That's because major tech companies have said they may be forced to suspend services that offer end-to-end encryption if the controversial legislation, known as Bill C-22, which would give law enforcement more access to private communications and data, comes into force.

"Shutting it down [would be] really a tragedy," Gukiina said of WhatsApp.

Alina Murad, director of federal government relations at The Refugee Centre, a non-profit group in Montreal, also described WhatsApp as "a very, very crucial tool" in the refugee resettlement and integration processes.

"It's a lifeline in many ways," she said.

"So if you take away this tool that, for the most part, everyone in the world is familiar with and knows how to use with ease, it leaves people vulnerable — extremely vulnerable."

WATCH | Meta would 'consider' pulling services over Bill C-22: Meta would consider pulling apps from Canada over 'lawful access' bill | Duration 1:58 Bill C-22 would force tech companies to adapt their systems so they all have the ability to hand over information to investigators with a warrant. It would also grant the public safety minister the ability to require electronic service providers to build surveillance and monitoring systems.

The legislation

Bill C-22, which is being studied in the Senate, would require technology companies to adapt their systems to be able to provide private communications to Canadian law enforcement and the CSIS spy agency during investigations.

Companies would also be forced to retain users' metadata for six months.

The government has said the measures will help create "a modernized legal framework that helps ensure that CSIS can investigate threats to the security of Canada and law enforcement agencies can effectively detect, deter and respond to crime."

But at a Senate committee hearing on Monday, representatives for Meta, which owns WhatsApp, and Signal, another encrypted messaging service, said Bill C-22 would hamper their ability to offer end-to-end encryption in Canada.

Rachel Curran, Meta's head of public policy for Canada, said the company "would need to consider" withdrawing affected services — effectively, WhatsApp — if the legislation passes.

"In a similar situation, when Apple was served with a technical assistance order that it could not comply with without weakening or breaking encryption in the U.K., it chose to withdraw those affected services from the market," she said. "And I think we would need to consider the same option."

Udbhav Tiwari, vice-president of strategy and global affairs at Signal, also told the Senate committee on Monday that the firm would be forced to either "engineer a vulnerability" into its platform or refuse to comply with the law.

"And at that point in time, we will have no choice but not to serve Canadian users."

David Taylor, a spokesperson for Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree, told CBC News in an email Friday that the legislation does "not permit or require companies to introduce systemic vulnerabilities or so-called 'back doors.'"

Amendments adopted in the House of Commons also clarify that "service providers cannot be required to break encryption or introduce systemic vulnerabilities, that ministerial authorities cannot be used in place of judicial warrants and that any data-related requirements are strictly limited to metadata, with reduced retention periods and clear legal thresholds," Taylor said.

"The proposals on encryption in C-22 are similar to those in Australia, where WhatsApp continues to operate. They are stronger than those in the United Kingdom, where WhatsApp is available."

Group chats key

Nevertheless, the legislation has fuelled fears that WhatsApp service could be affected.

WhatsApp says more than three billion people around the world use its platform. While usage varies by country, a 2023 survey by the U.S.-based Pew Research Center found that it had "broad reach" in middle-income countries in particular.

Ashika Niraula, a senior research associate at Toronto Metropolitan University's Global Migration Institute, studies how highly skilled migrants and international students use digital platforms before and after they get to Canada.

WhatsApp says more than three billion people around the world use the messaging platform. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)

She said WhatsApp groups — where more than 1,000 people can exchange messages in a single digital space — have emerged as a key place for newcomers to get information about life in Canada.

That ranges from how to rent an apartment, open a bank account or find affordable groceries to navigating the Canadian immigration process.

The group chats help newcomers feel less isolated while creating a place to speak openly with people who share their cultural backgrounds or languages and have gone through similar experiences, Niraula said.

"It can help [make] settling into a new country feel less overwhelming."

Encryption offers 'level of safety'

At the same time, WhatsApp remains an easy and cost-effective way for newcomers to stay in touch with relatives in their home countries, said Lauren Lallemand, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees.

"Not being able to get back in touch with your family members who you've been separated from" can have very real effects, including on peoples' mental health, she said.

"If it's no longer possible to use WhatsApp in Canada but it continues to be available across most other countries ... there's a sense of people in Canada being left behind."

Lallemand also said the fact that WhatsApp is encrypted "provides some level of safety" for people who fled persecution in their home countries — and losing that encryption could put them at risk.

"People who are journalists, human rights defenders, refugees in Canada — they often already face repression transnationally, like surveillance threats and intimidation by foreign governments," she said.

"So it is doubly dangerous to be introducing laws that could further target communities that are already very vulnerable."

World.title: Hegseth reportedly moves to restrict defence ties with Canada, but Ottawa sees no change
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has reportedly issued a classified directive restricting military co-operation between the United States and Canada — something that Canadian government and military officials were not aware of and have seen no evidence it has been put into practice.

The Washington Post reported late Friday that the directive was circulated last week in a secret memorandum. The report cited U.S. officials familiar with the decision.

Three Canadian defence officials speaking on background on Saturday said they were aware of the reports and were looking to substantiate them, as well as seeking clarification because there's been no change at the military operational level between the two countries.

A Republican senator attending the Halifax International Security Forum confirmed the existence of the memo and the restrictions but downplayed their impact, saying they have no effect on operations between the two countries.

"It does limit general flag officer meetings to those that advance [U.S. Department of War] objectives," said Sen. Mike Rounds, who sits on the armed services committee.

U.S. defence officials — uniform and civilian — must seek permission before attending social events or think-tank conferences.

The measures were drafted months ago but only signed recently, Rounds said, adding that it's unfortunate they were leaked.

The intent, however, was to put pressure on Canada.

U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds speaks to reporters in the U.S. Capitol Building on Monday in Washington, D.C. Rounds on Saturday confirmed the existence of Hegseth's memo and the restrictions, but downplayed their impact. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"Look, we really want you to bring up your defence spending," Rounds said, before quickly adding the U.S. delegation at the conference had a chance to be briefed on the latest measures.

"We just had a chance to talk with our Canadian friends, and they indicated and laid out the roadmap that they're using to significantly increase their defence spending."

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware says he was irritated by Hegseth's directive and its impact on relations with Canada.

"This is a completely unnecessary insertion of a negative tone," said Coons, who is also in Halifax and sits on the Senate foreign relations committee.

"I'm relieved this has no significant operational impact, but at the end of the day, as we've got our adversaries globally pulling together and working more closely — Iran, North Korea, China, Russia — the United States should be doing nothing to further aggravate some of the distance and division between the United States and Canada."

Defence Minister David McGuinty, who is also at the security forum, said the two countries continue to work "hand-in-glove" on various missions such as stopping the flow of illegal drugs in the Caribbean and on new policy initiatives such as integrated air and missile defence.

"It's the first time we heard of this — just yesterday," McGuinty said, referring to the directive. "It's clear there's some sort of document we haven't seen. I'm not aware of the contents of it."

Minister of National Defence David McGuinty rises during question period in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Nov. 3. McGuinty says Canada and the U.S. continue to work 'hand-in-glove' on various military missions and new policy initiatives. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

There was no mention of the directive from the Americans at the security forum dinner Friday night, according to two of the confidential defence sources, one of whom wondered if the congressmen and senators were even aware of it.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

In an interview with CBC's Adrienne Arsenault, McGuinty said he has not yet contacted Hegseth over the issue. He said Canadian officials are reaching out to U.S. counterparts on a host of security-related issues.

Asked if he thinks there were certain issues in Canada-U.S. relations that may have precipitated the memo, McGuinty declined to speculate, noting Ottawa has learned to take the often unexpected decisions of the Trump administration in stride.

WATCH | 'Business as usual' between Canada and U.S., McGuinty says: 'Business as usual' between Canada and U.S., McGuinty says following Pentagon restrictions report | Duration closed caption 2:02 In an interview with CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, Defence Minister David McGuinty responded to a Washington Post report that U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has issued a classified directive restricting military co-operation between the U.S. and Canada. McGuinty declined to speculate on what may have precipitated the memo and said it was 'business as usual' between the two countries.

"There have been curveballs of this kind," McGuinty said of the sudden nature of the directive.

"We've learned to move forward."

The existence of such a directive would only add to mounting tensions between the long-standing allies over trade and defence spending.

Canada, U.S. working on trade deal

The move comes as the Trump administration and the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney inch toward a trade deal that could see some relief in key sectors such as automotive and steel and aluminum.

The military and defence ties between Canada and the U.S. are deep, long-standing and would be difficult to restrict at an operational level without harming the security of the U.S. itself in one fashion or another, said one of the sources.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: Is it OK to start travelling to the United States again? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for this Sunday's show

The two countries co-operate in the defence of North America through NORAD. In Europe, they are founding partners of NATO and work side by side with the other 30 members of the Western alliance. They also work together in the Indo-Pacific in joint military exercises.

A third source said it would also be difficult and counter-productive for Washington to, for example, restrict access to U.S.-made weapons systems and equipment, which Washington has been eager to sell and pressuring Canada to buy.

WATCH | Carney says he's examined risk of U.S. military action in Canada: Carney says he examined 'extreme tail risk' of U.S. military action in Canada | Duration closed caption 8:20 Prime Minister Mark Carney said in an interview with the New York Times that he's studied the risk of a U.S. military attack on Canada. Matina Stevis-Gridneff, the newspaper's Canada bureau chief, said Carney took several seconds — 'a pregnant pause' — before responding as to whether such a scenario had crossed his mind.

Officially, the scope of Hegseth's restrictions is unclear, according to the Washington Post report. Since the memo is classified, the Department of War has not identified which military programs or activities might be affected.

In a statement to CBC News prior to Rounds's comments, the Pentagon's chief spokesperson, Sean Parnell, ruled out restrictions on operational level matters, but was vague on what precise impact the memo would have.

"The Department of War is taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defence objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defence relationship," Parnell said in a written response.

"DoW is prioritizing opportunities for bilateral cooperation that strengthens the defence of our Homelands and shared hemisphere, while supporting Canada's ability to meet NATO obligations. This guidance does not impact defence intelligence co-operation, our binational NORAD command or our co-operation through NATO."

The response left open questions about bilateral military exercises, training exchanges, defence planning and other forms of co-operation.

But even on that level, Canadian officials say they've seen no evidence thus far of any restrictions and point to the notion that the memo has been in circulation for a week.

WATCH | Pentagon withdraws from Canada-U.S. defence board: Pentagon withdraws from Canada-U.S. defence board | Duration closed caption 2:33 The Pentagon has announced it has paused its participation in a joint Canada-U.S. defence board that's been around since the 1940s, accusing Canada of not making enough progress on its commitments. Canada says it's always ready for constructive discussion on how to strengthen mutual security.

Last spring, the Trump administration paused U.S. participation in the Permanent Joint Board on Defence (PJBD) with Canada.

Halting the activity of the decades-old board, a bilateral advisory group that co-ordinates continental security and recommends defence policy to both governments, was considered largely symbolic because it met infrequently.

Canada has been routinely criticized in Washington over its lacklustre defence spending.

There has been change under Carney, and Canada has now hit the NATO target of spending two per cent of GDP.

Carney, however, has publicly stated he wants to diversify both the country's trading relationship and where it sources its military equipment. He has said it's not good for more than 70 cents of defence equipment dollars to be going to one market — the United States.

World.title: City of Regina plans to shut down public transit starting Monday
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There will be no public transit on Monday in Regina, according to the city.

The city's transit shutdown comes amid the ongoing collective bargaining agreement negotiations with the local transit workers' union, Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU) Local 588.

The city confirmed its director of transit operations sent employees a letter on Saturday advising them that only management and security personnel would be allowed to access Regina Transit facilities, yards and depots effective Monday at 3:00 a.m. CST.

A "formal lockout" will commence at 11:00 a.m. CST Monday.

The city says it cannot maintain a minimum level of service due to ATU Local 588 implementing an overtime ban starting Monday.

John Di Nino, president of ATU Canada, said the service suspension is the city's choice and the union does not want service to end.

"This is not something being initiated by the ATU. In fact this is the irresponsibility of city council who's allowing this to happen. They're penalizing their members because they can't come to the table and negotiate a fair contract for transit workers. "

He said workers have not had a new collective agreement for almost two years and he confirmed the city chose to suspend services after the union said it would implement a ban on voluntary overtime starting Monday.

John Di Nino, president of ATU Canada. (ATU Canada)

"The city is using a power play. They're suggesting that without the voluntary overtime that they cannot maintain their service levels, again that's a farce," he said.

"If an employer relies on overtime to fill shifts to provide a service, then they're not managing the property correctly. That only tells us that more workers are needed to maintain regular service."

He said workers will still report to work on Monday morning.

A statement the city provided to CBC said "The decision to impact transit service was not taken lightly. Resident safety is a top priority of the city, and as the weather continues to get colder the city needed to ensure transit service is reliable so that no one is left outside waiting for a ride."

Paratransit service will continue, according to the city's website.

"Transit employees are valued, both by the city and residents who rely on them every day. The agreement must balance staff needs with the interests of residents and taxpayers," according to the statement.

On Monday, Environment Canada projects the temperature of Regina to be –4 C during the day and –11 C at night.

According to De Nino and the city's letter to workers, they will not be paid after Monday morning while the suspension occurs.

The union has also raised other issues such as pay, benefits and safety while trying to negotiate the agreement, Di Nino said.

The city did not respond to CBC's additional requests for comment by time of publication.

World.title: A real '3 Body Problem': Astronomers discover a nearby 'weirdo' triple-star system
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Roughly 28 light-years from Earth lies a peculiar star system called IRAS 21500+5903.

For years, astronomers had known about the two stars that orbited one another. But then, when looking for exoplanets — planets that orbit other stars — a group of astronomers made a surprising discovery: there was another star in the system. Instead of being a binary star system, this was a triple-star system.

"It's a freak thing. It was an annoying object," said Étienne Artigau, a researcher at the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets (IREx) at the University of Montreal. "It's not what we were looking for."

Their findings were released this week in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

The system contains a red dwarf, a type of star that is very common in our galaxy, and two smaller, dense white dwarfs. One is roughly 1,000 astronomical units (the distance between the sun and Earth) away from the red dwarf. The other, they found, was a mere two astronomical units away, a little similar to the distance from the sun to Mars.

The inner white dwarf orbits the red dwarf, while the outer white dwarf orbits the pair.

A quirky neighbour

What's surprising is that no one had discovered it over the decades.

"It's weird that no one found the system, but it also says that there are weird things overlooked just next to us," Artigau said. "It's like not next door, but down the road, just one block away of a stellar neighbourhood."

When a low- to medium-mass star reaches the end of its life, it first swells into a red giant before leaving behind the dense and small white dwarf. It is what will happen to our own sun in roughly five billion years.

This artist concept depicts an ultra-dense dead star, called a white dwarf, passing in front of a small red star. (NASA/JPL-Caltech)

While looking for an exoplanet in this system, the international team of astronomers — led by the University of Montreal team — used an instrument at the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope in Maunakea, Hawaii, called SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou). It is used to detect exoplanets and does this by measuring tiny changes in a star's velocity, which can be caused by orbiting planets.

But the red dwarf wasn't doing what it was supposed to be doing. It was moving differently, with velocity changes of nearly 16 kilometres a second. That's a huge difference.

Initially, they thought it was a brown dwarf, a type of substellar object that has a mass of about 75 times that of Jupiter.

But that still didn't make sense.

More weirdness

The velocities were so off that they broke Artigau's code.

"At some point, we said, Okay, we should get to the end of it. Something's wrong with that object. And so I fixed the code," he said. "And then we just said, let me do the math of that brown dwarf. Okay, no, it doesn't work."

It was a real head-scratcher.

What they eventually discovered is that what was causing the perturbations was a high-mass… something. But it also couldn't be seen.

Could it be a black hole? A neutron star? A white dwarf?

The team turned to the Gemini North telescope, also on Maunakea. Using high-resolution images from its 'Alopeke instrument — a specialized high-speed camera — they found what they were looking for: a faint companion star — a white dwarf — orbiting closely around the red dwarf.

WATCH | The orbit of the Welopō'ai triple-star system:

Here's where it gets weirder.

Before becoming a white dwarf, the star would have become a red giant. As it swelled up, its orbit would have been so close to the red dwarf that the pair must have interacted with one another. Many times these types of stars envelop the red dwarf, or the two may even merge. This didn't happen.

And there was more.

The inner white dwarf should be spiralling inward toward the red dwarf. Instead, it is in a stable orbit.

It could be that the more distant white dwarf is somehow stabilizing the orbit, though they don't know yet how. That's for future research.

The image on the left shows the two components of the system: Welopō'ai A, a closely orbiting red dwarf and white dwarf pair, and Welopō'ai B, a second white dwarf located farther away. The image on the right provides a close-up view of the inner pair and their orbital paths. (Pan-STARRS1/STScI/MAST, left, International Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab, right. Graphical construction by Étienne Artigau & Heidi White (UdeM/IREx))

"We're saying it cannot exist," Artigau said. "Of course, it exists. It's there."

Paul Delaney, professor emeritus of physics and astronomy at York University in Toronto, believes that perhaps the more distant white dwarf was once much closer to the other pair.

"I mean, when planetary systems form now, one of the standard things is migration," he said. "I would bet that they were relatively proximate to each other and then they did engage in a bit of gravitational embracing, and the further white dwarf today was much, much closer in its heyday."

To add to the weirdness, the astronomers calculated that the system is roughly 10 billion years old, older than our own solar system of 4.6 billion years, and its stars are metal-rich. Typically, these older stars are metal-poor.

"It's tantalizing, and we just don't know if it means anything. It may just be a random draw basically of a stellar population," Artigau said.

Still searching for an exoplanet

The astronomers gave this system the Hawaiian name Welopō'ai, combining "welo" which means an inherited family trait, and "pō'ai," which means an orbit or circular path. The name therefore means "path of family traits."

The very popular book and Netflix show 3 Body Problem looks at a triple-star system and the effects it could have on a nearby planet, mainly to a civilization that has evolved on that planet.

One of the terms that is used to describe the triple-star system in the show is "chaotic," which affects the speed at which the civilization can evolve.

The issue is an age-old physics problem. Two-body systems are predictable. But add a third, and everything blows up. That's because Body A pulls on Body B and Body C. Body C in turn pulls on Body A and Body B, and because of these interactions, it changes their motions and their forces forever.

WATCH | Newton's three-body problem explained:

While researchers didn't find an exoplanet, Artigau said the search isn't over.

"It's such a weirdo system that Atanas Stefanov, one of the authors, he's applying for time to get, to look for planets around the red dwarf," he said.

Whether there is a planet there or whether an alien civilization could live on a planet in a triple-star system remains to be seen.

For Artigau, he said the fact that something new was thrown at him was very exciting.

"I like it," he said. "Little things that are just sideways in your life in research. It's fun."
