World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Sheinbaum in China, Rodríguez at the mic and a kingpin behind bars
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum spent most of the week in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. That left Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez running the mañaneras from Monday on. The Minnesota Vikings, meanwhile, were pumping thin air into a chamber in the Midwest to prepare for Sunday night’s kickoff in Mexico City.

It was a relatively calm week at home while the president was abroad. That changed Friday night, when Mexican special forces captured an alleged drug kingpin on the FBI’s Top 10 Most Wanted list, sparking violence in Sinaloa.

Didn’t have time to catch Mexico’s top stories of the week of Nov. 16? Here’s what you missed.

Sheinbaum touches down in Shenzhen

Sheinbaum left Mexico City’s airport at 11 p.m. on Saturday for a 12:35 a.m. flight to Tijuana. She then boarded China Southern Airlines flight CZ8032 to Shenzhen. It was another commercial flight, in keeping with the austerity symbolism started by her predecessor. She arrived at 11:30 a.m. Monday local time and went straight to the Tequila Coyote’s restaurant to meet Mexicans living in China, whom she called “extraordinary.” The economy-class journey also struck a chord online: Bloomberg reported that a hashtag about her arrival was seen 10 million times on Weibo.

Sheinbaum pitches Plan México at APEC

In a 13-minute speech at the APEC CEO Summit on Tuesday, Sheinbaum told more than 2,000 business and political representatives that Mexico “guarantees conditions for investment.” She said the government and private companies expect to invest US $432 billion in infrastructure under Plan México between 2024 and 2030. She also described the plan as having a “humanist vision.”

Mexico News Daily noted that foreign direct investment hit a record of almost $35 billion in the first half of 2026, though growth was only 2.1%. Insecurity, USMCA uncertainty and the recent judicial reform are seen as deterrents. On Thursday, she gave a four-minute address at the Leaders’ Meeting, calling this “a decisive moment for humanity.” Mexico will host APEC in 2028.

Meetings with Xi, Carney, Trump and more

Sheinbaum told Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday that her visit marks “a new era” in bilateral ties, focused on science, technology, clean energy and health. Neither side’s readout mentioned Mexico’s new tariffs on Chinese goods. She also revealed she had asked Xi for a panda for Chapultepec Zoo.

She also met Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney that day, and both reaffirmed support for renewing the USMCA. Carney said bilateral trade is up 18% this year.

On Wednesday came the one many were watching: a roughly 20-minute meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, her first formal in-person talks with him. Sheinbaum said trade negotiations are “very far along” but gave no timeline for a deal. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said 56 technical meetings have been held. Trump’s recent tariff threat over the migrant caravan went unmentioned, and the two agreed to meet again at next month’s G20 summit at Mar-a-Lago.

She also met leaders from Vietnam, Australia, Singapore and Peru, plus the IMF’s Kristalina Georgieva. At her closing press conference, Sheinbaum called the trip “very productive and very successful” but said Mexico has no plans for a free trade agreement with China.

Rodríguez takes the mañanera podium

With the president away, Interior Minister Rodríguez led this week’s morning press conferences. On Monday, the mañanera featured World Bank data showing that Mexico’s monetary poverty rate fell from 35.3% in 2018 to 21.1% in 2025, with 17.3 million fewer people in poverty projected by the end of 2026. Officials also touted a CB Global Data poll putting Sheinbaum’s approval at 69.8%, the highest in Latin America.

Sheinbaum joined Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday’s mañanera by video link, and on Thursday, Rodríguez praised her boss’s “composure” and “firmness, without confrontation or subservience.”

Mexico ranks fourth in APEC tech exports

An APEC report showed that Mexico ranks fourth among APEC economies in the share of exports that are medium- and high-tech goods, at 70.6%. Only Taiwan, Hong Kong and South Korea rank higher. Mexico sits ahead of China (61.6%), the United States (46.5%) and Canada (31.7%). APEC projects regional growth of 3.4% this year and 3.1% in 2027.

Revolution Day parade

Hours after landing from China, Sheinbaum presided over the parade marking the 116th anniversary of the Mexican Revolution. She invoked the 1917 Constitution and defended democratic freedoms. She also accused political opponents and foreign interests of trying to weaken her administration and delegitimize the 2027 midterms. Pageant floats and military contingents then rolled through the Zócalo and down Paseo de la Reforma.

What’s going on with the peso?

The peso sank past 19 per dollar on Thursday, hitting 19.04, its weakest level in 17 months. Bloomberg tied the move to Banxico’s dovish stance, after a 25-basis-point cut to 6.25%, and expectations of another Fed hike in December. That would narrow the interest-rate gap that supports the carry trade. The peso is down about 5.5% this year.

The November MND Peso Index™ offers some context. It found the peso 4.2% undervalued at 18.67 per dollar, versus a 0.7% undervaluation in October. The swing was driven almost entirely by depreciation.

Mexico and US lose measles-free status

The Pan American Health Organization revoked the measles-free status of Mexico, the United States and Bolivia after 12 months of continuous transmission. Canada lost its status a year earlier. Mexico has recorded 20,601 cases over 2025 and 2026, but only 14 are currently active, down from a February peak of 1,314. The government aims to end the outbreak in the second half of 2027 and regain recognition in 2028.

Migrant caravan trudges north

A caravan of about 1,500 migrants left Tapachula last Tuesday, and Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods if it isn’t stopped. By Tuesday, it had shrunk to 781 people in Mapastepec, Chiapas, as migration officials urged people to go home. On Thursday, Rodríguez responded to U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s remarks by saying Mexico “will continue detaining” people involved in smuggling.

Former Iguala mayor sentenced

José Luis Abarca, Iguala’s mayor during the 2014 Ayotzinapa tragedy, was sentenced to 60 years on Nov. 10 by a federal judge in Tamaulipas. He and 25 co-defendants, including the police chief, were convicted of six counts of aggravated homicide and attempted murder. Those charges stem from the attack on a bus carrying the Los Avispones soccer team. Abarca is already serving 20- and 92-year sentences. His lawyer argued police control had been ceded to then-Gov. Ángel Aguirre.

‘El Chapo Isidro’ captured in Sinaloa

Friday night’s big news came from Sinaloa. Mexican special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro,” and two other leaders of his organization.

The FBI lists Meza Flores on its Top 10 Most Wanted list and had offered up to US $5 million for information leading to his arrest. Agents came under fire from gunmen using explosives during the raid in Guasave, according to the Defense Ministry. Violence erupted afterward, with civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game and vehicles burning on a highway near Los Mochis. The Mexican government said U.S. intelligence helped, giving few details. The three were flown to Mexico City.

Looking ahead

The aftermath in Sinaloa is the story to watch, as violence following the capture may not end quickly. On trade, Sheinbaum and Trump are due to meet again at the G20 in Florida next month. Sheinbaum has said talks are “very far along,” but no deal date has been set, and the U.S. has still not agreed to any tariff reductions for Mexican automobiles, steel or aluminum. Financial markets, meanwhile, will be watching the Fed’s December meeting and Banxico’s decision on Dec. 17 for clues about whether the peso’s slide continues. Back at the Estadio Azteca, the Vikings and 49ers will find out Sunday whether their different altitude strategies paid off.

Mexico News Daily

This story contains summaries of original Mexico News Daily articles. The summaries were generated by Claude, then revised and fact-checked by a Mexico News Daily staff editor.

World.title: Mexican special forces capture top FBI fugitive ‘El Chapo Isidro,’ unleashing a night of fire in Sinaloa
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexican special forces on Friday detained Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro,” who was one of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation’s 10 most-wanted fugitives.

The arrest on Friday night in the municipality of Guasave in the northern state of Sinaloa triggered a violent reaction, with cartel operatives setting up narco-blockades and engaging in gun battles with military forces.

Se informa que, derivado de la coordinación entre organismos de inteligencia de la Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional y de los E.U.A., realizada en el marco de la cooperación bilateral con ese país, el 20 de noviembre del presente año, Fuerzas Especiales de la Guardia Nacional (Lobos) y del Ejército (Murciélagos), en coordinación con elementos de Fuerzas Especiales del Ejército comisionados en la Secretaría de Seguridad Pública del Estado de Sinaloa, detuvieron en el municipio de Guasave, Sin., a Fausto Isidro N (a) “Chapo Isidro”, jefe de la organización delictiva “Beltrán Leyva” y aliado al “Cártel del Pacífico” facción “Mayos”, a Germán N (a) “Serafín”, segundo al mando de esa organización delincuencial y a José N, operador financiero de este mismo grupo delictivo. (a) “Chapo Isidro”, cuenta con una orden de aprehensión en México por delincuencia organizada y por cometer delitos contra la salud, y una orden de extradición a los E.U.A. por asociación delictiva para distribuir droga en territorio estadounidense; además, se encuentra en la lista de los 10 fugitivos más buscados por el F.B.I. La operación para estas detenciones, fue realizada por fuerzas militares de élite, las que una vez ubicado con precisión el objetivo, mediante el empleo de diversos ingenios tecnológicos, la desarrollaron en 3 fases, de la forma siguiente: Arribo al área del objetivo: se realizó utilizando el sigilo y la sorpresa por diferentes vías de acceso terrestre al área de la detención. Establecimiento de la seguridad y captura del objetivo: esta se realizó a inmediaciones de la ubicación de los detenidos, mediante la colocación de un dispositivo de seguridad interna y externa, para evitar la huida o la llegada de refuerzos, habiendo sido agredidos con disparos de armas de fuego y explosivos, por lo que la fuerza de detención ingresó a la casa habitación para capturar a las personas indicadas. Evacuación del objetivo: confirmada la identidad de los detenidos, se procedió a su evacuación a la Ciudad de México, en una aeronave de la Fuerza Aérea Mexicana, para ser puestos a disposición de las autoridades ministeriales competentes. Derivado de esta detención, se registraron bloqueos en los municipios de Ahome, Guamúchil, Guasave y Navolato, para lo cual, en coordinación con autoridades locales, se activó el plan antibloqueo, movilizando fuerzas de seguridad para restablecer el tránsito en las vías de comunicación y proteger a la población. #NoticiadeÚltimaHora #ComunicadoDePrensa #EjércitoMexicano #FuerzaAéreaMx #GuardiaNacional — @Defensamx (@Defensamx1) November 21, 2026

Meza Flores, 44, is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organization and an ally of the “Mayos” faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, according to the Ministry of National Defense (Defensa), which announced his arrest in a statement early Saturday. He is considered one of the most powerful drug traffickers in Sinaloa, with the Reforma newspaper describing him as “the main active capo” in the state.

U.S. authorities have described him as the leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO) and a former high-ranking leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organization.

In its statement, Defensa said that the Beltrán Leyva Organization’s second-in-command, Germán N, alias “Serafín,” and a financial operator of the same group identified as José N were also detained in the operation in Guasave carried out by elite National Guard and Mexican Army special forces. The ministry said the three suspects were arrested at a home in Guasave, a coastal municipality in northern Sinaloa that includes a city of the same name. It said that “stealth and “surprise” were used in the operation to detain the three men, who were subsequently transferred to Mexico City on an Air Force plane.

Defensa said that the capture of Meza Flores was the result of coordination between Mexican and U.S. intelligence agencies. It said he was wanted in Mexico on organized crime and drug trafficking charges and noted that he is subject to a U.S. extradition request.

In 2017, U.S. authorities announced a reward of up to US $5 million for information leading to Meza Flores’ arrest.

In February 2025, the U.S. State Department said that “for over 20 years, the Meza-Flores TCO has been responsible for smuggling multi-ton quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, and marijuana into the United States.”

It noted that in May 2012, Meza Flores was indicted in the U.S. on drug trafficking and firearm charges and in November 2019 “a federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging … [him] with additional drug trafficking and firearms violations.”

On Saturday morning, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) said that the capture of Meza Flores “represents a significant victory against one of Mexico’s most violent criminal networks.”

“For decades, this organization has fueled bloodshed and instability in Mexico while trafficking deadly drugs, including fentanyl, into the United States, posing a significant threat to American lives and communities,” the DEA said on social media.

“#DEA commends Mexican authorities for this decisive operation and remains committed to dismantling the violent criminal organizations responsible for trafficking deadly drugs into our country.”

In a social media post earlier on Saturday, federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said that the arrest of “El Chapo Isidro” and the two other cartel suspects was “an important step” toward the “pacification of Sinaloa,” a state that has been plagued by Sinaloa Cartel infighting for more than two years.

However, it was violence rather than peace that immediately followed the arrests.

‘A night of terror’

The Defense Ministry reported that narco-blockades were set up in several Sinaloa municipalities, including Ahome, Guasave and Navolato, in response to the arrests on Friday night. Vehicles were set on fire to create the blockades on major roads in Sinaloa, including Federal Highway 15. Gas stations and convenience stores in Guasave were also set ablaze.

There were also gun battles between cartel henchmen and Mexican military forces. Video footage showed that military helicopters opened fire on ground targets in Guasave. Reforma reported that the helicopters targeted criminal cells seeking to “rescue” Meza Flores.

Mexico’s military captured FBI-wanted cartel leader ‘El Chapo Isidro’ in Guasave, Sinaloa. Armed clashes erupted as helicopters opened fire, vehicles burned and roads were blocked. Gunfire also halted a baseball game, sending players and fans scrambling for cover. https://t.co/URhPOTN512 — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) November 21, 2026

Authorities did not say whether anyone was killed during what media outlets described as a “night of terror” in Guasave and other parts of Sinaloa.

Shortly after 9 p.m. Friday, the Sinaloa Security Ministry (SSP) said that federal forces had come under attack in Guasave. In a social media post, the SSP instructed local residents to stay indoors.

A Mexican Pacific League baseball game between the Algodoneros de Guasave and the Venados de Mazatlán at Kuroda Park in Guasave was suspended amid gunfire in the city. CNN reported that an official broadcast showed players from the two teams “fleeing the field mid-game,” while baseball fans “scrambled out of the stands as a barrage of gunfire rang out.”

The arrest of Meza Flores is another high-profile blow against organized crime, following the fatal wounding of Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) leader Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes in a military operation in Jalisco in February.

Mexican authorities have arrested more than 74,000 people for allegedly committing high-impact crimes such as homicide and drug trafficking since President Claudia Sheinbaum took office in October 2024. Among the other cartel figures who have been detained are Audias Flores Silva, an alleged high-ranking member of the CJNG known as “El Jardinero” (The Gardener), and Axel Alfredo Cárdenas Rodríguez, son of a Gulf Cartel leader known as “El Contador.”

World.title: Mexico’s forgotten cactus spirit: An interview about colonche with César Iván Ojeda-Linares
World.content:
We all know the cactus fruit and have maybe tasted its juicy flesh and hard seeds protected by a spiny skin. But most of us have never tried — or even heard of — the fermented beverage that can be made from it.

César Iván Ojeda-Linares, a researcher at the Instituto de Ecología of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM), takes us on a journey through Mexico’s prickly pear landscapes, where he encountered colonche, a traditional fermented drink made from the fruit. He explores its connections with the people who make it, the vessels in which it ferments, and why this heritage is at risk.

What first drew you to Mexico’s fermented drinks?

During my master’s degree, I was studying evolutionary developmental ecology, and I went to Japan for a research stay. There, I realized I wasn’t enjoying working only with models, genes and model plants as much as I had expected.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Secretaría de Turismo Zac (@zacatecas_travel)

One evening, I was invited to a sake tasting by my mentor at Kyoto Sangyo University. I saw the diversity of sake and thought, “This is amazing — Mexico has a diversity of drinks, too.”

I returned to Mexico wanting to investigate fermented drinks, the plants used to make them and their relationships with people and microorganisms. Early in my doctorate, I noticed that plants and fermentation were often studied separately, and people were missing the big picture. What interested me was how people select or manage something invisible: microorganisms.

How did colonche become part of that research?

When I was applying for my doctorate, I wanted to study many things. I was living in Michoacán, a central region in Mexico, and I included pulque, mezcal and fermented corn drinks in my plans because of corn’s symbolic and cultural importance in Mexico.

Then I was reviewing an old book about Mexico’s drinks and came across colonche. There wasn’t much information. When I searched scientific databases, I found at most two articles at that time and only two records of yeast strains isolated. So I started looking for where it was made.

How did you find the colonche producers?

At first, I went to Guanajuato and couldn’t find anything. I would ask about colonche, and people would say they had no idea what it was.

Then I got hungry and stopped somewhere selling gorditas, in a community called La Chirimoya. After eating, already feeling a little discouraged, I asked whether they knew about the colonche fair. A woman told me, “My friend organizes it.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Casa Mercedes (@casamercedesgto)

That was the connection. I went there, began taking notes, met producers and started my fieldwork. I think I interviewed about 13 producers in the community at that time.

The landscape also astonished me. We were walking among nopales more than 3 meters tall. They rose above us and provided shade. Getting to know the producers and the territory was an exploration of a landscape that was new to me.

For someone who has never tried it, what is colonche — and how do people make it?

Colonche is a fermented drink made from prickly pears, especially the red fruits producers call cardonas. There are many ways to prepare it.

The one I particularly like comes from Laguna de Guadalupe, Guanajuato. Producers collect the fruit and peel it where they harvest it. They take it home, squeeze out the pulp, and put it into their pots to ferment. Some of those pots are more than 80 years old.

There is a detail I find beautiful: The peels are left where the fruit is harvested, and cows come along and eat them. Their mouths become stained red — it looks as though they are wearing lipstick.

In San Luis Potosí, I encountered another method. Producers heat the fruit in a metal pot to extract the pulp. Some add anise or other spices. To start fermentation, they may add colonche saved from the previous season or locally produced pulque. Many colonche producers there also make pulque.

In Zacatecas, I encountered a woman who heated the fruit juice and added aguardiente. She had spent time in the United States and, after being deported, did not know how to prepare colonche, so that was the method she used.

From a microbial perspective, what is happening in the pots used in Guanajuato?

Part of the microbial community carrying out fermentation is in the pots themselves. Producers do not necessarily need to add a starter culture or a fermentation “mother.” Their pot is, in effect, their fermentation mother or starter.

Those pots have been in families for generations. Their porosity gives yeast small spaces where they can remain and become active again when liquid and suitable conditions return.

There is another layer to this relationship: the pottery itself. San Felipe Torres Mochas, near Laguna de Guadalupe, specialized in making these pots. That production has been declining, and fewer people make them now. So the pot connects the microorganisms, the family and a local craft tradition.

Hopefully, the producers of these containers will survive or maintain the tradition; otherwise, it will shift to plastic containers and it might be a loss of flavors or aromas.

How does heating the juice and adding a previous batch change the fermentation?

Heating kills some of the wild yeast and bacteria, and it also changes the material they will ferment. It is no longer the same juice coming directly from the fruit, and that changes the possibilities for other yeast to establish themselves. It is like an open space to conquer.

Using a previous batch is also interesting because it involves selection driven by humans. Certain groups of yeast and bacteria survive and are carried over to the next fermentation, reproduced from one fermentation to the next.

In a study we published, we found much lower microbial diversity in the inocula — the material used to start fermentation. That allows us to identify selection for particular, more limited groups of microorganisms. So in a broad sense, the producers are selecting a consortium of microbes that helps them to reproduce what, culturally, they conceive as a good colonche.

What interests you about people selecting organisms they cannot see?

Selection is well studied in plants and animals. With corn, for example, you can see changes in the grain, its size and its uses — whether it is for pozole, tortillas or popcorn.

With microorganisms, it is fascinating because you are not selecting something you can see. You are selecting something you can taste or smell, and you are not selecting only one species; you select a community.

What pressures have you seen on colonche production?

There are fewer producers now than when I began. Some have died, and others have stopped making colonche because of poor seasons for prickly pears and other social and environmental conflicts.

The spaces where people collected fruit are also being fragmented. Land that was used for gathering and communal resources is being divided into plots. In some places, large areas once covered with nopales are being converted to bean monocultures.

Some producers have also told me that colonche no longer comes out the same — that it does not taste the way they remember it, mostly because different environmental factors changed the flavor of the cactus prickly pear fruits.

What did working with Comcáac producers in Sonora teach you about fermentation’s relationship with a landscape?

I worked in Punta Chueca in the northern state of Sonora with Indigenous Comcáac producers who make a drink from cardón fruit. We held a fermentation workshop: They explained how they made it, and I brought a microscope so we could see what was growing in the fermentation. Most of the producers were women, and they invited their children to participate.

One of the most valuable lessons came when we were collecting fruit. I asked why they did not collect fruit that had not opened. They explained that it was not fully ripe, and that if animals had not visited it, fermentation took much longer. They described bats, bees and flies visiting the fruit.

I have not been able to evaluate that relationship directly because of limited time and funding. But their understanding connects fruit availability, animal visitors and fermentation. So, I really see that Indigenous communities have a very detailed way to characterize how these interactions occur, and it has different layers of understanding their relationship with the environment, even with invisible beings such as microbes.

The drink is also part of their New Year celebrations and rituals associated with asking for rain and good harvests. Defending the territory therefore means defending not only the land, but also food systems and practices that depend on it.

Why is colonche difficult to separate from the place where it is made?

It continues fermenting, which makes transporting it difficult. I used to carry samples to the laboratory in a cooler. Once, I closed a container without leaving a way for the carbon dioxide to escape, and it burst. The car’s trunk was covered in red liquid and smelled for weeks.

That is part of what makes it so local. You need to visit the place to know the drink, the people and the ecosystem. In one sense, that protects its uniqueness. At the same time, it limits how widely it can become known.

I think drinking this beverage is a privilege: a chance to enjoy good conversation while taking in the landscape. I know that globalization encourages people to seek out new tastes, and that the “gastronomification” of food fuels this desire. But some things give a place its magic, and colonche is certainly one of them here. Perhaps part of that magic lies in enjoying it in the landscape and among the people who give it life.

Katy Alivraz is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Chicano baby: The Mexican lowriders challenging gang stereotypes
World.content:
Every Sunday, a special kind of meetup takes place in downtown Mexico City: a few dozen men and women gather in oversized white shirts and baggy jeans with blue bandanas hanging from their pockets, all sporting gleaming silver lowrider bicycles.

Inspired by the Mexican-American Chicano communities of 1960s and ‘70s California, their style is often associated with cholos: a Los Angeles street culture that has long been stereotyped as synonymous with gang violence.

But that’s exactly what this group wants to challenge. They are here to represent a subculture shaped by migration and marginalization, honor its heritage and scrap the stigma of violence attached to it.

“We represent culture, that’s it,” Hiram, a member for two years, explains.

Most members in this report chose to be identified by first name only, citing privacy reasons.

“We are not violent, we are not a gang. We’re here so people can see us, see we’re not bad guys.”

Finding support and love

This wanna-not-be gang is strikingly intergenerational. There are little kids in gangster white face paint running between the bikes, veteran-looking men covered in tattoos, a mother and her teenage son — a real family, as the group’s name “Mexican Family” would have it.

“Many of us come from a dysfunctional family; we find support and love from people who aren’t blood. That was the primary purpose of creating this group,” explains el jefe, Babo, who founded the group three years ago.

The members meet every week, tinker and ride their bikes — all hand-wrought from different bicycle parts and adorned with jewels — pose with passersby and invite people to try their bikes.

Contrary to what its aesthetics would suggest, not all of them share the Chicano identity.

At its origin, Chicano was used as a derogatory term for the Mexican-American working class in the U.S. before activists in the 1960s and ‘70s reclaimed the identity as a symbol of resistance and pride.

Some members of the group are Mexican-American, others have been deported from the United States over the years, and many of the youngsters are just Mexican.

What brings them together is a shared love of lowrider bicycles and cars, as well as an appreciation for what Chicano identity symbolizes.

“It’s tradition, history, resistance,” explains a young Mexican member with no ties to the U.S., who goes by the name Estonet. “Chicano means keeping Mexican culture alive anywhere in the world.”

Tessie joined a year ago to spend time with her teenage son, a lowrider fan. She wants people to stop associating the club with gangs. The point, she says, is to “go slow and happy on a bike, no matter which one it is.”

But the stigmatization of this culture mostly comes from its association with the cholos.

Unpacking the term ‘cholo’

Cholo also began as an insult, a colonial-era slur for people of mixed Indigenous and European descent, before Mexican-American youth in Los Angeles reclaimed it as a style, taking visual influences from Chicano culture such as the lowrider bicycles and cars.

Over time, however, police discrimination and popularization through gangster films such as “Blood In Blood Out” (1993) made the term synonymous with dangerous gangs.

“For better or for worse, culture changes,” el jefe continues. “The cholo has more to do with gangs, with prison.”

Some members’ own pasts are not far removed from those associations.

Hiram, who self-deported from the United States nearly two years ago after getting into a car accident and fearing imprisonment, says most of the older members of the group used to be in gangs.

“Arriving somewhere that receives you with open arms is very hard… you don’t know the problems you had, the gangs you were in.”

Joining the group, he says, has been “like going back to the place where something was missing.”

1 of 11

A family affair

Juan, who brought his lowrider car to one of Mexican Family’s Día de Muertos parades with his teenage daughter, shares the same sentiment. “We grew up in the street, but we’re here because we don’t need the street anymore,” he says.

“Ten years ago, you could not have seen us here all together, from different barrios,” he says, alluding to the fact that many of them were members of different street gangs here in the city.

For Alvin, who grew up without papers in the U.S. and voluntarily came back to Mexico five years ago, his membership in the group is a family homage.

“My father was a cholo. I grew up watching my dad with all the bikes, these cars,” he says.

In this way, Mexican Family seems to have also become an asylum for men with troubled pasts to start anew, without forgetting the culture that raised them.

Toeing the line between bravado and vulnerability, the group could be accused of glorifying the violence attached to gang aesthetics. But perhaps what it does best is hold space for the complexity of an identity crossed by a multitude of borders, subject to poverty, marginalization and all too often, violence — and seek to redefine it as a community united by culture, pride and family.

Mathilde Hourticq is a multi-platform journalist based in Mexico City covering breaking news, subcultures, youth issues and many other things in between. Her video-journalism has appeared on the Associated Press, AFP, and Press Association.

World.title: ‘Trading Places’: A new podcast by Mexico News Daily
World.content:
The team at MND is excited to be launching a new podcast series to complement our existing “Confidently Wrong” podcast and “MND Hits the Streets” series of videos.

Cesar Martinez will be joining me as the co-host of Trading Places. Both Cesar and I have, in fact, traded places. I was born in Wisconsin and now live in San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato, after having lived, studied, worked, or traveled in Mexico for over 30 years. Cesar was born in Mexico City and now lives in Los Angeles, California. Cesar has spent over 40 years living in the United States, between Texas and California.

Each episode, Cesar and I will speak about Mexico with a different person of Mexican heritage (first and second generation Mexican Americans) living in the United States. We will reflect on how the guests’ perceptions of Mexico have evolved and changed (and why) as well as their current thoughts on the country, its leadership and its future. We will explore if they are feeling more of a pull towards (or away) from Mexico, and if so, why. We will review how their children’s views on Mexico differ from their own, and how theirs differs from those of their parents. We will, of course, also discuss the evolving relationship between the United States and Mexico, and what that means for both countries.

The goal of the podcast is to encourage the nearly 40 million Mexican diaspora living in the United States to reflect on their own relationship with Mexico and hopefully inspire them — each in their own way — to build a stronger connection with the country. We believe that there is a significant opportunity for the U.S. population of Mexican descent to have an outsized impact on the economic growth and overall well being of Mexico and want to provide a platform to share inspiring case studies and stories.

Please tune in, get informed, and get inspired!

Check out the first episode of MND’s Trading Places here:

We Both Left Our Home Country—for Opposite Sides of the Border | Trading Places - Episode 1

Watch this video on YouTube

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.content:
Ghana’s governing party picks its chairman in four weeks. The aspirant who led a July poll is selling unity and pensions.

Edwin Nii Lante Vanderpuye, a former Ghanaian youth and sports minister, launched his bid to lead Ghana’s governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) in Kumasi, Ghana’s second-largest city, on Saturday 21 November 2026. He promised to “rebuild” the party and to start a pension scheme for its workers.

Ghana’s governing party picks its chairman in four weeks. The aspirant who led a July poll is selling unity and pensions.

In his launch speech in Kumasi on 21 November 2026, Vanderpuye said: “We are going to reset this party. Let’s go back to the NDC that cares for each other.”

He also set his sights beyond 2028, the year of Ghana’s next general election, saying: “we are going to win 2032.”He has also told supporters that the pension fund would draw on 1% of the salary of every government appointee, to be agreed with President John Mahama and his chief of staff, the head of the presidential office.

He said the money would be invested to pay long-serving party workers a monthly income.

Global InfoAnalytics, a Ghanaian polling firm, surveyed 5,637 NDC delegates between 8 and 14 July 2026 and put Vanderpuye first with 26.8%. Former party chairman Samuel Ofosu-Ampofo was second with 19.3%, but a statement issued on his behalf on 9 November 2026 said he had withdrawn to serve in other national roles.

World.title: Schumer Faces Rare Senate Leadership Fight
World.content:
Chris Van Hollen is challenging Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader on 1 December, in a secret ballot that has split the party's senators.

Senate Democrats are about to pick a leader in a way they have not done in decades: with a real fight. Chuck Schumer of New York, has led the party in the Senate since 2017, and Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen wants his job.

The vote on 1 December sits inside our US midterms 2026 dossier, because the winner will run the Senate agenda for the next two years. For US readers, it decides who sets the pace on spending, tariffs and judges once the new Congress sits.

Chris Van Hollen is challenging Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, in a secret ballot.

Support. About 15 Democratic senators back Schumer publicly and four back Van Hollen. Most are staying silent.

This story is part of our coverage of the 2026 US midterm elections. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Musk Says He Feels Foolish Over Midterm Cash

Why a Secret Ballot Makes This Hard to Call

Senate Democrats elect their leader every two years, behind closed doors and on a secret ballot. That means nobody outside the room can check who is ahead.

Schumer says he is confident he has the votes to stay on. Van Hollen calls his bid a call for new leadership and says Democrats need it to deliver for voters.

The US Capitol in Washington (file photo). Senate Democrats vote behind closed doors on 1 December.

Who Has Taken Sides

Around 15 of the 55 Democratic senators in next year’s caucus have said publicly that they back Schumer. Four have said they will support Van Hollen, and everyone else is keeping quiet for now.

The newcomers could matter most. Eight freshman Democratic senators join in January, but only two have said how they will vote: Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, both for Van Hollen.

Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who votes with the Democrats, endorsed Van Hollen as soon as he entered the race. Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin says she will not back Schumer, but she has not endorsed Van Hollen either.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, traders have bet about US$1.8 million on who will be the next Senate majority leader. At 2:25 a.m. ET on 22 November, Schumer traded at 92.5% and Van Hollen at 6.7%, with Brian Schatz of Hawaii at 0.7%.

Because Democrats are set to hold the Senate majority, the Democratic leader would become majority leader. These prices are bets, not polls, and traders cannot see the secret ballot either.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Where the Midterm Count Stands

Democrats won the House on 3 November and took back the Senate. In the Senate, the Alaska race with Democrat Mary Peltola was still uncalled in mid-November, so the party’s final seat count could rise by one.

Two dates are fixed. North Carolina’s State Board of Elections is scheduled to certify its results on Tuesday, 24 November, though it can adjourn for up to ten days if county results run late.

Louisiana then holds runoffs for two US House seats on 12 December. In the 5th District Democrat Pat Moore faces Republican Gabe Firment, and in the 6th Democrat Chauna Banks faces Republican Blake Miguez.

The Mood Behind the Vote

Schumer has drawn sharp criticism from the party’s base, which is one reason the race is so public. Van Hollen also wants Democrats to push harder to end the war with Iran and to consider a government shutdown next month to stop war funding.

Voters are in a sour mood. A Reuters/Ipsos poll of 1,705 US adults on 6–9 November, with a margin of error of about two points, put President Donald Trump’s approval at 32%.

A separate Economist/YouGov weekly poll on 9–11 November found 32% of US adult citizens approving and 63% disapproving. Among registered voters, 36% approved and 61% disapproved.

What It Means for You

The Senate leader decides which bills reach the floor and when, and shapes which judges and officials get confirmed. A new leader could mean a harder line on war funding and the budget, while Schumer would mean continuity.

Democrats will still be limited. President Trump keeps his veto, and Republicans with 44 seats can block most bills through the filibuster, the Senate rule that needs 60 votes to end debate.

What Is Not Known

Nobody outside the Democratic caucus knows who has the votes, and the ballot will stay secret. We also do not know whether Alaska will be called before 1 December or what time the vote will be held.

No certified House count exists yet, and we have not confirmed any development dated 21 or 22 November. The latest detailed public count of support dates from 17 November.
