World.title: Puma Hit by Vehicle in Guápiles Undergoes Two Surgeries
World.content:
A puma rescued Wednesday in Guápiles after apparently being struck by a vehicle has undergone two operations to repair severe fractures and remains under veterinary care at the National University, where specialists are now treating inflammation of its spinal cord. The animal arrived in critical condition at the university’s Small Species and Wildlife Hospital, known as Hems-UNA, in Heredia. Veterinarians first had to stabilize it before it could go into surgery.

Mauricio Jiménez, the hospital’s director, said the first operation addressed an open fracture that had badly damaged the bone. Surgeons placed two plates to hold it in position. A second operation followed the next day to stabilize the femur, which was splintered and damaged in several places. Jiménez said part of the bone was lost in the collision, explaining that fragments are often expelled from the body in an impact of that force.

The puma also has considerable inflammation around the spinal cord. It is receiving physical therapy along with regular wound care, and the veterinary team is monitoring how it responds. Environment officials said the cat came in with heavy blood loss and anemia, and that surgeons also repaired tissue that had torn away from its abdomen. As of Friday it was still in pain and unable to stand, though it had begun eating small pieces of food.

Jiménez said the goal is to return the puma to the wild, but stressed that recovery will not end when it leaves the hospital. It will need continued follow-up care, and specialists expect to move it to a wildlife center for the next stage of rehabilitation. No timeline has been given.

The puma was found Wednesday morning near Route 32, the highway that connects San José with the Caribbean coast. Officials from the Tortuguero Conservation Area sedated it at the scene with support from firefighters and police. José Joaquín Vargas Mora, who heads the conservation area’s wildlife program, said the leg fractures were the reason it was transferred to the university hospital.

Elena Vargas, director of the Tortuguero Conservation Area, urged drivers to slow down and stay alert near forested stretches of road, where wildlife crossings are common. Injured or at-risk wild animals can be reported to 1192 or 911.

World.title: Landing in San José? Your Taxi, Shuttle and Rental Car Now Leave From One Spot
World.content:
If you fly into Juan Santamaría International Airport this high season, your ride is probably waiting somewhere new. The airport has opened a ground transport center where official taxis, hotel shuttles and rental car transfers all pick up passengers. You’ll find it between the international arrivals area and the domestic terminal. Until now, those services were scattered around the outside of the building.

Aeris, the company that runs the airport, says the center began operating in November and covers about 2,800 square meters (30,100 square feet). Shuttle buses load at three covered islands, so you can wait out of the sun or rain. Cars come in one way and leave another, and marked crossings and sidewalks ring the site to keep people on foot away from traffic. There are restrooms, security cameras and controlled vehicle access.

Ricardo Hernández, executive director of Aeris, said the center improves the flow of vehicles and makes it easier for people arriving at or leaving the airport to get around. Two things the announcement does not cover are ride-hailing apps and private pickups. If a friend, relative or app driver is collecting you, agree on a meeting point before you board.

If you booked a hotel shuttle or a rental car, ask the company where its driver will be. Confirmation emails sent before November may still describe the old pickup point. The center belongs to the first phase of a westward expansion of the international terminal, a project budgeted at $62 million. Aeris has not said how much of that went to the transport center or when the next stages will open.

The same expansion produced the international arrivals hall that opened May 21, a 3,800-square-meter space (40,900 square feet) with a larger customs inspection zone, rental car counters and an outdoor meeting plaza. Give yourself a few extra minutes the first time you use the new layout, especially on a late arrival.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Dollar Slide Is Cutting Into Workers’ Pension Savings
World.content:
Workers in Costa Rica who are building retirement savings through the mandatory complementary pension system have seen part of those savings lose value this year, not because markets fell but because the dollar did. The Superintendencia de Pensiones (Supen), which regulates the pension funds, said in its November bulletin that the dollar’s slide has reduced the value in colones of the funds’ dollar-denominated investments.

According to Supen, the reference buy rate fell from about 496 colones per dollar in December 2025 to about 450 in October 2026, a drop of roughly 9%. Many of the Mandatory Pension Regime’s (ROP) foreign investments are held in dollars but reported in colones, so every dollar in those portfolios now shows up as fewer colones on workers’ account statements.

The regulator illustrated the effect with a simple example. An investment of $100 is worth 50,000 colones at an exchange rate of 500, but only 45,000 colones at 450. That is a 10% reduction in local-currency terms, even though the number of dollars has not changed. The slide has continued since October. The dollar closed Friday at 443.97 colones on Monex, the Central Bank’s wholesale foreign-exchange platform, setting a new record low for the third consecutive session. That is about 53 colones, or 10.7%, below where it started the year.

Supen stressed that savers’ total balances have not fallen by the same proportion. The impact depends on how much of each fund is invested abroad and on how its other holdings perform. The regulator noted that strong gains in international stock markets have offset part of the currency loss, citing year-on-year gains of 16.3% for the S&P 500 and 17.4% for the MSCI World index as of March 2026.

Costa Rican law allows pension operators to invest up to 50% of ROP funds in international markets, a limit Supen described as a way to diversify portfolios and reduce the concentration of risk. The cap is a ceiling, and not every operator holds that much abroad. Over longer periods the funds remain in positive territory. Supen reported nominal ROP returns through October 2026 of 10.85% over three years, 6.69% over five years and 8.63% over 10 years. The regulator cautioned that those figures do not represent any individual saver’s return this year.

Supen advised workers to review their account statements regularly and to judge fund performance over three-, five- and 10-year horizons rather than reacting to short-term swings. The pressure on the dollar has drawn heavy intervention from the Banco Central de Costa Rica. The Central Bank bought $39.65 million in stabilization operations on Friday alone to limit the decline. Through Nov. 20 it had bought $261.3 million in stabilization operations this month, the highest monthly total of 2026, ahead of the $259.1 million it bought in February.

Analysts see little short-term relief. Economist Pablo González of brokerage Mercado de Valores said that as long as dollar supply keeps outpacing weak demand, a major change in the trend is unlikely, and he noted that early December often brings additional downward pressure. That outlook is in line with earlier forecasts that the dollar would keep falling through year-end.

The stronger local currency cuts both ways. It makes dollar-priced goods cheaper in colones, but it reduces the colón income of anyone paid in dollars, from exporters to retirees living on foreign pensions, who already face some of the highest retirement costs in Latin America.

The currency hit to pension statements comes as Costa Rica also debates the future of its main public pension, with a proposed overhaul that could require 30 years of contributions instead of 25. For most savers, Supen’s message is one of patience. Pension savings are built over decades, and exchange-rate moves can reverse, as they did in 2022, when the dollar climbed from about 640 to about 691 colones in the first half of the year.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Grynspan Leads UN Race Again, but Two Veto Powers Stand in Her Way
World.content:
Costa Rican economist Rebeca Grynspan finished first again on Friday in the United Nations Security Council’s informal vote on the next Secretary-General, but the result made clear that two of the five permanent members still stand between her and the job. In the ninth closed-door straw poll since late July, Grynspan received 10 votes encouraging her candidacy, four discouraging it and one with no opinion, according to diplomats and a tally reported by the UN-focused outlet PassBlue. Two of the negative votes came from permanent members, each of which holds a veto.

The ballots were color-coded, the first time since Oct. 16 that the votes of the United States, China, Russia, France and the United Kingdom could be told apart from those of the 10 elected members. The ballots do not show which countries voted against her. The tally was a step back from early November, when Grynspan collected 12 encouraging votes and three discouraging ones on undifferentiated ballots. It also repeated the picture from the October color-coded round, when two permanent members likewise opposed her.

Even so, Grynspan remains the only candidate to reach the nine-vote threshold in every poll since September, and on Friday she was the only one backed by a majority of both the permanent and the elected members. Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, head of the International Atomic Energy Agency, came second with eight encouraging votes and six discouraging ones, three of them from permanent members. Lana Nusseibeh of the United Arab Emirates drew seven in favor and six against, also with three permanent-member objections.

Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett received six votes on each side. Türkiye’s Feridun Sinirlioğlu, who joined the race after the October color-coded round, received five encouraging votes and 10 discouraging ones, four of them from permanent members. PassBlue reported that every one of the eight candidates on the ballot drew at least two negative votes from permanent members.

Washington’s position remains the central question. US Ambassador Mike Waltz said Friday that the United States would welcome a Latin American candidate, in keeping with the informal practice of rotating the post among regions, while adding that Washington wants the best candidate to emerge and acknowledging there is no consensus yet. He also urged candidates with little support to withdraw so the Council can focus on a smaller field.

Diplomats cited by the development news outlet Devex said earlier this month that the United States and Russia had backed Nusseibeh, while China has signaled a preference for a Latin American without publicly endorsing anyone. Analysts have pointed to reports issued by UN Trade and Development under Grynspan that criticized the effect of Israeli policies on the Palestinian economy as a source of friction with the current US administration.

After the color-coded round in October, Grynspan said that because no formal vote had taken place, the results could not be described as vetoes, and that she would keep negotiating to broaden her support. To be recommended, a candidate needs at least nine votes on the Council and no veto from a permanent member. The 193-member General Assembly then makes the formal appointment.

Time is running short as António Guterres ends his second term on Dec. 31, and the UN Charter makes no provision for an interim leader. Reuters reported this week that UN officials are drafting contingency plans. Kirill Logvinov, a senior Russian Foreign Ministry official, said the options under discussion include temporarily extending Guterres’ term or naming another official to fill in. Daniel Safran-Hon, a former UN official, warned that senior appointments and the budget cannot move forward without a Secretary-General in place.

Grynspan, 70, served as Costa Rica’s vice president from 1994 to 1998 and later as UN Under-Secretary-General and associate administrator of the UN Development Programme. She led the Ibero-American General Secretariat from 2014 to 2021 before becoming the first woman to head UNCTAD, a post from which she took leave to campaign.

Costa Rica announced her candidacy in October 2025 and formally nominated her on March 3. If she clears the final hurdle, Grynspan would become the first woman and the first Central American to lead the United Nations.

World.title: Shakira Tickets for Costa Rica Go on Sale Monday
World.content:
Tickets for Shakira’s concert in Costa Rica go on sale Monday at noon, but only if you hold the right bank card. Everyone else has to wait until Friday, and by then you will be buying whatever the presales leave behind. The Colombian singer plays the Estadio Nacional in La Sabana, San José, on Sunday, Jan. 31, 2027, as part of her Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour. Organizers say 45,000 tickets will be available. It will be her first show in the country in almost 16 years.

The sale runs in three stages. The first presale opens Monday, Nov. 23, at noon and runs through Tuesday for holders of Visa cards from Davivienda and DAVIbank. The second opens Wednesday, Nov. 25, at 10 a.m. and runs through Thursday for holders of any Davivienda or DAVIbank card.

General sale opens Friday, Nov. 27, at 10 a.m. with any payment method. All three stages draw from the same pool of tickets, so if demand is strong early in the week there may be little left in the cheaper sections by Friday.

Prices range from 34,500 colones (about $77) to 124,500 colones (about $279). Those figures do not include service fees, which are added at checkout, so expect to pay more than the listed price.

VIP Waka Waka and La Loba, standing in front of the stage, adults only: 124,500 colones (about $279)

Platea east and west: 69,500 colones (about $156)

Balcony east and west: 64,500 colones (about $144)

VIP Las de la Intuición, standing on the field: 54,500 colones (about $122)

Sombra east and west: 44,500 colones (about $100)

South stands: 34,500 colones (about $77)

Dollar amounts use yesterday’s central bank’s rate of 446.48 colones, which, unfortunately, is when the dollar hit its third record low. This means that if you earn in dollars, the same ticket costs you more than it would have a few months ago.

However, if you find it difficult to afford at the moment and you really want to go, you can spread the cost as organizers are offering 12-month interest-free financing on ticket purchases. Children can attend from age four in every section except the two front VIP areas, which are restricted to adults. Promoter Juan Carlos Campos of ONE Costa Rica said the restriction is there for safety reasons.

Tickets are sold through publitickets.com, the only platform the organizers have named. Buy there and nowhere else, because a ticket from a reseller or a social media seller may not get you through the gate. Plan to arrive early on the day. An entertainment area outside the stadium will open at noon, with sponsor activities and stalls run by women-owned businesses.

If you miss out, there is a slim chance of a second night. Campos said the producers want to add another date but have not been able to confirm one because of the singer’s schedule.

World.title: Nearly 7 in 10 in Costa Rica Say Tourism Prices Are Driving Locals Out
World.content:
Nearly seven in 10 people in Costa Rica believe rising prices in tourist areas have forced local residents to move away, according to a national survey that also found crime is now seen as the biggest problem facing tourism.

The National Survey on Tourism in Costa Rica 2026, carried out by the Institute of Social Studies in Population (Idespo) at the Universidad Nacional (UNA), found that 68.6% of respondents said the displacement of residents by higher prices happens a lot in tourist areas. Another 71.4% said luxury housing is prioritized over affordable housing, and 75.2% said the profits from tourism benefit some sectors more than others.

The survey also points to unease about who shapes life in tourism towns. Six in 10 respondents, 60.3%, said tourism develops without taking the views of local communities into account, and 47.8% said foreigners have more influence in those communities than the people who live there. A further 41.7% said hotel and residential development has made basic public services worse.

Trust in oversight is low. Some 59.7% said authorities handle complaints about legal violations with little or no effectiveness. More than half of respondents, 52.9%, said they were unfamiliar with the work of the National Environmental Technical Secretariat (Setena), the agency that reviews the environmental impact of development projects, and 62% said the same of the Environmental Administrative Tribunal.

Asked to name the main problems of tourism in Costa Rica, 37.7% pointed to crime and insecurity, well ahead of the cost of travel at 17.6%. The deterioration of San José and the greater metropolitan area followed at 10.2%, then road conditions at 8.2% and pollution at 6.5%. The result contrasts with an international risk map released this week that ranked Costa Rica among the 10 safest countries to visit in 2027.

None of that has stopped people from traveling at home. Seven in 10 respondents, 69.8%, said they had taken a trip inside the country in the past two years, staying an average of three nights, and 75.7% of those travelers went by private car. Guanacaste was the preferred destination for 45.6%, followed by Puntarenas at 19.2% and Limón at 16%, and beaches were named as the main draw by 56.4%.

Budgets are tight. Some 44.2% said they spend less than 50,000 colones (about $112) per person per day on domestic trips, and nearly three-quarters spend less than 100,000 colones (about $224). Price was the most cited factor in choosing lodging, at 44.1%, in a place that has become Latin America’s priciest place to retire as the dollar hits a record low.

Views on where the industry is heading are mixed. Only 34.5% said Costa Rica has improved as a destination for domestic travelers, while 41.6% said it has improved for foreign visitors. Idespo interviewed 899 adults by cell phone between June 3 and 11, including Costa Ricans and foreign residents who have lived here for at least two years. The survey has a margin of error of 3.3 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

The research team identified three challenges from the results. They are narrowing the gap between what Costa Rica offers domestic and foreign tourists, strengthening environmental oversight, and giving communities an effective say in decisions about local development.

World.title: Expect Intense Heat and Almost No Rain in Costa Rica This Weekend
World.content:
Plan for heat this weekend. Costa Rica stays dry and sunny through Sunday, and the breeze that has kept things bearable is about to drop off. Saturday’s highs will reach 35.5°C (96°F), according to the National Meteorological Institute (IMN). Skies will be clear to partly cloudy across the country, with the odd gust near the mountain ranges early in the day.

If you are in the South Pacific, you are the exception: sea breezes pushing toward the mountains give that region the only chance of rain on Saturday. The bigger change is the wind. The trade winds that have been blowing over Guanacaste and the Central Valley will go through a weak spell this weekend, the IMN says. With less air moving, it will feel hotter and stickier than the thermometer suggests.

That matters if you are spending the day outside. Drink water before you feel thirsty, find shade around midday, and don’t leave children or pets in a parked car, even for a few minutes. Rain is not coming back in any real way. The IMN’s weekend outlook allows for scattered afternoon showers in the western Central Valley and the Central Pacific, and more often in the South Pacific. On the Caribbean side and in the Northern Zone, any rain should be brief and fall in the morning.

For most beach plans, that means good conditions. If you are headed to Limón or the Northern Zone, do your outdoor activities after the morning showers pass. This is what the second half of November normally looks like, as the dry season takes hold across much of the country. What is not normal is how hot the month has been.

The IMN counted more than 23 record highs in the first 11 days of November alone, with readings near 37°C (99°F) in the North Pacific. The institute links the heat to thinner cloud cover, El Niño and warmer seas. It is not expected to ease soon. The IMN projects above-normal temperatures nationwide through January, running 1.5 to 2°C (2.7 to 3.6°F) over the average in the Pacific regions and the Central Valley.

With little rain ahead and months of dry season still to come, water is worth saving now. Short showers and fixing a dripping tap make a difference when supplies run low later in the season.

World.title: A Slow Earthquake Equal to Magnitude 6.4 Happened Off Osa and Nobody Felt It
World.content:
A slow-motion earthquake with the energy of a magnitude 6.4 tremor took place off Costa Rica’s Osa Peninsula in Octobe and no one on land felt a thing. The Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (Ovsicori), part of the National University, detected the episode offshore of southern Osa, where the Cocos Plate meets the Panama Microplate. Its findings appear in a preliminary report updated on November 17.

In a slow earthquake, the strain stored between two plates escapes little by little across days or weeks rather than in one violent break. Because nothing shakes, only instruments that track ground position down to the millimeter can pick it up. Those instruments showed the observatory’s satellite positioning station in Puerto Jiménez sliding about 4.2 centimeters (1.7 inches) to the southwest over the month. Deeper down, Ovsicori’s model puts the largest slip between the two plates at roughly 13 centimeters (5.1 inches).

For comparison, the two plates normally close on each other at around 8 centimeters (3.1 inches) a year, as the Cocos Plate dives beneath the Panama Microplate. Ovsicori seismologist Cyril Müller stressed that the 6.4 figure measures the tectonic movement added up over the whole process and does not mean a quake of that size struck.

This is not the first such episode in the area. The observatory recorded slow slip in the same offshore area in 2018 and again in 2022, and both years brought a second episode, five months after the first in 2018 and two months after in 2022. The second 2022 episode covered more ground, spreading into a neighboring area to the northwest.

Since October’s slip sits in much the same place as the opening episodes of those earlier sequences, researchers consider a second episode possible in the coming months, though the report says the data cannot yet show whether, when or how far it would spread.

The report makes no forecast of a conventional earthquake and it neither claims the October episode will set one off nor estimates any rise in the odds. Studies published in 2023 and 2025 suggest slow slip can redistribute stress onto neighboring parts of a fault, a mechanism scientists are still working to understand.

The monitoring matters because parts of the plate boundary keep building up strain, among them the zone tied to the magnitude 7.4 Osa earthquake of 1983. Ovsicori will keep reviewing its station data for signs of a new episode or a spread to the northwest and will continue tracking ground deformation and seismic activity in the region.

The finding comes in a year when more earthquakes have been felt. Ovsicori data show felt quakes averaged 12 a month from January through April and 25 a month from May through October. The observatory’s researchers said the year’s activity shows nothing anomalous compared with recent years.

Costa Rica sits on one of the most active plate boundaries in the Americas, and strong earthquakes can occur at any time. Emergency authorities recommend keeping water, food, a flashlight and important documents within reach and agreeing on a meeting point with the people you live with.

World.title: International News: About 250 migrants enter Mexico in caravan hoping to reach U.S.
World.content:
International News: About 250 migrants enter Mexico in caravan hoping to reach U.S.

By Zoila Palma: A caravan of approximately 250 migrants, mostly from Central America, entered Mexico on Friday after crossing the border from Guatemala as they continued their journey toward the United States.

The group, made up largely of young men and families with children, crossed a border bridge into Tapachula carrying their belongings on their backs. They displayed a banner reading “God with us” and were not stopped by Mexican authorities.

Several migrants told AFP that they had previously lived in the United States but were deported during Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations.

Among them was 31-year-old Honduran national Saba Najera, who said she was determined to reach Houston to reunite with her newborn daughter. She described her deportation as painful but said the separation had strengthened her resolve to make the journey again.

The latest movement comes as several migrant caravans have entered Mexico hoping to reach the United States, despite warnings from President Donald Trump.

Mexican security forces have blocked some larger groups, while others have dispersed after immigration officials offered them the opportunity to seek asylum in Mexico.

World.title: Motorcycle collides with Sarita ice cream truck in Independence Village
World.content:
Motorcycle collides with Sarita ice cream truck in Independence Village

By Belize Live News Staff: A motorcycle and a Sarita ice cream truck were involved in a collision in Independence Village on Friday evening.

Reports are that the accident happened around 6:47pm on November 20 on Faden Street.

According to initial information, the driver of the motorcycle picked himself up after the collision and walked away from the scene.

The extent of any injuries is not known at this time. There are no reports of injuries to anyone in the truck.

The cause of the collision has not been established.

Breaking Belize News will provide more information as it becomes available.

World.title: Galen University offers free application opportunity at Christmas Extravaganza in Belize City
World.content:
By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizeans planning to pursue higher education in 2027 will have an opportunity to save on university application fees when Galen University participates in the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s Christmas Extravaganza.

The event is scheduled for Saturday, November 28, 2026, at the Belize City Civic Center, from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Galen University is inviting prospective students to visit its booth and apply for the Spring 2027 semester, with the university waiving the application fee for those who apply at the event and bring their supporting documents.

The initiative provides an opportunity for students preparing to continue their education, working professionals considering additional qualifications and individuals interested in returning to school.

Prospective applicants are encouraged to bring their supporting documents to take advantage of the offer.

In addition to accepting applications, Galen University’s presence at the Christmas Extravaganza will give visitors an opportunity to learn more about the institution and its educational opportunities.

The event is organized by the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry and will take place at the Belize City Civic Center.

For additional information about admissions, interested persons can visit www.galen.edu.bz, email [email protected] or call 614-6415.

World.title: Enrique Martinez and Sons announces Black Friday Super Sale with up to 20% off and free gifts
World.content:
Enrique Martinez and Sons announces Black Friday Super Sale with up to 20% off and free gifts

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizeans looking to save big this Black Friday can take advantage of two days of special discounts as Enrique Martinez and Sons Limited prepares for its Black Friday and Saturday Super Sale on November 27 and 28, 2026.

The Belize City business is offering discounts of up to 20% on selected products, including air conditioners, vehicle tires, ice makers and automotive lubricants.

Customers shopping for air conditioning units can enjoy 20% off LG air conditioners and 15% off CHIGO air conditioners.

Motorists can also benefit from a special GITI tire promotion, allowing customers to purchase three tires and receive a fourth tire free.

Among the featured deals is an AKT ice maker, reduced by 18% from $613.13 to $502.76. The appliance offers ice-making capabilities and a cold-water function.

Vehicle owners can also save 20% on CAM2 motor oils and lubricants during the two-day promotion.

As an additional incentive, Enrique Martinez and Sons will reward the first 20 customers with a free gift.

The sale comes as Belizean consumers prepare for the Christmas shopping season, offering an opportunity to purchase household appliances and automotive products at reduced prices.

The promotion will take place at Enrique Martinez and Sons Limited, located at 2 Miles Philip Goldson Highway in Belize City.

Customers can call 223-2572 or WhatsApp 606-4154 for additional information.

The special offers are available on Friday, November 27, and Saturday, November 28, only.

World.title: Caribbean sugar producers say region is now self sufficient; BSI to invest $50 million
World.content:
Caribbean sugar producers say region is now self sufficient; BSI to invest $50 million

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Sugar Association of the Caribbean (SAC) says the region can now meet its own sugar demand from regional production for the first time in generations.

The announcement followed the association’s 178th Board of Directors meeting, held last week in Bridgetown, Barbados.

According to the SAC, investments by member industries have brought combined regional supply capacity to more than 300,000 tonnes, enough to cover CARICOM’s estimated demand.

Directors verified final production of 241,500 metric tonnes for the 2025/26 regional crop and estimated more than 330,000 metric tonnes for 2026/27.

Belize features prominently in the plans. Belize Sugar Industries Limited (BSI) is investing $50 million over the next three to four years to expand output by 25 percent, with a long term vision of potentially doubling current production.

Santander is targeting one million tonnes of cane within three to four years, backed by $75 million to $100 million in capital spending that includes a new boiler and expanded acreage.

The SAC noted that producers in Belize are actively managing a mealybug infestation to protect yields.

The association also reported that Caribbean Sugar Refineries has begun producing refined white sugar within the single market, with product now available to CARICOM customers. The refinery is being inaugurated today, November 21.

BSI’s Mac McLachlan was reaffirmed as SAC chairman for the 2025/26 and 2026/27 terms. The board also approved relocating the association’s secretariat to Barbados.

McLachlan said private investment has unlocked self sufficiency, but full implementation of CARICOM’s trade rules remains critical. The SAC said the CARICOM Monitoring Mechanism for Sugar is not yet operational because member states have not submitted enough data, and it is preparing a paper for the next Council for Trade and Economic Development meeting.

“We are proving that the Caribbean can feed and supply itself,” McLachlan said.

Elsewhere in the region, Jamaica plans to break ground on a new sugar factory in January 2027, while Barbados is exploring rebuilding its mill with co generation using bagasse.

World.title: Belize gets a dry and sunny Saturday with almost no rain
World.content:
Belize gets a dry and sunny Saturday with almost no rain

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize can expect a mostly sunny Saturday, with clear to partly cloudy skies tonight.

The National Meteorological Service says a light and mostly dry airflow prevails over the country.

Little or no rain is expected.

Coastal areas will reach a high of 86°F (30°C) with a low of 74°F (23°C). Inland areas will hit 88°F (31°C), cooling to 71°F (21°C). The hills will see a high of 75°F (24°C) and a low of 64°F (18°C).

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region in the next 48 hours.

Today’s forecast was issued by forecaster Crystal Rosalez.

World.title: International News: France sees 6th consecutive weekend of protests over cost of living and public services
World.content:
International News: France sees 6th consecutive weekend of protests over cost of living and public services

By Zoila Palma: Thousands of people took to the streets across France on Saturday for the sixth consecutive weekend of demonstrations, protesting the rising cost of living, inequality and what they describe as declining public services.

The demonstrations come amid a wider protest movement spreading across Europe, with citizens demanding better living conditions and greater government investment, AFP reports.

The movement began in mid-September, initially led by high school students calling for improved learning conditions. It has since expanded into a nationwide campaign addressing soaring prices, inadequate public services and allegations of police brutality. Although participation in France has declined, demonstrations continue as similar rallies take place in other European countries.

In central Paris, several thousand protesters gathered at Place de la République in a festive atmosphere featuring musicians, food trucks, costumes and handmade signs. Flags representing trade unions, left-wing political parties, student organisations and the Yellow Vest movement were visible.

Protesters also displayed mock headstones symbolising what they described as the death of public services, including social security and education.

World.title: World Fisheries Day highlights importance of sustainable Fishing and Fisherfolk livelihoods
World.content:
World Fisheries Day highlights importance of sustainable Fishing and Fisherfolk livelihoods

By Zoila Palma: World Fisheries Day is being observed with renewed calls for responsible fishing practices, sustainable management of aquatic resources and improved working conditions for people employed in the fisheries and aquaculture sectors.

The annual observance recognizes the contributions of fisherfolk, aquaculturists and fish workers to food security, nutrition, economic development and the livelihoods of communities worldwide.

The Organization of the Fisheries and Aquaculture Sector of the Central American Isthmus (OSPESCA) highlighted the important role fishing plays in generating economic opportunities, preserving cultural traditions and supporting thousands of families across the region. The organization reaffirmed its commitment to promoting sustainable fishing, the responsible use of fishery resources and the conservation of aquatic ecosystems for present and future generations.

This year’s theme, “Empowering People for Change: Advancing Decent Work in Fisheries and Aquaculture, Particularly for Youth and Women,” also draws attention to the need for safer working conditions, greater opportunities and equitable participation in the sector.

World.title: Fragile cash
World.content:
A vendor displays torn $100 and $500 bills to the Jamaica Observer.

Vendors, cab drivers, bus conductors, and other Jamaicans whose livelihoods depend heavily on cash transactions say they are taking losses as some of the country’s most frequently circulated banknotes succumb to tearing and fading, prompting concerns about their durability.

The Bank of Jamaica (BOJ), acknowledging the problem, says it is exploring ways to make the notes more resilient.

“It’s too easy to tear, man; soon as you draw them so they split… I’m not comfortable with them,” long-time Coronation Market vendor Nadine Campbell told the Jamaica Observer.

“I have [so] much in my drawer, about $5,000 [worth of] $100, $50, all of them, I just throw them down,” Campbell added.

The polymer notes now in circulation were introduced in 2023, replacing cotton-based $50, $100, $500, $1,000, and $5,000 denominations, incorporating new designs and enhanced security features. The roll-out also saw the introduction of an entirely new $2,000 denomination.

At the time, then Finance Minister Dr Nigel Clarke said the upgraded notes have the latest in material technology for greater durability, which reduces the frequency of replacement. That would have a positive impact on the BOJ’s annual spend of about $1.4 billion every year to print banknotes.

Additionally, the new notes have specific markers to facilitate ease of use by visually impaired people.

However, Jamaicans who engage in cash-heavy transactions daily are now doubtful about the notes’ longevity.

“If there’s a little tear, nobody wants it, [and] it washes out easily,” shared a vendor who identified herself as Denneshia.

“It is easy to slide out of your pocket; I don’t like them. But we have to use them because… we have to use them,” she added.

Andrew, who loads taxis plying the Price Rite/Whitehall route, had several $50 and $100 bills with microtears along the edges in his hand when the Sunday Observer spoke to him in Half-Way-Tree.

“They are quick to tear and, as you get a tear on it, it rips off completely,” he said.

In June 2026 the central bank, in an interview with the Observer, had maintained that the new notes far outlast the old cotton-based currency

— up to three years compared to 1.5 years.

When contacted for this story, the BOJ declined to comment on the complaints. However, it did admit that the lower denomination notes, including $50, $100 and $500 bills, are coming back to the bank damaged more frequently than higher denomination notes.

Almost a quarter, around 22 per cent, of the notes in these denominations that it processes are deemed unfit for recirculation.

But anecdotal evidence suggests the number could be higher, as a familiar refrain among vendors and customers with whom the Sunday Observer spoke is that they don’t return the most damaged notes.

Some, like a cab driver who identified himself as Prince, showed the newspaper their stash of damaged notes.

This is not good, look at this,” Prince said, flipping through a wad of torn bills, mostly $50 and $100 notes.

Similarly, more than half of the vendors and customers who spoke to the Sunday Observer said they have damaged bills collecting dust at home.

One vendor, who identified herself as Grace, said she had taken the torn notes to a bank to have them replaced. But that effort failed as the bank refused to take them.

“When I bring it to the bank, they told me to go and find the other piece if there’s another piece to find, but they’re not changing it,” Grace said.

That, she insisted, was opposite to her experience with the former cotton-based notes. “We always could bring them to the bank as long as they have on the serial number,” Grace explained.

She said the serial numbers are visible on the damaged $500, and $1,000 bills she had, but she has since thrown them away “because we don’t know what to do with them”.

A vegetable vendor, Gem, who said she has been selling in Half-Way-Tree for more than 15 years, told the Sunday Observer she has her own collection of damaged notes.

“As you quint [blink] they tear,” she said. “The amount that I’ve gotten I have to carry them and put down at my house, because sometimes how people ginnal you and give you, you don’t even notice. Some of them you can use a piece of tape and it’s good to go, but others…”

“Maybe one day when I am broke and don’t have any money I can draw back for them and carry them to the bank,” Gem added, laughing.

A driver who travels through Spanish Town, Frankie, maintained: “Once they have a rip, that’s it; they don’t have any value unless you take them back to the bank.”

Despite the complaints, the bills seem almost impossible to rip. Jamaica Observer reporters who tried various methods to tear a $100 bill found that it merely bent and wrinkled.

When the Sunday Observer contacted De La Rue, the British company that manufacturers the notes, an employee explained that it would be very difficult to comment without knowing the state of the notes beforehand, including how old they were and how they had been used.

However, the employee said: “If you have to work really hard to destroy the notes and then you are seeing some that are damaged, it suggests that the notes have two very different histories.”

The BOJ has blamed rough handling, including stapling and graffiti, for the state of some of the bills.

It also said in June, that while replacement rates have dropped across all denominations, it is working with the manufacturer to “identify ways to further improve durability, particularly for the lower denominations”.

The Sunday Observer then asked De La Rue whether any changes have been signed off on with BOJ regarding the notes; if so, when are they due to begin production, and whether Jamaicans could expect any tangible changes, for example, a different feel or thickness. However, the manufacturer said it was not able to comment on any conversations it had with any central bank.

In the meantime, Jamaicans who use the lower denominations the most say it’s costing them money.

“It is a loss for me, because when a passenger gives me a torn note I have to just fold it up and put it somewhere; I can’t even pass it on,” said Prince.

Another issue that several bus conductors and drivers on the Spanish Town to Kingston route pointed out was that the notes tend to stick together when they get damp or moist, leading them to give away more bills than they intend.

They explained that this regularly causes conflicts between commuters and conductors.

Similar concerns were shared by a Coronation Market vendor who identified herself as Dimples.

“It is nice, but when it is wet it can be a little tedious because it sticks together… it poses a problem because suppose a shopper comes, and they come thinking it’s one note and… pass it on to me, and I give you the change, and you go to someone else thinking you have the other money, which you don’t; it’s gonna cause a problem… there’s a little friction, and we don’t really want that,” she said.

Regular consumers had fewer issues with the currency, though they still shared complaints about it tearing.

One customer in Coronation Market was complaining about the very issue when the Sunday Observer visited.

Displaying her $500 bill with a small piece missing from the edge, she said: “I don’t have a problem with the money, but there are times when you come and you will give someone, say, $1,000 or $2,000, and they tend to give you back money that is torn. And then now when you try to spend it, nobody will take it, and that is where I have a problem,” she said.

Another customer explained that she loves the fact that the notes can stand up to water, especially with accidental washing.

“So when you check the pocket now after the clothes dry, you find the money, and it’s still all right. It’s not crushed up… So you can use it again. The only problem with it, when it tears, you have a problem, because nobody want to take it from you. But I think it was a good switch. I appreciate it,” she explained.

World.title: Safety sells Jamaica
World.content:
CHANG... my job is simple: I want to make sure the only thing that takes your breath away in Jamaica is the view and the sunshine and the beach

WHITEHOUSE, Westmoreland — Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace Dr Horace Chang has declared that Jamaica’s continued success in tourism depends heavily on maintaining a safe environment for both visitors and residents, insisting that the country’s natural attractions mean little if people are afraid to enjoy them.

“Safety is part of the product. The most beautiful beach in the world means nothing if people are afraid to walk on it. My job is simple: I want to make sure the only thing that takes your breath away in Jamaica is the view and the sunshine and the beach,” Chang said to applause last Thursday at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the rehabilitated Sandals South Coast in Westmoreland.

The hotel, which reopened to guests on Wednesday after sustaining extensive damage during the passage of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, was restored over a compressed 10-month period by a combined team of Jamaican and American architects.

Chang said the Government’s investments in national security, coupled with the efforts of the security forces, were helping to create an environment in which tourists could move beyond hotel compounds and experience the wider Jamaican community without fear.

He said the ultimate goal was for visitors to feel comfortable travelling to nearby communities, visiting beaches and local attractions, and interacting with residents.

“[We want guests to] begin to feel free to go on the road and walk, take a taxi, go down to Whitehouse, go down to the beach, down to the fishing beach, buy some fried fish, and jump on any taxi and come back to the hotel without feeling fear,” he said.

“We have made significant progress, and as the ministry responded, with the support of the prime minister, we have made the investment in our security, and our police have responded,” Chang added.

He stressed, however, that safeguarding the tourism industry also means protecting the thousands of Jamaicans employed in the sector, particularly in the communities where they live.

The minister said hotel workers sometimes face criminal pressure as they return home at weekends, despite the industry’s move away from paying salaries in cash.

“Our security forces have delivered a sharp reduction in murder, and we will not ease up. We will keep strengthening policing in our resort areas and the communities where hotel workers live,” Chang assured.

He acknowledged that unemployment and other social challenges continued to contribute to criminal activity, adding that the police were also having to contend with domestic violence and less serious offences that could escalate into deadly confrontations.

Pointing to the impact of increased investment in policing, Chang highlighted an 82.14 per cent reduction in homicides in Westmoreland, which he said had previously recorded more than 100 and, at one stage, over 140 murders annually.

“Today, we have 25 for the year,” he said, while commending the work of the police leadership, including head of the Westmoreland division, Senior Superintendent Othneil Dobson.

Despite the significant decline in murders, Chang cautioned that domestic and interpersonal violence remained a troubling source of killings across the country, requiring more targeted interventions alongside conventional crime-fighting measures.

Describing the trend as “an unfortunate part of the social scene today”, he said the Government was developing a range of interventions involving communities, schools, and the police to address the problem and encourage behavioural change.

He said the police had established the Community Security and Safety Branch, while the Government intended to roll out a major anti-violence programme aimed at encouraging people to report domestic disputes before they turned fatal.

“We intend to embark on a major programme

— anti-violence

— to provide an opportunity for domestic disputes to be reported to the police early, and to avoid the fatal outcome,” Chang said.

He also disclosed that the Government had established approximately 20 domestic violence centres, with men accounting for about 30 per cent of those seeking assistance.

“Not sure what it’s saying

— men reporting threats of violence

— but we are getting responses, and we intend to expand those centres and ultimately begin to get the kind of behavioural change we want in that sector,” the minister added.

World.title: A separate Grammy category for dancehall?
World.content:
Since the nominations in the Best Reggae Album category of the 69th annual Grammy Awards were announced on November 16, there has been some uproar across social media platforms by fans and some members of the entertainment fraternity alike about the non-inclusion of some notable albums by dancehall artistes.

Some of the albums include God and Time by Vybz Kartel, Eminence by Beenie Man, Heights of Fire by Capleton, Forever Reign by Masicka, NPT by Alkaline.

Some have even suggested a bias towards dancehall artistes.

The 2027 reggae Grammy nominees are Too Too Bad by Buju Banton, The Art of Acceptance by Protoje, Supernova by Runkus, Exile by Chronixx, Brightside by Ziggy Marley, and Lottery by Shaggy.

There has been a call for a separate category for dancehall artistes, while others have argued that renaming the category to Best Reggae/Dancehall Album would suffice.

A few months ago, the JUNO Awards (Canada’s equivalent to the Grammys) announced the renaming of its Reggae Recording of the Year category to Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year for the 2027 staging.

The reality, some say, is that there are not sufficient releases each year by dancehall artistes to argue for a separate dancehall category in the Grammys. The Best Reggae Album category, instituted in 1985, was allegedly on the chopping block a few years ago due to the low number of submissions. This year, the number improved to 119, compared to 73 last year.

Recording artiste, producer, and music executive Ce’Cile, who is a registered member of the Recording Academy, says the Grammys aren’t obligated to do anything to drown out the noise created each year after the nominations are announced.

“They [Grammys] are not obligated to do anything. They gave us a category, and it would be nice to have an additional dancehall category, but there are many other genres that are still not a part of the Grammys,” Ce’Cile told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday.

She also argued that there hasn’t been the same enthusiasm and support for local award shows.

“The Grammys can do what they want to do. How many of us within the industry are voting members? We don’t even support our local award shows.”

Well-known entertainment attorney and music business consultant Lloyd Stanbury doesn’t support renaming the Best Reggae Album category. Instead, he supports the idea for a separate category for dancehall.

“The dancehall music genre, although born out of the reggae music genre, has evolved and grown to establish itself globally as yet another distinct music genre coming out of Jamaica. Dancehall music has earned and deserves its own standalone category in the Grammys. What is needed is more membership representation in the Recording Academy of both reggae and dancehall creatives to lobby and advocate for change.

“I think we will see more qualified submissions from both reggae and dancehall when Jamaican music creatives take their activities as serious business, inform themselves, and create support teams with qualified personnel,” the respected music industry insider told the Observer.

Music producer, artiste manager, publicist and podcast host Ralston Barrett, who has more than 30 years of experience in the industry and has represented Grammy-nominated and Billboard-charting acts, concurs with Stanbury that a separate dancehall category is needed.

“I think dancehall is more vibrant than reggae right now, so I expected to see more dancehall artistes nominated. To me, it’s a slap in the face to dancehall music. Buju Banton is the only nominee I’d put squarely in the dancehall camp. Some people would include Shaggy, but his music blends dancehall, reggae, and other genres. I was hoping to see Masicka, Vybz Kartel, and Alkaline among the nominees, and I would have liked to see Capleton nominated too,” said Barrett.

Barrett continued: “I’d like to see two separate Grammy categories: Best Reggae Album and Best Dancehall Album. Right now, I don’t think we have the numbers to make a strong case for that, though. Our industry needs to get more organised and united, do more to strengthen both genres, and encourage more eligible Jamaican music professionals to join the Recording Academy as voting members. Putting dancehall by itself could encourage more submissions. A category of our own would give artistes even more reason to submit.

“We also need more dancehall artistes making strong albums. Once the album is done, you still have to market it, network, and get people to hear it. When an artiste wins, people are quick to curse the artiste or the team. Give them credit for putting in the work. And where are our own award shows in Jamaica? We should be honouring our music and the people who make it right here at home,” he charged.

Music executive, Grammy-nominated producer, and former chair of the Grammy reggae committee Cristy Barber poured cold water on the assertion that no dancehall artistes were nominated this year.

“Although some of the predictions that were spoken about were not among the six nominees this year, there are three deejays nominated — Buju, Shaggy and Runkus — this year. So there is a dancehall presence. Hard-core, crossover, however you see it, they are still dancehall. So, renaming the category probably won’t change the problem some have with the title just being reggae. But the Academy looks at the category as all-inclusive — reggae and dancehall,” Barber reasoned.

Dancehall artistes who have won the Best Reggae Album award over the years include Shabba Ranks, Beenie Man, Sean Paul, Buju Banton, and Shaggy.

World.title: ODPEM chief saw trouble long before audit
World.content:
Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management head office at Haining Road in St Andrew.Photo: Joseph Wellington

INTERNAL Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) correspondence seen by the Jamaica Observer show that Director General Commander Alvin Gayle had long held concerns about several of the issues raised by the auditor general in a report tabled in Parliament last Tuesday.

In its report the Auditor General Department said its team members who inspected warehouses holding Hurricane Melissa relief supplies found 359 boxes of crackers past their best-before dates, insects on the packaging of some consumables, and 15 unopened containers that had not been recorded in ODPEM’s inventory, exposing serious gaps in how the agency accounted for and safeguarded donated goods.

The report also identified approximately $780 million in shipments that were not included in the donation schedules maintained by ODPEM.

The auditor general also raised concerns about the conditions in which relief supplies were being stored, given the presence of insects on the packaging of some consumable items.

Additionally, the inspection exposed a basic problem with the agency’s record-keeping. ODPEM did not provide auditors with store records showing the quantities of goods that should have been in Warehouse 3. This meant the auditors could not compare what they physically counted with the supplies recorded as received since November 2025 or those distributed during the period under review.

Sunday Observer sources have since pointed to repeated efforts by Gayle to address the issues before the auditor general’s report.

These include a memo dated June 22 in which Gayle wrote to the entity’s then logistics manager seeking urgent information on the agency’s readiness for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.

In the memo Gayle pointed to a previous correspondence one month earlier in which he had already requested the information which had not been submitted by the logistics manager.

“Reference is made to my memorandum dated May 21, 2026, directing the completion and submission of the Hurricane Inventory Template to facilitate the consolidation and verification of the office’s operational readiness inventory for the 2026 Atlantic Hurricane Season.

“A review of your submission has revealed that the information provided was materially incomplete and required significant intervention by the Office of the Director General to address critical gaps. This situation is both disappointing and unacceptable,” said Gayle in the June memo.

He pointed out that the initial response from the logistics manager failed to adequately capture or provide the required information relating to all Starlink devices, including their current locations, operational status, assigned custodians, deployment details, and other relevant tracking information;

Gayle added that the logistics manager failed to provide generator inventories, including donor information, generator capacities, current locations, operational status, and additional information required under the General Stores section, including inventory balances, stock status, and other supporting details necessary for effective operational planning and reporting.

“The purpose of the exercise was to provide the Director General’s Office with a comprehensive and accurate inventory position. It is therefore unacceptable that such fundamental omissions were not identified and addressed prior to submission. The information requested falls squarely within your remit and should already have been known, maintained, and readily available through established inventory management processes and systems.

“The fact that the Office of the Director General found these significant gaps in the records that have been provided by you demonstrates a serious deficiency in the preparation, verification, and quality assurance of the submission,” added Gayle.

He directed the logistics manager to immediately review the inventory management and reporting processes within the Logistics Unit and provide a written report to include: The reasons for the incomplete submission; the measures being implemented to ensure inventory records are maintained accurately and in real time; the quality assurance mechanisms that would be instituted to prevent a recurrence of this issue and; any outstanding inventory information that remains to be verified.

“The maintenance of accurate inventory records is a fundamental operational requirement, particularly in the context of disaster preparedness, emergency response, donor accountability, and audit compliance. I expect immediate corrective action and sustained improvement in this regard. Please treat this matter with the urgency and seriousness it warrants,” said Gayle.

Days later Gayle again wrote to the logistics manager expressing concern about the receipt, storage, issue and status of the generators donated by the Government of Mexico to Jamaica following Hurricane Melissa in October 2025.

The ODPEM director general demanded details on when the generators were received, amount issued and how many were still in storage.

By August an obviously frustrated Gayle wrote to the logistics manager expressing displeasure over the management of the department and his failure to maintain proper records of the supplies and donated items donated to ODPEM.

“These matters fell directly within the core responsibilities of the logistics manager, particularly the maintenance of accurate and up-to-date inventory records, the proper accounting for equipment and supplies received and distributed during disaster and relief operations, and the preparation and maintenance of records showing the final disposition of items donated by local and international partners.

“ODPEM’s mandate requires the organisation to maintain effective systems for the management, control, and accountability of resources entrusted to it in support of national disaster preparedness, emergency response and relief operations. Proper accountability for these resources is therefore fundamental to the effective discharge of that mandate and to safeguarding the wider public interest,” said Gayle to the logistics manager who resigned from ODPEM in August.

World.title: HORSE POWER
World.content:
Constable Achasha Madden of the Mounted Troop Division shows her affection for Behave after visting Caymanas Park for the first time on Saturday, November 7. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

There is life after racing — and at Caymanas Park, it is a life worth living.

That was the powerful message on Saturday, November 7, as the Racehorse Retirement Programme took centre stage, celebrating almost 500 horses that have been retired from racing in the past five years and given a second career, a new home, and a new purpose.

This year’s showcase featured two of the programme’s key retirement partners — the College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) and the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Mounted Troop Division — along with the launch of a new QR code that takes the public directly to the Racehorse Retirement webpage.

The page is a one-stop hub for the programme. It lists the names of the almost 500 horses retired from Caymanas Park in the past five years, provides access to the horse ownership transfer form, shares testimonials on race horse retirement, and carries media articles on the programme’s work.

For Sergeant Everal Alexander of the Mounted Troop Division, retired race horses are not just animals — they are partners in service.

The Mounted Troop is the oldest division in the entire Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), and at present it has 15 equines, ranging in age from two years old to 24 years old.

“We have a veteran in TJ, from a race horse. He’s pretty much retired. So what we do there is pretty much ceremonial duties, regular mounted patrol, school visits — it’s really the lighter side of policing,” Alexander explained.

Alexander said that getting a race horse ready for that lighter side takes patience and skill.

“We normally take them onto the street because some are not used to vehicle traffic, some are not used to noise, and so we use different apparatus like flags. What we do is to take a horse out of its competitive spirit and into a slower, calmer spirit that can be manoeuvred safely through traffic and crowds, in schools and on parade.

“We are members of the retired race horse association, so when a horse is not competitive enough to win, sometimes we are fortunate when we get them, and we just automatically transition into what we do there,” Alexander told the Sunday Observer.

The need, he added, is growing.

“The programme is good and we are on the hunt for more horses because the ones that we have are pretty much aging, so we need to replenish the stock. Wherever we can get those horses, we do most greatly appreciate it,” he said.

The Mounted Troop is also breaking new ground in its own ranks. In 2025, it trained 17 persons at the National Police College of Jamaica — including five females, the first time that has ever happened in the constabulary. At present, out of a cohort of 18 riders, six are female.

Derrick Deslandes, president of CASE, said that retired race horses, have become a critical part of teaching and learning.

“We teach agriculture, and its equine science course focuses on horses and so part of our programme is to expose the students to the horses.

“The programme has been around for quite a while, but we have always done equine sciences. We have just brought in the animals so the students can actually work with the animals directly,” Deslandes told the Observer.

The partnership with Caymanas Park, he said, works for everyone.

“So the horses are finished racing and you may not have the time to feed them and the cost to feed them, so institutions like mine will take them. And we’ll grow them out and raise them and they’ll become part of our programme, our teaching and learning programme,” Deslandes said.

CASE currently has 11 or 12 horses from the programme, but like the police, it is always looking to replenish as horses age or pass on.

“We’re also looking to do a programme to train young people to ride horses. We are looking to establish a programme to train people in Portland to ride horses,” Deslandes revealed.

And fittingly, it was also revealed that the Richard Azan-trained Mojito — one of the most popular horses of his generation — is now preparing for his own next chapter. He will be a stable pony at his barn in 2027.

World.title: Why cybersecurity matters from your phone to your fridge
World.content:
Jevon Davis, Chief Operating Officer from Guardsman Cyber Intelligence Limited

Cyberattacks targeting supermarkets and cooling systems across Europe earlier this month reaffirmed the expanding threat to digital security, where hackers aren’t just going after personal information.

Guardsman Cyber Intelligence Limited Chief Operating Officer Jevon Davis told Observer Online that as homes and items become more interconnected and people depend more on operational technology, the Internet of Things (IoT) grows, including everything from smart cameras to televisions and appliances.

He also noted that what hackers want isn’t always clear-cut or financially motivated.

“It’s a matter of risk versus reward… what happened in Europe demonstrates that cyberattacks can also be a case where it affects physical equipment and basic operations,” Davis explained.

“Let’s use the supermarket as an example: if an attacker gains access to a food system and manipulates, let’s say, the temperatures, the business could potentially lose significant amounts of inventory and experience operational disruption…something that sounds unusual, like hacking a refrigerator, can reward hackers,” he shared.

Davis stressed that the “reward” can extend past stealing financial information.

“Even in the case of the everyday user, you may say that hackers don’t want to necessarily hack me, You might think so, but at the same time, some of them are just in it for just causing disruption, so sometimes the motivation isn’t financial gain or extortion. It’s sometimes just deliberate disruption,” he said.

The Europe attack, now being described as unprecedented, affected France in October and around seven other European companies in November, hitting over 700 stores. Hackers gained control of refrigerators remotely and increased the temperatures, resulting in millions of euros in losses.

Jamaica is not exempt from attacks because it is a small country, Davis explained.

“We do see where it happens every day, every minute, every second. So at Guardsman Cyber Intelligence, one of our duties is to protect the existing client environment. So we see live attacks happening every day,” he explained.

Davis added that hackers are also always looking for the next way to compromise an organisation or even a country.

As the government and populace prioritise efficiency and Jamaica continues to move toward increased digital infrastructure, there is more at risk, according to Davis.

“Any time technology tends to grow more and more, whether it would be in an organisation or even at an individual level, there’s always more risk. But one of the things that we can do is to essentially have an idea of what we’re implementing or growing from a technological perspective,” he said.

He urged businesses to maintain an inventory of connected equipment, understand their purpose, identify who is responsible for managing them, and review where they can be accessed.

“It shouldn’t just be limited to traditional computers and servers. It should include the relevant IoT devices and operational equipment, just like we discussed earlier with the fridge,” he explained.

Davis also said it was important to reduce unnecessary exposure.

“Not every device needs to be directly accessible from the internet; in fact, for critical operational equipment, direct internet exposure should generally be avoided,” he said.

For individuals at home, the recommendation is to have a good internet router that is properly secured.

“That is often the main connection between your devices on the internet… If you have bought a recent appliance and you have to set up the internet on it, change the default password…that is something that attackers like to take advantage of,” he added.

World.title: Special Olympics officials request privacy for loved ones after Beach Games tragedy
World.content:
Onlookers at the Harmony Beach Park in Montego Bay, St James, after an athlete went missing in a swimming competition during the Special Olympics Caribbean Beach Games on Friday. (Photo: Collin Reid)

MONTEGO BAY, Jamaica — Special Olympics officials are requesting privacy for the friends and family of the Rwandan athlete who died during the Caribbean Beach Games at Harmony Beach Park on Friday.

The athlete went missing during swimming competition on Friday morning, and his body was later discovered in the water.

READ: Rwandan athlete at Special Olympics Beach Games believed to have drowned

“We are saddened to confirm that an individual involved in a water-related incident during the Beach Games event has died. The cause of death has not yet been determined.

“Our deepest condolences are with their family and friends, and we ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time,” said a statement from Special Olympics North America, which has oversight of the Caribbean programmes.

The 2026 Caribbean Beach Games — the first of its kind to be held in Jamaica — officially began with the opening ceremony on Thursday. The closing ceremony is set for this evening.

The Beach Games comprise delegations from 18 Special Olympics regional programmes, as well as the invited contingent from Rwanda. Athletes have been competing in swimming, football, volleyball, basketball, and bocce.

World.title: From House to court
World.content:
The war of words between the Government and Opposition triggered by the November 3, 2026 ruckus in Parliament has spiralled into a legal battle with House Speaker Juliet Holness taking her allegations against St Andrew South Western Member of Parliament (MP) Dr Angela Brown Burke to the Supreme Court.

In a claim filed on November 19, Holness is seeking damages for assault and battery, alleging that Brown Burke stepped towards her and made physical contact with the left side of her body as she was leaving the parliamentary chamber.

According to the particulars of claim, the incident occurred after the House had been adjourned and Holness was making her way out of the chamber. The Speaker alleges that Brown Burke pointed at her while shouting “Coward! Coward!”, before stepping towards her and lunging with her upper body, causing contact with the left side of her body.

Holness claims that the contact was intentional and occurred without her consent or lawful justification. She is seeking general and aggravated damages, interest, and legal costs.

Attorney-at-law Alexander Shaw, who represents Holness, confirmed that the court documents had been served on Brown Burke. He also disclosed that a police report concerning the incident was made on November 9.

“My client has placed her allegations before the court and will pursue the matter through the established legal process. Holding public office does not diminish a person’s right to personal safety or to seek redress through the courts,” Shaw said in a release on Friday.

The November 3 confrontation followed a tense sitting of the House during debate on a motion concerning Jamaica’s decision to abstain from a United Nations resolution calling for an end to the United States’ decades-old trade embargo against Cuba.

Opposition members objected to the way the debate was brought to a close, arguing that their participation had been curtailed. The disagreement continued after the sitting was adjourned, with a separate heated exchange involving Opposition MP Mikael Phillips and Government MP Desmond McKenzie.

It was during that disorder that the Speaker left the chamber.

Brown Burke has since denied physically assaulting or pushing Holness, although she has acknowledged using the word “Coward” during the exchange.

Brown Burke had also taken steps to challenge public statements alleging that she physically assaulted the Speaker.

On November 10, her attorneys at Chen Green & Company wrote to Holness, Senate President Tom Tavares-Finson, and Deputy Senate President Charles Sinclair demanding that they withdraw statements alleging that Brown Burke had pushed or physically assaulted the Speaker.

The attorneys said the statements had damaged their client’s reputation and demanded written withdrawals, apologies, and compensation. They gave the three parliamentarians 10 days to respond.

The People’s National Party subsequently indicated that Brown Burke could pursue claims in the Supreme Court if the matter was not resolved. However, as at November 20, there had been no public confirmation that she had filed a civil claim against the three.

The November incident was not the first major clash between the two parliamentarians. On April 28, Brown Burke was suspended for the remainder of a sitting after liftng the ceremonial mace during proceedings on the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority (NaRRA) Bill.

The incident occurred during the Committee of the Whole House’s examination of the Bill. Brown Burke removed the mace from its designated position, prompting the chair, Holness, to name her. The House subsequently suspended Brown Burke for the remainder of that sitting.

That incident was later cited by the Government when it moved to suspend Brown Burke again following the November confrontation.

At last week’s sitting of Parliament, Leader of Government Business Floyd Green moved a motion under Standing Order 43(13), accusing Brown Burke of obstructing the Speaker’s path as she left the chamber, making physical contact with her, and shouting “Coward!”

The motion described the alleged conduct as a breach of the respect owed to the authority of the chair and the dignity of Parliament.

Green also relied on Brown Burke’s earlier suspension in April, arguing that the seriousness of the November incident, together with the previous disciplinary action, warranted a further suspension.

The motion proposed that Brown Burke be suspended from the service of the House until the conclusion of the sixth sitting following November 17. It also required her to leave Parliament immediately and barred her from attending House or committee meetings or entering the parliamentary precincts during the suspension.

World.title: Europeans dare to believe Trump could deliver security for Ukraine
World.content:
Neither is yet certain, and one Russian official dismissed the idea.

But Russian President Vladimir Putin himself has not yet publicly rejected Kushner’s plan, and European negotiators are taking it seriously, even if they want more information about how it would work.

A security guarantee for Ukraine based on NATO’s Article 5 collective defense clause, which states that an attack on one member shall be treated as an attack on all, would change the game when it comes to deterring Russia from invading Ukraine again after this war ends. That is particularly true if, as implied, America, with its mighty military, is bound into such a guarantee.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, French President Emmanuel Macron, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, back, and U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner leave a Coalition of the Willing media call in Berlin on Nov. 19, 2026. | Pool photo by Hannah McKay/Getty Images

While few details are known about the proposal, it would, if backed up by robust legal, military and political commitments, mean that a new attack on Ukraine would risk a direct conflict with the U.S.

An aide in French President Emmanuel Macron’s office said the U.S. is heading in “the right direction” but called on the White House to go a step further and give Ukraine full NATO membership.

An Article 5 guarantee “is obviously the best guarantee of solidarity among allies,” said the aide, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “So, if we say we’re giving Ukraine Article 5-type guarantees, we shouldn’t overcomplicate things: It means that Ukraine is joining NATO. The alliance’s credibility rests above all on Article 5. Article 5 is an article of faith.”
