World.title: Effort to regulate ‘killer robots’ delayed to 2028
World.content:
But resistance from several countries, and especially Russia, blocked those efforts. In the end, the 128 member countries agreed to launch "the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems," over the next two years, Julien Thöni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the talks, told reporters.

The issue is of growing importance as AI gains new capabilities and autonomous systems become increasingly powerful. Ukraine, Russia, Israel and others are using drones and robots in warfare, although they insist that humans still have ultimate control over pulling the trigger.

However, Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of more than 300 organizations, said such systems have already been tested or deployed, including in Ukraine and Gaza.

“Autonomous weapons technology, including AI in the targeting cycle, is being deployed on the battlefield — delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” said Nicole van Rooijen, the executive director of Stop Killer Robots.

Informal talk

Because consensus is required for any decision, Russia was able to block formal negotiations all week, refusing to allow observers — including the European Union — to take part in the talks. Instead, negotiations were held informally to circumvent Russia’s veto.

A Brazilian diplomat suggested it wasn't only Russia trying to block the effort. “You can blame Russia, but they are not the only ones. Some people are hiding behind Russia,” the diplomat said.

World.title: Russian ship damaged by drone attack in Gulf of Finland, Helsinki and Moscow say
World.content:
The Finnish coast guard said the ship was known to have ties with Russian armed forces.

A cargo ship sailing under the Russian flag was damaged by a drone attack in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday morning, the defense ministry in Helsinki said.

Finnish authorities said at a press conference Saturday afternoon that Ukraine carried out the attack in international waters, and that the ship then drifted into Finnish territorial waters in the Eastern Gulf of Finland, according to Yle.

Authorities also said that the ship is known to have links with the Russian armed forces, but that it could not be confirmed whether military equipment was on board. Russian state-owned news agency Tass said the vessel was transporting “paints and coatings,” citing a single unnamed source.

World.title: Russian threats ‘less and less hybrid,’ Von der Leyen says after assassination plot in Denmark
World.content:
Officials said at a press conference that a Russian intelligence service had hired two members of the Copenhagen-based gang Loyal to Familia to carry out the attack, but that police managed to stop them before it took place. The concert was then cancelled.

The suspects deny the allegations.

The Danish government reacted on Friday by expelling the Russian defense attaché, giving him seven days to leave the country.

“Moscow will respond accordingly,” Russia’s foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told state-owned news agency Tass.

“The accusations against Russia are again not supported by any evidence, except for the unsubstantiated and unverifiable ‘conclusions’ and ‘data’ of Danish intelligence services,” the Russian embassy in Denmark said in a statement.

Von der Leyen said in her statement that the EU has “the tools to act” against cases like this. She said actions could range from “rapid response teams” to sanctions. She added that an upcoming European Security Strategy, which she announced in her State of the EU speech in September, could reinforce the bloc’s “preparedness and deterrence.”

It is the second time Kyivstoner has been targeted in an attempted murder plot this year. On Aug. 7, a Russian man was detained in Poland for planning an attack against the musician, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.

Russia’s FSB security service accused the rapper in July of helping to plan drone attacks on a defense facility in the Moscow region, an allegation he denied on social media.

World.title: Costa cuts proposed EU budget by €44B
World.content:
"This proposal is fit for tackling the challenges we are facing in our societies, and gives the European Union the necessary capacity to act," Costa said on Saturday morning.

Costa, who is guiding discussions over the 2028-2034 budget which needs to be agreed by all EU governments, suggested the reductions, which are based on current prices, from the previous proposal presented by Ireland, in its role holding the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, last month.

Overall, the cuts amount to a reduction in size of the budget by €204 billion, or 10.2%, from the European Commission’s original proposal in July last year.

In another major development, Costa suggested introducing a new tax on large digital companies such as Google and Meta to help finance the budget over the coming years.

In recent years, Brussels held back from levying this tax for fear retaliation from Washington, but the Republicans' bruising defeat in the midterm elections earlier this month created an opening.

These ideas set the scene for fraught discussions among the EU’s 27 leaders during a summit next week. Even then the agreed budget will have to be approved by the European Parliament.

World.title: UK will take its time setting out Brexit options, says minister
World.content:
Andy Burnham pledged in September to set out “options” to fix the U.K. relationship with the bloc — which he said could include rejoining its single market, customs union, or even the EU itself.

But speaking in Brussels on Friday, the prime minister suggested the process could take longer and signaled the start of an “informal brainstorming process” with the European Union to conclude at the next U.K.-EU summit near the end of 2027.

It comes after rumbles of Cabinet discontent over the policy shift and speculation the prime minister may be taking a more cautious approach to avoid spooking his own government allies.

Defending the length of the process, Falconer said there was “a lot of variation” in the different relationships Britain could have with the EU and detail to work through.

“People say, ‘Oh, the options are obvious’ … but I think most people would struggle to describe the precise difference between the different arrangements,” he said.

Burnham has said he will be led by the public on the issue and told reporters in Brussels on Friday that he would “not be running ahead of public opinion on the issue.”

World.title: The biggest winners and losers of the EU-UK summit deals
World.content:
British renewable energy producers have double reason to celebrate. The decision to link the U.K. and EU emissions trading schemes from 2028 means clean energy exported to the continent will no longer be subject to the EU’s carbon border tax — making British clean energy exports more competitive.

Perhaps even more significant is a plan for the U.K. to join the EU internal electricity market, which they hope to finalize next year. If that comes off, it will make it much easier for British electricity generators to sell power to EU customers.

“That would be a major prize for consumers and the renewable energy industry,” RenewableUK chief executive Tara Singh said in a statement Friday, adding it would allow “electricity to be traded more efficiently across our interconnectors and enabling Britain and Europe to make better use of the cheapest clean power available at any given time.” EU renewables groups have made the same point.

The tech industry



The plan to launch an EU-U.K. Digital Partnership early next year is a win for the tech industry on both sides of the channel.



The statement’s wording is loose and doesn’t provide a ton of detail for industry types to sink their teeth into, but it spans a wide range of potential areas that “could cover” secure connectivity, quantum, online safety, as well as AI and its safety — areas that have seen considerable divergence since Brexit.



The statement also includes digital wallets and credentials, which are of interest to U.K. businesses, especially since Andy Burnham ditched the British government’s plans for digital ID.



Of the more political parts of the agreement, the youth visas scheme element is a big win for smaller U.K. tech companies who want to welcome keen young Europeans and entrepreneurs to the British tech scene.

The City

While there was nothing of great direct benefit to the City of London in today’s deal, the mood music matters for the U.K.’s financial services industry.

World.title: Reported FBI hack 'not good' but could have benefits, Trump says
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has said that a reported hack of the Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI) criminal justice database was "not good" but that it could have some benefits.

 

US media outlets reported earlier this week that the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) appeared to have been breached by hackers and that the agency had launched an investigation.

Asked about the subject on Saturday, Trump told Fox News: "We just heard about it, and I will say that it's not good. I don't like that."

"But maybe we'll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise," he continued, before referring to the "Russia hoax," the "Ukraine hoax," and alleged voter fraud.

"Maybe we'll learn about them, maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place," Trump said. "I always like to put things in a positive spin."

The NCIC is a computerised index of criminal justice information and includes records on criminal history, fugitives, missing persons and stolen properties, among other topics.

The reported hack comes amid a wave of tech outages in the US, which have impacted travel, communications and banking, as well as an internal system used by the National Security Agency.

National cyber director Sean Cairncross was ousted from his role as the issues mounted, with Trump telling reporters on Friday that he "didn't think that person was good enough." The national cyber director is tasked with advising the president on cybersecurity policy and strategy, including information security and data protection as well as deterrence of "malicious" activity.

World.title: Hot freezers, lost GPS and fake bombs: Europe's month of cyberattacks
World.content:
On 2 and 3 November, supermarket freezers across Europe started switching themselves into defrost mode. In some stores, attackers set the temperature as high as 50°C.

 

Shops in Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Romania and Sweden threw away spoiled meat and frozen food, while several blood banks in France were also hit. The UK reported attacks too.

EU food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen called it a "deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain". Nearly three weeks later, nobody has claimed responsibility and the motive remains unclear.

One month, 16 incidents

The fridge attacks were one of 16 incidents mapped by DigitalEurope, the trade association for Europe's digital technology industry, based in Brussels, Belgium, between 18 October and 18 November.

Eleven were cyberattacks. Hackers took an energy company's IT systems in Norway, closed a district hospital's emergency room in Germany and stole data from a tunnel builder working across Denmark and Germany.

At an unnamed EU institution, HR, payroll and medical systems were knocked offline. The personal data of 18 senior officials from Italy, Germany and the Netherlands was published, and espionage malware was found in Romanian government email.

About €100 million was taken from a French bank through one of its suppliers, more than 700 fintech customer accounts were exposed in Italy, and a Danish shipping group's legacy system was raided for data.

The other five incidents were physical, including two sabotage plots. About 80 aircraft lost GPS over the North Sea, drones forced Moldova to close its airspace, and hoax bomb threats hit more than 35 flights across Europe.

"Resilience is no longer just an IT department job," said Cecilia Bonefeld-Dahl, DigitalEurope's director general. "It is security policy and industrial policy."

The group says its list is not exhaustive. Ransomware gangs alone list dozens of European victims every month.

The password is 12345

The November wave was not the first. In mid-October, hackers took over refrigeration units in at least 350 supermarkets in France, including Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché and Coopérative U stores, and manually overrode their temperatures.

France's cybersecurity agency said the units ran software from Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell systems. Danfoss said many had reached the end of their life, no longer received security updates or ran outdated firmware.

Supermarket refrigeration is often connected to the internet so contractors can monitor and repair it remotely. Security firm Forescout found nearly 13,000 refrigeration control services openly reachable online in 99 countries.

In November, attackers exploited weak security and known flaws in Danfoss's AK-SM system manager. Many systems still used factory-default logins such as "Supervisor" and "12345".

George Nott, technology editor at trade magazine The Grocer, said the attackers found exposed login pages and used vulnerabilities that had already been patched. In Sweden, the Coop chain said the equipment in its seven affected shops was connected over old 4G mobile networks.

Xavier Bellekens, chief executive of cybersecurity firm Lupovis, said routing the controllers through VPNs would largely have removed the risk.

Who did it?

Of DigitalEurope's 16 incidents, seven have no named culprit. Attackers claimed four themselves, investigators suspect an actor in two without formally naming it, and only three have been publicly attributed by a government or researchers.

"That is what makes hybrid attacks work: cheap, deniable and hard to pin on anyone," the group said.

The fridge attacks show how hard the question is. Lupovis said its decoy systems recorded more than 276 attempts by 91 threat actors to probe Danfoss controllers over 10 days, peaking on 26 October and stopping at the end of the month.

The activity was traced to "bulletproof hosting" services, built to resist takedowns and law enforcement, some of which Russian groups have used before. Bellekens said that did not prove Russia was responsible, but there was "a bit of a pattern". The coordination within about 24 hours pointed to a well-planned operation, possibly by a state, he added.

Others are less sure. Dan Cimpean, director of Romania's National Cyber Security Directorate, called the attacks "semi-amateurish" and said he did not suspect a state actor. After the French attack, Ken Munro of British firm Pen Test Partners said it could be "kids messing around".

No ransom was demanded, which investigators found puzzling: criminal and hacktivist groups usually move quickly to profit from or publicise an attack. Agencies cannot even agree on what to call it. Belgium, Italy and Estonia labelled it a cyberattack, Sweden and Ireland a "cyber incident", while the EU's cybersecurity agency ENISA stopped short of calling it an attack.

Same targets, different weapons

DigitalEurope's tally suggests the line between online and offline attacks is blurring. In the same month, one military drone maker in Germany was hit through a hijacked software update, while an arson attack on another in Estonia was foiled.

DIGITALEUROPE analysed the recent wave of cyberattacks affecting Europe. DIGITALEUROPE

The group also counted a plot to start fires next to a railway and a power line in Germany.

"Digital and physical attacks hit the same targets," it said. Its map shows the incidents stretching from the North Sea to Romania and Moldova.

Find, fund, buy

Bonefeld-Dahl wants Europe to go further. "Europe needs the technology to detect, deter and recover – and it must FIND. FUND. BUY," she wrote on LinkedIn.

DigitalEurope is calling on EU leaders to spend at least 25% of the next EU budget, worth almost €2 trillion, on technologies to deter, defend and recover. It says only 14% currently goes to digital.

"There is no more time to waste," Bonefeld-Dahl wrote, in a message addressed to the bloc's prime ministers.

The 14% figure is the digital share of the EU's 2021–2025 spending, including its post-pandemic recovery fund, rather than of the budget now being negotiated. And as an industry lobby, DigitalEurope speaks for many of the companies that would sell Europe that technology.

In Brussels, the response is taking shape in the revision of the EU's Cybersecurity Act, led in the European Parliament by Czech MEP Markéta Gregorová.

What next?

Experts warn that fridges are only the start. Nott said heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems, electronic shelf labels and even floor-cleaning robots could have similar weaknesses.

Kumar Sokka, chief executive of Acre Security, said the same type of controller can run doors, access control, cameras, alarms and building climate systems. Organisations often leave them to facilities teams rather than treating them as part of their obligations under NIS2, the EU's cybersecurity law, he said.

Artificial intelligence could make the problem worse. Gianni Cuozzo, founder and chief executive of Exein, said AI was shortening the time between finding a vulnerability and building an attack, so connected devices needed to defend themselves as they run.

Bonefeld-Dahl will discuss Europe's response in Vilnius, Lithuania, next week. She ended her post with a question: "What's the next critical target?"

World.title: New COP31 draft deal tabled as countries scramble to salvage climate talks
World.content:
A new COP31 draft agreement was published early on Sunday as nations continued to struggle to reach a climate deal.

 

The new draft, published deep into overtime, kept a much-sought goal to electrify the global economy but again failed to mention fossil fuels, deepening divisions at the UN conference - which is being held in Antalya, Turkey.

The latest text needs consensus approval from almost 200 nations at a closing session on Sunday.

An EU official told the AFP news agency that the draft was a "backwards" step and warned that there was a "very real possibility" of the talks ending without a deal.

"I am more pessimistic today than I was yesterday," they said.

"The situation is difficult, and the outcome is uncertain. The oil-producing countries are putting up a fierce fight," a German official added.

Planet-heating fossil fuels have become a flashpoint at the talks, which come amid soaring energy prices and simmering global tensions stemming from the Iran war.

A draft deal unveiled earlier this week had called for a sped-up phasing out of fossil fuels. But a second version released on Thursday removed all mentions of the energy sources, forcing negotiators back to the bargaining table.

A group of countries including France and Panama had released a letter on Friday insisting that a deal include "a clear transition away from fossil fuels."

COP31 President Murat Kurum, center, speaks during a plenary session at the COP31 U.N. Climate Summit, Friday, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

The latest offering acknowledged a previous global deal to transition away from fossil fuels but stopped short of naming them explicitly.

It also kept a contentious push to expand carbon capture and storage, a technology backed by the fossil fuel industry but criticised by opponents as costly and ineffective at reducing emissions.

"We are very disappointed with how the text looks," Michael Joseph, the environment minister of Antigua and Barbuda, told AFP.

"I can't honestly say that I'm okay with it passing" as it is, Joseph said, adding that the draft was "quite silent" on fossil fuels.

World.title: Gadi Eisenkot invites Netanyahu's Likud party for 'marathon' coalition talks
World.content:
Gadi Eisenkot has invited the right-wing Likud party of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for "marathon" coalition talks as he continues to work to form Israel's next government, his party said on Saturday.

 

The talks are due to begin on Sunday and represent a "sincere and genuine effort to form a government that is as broad as possible," the centrist Yashar party said.

"The Yashar negotiating team will leave no stone unturned, enable bold moves and bring about a breakthrough that will lead to the formation of a government," it added.

Eisenkot has until early December to form a new government after both his and Netanyahu's blocs fell short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset in Israel's October legislative elections. Netanyahu's camp finished on 53 seats, while the opposition, led by the Yashar party, ended on 48.

In Israel, a candidate tasked with forming a government has 28 days to carry out the job. The president is able to extend this by a maximum of 14 days if necessary.

Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, congratulates newly elected Knesset Speaker MK Matan Kahana following a vote to elect a new Speaker at the Knesset. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Likud on Saturday outlined its position on forming a national unity government, which Netanyahu has been pushing for, including demands to halt "all personal attacks and incitement" as well as political "boycotts" against Netanyahu and the government.

It also called for a joint declaration committing to a unity government comprised of "all parties that support the existence of the State of Israel as the nation-state of the Jewish people" and without the involvement of Arab parties - which secured a record 19 seats between them in last month's elections.

"As for the talks with the Likud, we are making sincere and genuine efforts, but unfortunately there is a wide gap between rhetoric and actions, and between the Likud’s rhetoric and its actual willingness to cooperate," Eisenkot wrote in a post on social media on Friday.

He added that he intended to continue trying to "achieve a breakthrough in each of the options before us for forming a coalition that is as broad as possible" but that he did not plan to "drag this out."

"They must understand that, at the right time, I will bring a new and strong government headed by me to the Knesset for approval," he said.

World.title: Madeira's ocean survey finds evidence protection works – and some worrying signs
World.content:
Madeira's waters sit at an ecological crossroads in the North-East Atlantic. Migrating whales, seabirds and turtles pass through, and the archipelago is home to cold-water corals and one of the world's rarest seals. Yet large stretches of the sea around the Portuguese islands have never been properly studied.

 

The Madeira Ocean Expedition, which ran throughout October, set out to fill those gaps. Its findings will feed into decisions on how to manage and expand Madeira's marine protected areas, as the region works towards protecting 30 per cent of its sea by 2030, with at least 10 per cent fully protected.

"We cannot protect without understanding how the biodiversity functions and works," says João Canning-Clode, director of the MARE-Madeira research centre.

A health check at sea: 500 dives in Madeira's ocean

Madeira's regional government organised the expedition with the Oceano Azul Foundation, National Geographic Pristine Seas, the regional research agency ARDITI and Oceanário de Lisboa. Teams worked from the historic tall ship Santa Maria Manuela and a fleet of smaller boats around Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas Islands.

"In an expedition like this, we want to take a snapshot about the health of the marine environment," says Emanuel Gonçalves, chief scientist at the Oceano Azul Foundation.

Scientists completed nearly 500 dives, lowered more than 300 baited cameras, filtered seawater for traces of DNA, mapped the shoreline with drones and sampled for microplastics.

With no research vessel of its own yet, MARE-Madeira also hired a fishing boat. "The fishermen could see for the first time live images of some of the biodiversity that they are actually fishing," Canning-Clode says. "On the other hand, the scientific community can see firsthand how difficult their life is."

Signs that Madeira's ocean protections work

Early results suggest Madeira's reserves are making a difference. Limpets – grazing sea snails harvested as a local delicacy – were bigger and more abundant inside protected areas, a sign that limits on collecting them are working, and the largest groupers were recorded there too.

"The good news is that we have the science to show us that when we fully protect the ocean, the ocean responds," Gonçalves says.

The Mediterranean monk seal is another case in point. Hunted for centuries, it had almost vanished from Madeira by the late 1980s, when only six to eight animals were thought to remain. The Desertas Islands became a nature reserve in 1990, partly to protect it. Today the species "is a beacon of hope", Gonçalves says. "The population is increasing in numbers. Now that increase is very slow because they are very slow breeders."

The expedition also achieved the first-ever satellite tagging of a Blainville's beaked whale in the North-East Atlantic. Early tracking data show the animal favouring waters south of the Desertas, close to the fully protected area.

But one finding stands out for the wrong reason. Fewer than 10 sharks were recorded across the entire expedition. The organisers call this scarcity concerning and in line with wider worries about sharks in the Atlantic.

Into the deep: The difficulties of exploring Madeira's ocean

By area, Madeira is mostly deep sea. "It's an ocean state, a deep ocean state," says Diva Amon, a marine scientist on the Oceano Azul Foundation's board. "And the deep sea is a very difficult place to study."

Drift cameras developed by researchers in the Azores and lowered from a fishing boat reached 1,060 metres. They revealed sponge fields and large black corals that may be several hundred years old – alongside lost fishing lines and a glass bottle.

Closer to the surface, the habitat-mapping team's highlight was a dense black coral garden off Porto Santo, known as Ariel's Garden after the team's pink underwater robot. "Our torpedo is pink, so by majority vote it's called Ariel, after the little mermaid from the Disney film," says João Monteiro, a researcher at MARE-Madeira and the University of Madeira.

A second expedition in 2027 will explore the deepest waters. Amon hopes it will reveal "places that are as iconic as the Grand Canyon or the Okavango Delta".

For Paul Rose, head of expeditions at National Geographic Pristine Seas, Madeira's location matters. "People think about ocean protection, they think about the Pacific... It all seems a bit remote," he says. "But if they see huge, beautiful, functioning, proven marine protected areas in Europe, it's closer to home."

Just over 10 per cent of the global ocean now lies within protected areas, according to IUCN and UNEP-WCMC – a third of the way to the 2030 goal. "We've really got to protect 30 per cent or we're in big trouble," Rose says.

World.title: Is Europe ready to judge workers by skills, not just diplomas? Who leads skills-first hiring?
World.content:
The labour market is constantly changing. New jobs are emerging and new skills are required. Degrees still matter in Europe’s job market, but employers are paying more attention to what people can actually do, experts say.

 

“The currency of the labour market is shifting from traditional credentials alone towards a stronger focus on skills,” OECD’s ‘A Skills‑First Labour Market’ report says.

This is known as a skills-first approach.

“In practice, skills-first hiring is not about replacing degrees altogether, but about giving greater weight to individuals’ demonstrated skills, wherever they were acquired, to improve the matching of talent to jobs,” Glenda Quintini, senior economist at OECD, told Euronews Business.

Dr Soon-Joo Gog, senior director at the Centre for Skills-First Practices at the Singapore University of Social Sciences, emphasised that skills-first does not mean skills only. It is an operating principle. Individuals and employers use demonstrated skills, alongside qualifications.

The OECD’s Skills-First Readiness and Adoption Index measures how ready each country is for this approach.

How does the index work?

The index gives each country a score between 0 and 1. A higher score means a country is better prepared for skills-first practices and uses them more widely.

The index looks at how well countries identify, develop, recognise and reward skills. This includes adult learning, the use of skills data, public support for training and how far employers value what workers can show they are able to do.

Sweden and France lead the way

Sweden has the highest score in Europe at 0.70, followed by France (0.69), the UK (0.65) and Belgium (0.64).

“Countries such as Sweden and France perform strongly overall, although there is no single pathway to building a skills-first labour market,” Quintini said.

“Sweden, for example, stands out for its strong enabling framework, including the use of skills intelligence data and public support for skills development.” she added.

Finland (0.63), Czechia (0.61), Norway (0.61) and Latvia (0.61) also score above the European average.

The average across 23 European countries is 0.58. Spain (0.59), Denmark (0.58), Portugal (0.58), Italy (0.58), Lithuania (0.58), Poland (0.58) and Austria (0.58) are close to this average.

Germany (0.57), Switzerland (0.57) and the Netherlands (0.56) are slightly below it.

Hungary (0.45) and Greece (0.46) have the lowest scores. Turkey (0.52), Slovakia (0.54) and Slovenia (0.54) also score low.

Quintini noted that countries at the lower end of the index often face greater barriers related to adult learning participation and the development of broader learning ecosystems.

“The gap is therefore not simply about education systems, but it reflects how effectively countries identify, develop, recognise and reward skills in the labour market,” she said.

The US scores slightly above the European average at 0.60. Canada (0.55), Japan (0.51) and South Korea (0.48) are below it.

Gog pointed out that most European countries have laid the foundations but the harder step is to make these practices routine.

“That takes time and requires coordinated effort across the system,” she said.

Degrees still matter, but they are not the only signal

Experts agree that degrees remain important. But employers increasingly want to see skills as well.

“Degrees continue to matter in OECD labour markets, particularly because they remain a widely recognised signal of knowledge and capabilities,” Quintini said.

“However, employers are increasingly looking beyond formal qualifications and paying greater attention to the actual skills that workers possess and can demonstrate.”

She said skill shortages are driving this shift. Firms also need to find talent from a wider range of backgrounds, and skill needs are often changing faster than education systems can adapt.

As of 2025, more than 70% of employers across OECD countries report difficulties filling vacancies because of a lack of skilled talent. At the same time, around a third of workers say they are either over-skilled or under-skilled for their current job.

Significance of degrees varies by occupation

“Degrees still matter but their importance varies considerably by occupation and the real requirements are not always made transparent to jobseekers,” Pawel Adrjan, director of economic research at Indeed, told Euronews Business.

Indeed research found that only 14% of UK job postings explicitly mention formal education requirements, compared to 50% in the US.

He underlined that degrees remain important in specialist and highly regulated professions in practice.

“The key distinction is that a degree remains a valuable signal of knowledge and capability but it is not necessarily the only way candidates can demonstrate the skills required to do a job,” he added.

Skills need to evolve rapidly

Anna Toni, senior specialist at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment in Finland, emphasized that stakeholders increasingly recognise that valuable skills are acquired not only through formal education, but also through work experience, volunteering, hobbies and other life experiences. New tools and methods are being developed to identify and validate these skills.

“Labour markets are changing faster than before, driven by factors such as digitalisation, the green transition and AI. Skills need to evolve rapidly, and education and employment policies must adapt accordingly,” she told Euronews Business.

Skills or degrees: Which pays more?

The OECD found that on average, extra education raises wages by about 16%, while better numeracy skills raise them by about 9%, when comparing gaps of similar size.

This finding shows that employers still place substantial value on educational credentials as signals of productivity, especially when information on workers’ skills is limited according to Quintini.

In the OECD index, below 1 means education pays more than skills. France is the only European country above 1 at 1.33. This means a numeracy gap pays about a third more than an education gap of the same typical size.

“This [in France] may reflect a labour market and policy environment that is more conducive to recognising and valuing demonstrated skills,” she said.

Gog warned that the test covers numeracy only, so it misses the technical, social and job-specific skills that many jobs need.

World.title: Suffolk village votes to ‘leave UK’ in protest over asylum seeker plans
World.content:
A village in eastern England has voted overwhelmingly in favour of symbolically leaving the United Kingdom in protest against government plans to accommodate hundreds of asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.

 

Residents of Barnham, in Suffolk, voted 257 to 16 in favour of seeking a special status similar to that enjoyed by the Crown Dependencies of Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man. One ballot was spoilt in Saturday’s vote, in which around 500 residents were eligible to take part.

The vote is purely symbolic and has no legal force. It does not mean Barnham can leave the United Kingdom or acquire Crown Dependency status. Any such change would require formal agreement and constitutional action by the UK authorities.

The former Royal Air Force site has been identified as a potential location for accommodating around 930 asylum seekers while their applications are processed. The government is seeking to move away from using hotels and towards accommodation at former military sites.

No final decision on RAF Barnham asylum plans

The government has stressed that no final decision has been made on whether RAF Barnham will be used to accommodate asylum seekers.

It said that, should the plans go ahead, it would work closely with local authorities and Suffolk Police to ensure the safety and security of the community.

The Home Office also cited the example of Wethersfield in Essex, where male asylum seekers have been accommodated since July 2023, saying there was “no evidence of rising crime in the area”.

A Home Office spokesperson said the government was pursuing a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country and had saved more than £1bn (approximately €1.19bn) in costs since the general election.

The plans include closing all asylum hotels and relocating people to alternative accommodation, including former military sites.

The spokesperson added that the proposed facilities would be self-contained and equipped with round-the-clock security and CCTV to minimise the impact on surrounding communities.

Residents protest over lack of consultation

The proposal has prompted protests among residents, who say they were not adequately consulted about a development that could have a significant impact on their small community.

A similar vote took place in Piddington, Oxfordshire, in September, where residents also backed a symbolic move to leave the UK in protest against plans to accommodate more than 1,000 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base.

Piddington’s symbolic vote failed to halt the plans, and the village is now preparing a legal fight after the government granted planning permission.

World.title: Turkey seizes control of last major independent news channel amid fraud scandal
World.content:
Turkey's last operating independent TV news channel has fallen under state control, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan scrambles to contain a wave of public fury over a $20 billion investment fund scandal that has swallowed the life savings of hundreds of thousands of people in the country.

Advertising

Sozcu TV vanished from the airwaves before dawn on Tuesday as police enforced a court order installing a state trustee, cutting the channel's transmission as it was broadcasting a programme on the latest revelations in the investment fraud scandal.

The move echoes a similar state takeover last month of Halk TV, another major independent broadcaster.

The silencing of Turkey’s two largest independent news channels has drawn sharp condemnation from opposition parties and human rights groups. While the government maintains that the judiciary operates independently, critics argue the court orders are politically motivated.

“This is part of a process of basically closing down all independent media that might risk reaching followers of the ruling party,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb of Human Rights Watch.

“The whole tactic of the Erdogan government has been to use court orders. The court orders are so problematic in themselves, so overreaching, so disproportionate, that this has nothing really to do with the legal process. This is all about a political crackdown.”

Turkey talks green at Cop31 while cracking down on activists

Sinclair-Webb noted that television remains the primary news source for most Turks, making both networks and individual journalists who question government policies prime targets.

Four journalist have been detained or placed under house arrest for reporting on the investment scandal.

Authorities accuse Sozcu TV of ties to followers of the late cleric Fethullah Gulen, whom Ankara blames for masterminding a failed 2016 coup. Four of its executives and officials have been detained. Halk TV faces separate corruption allegations.

Both broadcasters strongly deny the charges.

Investment scandal

The closing of the channels comes amid fallout from the collapse of more than 100 investment funds, which wiped out $20 billion, stranded more than 500,000 investors and triggered a stock market crash.

The scandal has implicated numerous figures linked to Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party).

According to recent polls, 80 percent of Turks are closely following the scandal, with a similar majority blaming the government.

On Thursday, protesters demonstrated outside the Capital Markets Board, the country's financial regulator, in Ankara.

Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next

Around 500 people are under investigation and more than 100 suspects have been jailed. Erdogan vowed this week that no one would escape justice and promised to expedite repayments to affected investors.

Political analyst Sezin Oney said the government is scrambling to control the public narrative as its reputation among its own voter base unravels.

“Up to now, AK Party and government circles were able to project to their base the idea that the opposition [is involved in] all sorts of corruption. So all of a sudden, that facade, that rhetoric has collapsed. Now it’s the government circles who are massively corrupt."

Debate moves online

Atilla Yesilada, a Turkey analyst at New York-based consultancy firm Global Source Partners, warned that the scandal has exposed deep flaws in financial oversight, threatening severe economic and political fallout for Erdogan.

“Turkey is heading for a recession because the institutional structure has completely collapsed,” Yesilada said. “In a free market economy, you really need regulatory boards to do their work which clearly, as we see in this instance, they don't. In fact, they enable or incentivise thieves [and make] their jobs easier."

Yesilada added that Erdogan lacks a clear path to resolve the crisis, as opposition figures release new allegations implicating AK Party associates daily.

Turkey's new opposition party offers hope, but its future is already in jeopardy

Following the state takeover of another broadcaster last year, the loss of Sozcu TV and Halk TV marks a grim turning point for Turkish media, Oney said. However, she questioned whether the government can successfully suppress public discourse.

“It’s the end of the road for TV journalism, you don’t have any oppositional voice or oppositional debate. But people talk, people think, one way or another. Because Turkey was a thinking and talking nation before, it's very difficult to stop [that]. It is just [being done now] on social media.”

The government has accelerated efforts to police online dissent, shutting down hundreds of critical social media accounts, although new ones are emerging just as rapidly.

Meanwhile Koza TV, a previously fringe station, has seen its ratings surge after becoming a new outlet for independent reporting on the scandal – although mounting regulatory fines make its future uncertain.

World.title: Podcast: Living on the breadline, France's 35-hour week and a divisive tax
World.content:
The French government's decision to raise the minimum wage has failed to satisfy protesters struggling to make ends meet amid the cost-of-living crisis. Also, did the introduction of the 35-hour working week actually help reduce unemployment? The evidence is mixed. And a look at the history of France's second-largest tax, the CSG, and why it's dividing politicians.

Advertising

French unions and workers have been protesting over the rising cost of living and wages that are failing to keep up with inflation. In response, the government has agreed to increase the minimum wage, known as the Smic, by 1.6 percent – putting an extra €24 a month into the pockets of the lowest earners. But the measure has failed to satisfy unions and public sector workers, who took to the streets again this week for a day of strike action. We hear what it's like to live on the breadline and the arguments for raising public sector wages. (Listen @0')

France introduced the 35-hour working week in 2000, aiming to reduce high unemployment by spreading work among more people. After five years of research, labour economist Elio Nimier-David has found that the reform failed to achieve its intended goals, while the question of how much people should work continues to divide politicians today. (Listen @19'20'')

The CSG, or general social contribution, was introduced in 1990 and is now France's second-largest tax after VAT, raising billions of euros to fund the country's social security system. But its broad reach and proportional rate have made it a political target, as presidential candidates debate how to ease the cost-of-living crisis and put more money back into people's pockets. (Listen @15'10'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: China, ASEAN countries struggle over South China Sea code of conduct
World.content:
The Philippines wanted a South China Sea code of conduct in place by 2026. But persistent disagreements between China and ASEAN countries are slowing progress toward a deal.

It was supposed to be a breakthrough year. The Philippines had intended to set up a code of conduct with China for the South China Sea during its 2026 ASEAN presidency. However, at the summit in Manila in mid-November they had to abandon their goal. Some 80% of the text had been negotiated, declared Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro, but the key areas of dispute had remained unsolved.

Much more than diplomatic wording is at stake. The South China Sea is one of the world's most important shipping routes, it is rich in fishing grounds and may harbor significant oil and gas reserves. Primarily, however, it's a region of strategic competition: With its so-called Nine-Dash Line (often drawn in red), China claims a large portion of the sea. Its claims overlap with those of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei.

A code of conduct is to set up rules for parties dealing with one another and prevent incidents at sea from escalating. However, opinions differ, particularly with regard to its binding nature and its geographic scope.

"The basic problem with establishing such a code of conduct is that China is supremely powerful and has no real interest in a legally binding agreement," said political scientist Andreas Ufen, Southeast Asia expert at the German Institute of Global and Area Studies (GIGA). Beijing had little incentive to impose restrictions on itself as long as it was able to pursue its interests in the region even without such an agreement, Ufen told DW.

The 2026 ASEAN summit in Manila Image: Reuters

Mere recommendations or legally binding set of rules?

The Paracel Islands serve as an example of just how difficult the unresolved issues are. In China, the group of islands is known as Xisha, in Vietnam as Hoang-Sa. Hanoi apparently wants to include them in the code's geographic scope, but China rejects this. An agreement within the ASEAN framework could indirectly affect the territorial claims of the parties involved.

"A fundamental problem is that so far there's no consensus on whether the code of conduct should be legally binding," said Felix Heiduk, head of research division Asia at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). China and the ASEAN nations have been negotiating an agreement for 12 years without major progress so far.

There were reservations about such a treaty not only in China but also in other ASEAN countries. They would subsequently have to ratify a legally binding agreement under international law in their own countries. A non-binding code of conduct, by contrast, would be little more than a voluntary declaration of intent, Ufen told DW.

The definition of an "incident" is controversial as well. Are coast guard missions with use of water cannons included? Or blockades of supply vessels? Or is the code only applicable when military force is involved? This will determine which actions will be covered by the regulations in the future.

"These are by no means just technical details. Their clarification determines to a great extent whether the code of conduct will in fact be effective or will ultimately remain only a non-binding declaration of intent," Heiduk said. An agreement without valid commitments would bring about little change.

How a small, disputed island wards off China's power claims To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Diverging interests

Ufen views China's attitude as a strategic calculation. "I believe that China is interested in keeping the conflict simmering, so to speak, without having to commit itself to a truly binding legal regulation," he said. In this way, Beijing could strengthen its position in the South China Sea without limiting its room for maneuver.

At the same time there are also diverging interests within the ASEAN group. The 11 member states are by no means united. The Philippines and Vietnam are particularly vocal in their opposition to China. Malaysia and Indonesia pursue a more restrained approach. Cambodia and Laos have close economic ties with Beijing and don't have any territorial claims in the South China Sea.

"From the start of the negotiations, the lack of unity within ASEAN has been a problem. In a way, it's a permanent obstacle," Heiduk said. The group makes decisions based on the consensus principle, which basically means that every member state can block a unified position. Recurring confrontations between China and the Philippines exacerbated the problem by undermining trust and making it more difficult to reach compromises.

Ufen also believes that diverging interests are a key impediment. "Reconciling them is extremely difficult," he said. China could take advantage of the discord. Beijing preferred bilateral negotiations with individual countries rather than dealing with an entire, united group of nations.

Fundamental conflicts unresolved

A study published by the Singapore-based Yusof Ishak Institute (ISEAS) reaches similar conclusions. Not only China but internal divisions within ASEAN stalled negotiations. The authors warn against exclusively relying on a comprehensive, legally binding treaty. Initially, partial agreements — for example, on crisis communication, rescue operations at sea or maritime environment protection — could be a first step. Developing the 2002 agreement on a non-binding Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea could also be an intermediate step.

A Chinese Coast Guard and a Philippine Navy vessel during an encounter in the South China Sea on July 20, 2026 Image: Jay Tarriela via X/Handout/REUTERS

Ufen doubts whether Beijing is interested in a binding result. "For this reason, I can't really imagine that China has a real interest in a code of conduct that includes legally binding regulations," he said.

Heiduk warns against overestimating the significance of a potential agreement. "Even if the code of conduct was signed at some point, in whichever shape, that would in no way solve the conflict in the South China Sea," he said. The code could regulate how to handle incidents, but it could not eliminate territorial disputes and competing claims to maritime areas.

Can ASEAN do more to stop the violence in Myanmar? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hopes for future negotiations

This constitutes the dilemma for ASEAN nations as well, whose foreign policy oscillates between China and US ties: An agreement that's as binding as possible could fail because China and individual member states have reservations. A weak, non-binding code, however, could give the impression everyone agreed but would hardly change conduct at sea.

The American Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) summed up the situation after the summit in Manila: "Whatever progress was made this year, it is almost certain that the hardest sticking points remain unresolved."

Negotiations will be continued in 2027 under Singapore's chairmanship. Whether this will turn into more than just another diplomatic effort will depend on whether China is prepared to submit itself to regulations which limit its scope of action and whether ASEAN will be able to reach a consensus.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Inspired by Bernie Sanders: A German agency is using US-Style campaigning to boost the left in 2029
World.content:
"The Goodforces" wants to see a swing to the left in the 2029 German elections. The agency counts New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Bernie Sanders among its inspirations. Could it transform the political landscape?

Red, red, green — those are the party colors of the left-leaning coalition recently formed in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Now a Berlin-based agency wants to see the same alliance between the center-left Social Democrats, the socialist Left Party, and environmentalist Greens win the 2029 national elections.

The Goodforces wants to help make that a reality with their campaign neunund20 (twenty-nine), taking its cue, in part, from the American left. The agency was set up in response to the rise of the far right across Europe.

Co-founder Patrick Haermeyer told DW that the campaign's aim is "to give people hope and an alternative narrative to: Things are getting worse and worse." He worked as an online organizer for the election team of Bernie Sanders in the US Democratic presidential primaries in 2016 and cites Sanders' "not me, us" campaign as an inspiration.

Patrick Haermeyer got his inspiration from working with the campaign of US Senator Bernie Sanders Image: Karol Roller

Content creation, sharing, networking, campaigning

Neunund20 currently has two strategies: It provides digital space for short-form videos and social media content on political and social topics on Instagram , Tiktok, and Bluesky. At the same time, it tries to connect content creators, activists, NGOs, and political initiatives around shared "progressive" issues.

Users with a particular interest can click to get a link giving them access to archives of relevant social media material that they can then reshare. That feature is modelled on the campaign of New York's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani.

And there are other projects. The Goodforces was recently involved in a tactical voting initiative in the September elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, intended to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from winning an absolute majority. Haermeyer says physical campaigns of that kind are necessary to provide essential "interim victories" en route to the next parliamentary elections.

The Greens and the SPD, the two parties recommended by the app created by the organization, made it over the 5% hurdle and into parliament. The help that they received was declared by each party in the form of a €40,000 ($43,900) donation.

Germany's public broadcasters under fire from far-right AfD To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Super PAC-style campaigning is new in Germany

The agency sees itself as a kind of Super PAC, modeled on political organizations in the United States that collect money to carry out campaigns without directly supporting a single party or a special candidate.

For Christoph Bieber, political scientist at the University of Duisburg-Essen, the Goodforces is an interesting new type of player on Germany's political scene because it operates outside the country's political parties.

But many of those parties are eyeing the development with disquiet. The far-left, populist, immigration skeptical Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) criticized the Goodforces' intervention in Saxony-Anhalt, telling the newspaper FAZ that it was an "infantilizing, and perhaps even antidemocratic action." The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) called the tool "wrong and intentionally misleading." The FDP failed to clear the threshold, while the BSW only just squeaked in. The AfD gained 43% of the vote and its candidate may soon become Germany's first far-right state premier since the Nazi era.

What's behind the rising polarization in German politics? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Haermeyer set up the agency in 2024 along with Peter Jelinek, and both men previously worked for Green Party European Parliament member Michael Bloss. Ahead of that year's European elections, the EU's Green Deal began to come under increasing attack.

That year also ended with the collapse of Germany's first federal coalition between the SPD, Greens, and FDP, after much infighting and attacks from right-wing quarters.

"We noticed that more and more successes and freedoms that we had fought for were being reversed: Things like freedom of movement, border checks, and other things that were coming more and more under fire," Haermeyer told DW. "And we noticed that it was primarily democratic and progressive forces that were being drawn into defensive battles."

Stemming the rise of far-right AfD with digital know-how

The AfD, founded in 2013, already in the age of social media, has successfully targeted younger voters with in its online campaigns. But the older parties, in particular, have struggled. The Goodforces saw a need for support in the online environment and is now seeking to plug this gap.

The social media accounts of the campaign neunund20 contain posts on domestic German topics, such as the current negotiations to form a red-red-green coalition government in Berlin, and the country's new military service law. They also highlight "wins" in Spain in the protests for affordable housing and for US Democrats in the midterms.

Haermeyer stresses that the issues the agency highlights are determined together with a wide range of grassroots organizations and activists. "The campaign is not agreed in conjunction with the SPD, the Left Party, and the Greens," he said.

Agency funding comes from commissions and small donations. Haermeyer says that contributions generally range from $20 to $50.

Why Germany's political center is losing ground To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Big-tent parties in Germany in decline for decades

Bieber sees the emergence of non-party campaigning, long an accepted practice in the US, as a bid to compensate for the shortcomings of traditional parties.

"It is an omission of the parties," he said. "For years they have been saying we have to modernize, we have to become more open and get away from rigid membership structures. There are legal regulations governing the organization of political parties in Germany, but perhaps it could be more flexible and open."

The center-left and center-right big-tent parties have been in decline for decades. Membership of the SPD dropped from 943,000 in 1990 to some 348,000 at the end of 2025. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has seen a fall from 750,000 to under 357,000.

Party membership is particularly low in former communist eastern Germany. Centrist parties have also struggled to attract younger voters. A report by the Deutsche Kinder und Jugendstiftung (German Children and Youth Foundation) showed that only 20% of young people felt their concerns were taken seriously in the 2025 German elections and that trust in parties was low.

In the United States, campaign financing comes predominantly from donations, and lobby groups can buy influence by contributing unlimited amounts to super PACs. In Germany, party funding comes, in part, from taxpayers and membership fees, and donations are capped. However, Bieber warns that whereas there are strict rules regarding the disclosure of donors to US Super PACs, these do not exist in Germany.

The political scientist does not believe that US-style campaigning is going to take hold in Germany, but he does see potential dangers: "This could be a door opener to make others consider whether they want to go in this direction in the field of campaigning. And he added: "If it becomes rife, it could lead to a further devaluation of parties and their structures."

World.title: Germany news: IG Metall union calls for new 24-hour strike
World.content:
Hubig has been justice minister since May 2025 Image: Thomas Imo/IMAGO

Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig says that she intends to tighten the law on murders committed with "gender-specific" motives, with a particular focus on femicides perpetrated by men who are unable to accept a separation or the desire of a woman to live a self-determined life.

"A man kills, or attempts to kill, his partner or ex-partner almost every day in Germany," Hubig told the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild newspaper.

"Any man killing a woman because she wants to leave him must be punished as a murderer," she said, noting that in some cases, courts cite a man's deep sadness or fear of losing a partner to someone else as extenuating circumstances. This can lead to a lesser conviction of manslaughter.

She said that in future, courts should look more closely at such motives to determine whether they were based on sentiments of patriarchal possessiveness.

However, Hubig, who belongs to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), said she was opposed to making femicide a separate category of crime, as some women's rights organizations have demanded.

She said that, in her opinion, doing so would have "no advantages over what we are intending — and much bigger disadvantages."

The proposals are currently being debated within the coalition government and are expected to be presented to the states and associations for consideration before the end of the year.

They will then have to go before the Cabinet before being put before the parliament.

World.title: US: ICE arrests 2 at Seattle airport in 'chilling' scenes — governor
World.content:
Washington's governor has denounced the arrests made by ICE officers at Seattle's airport, calling the incident "horrific."

Masked US immigration officers have detained two people on an airport jet bridge in Seattle as passengers boarded a flight to Los Angeles, prompting criticism from Washington state Governor Bob Ferguson and concerns from Alaska Airlines.

The arrests took place at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport around 8 a.m. local time (1600 UTC) on Saturday. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said the operation targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who had overstayed his visa.

Agents also arrested Sofia Hernandez Mejia, who they alleged threw hot coffee at the ICE officers during the confrontation. ICE said she had also overstayed her visa and would face a charge of assaulting a federal officer.

When ICE comes knocking: the fight against Trump's deportations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Videos of the incident circulated on social media, showing officers struggling with a person on the ground as passengers look on. One woman could be heard shouting that her daughter was being taken away and that she had a work permit.

Washington governor slams 'out of control' ICE

Governor Ferguson, a Democrat, described the footage as "horrific" and "chilling", accusing ICE of being "completely and totally out of control."

He urged Alaska Airlines to ask federal immigration authorities to leave the state's airports and said he would make the same appeal to other airlines operating at Seattle-Tacoma.

Alaska Airlines said it had received no advance notice of the enforcement operation and was working to understand the circumstances.

The airline also expressed concern over the incident, which it said had been distressing for passengers and employees.

The operation drew criticism from April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, who said it had caused fear and disruption during one of the busiest travel periods of the year.

The flight was delayed, with Alaska Airlines saying many passengers were transferred to other flights. The original service eventually departed at 11 a.m. local time.

World.title: India: Nepal PM Balendra Shah heads to Delhi for first bilateral visit
World.content:
Skip next section Nepal PM Balendra Shah set to arrive in Delhi

11/22/2026 November 22, 2026 Nepal PM Balendra Shah set to arrive in Delhi

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah is set to arrive in New Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, his first bilateral trip since taking office in March.

The 36-year-old former rapper will meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday. He will also meet Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and briefly visit President Droupadi Murmu.

Reconstruction after August's devastating floods is expected to dominate the talks. The disaster left some 1,500 dead and more than 5,200 missing, with roads, bridges, power plants, farms and homes destroyed.

Nepal estimates rebuilding will cost $4.78 billion.

Nepal flood victims come to terms with massive loss To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nepal is also pressing for an extra route for commercial flights to Bhairahawa and Pokhara.

"India is a major and important partner for Nepal," Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai told reporters, saying the leaders would discuss trade, transit, investment, energy, connectivity and infrastructure.

New Delhi said the visit "reflects the importance India attaches to its relations with Nepal," AFP reported. Local media reported that talks may also touch upon unresolved border disputes.

India is Nepal's largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60% of its imports, worth $8.6 billion, versus China's 13%, according to World Bank figures. India and China regularly compete for influence in Nepal.

Shah will be accompanied by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal.

World.title: Dozens missing as deadly fire hits Indonesian candy factory
World.content:
A fire at a confectionery factory in Indonesia's Banten province has killed at least three people. Dozens are also unaccounted for after the blaze, which destroyed large parts of the facility.

Indonesian rescue teams are searching for 36 workers who remained unaccounted for after a fire at a candy-making factory killed at least three people, officials said on Sunday.

The fire occurred at the Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, around 50 kilometers (31 miles) west of the capital, Jakarta, in the Serang district of Banten province.

What do we know about the Indonesian confectionery factory fire?

The factory caught fire on Saturday afternoon, local search and rescue agency official Rizky Dwianto said.

"All elements of the joint SAR (search-and-rescue) team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritizing the safety of personnel in the field," he added.

Rizky said four people injured in the blaze had been taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic. Eleven more were said to have been rescued alive.

Rescue teams have been scouring the factory for survivors Image: BASARNAS/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

The governor of Banten province, Andra Soni, told reporters overnight that 60 people were believed to have been inside the factory when the fire broke out.

Drone footage shows the fire destroyed large sections of the three-story building, bringing down the roof in some places.

Survivors said the fire started in a cooling unit on the third floor.

The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products.

Deadly industrial fires in Indonesia

Indonesia has seen a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising questions about the country's workplace safety standards into question.

Among other disasters, at least 22 people were killed in a fire last December that broke out in a seven-story building in Jakarta after a suspected drone battery explosion, police said.

An explosion in a nickel-processing plant in the east of the country killed at least 13 people in 2023.

World.title: COP31: Fossil fuels still missing from draft deal at UN climate summit
World.content:
Climate activists have condemned what many feel is the 'worst COP ever' Image: Yasin Akgul/AFP

Welcome back to our coverage of the UN's COP31 climate summit in Turkey.

The latest, and potentially final, version of the deal still makes no explicit mention of fossil fuels.

It does refer to a 2023 agreement that committed the world to transitioning away from fossil fuels — but stops short of naming them directly.

The third and presumably final draft text to emerge from negotiations at COP31, which lacks any mention of fossil fuels or how to transition away from them, has been rejected by NGOs.

In a statement, Teresa Anderson, Climate Justice Lead at ActionAid International, said the people who will benefit most from the new "35-by-35" electrification targets and carbon capture "are the fossil fuel, nuclear, data and CCUS (carbon capture, use and storage) industries.

"This text will help elites to profit while leaving people in the dark," Anderson said.

Brandon Wu, AAUSA's Director of Policy and Campaigns, said: "Rich countries came to the COP31 talks with nothing to offer other than red lines.

"They put forward meaningless fossil fuel transition roadmaps that were nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy, then hypocritically blamed developing countries for failing to take action on phasing out fossil fuels.

“This is the behaviour of an arrogant bully who cares about nothing but himself and it is no way to have a proper negotiation. COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it’s because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise."

World.title: Nigeria: At least 24 dead after boat capsizes
World.content:
The boat carrying mourners for a funeral overturned in southern Nigeria. It was the latest in a series of deadly boat accidents in the country.

A boat capsized in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, the country's emergency agency said on Saturday.

"So far, 24 bodies have been recovered from the scene of the incident, while search and rescue operations are ongoing," said Manzo Ezekiel, a spokesman for the National Emergency Management Agency.

The boat was carrying mourners for a burial ceremony from the town of Ayama to Ukubie in the southern Bayelsa State on Friday when it sank.

Boat reportedly suffered mechanical failure

Authorities have not confirmed how many passengers were on board.

"Those who lost their lives in the tragedy did not deserve to die that way," Nigerian President Bola Tinubu said in a statement on X.

Two children were among the four bodies initially recovered from the water on Friday, when 24 survivors were rescued, according to police.

Police spokesman Musa Mohammed said that preliminary reports suggested that the boat suffered a mechanical problem.

Deadly boat mishaps in Nigeria

Boat accidents are common on Nigeria's busy river networks. Overloading, poor vessel maintenance, and failure to comply with safety norms usually cause them.

In August, at least 51 died after a boat capsized in northwest Nigeria's Sokoto State.

In September 2025, a boat carrying over 100 passengers sank in north-central Niger State, leaving dozens dead.

World.title: ¿Se ha movido el voto útil? Las opciones de izquierda y derecha en cada provincia con las últimas encuestas
World.content:
El modelo de EL PAÍS dice que hay 40 escaños en el aire. Consulta a qué partido le sirve más tu voto

Las encuestas tratan de predecir los votos del próximo 29-N, pero el modelo electoral que publicamos en EL PAÍS desde hace una década va más allá: estima los escaños en cada provincia, les asigna probabilidades, e incluso señala el llamado voto útil. A continuación mostramos sus pronósticos actualizados con las encuestas del 20 de noviembre, incluido el sondeo posterior al debate de 40dB.

En el primer interactivo puedes ver los escaños seguros (99% de opciones), probables (75%-99%) y en juego (25%-75%) de cada partido. En total hay 175 seguros, 135 probables y 83 en juego (suman más de 350 porque varios partidos se disputan los escaños). También puedes elegir una provincia y ver nuestra estimación allí.

Voto útil: ¿qué voto ayuda a tu bloque?

Muchas personas votan para maximizar las opciones de un gobierno de izquierdas o de derechas. Quizás tienen un partido favorito, pero se hacen otra pregunta: ¿a qué partido de su bloque le sirve más su voto? Es lo que se llama voto táctico o estratégico. La respuesta cambia en cada provincia: por el método D’Hondt, un voto al PP y otro a Vox no valen lo mismo en escaños, porque uno de los dos suele estar más cerca de ganar el último diputado. Y lo mismo pasa con PSOE, Frente Amplio o BNG.

¿Cuál es el voto táctico en tu provincia? Puedes verlo en el mapa. Primero elige un bloque. Entonces el mapa mostrará, para cada provincia, el partido de ese espectro que tiene más probabilidades de ganar (o salvar) un escaño para su bloque.

Para un votante de derecha, existe voto táctico en 34 provincias. Hay 18 donde le conviene votar al PP (probablemente) y 16 donde le conviene hacerlo por Vox. A veces la diferencia es grande: en Gipuzkoa, Lugo y Ourense, un voto a Vox casi nunca decide un escaño, mientras que el PP se disputa el último con Bildu o el BNG. En Álava o Melilla, un voto al PP vale más de cinco veces lo que uno a Vox. Pero hay territorios donde un votante indiferente entre PP y Vox maximiza sus opciones eligiendo al partido de extrema derecha. Es lo que pasa en La Rioja, por ejemplo.

En la izquierda, el voto táctico favorece al PSOE en 35 de las 52 provincias. En 19 provincias es el único del bloque que mueve escaños en nuestras simulaciones, porque los Frentes y Podemos tienen números débiles en los sondeos. Hay excepciones en territorios con fuerzas locales: por ejemplo, en Lugo y Ourense parece que un voto al BNG es mejor para los intereses del bloque. Y ocurre algo parecido con Adelante Andalucía en Córdoba y con la Unidad del Pueblo Canario en Santa Cruz de Tenerife.

En las provincias grandes, en cambio, el voto táctico apenas existe. En Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia o Sevilla da casi igual votar a un partido u otro del bloque: las fuerzas principales tienen todas opciones de lograr representación.

Nuestra simulación también muestra otra cosa: mover un escaño es mucho más barato en las provincias más pequeñas. La probabilidad de que justo tu papeleta sea la decisiva es siempre minúscula (un voto cualquiera tiene una posibilidad entre 117.000 de decidir un escaño). Pero no es siempre igual de minúscula. En Lleida un voto al PP pesa seis veces más que la media: una posibilidad entre 19.000. Y en Ávila o La Rioja, uno al PSOE pesa unas cinco veces más. En el otro extremo, un voto al PP o a Vox en Madrid vale la mitad de lo normal, en parte porque allí cada escaño cuesta más votos: hay unos 94.000 votantes por diputado, frente a 25.000 en Soria.

Una advertencia: esto no es una recomendación de voto. Es la aritmética de los escaños según las encuestas de hoy, que todavía pueden moverse y que son siempre una aproximación. Además, el voto táctico solo mide la probabilidad de mover un escaño, pero un voto puede tener utilidad para apoyar unas ideas o una formación incluso cuando no se traduzca en asiento del Congreso.

¿Cómo funciona el modelo?

El modelo parte de nuestro promedio de sondeos, lo proyecta a cada provincia con su historia y microdatos del CIS, y le añade la incertidumbre de las encuestas en el pasado. Después simulamos las elecciones 20.000 veces y contamos cuántas veces gana cada partido cada escaño. Así podemos clasificarlos en tres grupos: seguros, probables y en juego.

El siguiente gráfico muestra qué significan estas probabilidades. Puedes simular las elecciones una, dos, tres o cien veces para hacerte una idea intuitiva de cuántas veces se gana un escaño de cada tipo.

El modelo es sólido. Cada pieza la hemos puesto a prueba con otras elecciones generales. Por ejemplo, hemos probado varias formas de repartir el voto entre provincias, siguiendo técnicas habituales, y nos quedamos con la más precisa en votos y escaños.

El modelo es cauteloso. Y lo es por diseño: predecir cada provincia es difícil porque las encuestas pierden precisión a escala provincial. Un sondeo de 2.000 o 5.000 entrevistas no basta para estimar directamente el voto de Soria, Pontevedra o Castellón. Por eso no lo intentamos: lo que hacemos es usar el voto histórico de cada partido en cada provincia y lo que dicen en cada comunidad los microdatos del CIS, que acumulan decenas de miles de entrevistas. Además, las fuerzas locales no siempre salen en las encuestas y pueden sorprender al final: Teruel Existe gana escaño en una de cada cinco simulaciones. Y pasa algo similar con partidos pequeños en las provincias grandes: Podemos consigue un diputado por Madrid en el 60% de las simulaciones, y SALF, en el 24%. Si detectas cualquier omisión, escríbenos.

Y el modelo es confiable. Estas predicciones las hemos hecho muchas veces. Por eso sabemos que el modelo funciona y está bien calibrado. En 2023 dimos 189 escaños como seguros y se cumplieron todos, igual que en las dos elecciones de 2019 (156 y 153). Los que dimos como probables se cumplieron el 94% de las veces (365 de 388), en la parte alta del 75%-99% que prometíamos. Los errores de cada provincia se compensan en parte al sumarlos, así que el total es más fiable que cada provincia por separado. El modelo también acierta en el total nacional: en las generales de 2016 a 2023, los escaños de cada partido grande cayeron dentro de nuestra horquilla del 80% en 19 de 20 casos, más de lo prometido: es la cautela de la que hablábamos.

Si quieres seguir todas las encuestas del 29-N, apúntate el nuevo pódcast de Kiko Llaneras, en Spotify, YouTube, Apple Podcasts o iVoox.

Metodología

Las predicciones las produce un modelo estadístico basado en sondeos y en su precisión histórica. Es una versión renovada del que hemos usado en unas 40 elecciones desde 2016: en Andalucía, Castilla y León, Aragón, Extremadura, las europeas, las generales de abril y noviembre de 2019 y de 2023, y otras en México, Francia o el Reino Unido.

Funciona en cuatro pasos. 1) Un promedio de encuestas que pondera cada sondeo por su tamaño, su fecha y la precisión histórica de su encuestadora, según nuestro comparador. 2) Una proyección del voto a cada provincia con un modelo logístico, que parte de las generales de 2023 —y, para los partidos nuevos o que ahora concurren por separado, de las europeas de 2024 y las andaluzas de 2026— y se alimenta también con microdatos del CIS de cada comunidad. 3) La incertidumbre de las encuestas, calibrada con los errores de 44 elecciones en España desde 1986 y con una base internacional de miles de sondeos, según el tamaño de cada partido y los días que faltan para votar. Usamos distribuciones t de Student, con colas más anchas que una normal, y errores correlacionados entre partidos. Esos errores tienen una parte común a toda España, porque las encuestas suelen fallar en la misma dirección en todas partes, y otra propia de cada provincia. 4) 20.000 simulaciones de las elecciones, repartiendo los escaños según D’Hondt con barrera del 3% en cada circunscripción.

Un escaño es seguro si un partido lo gana en más del 99% de las simulaciones; probable, entre el 75% y el 99%, y en juego, entre el 25% y el 75%. En nuestras pruebas con las generales de 2016 a 2023, esas probabilidades están muy bien afinadas: los escaños en juego se cumplieron 202 veces, frente a las 195 que predecía el modelo.

Para calcular el voto táctico usamos las mismas 20.000 simulaciones. En cada una añadimos (o quitamos) un puñado de votos a cada partido en cada provincia, y miramos si su bloque gana (o pierde) un escaño. Solo contamos cuando el escaño cambia de bloque. El resultado es la probabilidad de que un voto decida un asiento para su bloque ideológico. Los bloques son derecha (PP, Vox y SALF), e izquierda (PSOE, Frente Amplio, Podemos, ERC, EH Bildu, BNG y Adelante Andalucía). PNV, Junts y CC quedan fuera.

En los gráficos nacionales agrupamos como Izquierdas a Frente Amplio, Podemos y las coaliciones Compromís-Front Valencià, Unidad del Pueblo Canario y Ara Més-Front Ampli; en cada provincia aparecen por separado.
