World.title: NCW seeks report on rape and murder of woman inside stationary train in Nagercoil
World.content:
The National Commission for Women (NCW) has written to the Tamil Nadu Director-General of Police seeking an investigation into the alleged rape and murder of a woman inside a stationary train coach at Nagercoil Junction railway station.

Also read | Decomposed body of woman found in train at Nagercoil junction yard

The organisation in a social media post on Sunday (November 22, 2026) said NCW chairperson Vijaya Rahatkar has written to the DGP seeking a thorough and time-bound investigation, examination of possible security lapses and preservation of CCTV footage and forensic evidence.

Taking suo motu cognisance of a media report published on November 21 alleging the victim’s body was discovered four days after the incident, the Commission called for expeditious identification of the deceased and tracing of her family.

The Commission has sought a comprehensive review of railway station security, particularly the monitoring of unoccupied coaches, night patrolling and coordination among the GRP, RPF and railway authorities. It has called for a detailed action taken report within seven days.

Also read | Man arrested for sexual assault and murder of woman on train in Nagercoil

“The safety of women in railway premises and public transport spaces cannot be compromised. Such grave incidents demand strict accountability, effective security measures and swift action to ensure justice for the victim,” the Commission said in the post.

World.title: Nitin Nabin announces his team; Smriti Irani, Ram Madhav make a comeback, Amit Malviya out
World.content:
Seven months after he took charge as the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) president, Nitin Nabin on Monday (August 17, 2026) unveiled his national organisational team. Although peppered with some new faces, the list signals continuity and organisational experience in major positions; the return of some important party men and women; and a clear imprint of recent events, including the Gen Z protests on the appointments related to the party’s social media communications.

Former Union Minister Smriti Irani as general secretary, and former party general secretary (during the presidentship of Union Minister Amit Shah) Ram Madhav as vice president have made a comeback to the BJP’s organisation.

World.title: The new BJP team’s piecemeal reset
World.content:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi walked into a meeting of the newly appointed Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national office-bearers on August 22. The 64 office-bearers present assumed he would address them on how they should approach their assignments. Instead, he spent the next four-and-a-quarter hours individually querying them on their past organisational work.

The exchange was unhurried, with PM Modi at one point telling the audience that he too was once like them, a national office-bearer of the party during the late Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s tenure as Prime Minister (1999-2004), say some of the new office-bearers.

The identification was interpreted in some quarters as a pep talk to the new team of how far organisational service can take you in the BJP, but for others it pointed to a unifying characteristic in a list of names that otherwise lacked a meta narrative, and instead, in a piecemeal fashion exhibited the political anxieties of the BJP.

This privileging of organisational experience by the Prime Minister was the highlight of the new team. The BJP, now in its third term in power and seeking a fourth in 2029, is, with this new team, attempting a reset amid various political anxieties.

Journalist Shekhar Iyer, who has tracked the BJP for decades, says, “The new team marks a big shift in the party top brass’ approach to the challenges ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha poll. Increasingly, the BJP is signalling to itself that, henceforth, the chosen men and women will represent less of their individual personality and more of their abilities and capabilities for the tasks to be accomplished.”

World.title: BJP appoints Yuzvendra Chahal as special invitee to OBC Morcha executive committee
World.content:
Indian cricketer Yuzvendra Chahal has been appointed as a Special Invitee to the Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) National Other Backwards Classes (OBC) Morcha executive committee.

Also read | Nitin Nabin announces his team; Smriti Irani, Ram Madhav make a comeback, Amit Malviya out

BJP national president Nitin Nabin on Saturday (November 21, 2026) announced fresh appointments of national office-bearers, national executive members, and department heads for its OBC Morcha with immediate effect.

According to the official communication issued by the party’s central office, the list includes seven national vice presidents, three national general secretaries, and seven national secretaries representing various states across the country.

The seven newly appointed national vice presidents of the BJP OBC Morcha are Jogen Mohan (Assam), Mamata Mohanta (Odisha), Sangam Lal Gupta (Uttar Pradesh), Babanrao Ravji Choudhary (Maharashtra), Sat Prakash Rana (Delhi), Arjun Sahani (Bihar), and Sangeeta Balwant Bind (Uttar Pradesh). Gajendra Yadav (Delhi), Pramod Madhwaraj (Karnataka), and Lalit Chandrakar (Chhattisgarh) have been named as national general secretaries.

The party also appointed seven national secretaries: Dashrathji Thakor (Gujarat), T Varatharajan (Tamil Nadu), Sanjeev Kumar alias Bablu Bhagat (Jharkhand), Sarita Jangid (Haryana), Kadaganchi Ramesh (Telangana), Vaibhav Panwar (Madhya Pradesh), and Bhim Kumar Sahu (Bihar). Under the organisational appointments, Radheshyam Yadav from Uttar Pradesh has been given charge as the national treasurer. Sanjay Kumar Gurjar and Dr Arun Yadav (both from Delhi) have been appointed as national office secretary and co-office secretary, respectively.

Ajay Gupta from Bihar has been named the media coordinator for the Morcha. For digital communication, Parikshit Dagar (Delhi) has been appointed social media coordinator, with Pradeep Mahaur Soni (Madhya Pradesh) named co-coordinator.

Prof. Pankaj Choudhary (Delhi) will head the policy and research wing as coordinator, assisted by co-coordinators Ashutosh Behera (Odisha) and Rahul Yadav (Uttar Pradesh).

The party also notified the initial names of the national executive committee members, including Sanjeev Rangaiya (Andaman & Nicobar), Srinivas Rao Kantubukta (Andhra Pradesh), Rajiv Ranjan alias Vishal Yadav (Bihar), and Sanjeev Verma (Chandigarh).

World.title: Palaniswami criticises TVK-led government over SC dismissal of TN’s Cauvery pleas
World.content:
AIADMK general secretary Edappadi K. Palaniswami on Sunday (November 22, 2026) criticised the Tamil Nadu government, led by Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, after the Supreme Court dismissed two applications filed by the State in connection with the Cauvery water dispute.

In a social media post, Mr. Palaniswami claimed the CM was not aware of the Supreme Court’s decision. .

“You (Mr Vijay) will not convene an all-party meeting over the Cauvery dispute. You will not engage with the Congress leadership on the issue or pursue the legal battle effectively. And you will pose for photographs without condemning Karnataka CM, who has been speaking against Tamil Nadu,” Mr. Palaniswami said.

The AIADMK leader warned the inadequate release of Cauvery water by Karnataka along with the “TVK-led alliance government’s failure” to secure Tamil Nadu’s rightful share, could adversely affect the samba cultivation season.

Questioning the Chief Minister’s priorities, Mr. Palaniswami charged that the CM had failed to raise the concerns of Tamil Nadu’s farmers during his recent meeting with Congress leader Sonia Gandhi in New Delhi. [Mr Vijay had gone to attend a function to mark the launch of Ms Gandhi’s memoirs.]

Mr. Vijay was playing with the rights linked with the lifeline of Tamil Nadu and the lives of the farmers in the State, Mr. Palaniswami said. Recalling the AIADMK’s efforts under former CMs M.G. Ramachandran, Jayalalithaa and himself, Mr. Palaniswami contended the party had fought to secure the State’s Cauvery rights over the Cauvery issue.

World.title: University of Hyderabad students continue protest, demand termination of faculty member over alleged casteist remarks
World.content:
Students at the University of Hyderabad, led by the Students’ Union, continued their protest for the third consecutive day, demanding the termination of Vijaya Ramadas Mandala, a faculty member in the Department of History, over his alleged derogatory and casteist remarks in a purported email correspondence.

The email communication between April 14 and 16, 2026, contains references to former students from the Scheduled Castes community as “untouchables”, remarks against students from marginalised backgrounds in Bihar and Jharkhand, and Islamophobic comments.

Students said such statements raise questions about the ethical responsibilities of faculty members and the dignity of students within an academic institution. Allegedly, Mr. Ramadas had also threatened some students associated with progressive student organisations for working against him.

The SU maintained that the university administration continues to remain silent despite the seriousness of the issue. Seeking solidarity, its members have written to Member of Parliament V. Sivadasan, historians Romila Thapar, Ramachandra Guha, K. N. Ganesh, Rajan Gurukkal, and Irfan Habib.

Taking a firm stand, the students said the protests would continue until the university administration takes clear action and addresses their demands.

World.title: Adani Group forays into West Bengal’s power sector, Trinamool calls for transparency
World.content:
As Adani Group forays into West Bengal’s power sector by securing a letter of award for supply of 1,750 MW of renewable power for 25 years, the Mamata All India Trinamool Congress has claimed that long-term power contracts deserve transparency, not preferential access for corporate giants.

“West Bengal’s resources and long-term power contracts deserve transparency, not preferential access for corporate giants. Adani’s subsidiary has received an LoA from West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd (WBSEDCL) for supply of 1,750 MW of renewable power for 25 years,” the party posted on social media.

Adani Energy Solutions Ltd. (AESL) has received a Letter of Award (LoA) from West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) for supply of 1,750 MW of Renewable Energy Round-the-Clock (RE-RTC) power for a period of 25 years, a press statement by Adani Energy Solutions said. The LoA provides a 750 MW greenshoe option, which upon exercising, would take the aggregate contracted capacity to 2,500 MW, the statement said.

The award follows a competitive bidding process in which PTSL (Powerpulse Trading Solutions Ltd), a wholly owned subsidiary of AESL, emerged as the successful bidder after the e-reverse auction. Power Supply is scheduled to commence from July 1, 2028 for 1750 MW capacity and from April 1, 2029 for 750 MW, once greenshoe option is exercised.

Also Read | Big players will invest in West Bengal for the love of the country: Adhikari

The Trinamool’s social media post referred to allegations by Abhishek Banerjee where he had pointed out, “while some appear to receive out-of-turn favours, ordinary people are still forced to run from pillar to post for basic services”.

“Questions of favouritism and accountability deserve answers....Who is this government really accountable to and why this favouritism? People need answers!” the party said.

Gautam Adani, Chairman of Adani Group, had on September 24, 2026, inaugurated a 2000-bed hospital in Kolkata. Mr. Adani announced an investment roadmap of over ₹1 lakh crore in West Bengal by 2035 in presence of Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari. After the Bharatiya Janata Party government came to power, Mr. Adhikari has been trying to bring big industrialists to invest in the State.

World.title: NHAI’s Telangana Region witnesses drop in fatalities
World.content:
Road fatalities on National Highways Authority of India (NHAI)-operated roads in Telangana declined by 14.8%, following measures such as the identification and rectification of accident black spots and improvements in emergency response services.

P. Shiva Shankar, Regional Officer, Hyderabad Region, NHAI, stated that road fatalities declined from 1,245 in 2024 to 1,061 in 2025. Telangana’s emergency response time of 13 minutes, compared with the national benchmark of 21 minutes, was also a factor in reducing fatalities. The response time in Telangana was 38.1% lower than the national benchmark. The NHAI has signed a memorandum of understanding with HLL Lifecare Limited.

With an investment of ₹2,304 crore to rectify black spots on highways in Telangana, accidents at these locations have declined by 47%. For instance, authorities undertook black spot rectification work at the Golden Dhaba Y-junction and Kadthal Bypass, both on NH-44.

As part of efforts to improve highway-side amenities, the government plans a ₹127.68 crore upgradation programme. It envisages the construction of 38 modern toilet blocks and improvements to 24 toll plazas. The presentation also covered the ‘Look and Feel’ programme, green median development, QR-code-based project information boards and improvements to highway amenities.

Leveraging artificial intelligence, an AI-powered Machine Control pilot project on NH-167 is supporting precision-based construction through digital models and machine-guided operations. The NHAI also highlighted Digital Highway Monitoring Systems, Centralised Control and Monitoring Systems, and Advanced Traffic Management Systems to improve highway monitoring, lighting management, surveillance and incident response.

Touching upon the National Highway network in Telangana, the NHAI stated that of the State’s 4,971-km network, 2,707 km is under its jurisdiction. As many as 11 projects, covering 391 km, are under way at a cost of ₹12,640 crore.

Along NH-163, 765 banyan trees were retained and 366 were translocated, with a reported survival rate of 94%. Projects involving a 150 m animal overpass and a 200 m animal underpass were also undertaken to facilitate wildlife connectivity on NH-363.

World.title: Portuguese foreign minister arrives in Pakistan for official visit: FO
World.content:
Minister of State and Foreign Affairs of Portugal Paulo Rangel arrived in Pakistan on Sunday for an official visit, the Foreign Office (FO) said.

Rangel is visiting Pakistan at the invitation of Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar from November 22 to 23. He was received upon arrival by Additional Secretary Europe Ambassador Ayesha Ali.

According to FO, Rangel will hold delegation-level talks with DPM Dar as well as meetings with Pakistani leadership.

“He is accompanied by a business delegation for the inaugural Pakistan-Portugal Business Forum,” FO said, expressing hope that the visit will provide an opportunity to review the full spectrum of the bilateral relationship.

The visit comes as Pakistan and Portugal mark the 77th anniversary of their diplomatic relations, established on Nov 7, 1949, FO spokesperson said in a statement on Saturday.

The two leaders will review bilateral relations and discuss ways to expand trade and investment.

“The visit will also feature a Pakistan-Portugal Business Forum. Companies from both countries will hold business-to-business meetings to explore commercial partnerships and investment opportunities in agri-food, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals, information technology and textiles,” the spokesperson had added in his statement.

Foreign Minister Rangel’s visit will provide an opportunity to build on the longstanding ties between Pakistan and Portugal and to broaden bilateral cooperation across diverse sectors.

World.title: 3 TTP-linked terrorists killed in village on outskirts of Peshawar: CTD
World.content:
PESHAWAR: Three terrorists were killed during an exchange of fire with Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) and military personnel in the Passani village, located on Peshawar’s outskirts, late on Saturday night, the CTD said in a statement on Sunday.

The statement said the CTD received intelligence about the presence of a group of terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Khawarij on Passani Road — an area located 23 miles south of Peshawar, falling within the jurisdiction of Mattani police station.

Fitna-al-Khawarij is a term the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).

The CTD said the terrorists planned to carry out attacks on government installations.

“Based on the confirmed reports, CTD’s Special Weapons and Tactics Teams (SWAT), along with personnel of the Pakistan Army, equipped with modern weapons, reached the area to arrest the terrorists,” the statement added.

However, upon seeing law enforcement and security personnel, the terrorists opened fire, to which the teams responded effectively in self-defence, the statement further said.

Following an exchange of fire, a search operation was launched in the area during which the bodies of three terrorists were found, it said. The CTD identified the terrorists as Abdul Rashid, Saeedullah, and Saeed Nawab — members of the banned TTP.

The statement added that other terrorists present at the site managed to escape; meanwhile, the teams recovered two Kalashnikovs, a pistol, three hand grenades, five magazines and computerised national identity cards (CNICs) from the slain terrorists.

A search operation was under way to arrest the escaped terrorists, the statement added.

As per the CTD statement, KP Inspector General of Police Zulfiqar Hameed and Additional IG CTD Jawad Qamar vowed that terrorists would never be allowed to succeed.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif lauded security forces for the successful operation, observing that “timely and decisive action” thwarted a “major threat”, state-run APP reported.

The operations of the security forces against terrorism are a reflection of national resolve and morale, the report quoted him as saying.

KP continues to actively face terrorist threats. Last week, 43 terrorists were killed during operations conducted in KP, including 35 in Mir Ali, North Waziristan district, and eight in Orakzai district, the military’s media wing said.

On the other hand, the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based independent think tank monitoring conflict and security developments, has reported encouraging trends in KP in its monthly assessment for October.

In mainland KP, PICSS recorded 40 attacks during October, compared with 58 in September, representing a reduction of 31pc. Meanwhile, deaths resulting from these attacks declined from 90 to 38, a decrease of approximately 58pc, while injuries fell from 165 to 19, representing a reduction of 88pc.

The merged districts of KP recorded 30 attacks during October, compared with 34 in September, and deaths resulting from these attacks decreased from 33 to 25, while injuries increased from 11 to 13, the report said.

World.title: Lahore once again ranks as world's most polluted major city as AQI crosses 500
World.content:
Lahore topped the list of the world’s most polluted major cities once again on Sunday morning with an hourly air quality index (AQI) reading of over 500, according to real-time air quality data.

Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir’s live global major city ranking placed Lahore first with 538 between 9am and 10am, classifying the quality as ‘hazardous’, indicating extremely polluted conditions and serious health risks for residents.

It was followed by Delhi with an AQI of 207, Karachi with 180, Mumbai with 177 and Cairo at 162. The ranking showed Lahore’s pollution level to be more than twice that of the second-ranked city, Delhi.

The deterioration was not confined to the provincial capital.

IQAir’s live ranking of Pakistani cities on Sunday morning placed eight Punjab cities among the country’s 10 most polluted urban centres.

Kahna Nau in Lahore district topped the list with an AQI of 606, followed by Lahore at 538, Bahawalpur at 536, Sargodha at 392 and Gujranwala at 347.

Other cities in the top 10 included Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan, Skardu, Faisalabad and Peshawar.

IQ Air rankings for the most polluted cities on Nov 22. — Screengrab IQAir

According to global health statistics, air pollution, both outdoor and indoor, is the second-leading risk factor for deaths worldwide, claiming an estimated 8.1 million lives annually. Outdoor particulate matter alone accounts for 4.7m deaths.

Lahore has consistently ranked as the world’s most polluted major city in the past few weeks. On Saturday evening, it recorded an AQI of 266, showing Lahore’s air quality in the hazardous category.

On Friday, heavy smog pushed air quality in several Punjab cities into the hazardous category, with Lahore recording an hourly AQI reading of 465 between 7am and 8am.

Punjab govt intensifies crackdown against smog violations

Amid the worsening air quality, Punjab’s Environment Protection and Climate Change Department (EPCCD) has intensified its province-wide crackdown against environmental violations, imposing fines amounting to Rs449.5 million, sealing 6,476 premises and carrying out 1,808 demolitions during the first 11 months of 2026.

According to the latest enforcement figures compiled by the Environment Protection Agency (EPA) Punjab, enforcement teams conducted 187,588 field visits across the province between January 1 and November 21, targeting industrial pollution, non-compliant brick kilns, illegal plastic businesses, commercial establishments and fugitive dust.

The enforcement drive has also yielded a 60 per cent increase in fines compared with the corresponding period last year, reflecting intensified regulatory action against major sources of pollution.

Industrial units accounted for the largest share of penalties, with fines reaching Rs231.6 million against Rs108.8m during the same period in 2025.

Brick kilns attracted Rs183.3m in fines, while penalties against plastic-related violations increased 4.5 times to Rs34.5 million.

Brick kiln inspections remained a major component of the campaign, with 85,768 visits recorded during the reporting period. Enforcement teams demolished 1,431 units and sealed another 1,018 premises. Industrial enforcement operations involved 50,555 inspections, resulting in 1,525 premises being sealed and 377 demolitions.

The department has also stepped up enforcement against restaurants and commercial establishments operating without the required suction hoods. A total of 10,766 inspections were conducted, leading to the installation of 4,385 suction hoods and the sealing of 1,287 premises. Significantly, 1,130 suction hoods were installed during November alone.

The daily enforcement figures for November 21 further illustrated the scale of operations, with teams conducting 1,022 inspections across Punjab and imposing fines of Rs1.87 million.

The operation resulted in 20 premises being sealed, seven FIRs registered and one brick kiln demolished. Officials also confiscated 390 kilogrammes of plastic bags and oversaw the installation of 72 suction hoods.

Brick kilns accounted for 499 of the day’s inspections, followed by 275 industrial units, 153 plastic-related inspections and 95 suction-hood inspections. All seven FIRs and the demolition recorded on the day were related to brick kilns.

Director General Environment Abdullah Nayyar Sheikh said the department was maintaining strict enforcement against all major sources of pollution through continuous monitoring, field inspections and action against non-compliant units. He emphasised that the strategy was aimed at ensuring compliance with environmental laws and preventing pollution at its source.

EPCCD Secretary Silwat Saeed also stressed the importance of sustained institutional monitoring and effective implementation of environmental regulations to address pollution through a coordinated enforcement approach.

A day earlier, the Lahore Traffic Police claimed to have intensified enforcement operations against vehicles contributing to air pollution.

Chief Traffic Officer Syed Abdul Rahim Shirazi on Saturday claimed that the traffic police have issued challan tickets to 14,653 smoke-emitting vehicles.

Action has also been taken against 10,306 vehicles transporting sand, soil and other materials without covering their loads with tarpaulins. The police have also proceeded against 31,618 unfit and dilapidated vehicles and taken action against 272,760 vehicles for overloading, he said.

Pakistan’s average PM2.5 concentration stood at 67.3 micrograms per cubic metre in 2025, nearly 14 times the World Health Organisation’s annual guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, according to the 2025 World Air Quality Report.

This concentration corresponded to an average AQI of 156, placing Pakistan among the world’s most polluted countries.

World.title: Veteran journalist Husain Naqi passes away in Lahore
World.content:
LAHORE: Veteran journalist and human rights activist Husain Naqi passed away in Lahore on Sunday of a cardiac arrest.

He was a former editor of The News and had also been associated with the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP).

On Saturday, a day before his passing, Naqi attended a book launch organised by HRCP. Later in the day, at 6pm, he suffered a cardiac attack, after which he was admitted at a private hospital, according to HRCP official Muhammad Ilyas.

Naqi passed away on Sunday morning at 5am. He left behind three sons.

President Asif Ali Zardari extended his condolences on Naqi’s passing to the bereaved family, expressing “deep sorrow”, a statement issued by the Presidency said.

The president paid tribute to Naqi’s “services to journalism, freedom of expression and human rights”, the statement said.

It further quoted the president as saying: “Husain Naqi played a prominent role in promoting journalism and democratic values. His contributions will always be remembered.”

The President offers condolences to Hussain Naqi’s family and prays for the forgiveness of the deceased.

The HRCP also released a statement, saying it “deeply mourns” Naqi’s passing.

“Over a career spanning more than 70 years, from student leader to newspaper editor to treasurer of HRCP, neither multiple incarcerations nor vindictive acts by the authorities ever weakened his resolve to speak truth to power. Naqi sahib served HRCP in different capacities for three decades and was an active council member at the time of his passing. One of the strongest voices for people’s rights and democracy in Pakistan has gone silent,” the statement said.

Senator Sherry Rehman expressed her grief on Naqi’s passing in a post on X.

“His passing signals the end of an era. Naqi Saheb always spoke unflinching truth to power,” she said.

She said many “cub journalists” had learned at his desk and walked in rallies under his leadership.

“We often called him the rebel angel of our times, yet he never stoked anger. He sought the right to dissent with respect,” Rehman wrote.

PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja also expressed his condolences on Naqi’s passing, saying that he had met the veteran journalist on Saturday at a book launch at HRCP.

“My acquaintance and admiration for him spanned decades,” Raja said in a post on X.

Naming I.A. Rehman, Asma Jahangir and Amin Mughal, he said, “The most precious gems who dreamed of and championed the dignity of human beings and the voices of the poor in Pakistan are leaving us.

“Their dreams have yet to be realised. Their dreams are the dreams of 250 million people.”

Who was Hussain Naqi?

Naqi was born in Lucknow, India before partition. In his autobiography Mujh Se Jo Ho Saka, Naqi said he was perhaps born a year before his officially recorded birthdate, 1936.

His great-grandfather had moved to Lucknow from a village in what is now Haryana, in the then-undivided Punjab. It was a well-heeled and well-educated family that flourished in Lucknow over the next few generations.

However, Naqi subtly confronted the conservatism of his traditional family from a very young age. Outside, he was not subtle. He began his student activism in secondary school and started taking on the minor establishments of power at a fairly young age.

After early schooling and college education in Lucknow, Naqi moved to Karachi in the 1950s, where he subsequently developed into a quintessential student leader.

As a student in Karachi, Naqi played a key role in several demonstrations and protests. During the 1956 Suez Canal crisis when Egypt was attacked by Israel, France and Britain, Naqi was part of the executive committee of the National Students Federation (NSF). At the time, the NSF organised a march to the British High Commission in Karachi to protest against the attack and was faced with police batons and tear gas.

As president of the Karachi University’s students union, Naqi made a deal with the university’s vice-chancellor for Naqi to be rusticated for three years instead of three Baloch students who had been rusticated in response to an incident at the hostel.

Naqi’s activism during his student days was not just centered around protests, but also had to do with improving conditions in the institution. He fought for adding a new campus with better facilities, providing safe transport for girls and ensuring that exams were held on time and not postponed.

He was a strong advocate for student unions. In an interview published in 2011, he said, “it was the banning of student unions that destroyed campus peace. In our time, student unions were a positive influence. We organised cultural activities. We tolerated diversity. Representatives with various political leanings were able to work together despite their ideological differences.”

After a few turbulent years in Karachi, Naqi permanently settled down in Lahore — the city that he has long identified with as his own and the city that itself identifies with Naqi as a source of resistance to power.

As a journalist, Naqi found his first mentor in Javed Bokhari, with whom he worked for a couple of years. “In those days I used to literally live at the PPI office,” he said of the time.

He ended up working as bureau chief of PPI. However, he eventually had to leave the position following a reporting incident in which he refused to accept a false news of desecration of the Holy Quran.

Nonetheless, he continued to write for various newspapers, including the Viewpoint, Holiday, Outlook, Frontier Post, Frontier Guardian, Daily Star, Punjab Times and Punjab Punch.

Naqi consistently campaigned for the preservation and promotion of the Punjabi language in Pakistan, starting the first-ever daily newspaper in the Punjabi language — Sajjan.

Naqi had also been imprisoned a couple of times because of his outspokenness. In the 2011 interview, he recalled those instances with a sense of humour. “I was lucky to invariably have someone favourably disposed towards me at the jail premises, who made sure that I was not mistreated.”

World.title: Presidential ordinance withdraws most privileges of KP MPAs, including protection against preventive detention
World.content:
PESHAWAR: President Asif Ali Zardari has promulgated five ordinances, doing away with most of the “privileges” of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa lawmakers, including protection against “preventive detention” and providing a legal framework for special initiatives in the designated 12 districts and other districts in the province.

With the imposition of emergency in KP on Oct 11, an Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC) was formed to oversee 12 districts that were deemed to face intense security challenges, including the merged districts.

Two of the ordinances envisage setting up an executive committee with wide-ranging powers to oversee special initiatives, including developmental schemes, in the 12 designated districts and the rest of the province, respectively.

The committee will have powers to identify and recommend the executing agency for special initiatives in the designated and other districts, including military formations.

In a statement on Saturday, President Zardari’s office confirmed he had promulgated five ordinances pertaining to KP. Of these, the following four had been published in the Official Gazette on Nov 19 after their promulgation:

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Societies (Registration) (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026;

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Special Initiative Ordinance, 2026 (specific districts);

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Special Initiative Ordinance, 2026 (other districts);

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Provincial Assembly (Powers, Immunities and Privileges) Ordinance, 2026 (XI of 2026).

The fifth was the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Speaker and Deputy Speaker (Salaries, Allowances and Privileges) Ordinance 2026.

Through the amendment ordinance related to privileges of MPAs, drastic changes have been made in the KP Provincial Assembly (Powers, Immunities and Privileges) Act 2026, as 21 of its 40 sections have been omitted, including those providing protection to the MPAs against “preventive detentions” and offences related to “breach” of privileges.

The schedule of offences related to “breach of privileges” of the Assembly, its members and committees has also been omitted, thus leaving them without significant privileges.

It may be mentioned that Sohail Afridi — whose role as the chief minister was rendered non-functional due to governor’s rule — Speaker Babar Saleem Swati and other lawmakers have been in “preventive detention” since emergency was imposed, according to police.

KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi also said last month that they had been placed under house arrest.

The important provisions omitted through the ordinance include sections 5 (attendance of MPA detained or arrested), 6 (members not liable to civil or criminal action), 10 (preventive detention), 11 (permission of speaker before arrest, detention, etc. of a member), 15 (power to summon), 22 (power to arrest), 31 (breach of privilege), 32 (breach of privilege to be an offence) and 34 (cognisance of offence).

Special initiative ordinances

The two ordinances relate to special initiatives in the 12 designated districts and the remaining districts in the province, respectively.

Both the ordinances provide for the establishment of an executive committee comprising a chairman, vice chairman and other such members as nominated by the prime minister, in case of designated district, and by the governor of the province, in case of the remaining districts.

For the designated districts, the Area Development Secretariat shall serve as secretariat of the executive committee, whereas for the other districts, the planning and development department shall serve as the secretariat of the committee.

Under the new laws, “special initiative” includes any work, developmental scheme, rehabilitation or reconstruction work, procurement of goods and human resources, consulting or non-consulting services or any other activity involving expenditure of public funds as determined by the executive committee.

The executive committee, in both the ordinances, has extensive powers including:

Identify an initiative as a special initiative of urgent or emergent nature;

Scrutinise and approve proposals, concept papers and PC-Is for the special initiatives;

Grant anticipatory approval for the initiatives, proposals, concept papers and PC-Is of the special initiatives;

Identify and recommend the executing agency, including military organisations and formations, for the execution of the special initiatives;

Provide a mechanism for the monitoring and evaluation of the special initiatives, including third-party monitoring and evaluation;

Review progress of the special initiatives;

Constitute committees or designate persons to carry out functions assigned to them by the executive committee;

Perform any other act to carry out the purposes of the ordinance.

The ordinances provide that the executive committee should meet at least once a month or as and when required.

The decisions of the committee shall be made on the basis of majority vote of its members, and in case of a tie, the chairman shall have the casting vote.

The chairman is also empowered to co-opt any other member or technical expert, to offer advice to the committee, as required.

Both the ordinances have overriding effect on other laws, including the KP Public Procurement Regulatory Authority Act 2012 and the KP Public Private Partnership Act 2020.

Moreover, no civil court shall have jurisdiction in relation to an act done, order passed, and any proceedings done under the ordinances.

Madressah registrations

Through the KP Societies (Registration) (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, a sub-section 1-A has been included in Section 21, dealing with the registration of “religious madressahs”.

The newly included provision provides that madressahs which are or may be registered with the Directorate General of Religious Education, Ministry of Federal Education and Professional Training, shall not be required to be registered under the Act (Societies Registration Act).

World.title: Forensic evidence points to servant in Hina Javaid murder as probe clears husband
World.content:
• After nearly three-month delay, police submit charge sheet in high-profile murder case

• According to the DNA analysis report, Hina Javaid was reportedly sexually assaulted after being murdered by her domestic servant

RAWALPINDI: Rawalpindi police have completed their investigation into the high-profile murder of digital media executive Hina Javaid, who was found dead with signs of torture and strangulation at her husband’s apartment in Lal Kurti in August. The police submitted the challan to the court after about three months.

The development was disclosed by newly appointed City Police Officer (CPO) Rawalpindi Sardar Ghias Gul during his first interaction with media persons on Saturday.

Hina Javaid was murdered on August 20, 2026, at her husband’s house, and her domestic servant has been identified as the main suspect in the case following a forensic DNA match and a report by a high-level inquiry committee.

Hina Javaid’s husband and his father have been cleared of any involvement in the murder by the police investigation, as no evidence linking them to the crime has been found.

At one point during the course of investigation, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz noted that “DNA test results and polygraph test suggest that the murder and rape were committed by the servant.”

However, he said the investigation was ongoing. On Oct 29, First Lady Aseefa Bhutto Zardari also met with Hina’s family at the Parliament and called for the family’s demand for a judicial commission to be “given due consideration”.

Although Hina Javaid’s husband and her father-in-law were named in the initial FIR registered on murder charges, they were given a clean chit in the police investigation. However, Hina’s husband was arrested, while her father-in-law was only questioned by the police.

It will be up to the court to decide whether Hina’s husband and father-in-law had any link to her murder. The police are required to submit a challan in a murder case within 15 days after a suspect is sent to judicial remand.

Meanwhile, Hina’s family had expressed dissatisfaction over the police investigation and demanded a judicial inquiry.

The family claimed to have proof of evidence tampering by the husband’s brother, who allegedly cleaned the accused’s room, tampered with evidence, and colluded with the police.

The police have already added Section 376 of the Pakistan Penal Code (rape) to the case following the forensic DNA findings.

CPO Sardar Ghias Gul told media persons that the challan had been submitted to the court for legal proceedings. He also acknowledged shortcomings in police prosecution, which result in the release of criminals, and said these would be addressed by appointing the right people to the right positions.

The Punjab government had constituted a three-member high-powered committee to review the investigation into the murder case, in which her husband and a domestic servant had been placed on judicial remand at Adiala Jail.

As part of the investigation, the committee also visited the crime scene, questioned the deceased woman’s husband and the domestic servant in jail, and met members of her family.

The committee comprises Additional Inspector General of the Crime Control Department (CCD) Sohail Chattha, DIG Lahore Shoaib Khurram Janbaz and SSP Investigation Rawalpindi Saifullah.

Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

World.title: Three dead, 36 missing after Indonesia factory fire
World.content:
A fire at a confectionery factory west of Jakarta killed three people and 36 remain missing, an Indonesian rescue official said on Sunday.

Drone footage showed large parts of the factory destroyed, with the roof collapsed in places and smoke still rising from the complex.

Photos and videos shared by rescuers also showed officers entering the charred building in search of the missing victims, with small fires still burning in some spots.

Relatives of the missing victims flocked near the factory’s entrance, seeking updates about their loved ones, footage aired by local broadcasters showed.

The Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, located in the Serang district around 50 kilometres from the capital, caught fire on Saturday afternoon, local search and rescue agency official Rizky Dwianto said.

“All elements of the joint SAR (search-and-rescue) team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritising the safety of personnel in the field,” he added.

Rizky said four people were injured and taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic.

Firefighters were alerted around 4:30 pm (2:30 pm Pakistan time) on Saturday and found the building already engulfed in flames when they arrived, fire official Tubagus Machfudz told local broadcaster Kompas TV.

“When we arrived (on location)… a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company’s protection system was functioning properly or not,” he said.

Banten province governor Andra Soni told reporters overnight that an estimated 60 people were inside the factory when it caught fire.

Confectionery maker Fonusa Agung Mulia describes itself on the professional networking platform LinkedIn as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of the Southeast Asian nation’s major consumer-food companies.

The cause of the incident is still under investigation, the local disaster agency said in an Instagram post on Sunday.

Deadly fires are not uncommon in Indonesia.

In December last year, a blaze that was likely caused by a drone battery explosion tore through a seven-storey building in Jakarta and killed at least 22 people, police said.

In 2023, at least 13 people were killed in the country’s east after an explosion at a nickel-processing plant.

World.title: Focus on public issues, avoid new fault lines: PPP
World.content:
President Asif Ali Zardari meets with Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar and National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq at the Presidency.—X/PresOfPakistan

ISLAMABAD: Seeking to ease tensions between her party and PML-N amid the ongoing debate on need for new provinces, PPP Vice President Senator Sherry Rehman on Saturday urged the government to focus on people’s problems rather than create new political fault lines.

Provocative statements by ministers should be avoided, she said, adding that PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari wanted politics to address people’s problems rather than create new divisions.

“Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari is looking to prevent bloodshed, not shed it,” she said.

Her statement came before Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar and National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq met President Asif Ali Zardari at President House to discuss the overall political situation. Besides Senator Rehman, PPP leader Raja Pervez Ashraf was also present.

The meeting followed an apparent easing of tensions between President Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif who also discussed the matter with Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi after the PPP chairman’s remarks at a ‘Meet the Press’ event at the Karachi Press Club. He had opposed the creation of new provinces, warning that dividing Sindh would lead to bloodshed.

He also criticised the coalition over several issues, including the treatment of JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, PTI founder Imran Khan’s incarceration and the 27th Amendment. He later clarified that he was raising an alarm, not issuing a threat, and complained that the PPP was not being consulted.

The remarks drew sharp reactions from PML-N ministers Khawaja Asif and Tallal Chaudhry, while MQM-P chief Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui urged the courts to take notice. Mustafa Kamal also criticised Mr Bhutto-Zardari.

President Zardari subsequently met Prime Minister Shehbaz and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, with the meeting calling for dialogue and restraint in public statements.

A separate PPP meeting reaffirmed the party’s opposition to Sindh’s division. A meeting between Mr Bhutto-Zardari and the prime minister is also expected in the coming days.

Senator Rehman also warned of a difficult winter, with gas and resource shortages and extreme weather in many areas, urging politicians not to add to people’s troubles by creating new fault lines.

Constitutional process

She also drew a constitutional line on demands by some ministers for a referendum on new provinces. “They [the ministers] should know that the Constitution will still refer the matter to parliament. There is no walking away from the votes of the assemblies.

A referendum does not override the Constitution, nor does it change any ground reality where any given province has spoken with its majority,” she said.

The PPP’s message was that it wanted the truce to hold but would oppose the creation of new provinces outside the constitutional parliamentary process.

Whether the easing of tensions lasts will depend on whether the parties pursue consultation and consensus through parliament or revive the referendum debate.

Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
