World.title: Agnes Callamard: US sanctions vs ICC could jeopardize Rodrigo Duterte case
World.content:
LAUNCH. Amnesty International Secretary General Agnès Callamard calls for justice for drug war victims during the November 20 launch of 'Walang Pahimakas' in Quezon City, on November 20, 2026.

'There is only one response to the USA threats and sanctions: it must be protecting the ICC. Not appeasing the predator,' Callamard says

MANILA, Philippines – Amnesty International secretary general and human rights activist Agnes Callamard warned that the United States’ sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) could imperil the court’s operations, including the case of former president Rodrigo Duterte.

At the sidelines of the event, the Amnesty secretary general told Palawan News that these sanctions could cause the collapse of the court. “If the ICC is unable to function, the ICC will collapse. Or the trial will deliver the verdict that will have lost its credibility. At all levels, whether it’s operational or political, it’s bad news.”

Callamard was in the Philippines for Rappler’s Social Good Summit on Saturday, November 20, where she and other advocates talked about the need to build a community amid threats of Artificial Intelligence. As United Nations Special Rapporteur on Extrajudicial Killings, she was barred by the Duterte administration from entering the country. The Marcos government lifted this ban only last September.

Callamard told Rappler, “The trial of ex-president Duterte is due to start on 30 November. It could take one year or probably more until judgment. If no action is taken to protect the ICC against the US sanctions, the trial may never proceed.”

In an interview with Rappler, Callamard said: “I was told that just this week, in a meeting of the state parties to the ICC, the diplomats of the most powerful countries, including Canada and the UK, and other G7 states, have insisted the only way forward is to negotiate with the US and agree to their demands. They continue to refuse to protect the ICC.”

According to Callamard, the US is giving the ICC until April to comply with the following:

No ICC jurisdiction over non-state parties or “an impunity carve-out for the USA”

Dropping of ICC investigations and arrest warrants in the Palestine situation

Immunities for heads of state

The Amnesty secretary general said that if the powerful countries that are part of the ICC “are prepared to negotiate with the US, the ICC will lose its independence and credibility.”

“The failure to protect the ICC is a betrayal of the mothers and fathers, sons and daughters of the Philippines that have spoken up against Duterte’s senseless war, against threats and intimidation,” she added.

Duterte has been detained in The Hague, Netherlands since March 2025 after he was arrested due to three counts of crimes against humanity case. His case stemmed from the alleged killings of the Davao Death Squad and his bloody war on drugs that killed nearly 30,000 people, according to several human rights organizations.

In April, the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I confirmed all three charges against the former president. His trial will start on November 30 at the ICC Trial Chamber III.

Why trump wants sanctions vs ICC

US President Donald Trump, in the last years, has been pushing to sanction the ICC which has jurisdiction over genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and crimes of aggression.

In February 2025, Trump authorized economic and travel sanctions against those involved in the ICC probe into US citizens or allies like Israel. He imposed sanctions, in the same year, against four ICC judges over the issuance of an arrest warrant for Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu and a past decision to open a case into alleged war crimes by US troops in Afghanistan.

Just last August, the US government imposed sanctions against ICC President Tomoko Akane and Abdoulaye Seye, a senior ICC trial lawyer. But the most concerning development is the ICC-wide sanctions that the Trump administration is planning to announce soon.

Entity-wide sanctions would bar US citizens and companies from giving the ICC funds, goods, or services without permission from the US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control. This would be tricky because banks often comply with these sanctions since they are dependent on access to the American financial system, according to Reuters.

Apart from this, ICC-wide sanctions could affect the court’s IT services and insurance, investigations, and payments to employees.

Callamard urged European governments to “use their ‘blocking’ law, which bars European companies from complying with foreign sanctions. She also called on central banks in Europe to give the court bank accounts,” Palawan News reported.

She told Rappler: “There is only one response to the USA threats and sanctions: it must be protecting the ICC. Not appeasing the predator. They continue to refuse to protect the ICC. They are betraying decades of efforts forged in blood and tears to ensure that no one, absolutely no one should be above the law.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Gilas Hiraya out to chase Philippine women’s basketball dreams
World.content:
STALWARTS. Gilas Hiraya stars Amyah Español (left) and Kacey dela Rosa hope to carve out a new era for Philippine women’s basketball.

Armed with a new name and fresh off an Asian Games silver-medal breakthrough, Gilas Hiraya sets its sights on historic women’s basketball milestones in 2027

MANILA, Philippines – Shifting to a refreshed identity, the newly christened Gilas Hiraya looks to bear the fruit of the hoop-crazy nation’s hopes, dreams, and aspirations in a huge 2027.

Gilas Hiraya, the new name of the Philippine women’s basketball team, was unveiled this month to establish its own identity as an emerging force in Asian hoops.

The rebrand comes ahead of a pivotal year in which both the 3×3 and 5-on-5 squads will chase a spot in the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, alongside the country’s hosting of the FIBA Women’s Asia Cup at the SM Seaside Arena in Cebu next year.

“It’s really a deliberate decision to give them an identity of their own in order to shape a pathway that is unique for them,” Samahang Basketbol ng Pilipinas (SBP) executive director Erika Dy said.

“We don’t want them to just follow the footsteps of the men’s team or the men’s program,” she added. “We want them to be able to create their own dreams and aspirations for Philippine basketball.”

According to Dy, the idea of giving the women’s team its own name was suggested by FIBA secretary general Andreas Zagklis during a meeting in Shenzhen, China, in July 2025.

Zagklis pushed for the rebrand upon learning that the women’s team used to be known as “Perlas Pilipinas” before aligning its identity with the broader Gilas Pilipinas program in 2019.

Following lengthy discussions with numerous stakeholders, including the UAAP and the players themselves, Hiraya stood out among the other shortlisted names and was officially picked by the SBP on October 27.

“Part of why we chose the word Hiraya, which represents dreams, hopes, and aspirations — it’s a deep Tagalog word,” explained Dy, herself a former basketball player and coach for Ateneo.

“It’s because we really believe that our women’s program can represent that for all the women in the Philippines. It actually goes beyond basketball.”

With a fresh identity, Gilas Hiraya is riding a wave of sustained success, buoyed by a 3×3 silver-medal finish at the Asian Games and a deep tournament run by the 5-on-5 squad in the same meet.

Helping lead the way are Asiad silver medalists Kacey dela Rosa of Ateneo and Amyah Español of Far Eastern University.

“I’m just grateful that we have our own identity now as a women’s basketball team. And I just think every player on the women’s team is very dedicated to growing the sport of women’s basketball in the Philippines,” said Español.

“I’m just thankful that we have such a great support system who believes in us to have our own identity as the women’s team.”

For Dela Rosa, a two-time UAAP MVP, the identity shift reflects the program’s continued development under program director Bacon Austria and head coach BT Toews.

“As Filipinos, we put in a lot of work, like hard work, and we want them to know how much hard work we put in and sacrifices outside the court,” Dela Rosa said. “We also want them to recognize us — we are a team that dreams big.” – Rappler.com

World.title: COP31 climate talks close to final deal, says summit president
World.content:
JUSTICE. A member of Fridays for Future holds a placard at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 16, 2026.

The draft omits mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving climate change, an issue that has been at the center of the fractious talks

ANTALYA, Turkey – UN climate talks in Turkey approached a final deal on Sunday, November 22, with the announcement of a new package that COP31 presidents Australia and Turkey hope will achieve consensus on how to advance the fight against global warming.

The new draft deal was released two days after the conference in Antalya was scheduled to end.

If approved, it would acknowledge for the first time that global warming is on course to exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that countries had sought to preserve, while calling for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse the overshoot.

The draft omits mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving climate change, an issue that has been at the center of the fractious talks. Instead, it includes language referring to a previous COP at which governments had agreed to transition away from oil, gas, and coal.

“We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” COP31 President Murat Kurum told a plenary session early on Sunday.

He said the conference would reconvene in the morning to approve the deal.

Environmental group 350.org said it was disappointed by the draft’s failure to mention fossil fuels explicitly, as well as its encouragement of carbon-removal technologies.

“Carbon capture is one of the biggest scams of the overshoot era, and our leaders are on the verge of falling for it,” said Sara Shaw, the group’s campaigns and networks director, referring to the practice of trapping carbon dioxide before it reaches the atmosphere.

Shaw said the draft deal opens the door to more fossil fuel development.

Observers to the closed-door talks said Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producer nations had pushed hard in negotiations for keeping fossil fuels out of the text, and carbon removal in.

A representative for the Saudi delegation declined to comment.

The new text followed intensive consultations between Australia, which is leading the talks, Turkey, which is hosting the meeting, and nearly 200 delegations from many of the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations.

The presidency gave delegations several hours to raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled at 0700 GMT to begin approving it.

Australia’s task, supported by Turkey, has been to find a deal that balances the needs of nations most vulnerable to climate change with those whose economies depend on either the production or consumption of fossil fuels.

This year’s COP is the first since the UN’s environmental body confirmed that the rise in global temperature was set to blow past 1.5 degrees, a threshold all countries agreed over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Tech Thoughts] Considering AI to help you think through problems? Same here.
World.content:
Would inviting a little AI into my life help with brain fog at work? It might be able to help, but it'll take time to know how useful it'll be in the long run.

It’s been a strange few years since COVID-19 came about.

I fell ill from it a few years back, and without noticing it, it slowly dawned on me that I’d been struggling with my thoughts. In the years following getting sick with COVID-19 and recovering from it, it felt as if I had never completely recovered.

I felt like I was suffering from brain fog and had trouble imagining what my days would look like or how to plan and organize my writing.

For a while, reading would help. I’d read up on topics I wanted to discuss for this column, for example, and I’d be able to react to the information. There was, however, a decided difficulty in being proactive.

It’s as if I wanted to go for a walk in a field and was suddenly stopped by vision-obscuring trees everywhere I looked. I had information and things I wanted to do (and deadlines, to boot), but I had trouble planning properly because I couldn’t connect my thoughts into plans, and put plans into action.

There’s no definitive way to test for what caused my brain fog — the American Brain Foundation says it could be a symptom of being sick from COVID-19, chronic fatigue syndrome, insomnia, or even lyme disease. Adding to that, there’s no official diagnosis for this feeling or sensation of being slower than I used to be, but it has threatened one of the things I hold dear to me: my ability to write stuff the way I want to.

My wife, whom I recently shared these feelings of anxiety with, told me something that felt both logical and like a betrayal of the things I write about here when it comes to artificial intelligence.

She advised me to get used to the idea of adding even just a little AI to my life. I tried to imagine it in much the way I would use eyeglasses, or to put it back to the analogy of my suddenly-appearing mental forest, perhaps I could use it like a chainsaw that wouldn’t cut down everything in my path, but would help with some of the trees in front of me.

Maybe using AI could help me see the outlines in my mind a little better.

It started with little things, like audio transcription for work quotes, which worked well enough.

Like any other tool, it felt like I was being forced to adjust to or relearn something I could do myself. But I kept trying anyway.

Quietly, I’d rely on AI search results to help me sift through information just a little faster, or use the work-based AI-powered summarizer on our content on Rappler for a three-sentence overview. I’d check the outputs for accuracy or truthfulness, fix any issues and, in the case of AI searches, make sure to cite the appropriate sources.

These were helpful, but it left me scared too. Could it help me be more proactive? Can it plot out points of action so I could have more information as to what story leads might be pursuable?

Honestly, I wasn’t sure and I didn’t know, and that’s one other point of fear.

I’d been focused on the potential problems AI can bring — from the environmental to the economic and moral implications of AI use — that it didn’t dawn on me that with some work, it could be just a simple tool for helpful solutions for people having trouble with cognition or planning.

My wife, who put this idea in my head, knows well-enough about using AI to help with her unfathomable workload.

Tonight seems like a good time to ask about what tools she uses to get her job done, and maybe learn how to better use AI to shore up my now-glaring weaknesses. – Rappler.com

World.title: Keep the faith: Nisperos rediscovers confidence after yearlong PVL injury layoff
World.content:
Once one of the Philippines’ biggest names in high school and college volleyball, Akari star Faith Nisperos now fights to stay healthy and finally unlock her true potential in the PVL

MANILA, Philippines – For years, Faith Nisperos was a name thrown around in numerous conversations as one of Philippine volleyball’s brightest future stars.

From her time in high school with the dynastic Nazareth-NU Lady Bullpups, to her stint with the Ateneo Blue Eagles in college, and finally, to her jump to the pros with the PVL’s Akari Chargers, Nisperos always had hype surrounding her, and lived up to it for the most part.

In recent times, however, Ateneo’s former “Queen Eagle” had quietly faded into the volleyball landscape’s backdrop, grounded and clipped by a major knee injury that kept her sidelined from April 2024 until July this year.

Save from a brief and scoreless one-game appearance last January 31, Nisperos sat out more or less 15 months’ worth of a budding volleyball career, before finally shaking off her injury tag for good at the start of the 2026 PVL On Tour, and played every game since then.

The 26-year-old spiker then marked the end of a breakthrough 2026 with a 15-point winning effort — her highest scoring mark since November 2024 — in what was otherwise a no-bearing game against ZUS Coffee last November 17.

Though Akari failed to make the playoffs for the 2026 All-Filipino Conference Siklab Series, Nisperos nonetheless felt like a champion after ending the year on a winning and, more importantly, healthy note.

“I’m really happy because I’m finally here. This is me, and this is my territory,” she said in Filipino. “I have to also give credit to my coaches and my teammates who are beside me throughout my process of going back into the game.”

Despite only playing one to two sets at a time due to the Siklab Series’ “all-to-play” requirement, Nisperos still averaged a respectable 6.5 points per game, and played in all of Akari’s eight elimination round matches that netted a 3-5 record.

Winning the mental war

Though restrictions were in place, Nisperos did not downplay the difficulty of both finding her confidence back, and striving for consistency amid the ever-present dangers of reaggravating her injury.

“It has been months of mental preparation, because I knew that I would return to form one day, I just didn’t know when,” she continued. “Part of the mental preparation was us getting back under pressure again, going through so much scrutiny, and so much responsibilities.”

“I also had people who helped me throughout that mental process. Again, I go back to my coaches and teammates, who also reminded me that I got this. ‘You’re Faith, remember that. You’re strong,’ they said. They always reminded me who I really am.”

Heading into 2027 for the next two All-Filipino Conferences, Sigla and Sinag, Nisperos is raring to further rediscover her true, peak form — the Faith Nisperos that once won V-League MVP in college and led Ateneo to the Final Four as the main star.

“It’s a common denominator for us athletes that we want to get better as time proceeds,” she continued. “I feel like I just want to be more consistent, and improve my non-scoring skills like receiving and defense.”

“Improvement is always one of my biggest goals as a player. I’ve wanted that for such a long time, to improve myself further.”

Stars who faded into obscurity due to injuries are a dime a dozen in all sports. Nisperos could have gone that route, and could very well still go that route, if her fortunes don’t hold.

After all, she’s never had the best of luck. Prior to her yearlong injury spell, Nisperos also lost two more years of her career after her college rookie season was cut short due to the onset of the 2020 pandemic.

But she’s not holding herself to what-ifs stemming from a rocky past.

True to her name, Nisperos always kept the faith — faith in the process, in her potential, and in the light of a future that she fought hard to keep bright. – Rappler.com

World.title: People should shape AI’s future, says UN panel member Leslie Teo
World.content:
'AI is a powerful tool we should build, we should share, but we should always make sure that humans — all stakeholders — have a say in this future that we create,' Leslie Teo says at the 2026 Social Good Summit

MANILA, Philippines – “What can you do to make sure our future, our children’s future, is one that we would wish, not one that is imposed on us?”

Leslie Teo, a Singaporean economist and artificial intelligence executive who serves on the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, posed that question during his speech at the 2026 Social Good Summit on Saturday, November 21. He outlined ways to develop AI as a positive force for society.

Teo challenged the notion that AI is beyond people’s ability to shape and control.

“Today AI gives us powerful possibilities, but, just like the ideas of economists, the future is for us to determine,” Teo said.

Teo compared the potential benefits of AI development to a pie that economists envision growing larger.

“The fact that the pie grows doesn’t mean that you as an individual benefit. The fact that a consumer benefits doesn’t mean that a society grows. And even if the pie is larger, who gets the slice? Who chooses? Who has a say?” Teo explained.

He said responsible AI development could help address gaps in expertise and efficiency, along with other problems countries face.

An open approach to solving local problems

Teo advocated for open access to AI tools, saying this would allow communities to shape how the technology is developed and build tools that address their own needs.

“We all don’t need to build frontier models; in fact, that would be very foolish. But many AI tools — many things that matter when it comes to real impact — are open and free,” said Teo.

He added, “If we don’t understand the technology, we can never trust it, we can never use it.”

Teo said learning about AI and building tools to solve specific problems may be easier than people imagine. Developers can also set their own criteria for measuring the tools’ success.

Defining their own benchmarks for success, Teo said, allows developers to retain control over the tools they build.

“If you give someone else the ability to define what is success, you are giving away your sovereignty,” Teo said.

As an example, Teo said there were 8,000 languages in the world, with 1,300 languages in Southeast Asia, but that most models can do 10 at best.”

He asked, “What happened to the rest? Who defines what is good?”

Teo said communities can maintain their sovereignty and address local problems by developing specialized tools that reflect their own needs, rather than relying on Western standards of what is “good.”

Teo also envisioned a future in which AI development becomes more like Linux: frontier models would continue to exist, but open-source and free models would become more widespread as developers share and build on existing technology.

Who has control of tech?

Teo also emphasized that humans should remain in control of AI and other emerging technologies, rather than allowing these systems to dictate how people can act. To illustrate his point, he compared two call centers with different approaches to using AI.

In the first call center, technology helps human agents find accurate information about customers’ problems, acknowledge mistakes, and resolve issues. In the second, AI monitors agents’ productivity and time spent on calls. They must follow a script and cannot or do not deviate from it.

“AI is a powerful tool we should build, we should share, but we should always make sure that humans — all stakeholders — have a say in this future that we create,” Teo said.

This human-centric approach to AI, he explained, is meant to keep AI development sustainable and pointed toward future growth,

‘Not about the pie’

Teo ended his speech by returning to the pie analogy, saying his vision of a better world was not about who got the biggest slice.

“It’s about relationships. It’s about society. For me, this is what we want to build with AI. We want to build a better place for our children, where relationships matter, creativity — notwithstanding all the things AI can do — is still very much a human thing, and so is understanding meaning,” Teo said.

“It’s not about a bigger pie. It’s about a meaningful world — much, much more important than just the pie.”

The 2026 Social Good Summit, themed “We, The Humans,” focuses on promoting and defending human rights, community, and shared values as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly widespread. – Rappler.com

World.title: Rappler’s Dwight de Leon, Patrick Cruz nominated for best journalist at Paragala Awards
World.content:
Rappler multimedia reporters Dwight de Leon and Patrick Cruz are recognized for their in-depth stories on the anti-dynasty bill and the Navotas landfill fire, respectively

MANILA, Philippines – Rappler multimedia reporters Dwight de Leon and Patrick Cruz have been nominated for the Paragala Central Luzon Media Awards, which describes itself as the biggest student award-giving body in Luzon.

The two reporters are nominees in the Best National Journalist category, alongside Christian Esguerra of Facts First and Guinevere Latoza of the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism.

De Leon was recognized for his in-depth story examining how House leaders justify and promote a toothless anti-political dynasty bill to the public.

Cruz’s nomination, meanwhile, is for his special interactive story on the weeks-long landfill fire in Navotas, which displaced hundreds of residents.

The Paragala, organized by the Communicators’ League of Holy Angel University, is now in its 13th year.

The awards recognize communicators “whose work embodies integrity, purpose, and conviction — those who deepen public awareness, preserve collective memory, encourage critical reflection, and inspire compassion toward the realities of Filipino society.”

Visit Paragala’s social media pages for the complete list of nominees across categories. Winners will be announced on Friday, November 27. – Rappler.com

World.title: Aagos ang Kundiman: 100 Years of the UP College of Music
World.content:
This event marks the start of a yearlong partnership between the UP College of Music and the Pasig local government

(This is a press release from the UP College of Music and the UP Office of the President.)

The UP College of Music presents a special commemorative concert on Tuesday, November 24 6:30 pm at the UP Theater Lobby in cooperation with the UP Office of the President and the Pasig Chamber of Commerce and Industry through Deep Echoes International.

Play Video

Titled Aagos ang Kundiman, this commemorative concert honors the centennial of Nicanor Abelardo’s iconic kundiman-kumintang “Mutya ng Pasig“ (composed in 1926, lyrics by Deogracias del Rosario) as it simultaneously celebrates the 110th anniversary of the UP College of Music (founded in 1916), where Abelardo studied and later taught.

The project frames the Pasig River not merely as a geographic landmark, but as an important lifeline and artery of economic activity, and as a living muse that shaped the romantic, nationalistic, and sonic landscape of traditional Philippine art music.

Play Video

As the Pasig River flows relentlessly from Laguna de Bay to Manila, through time and history, bisecting the city and changing form through the seasons, so does the kundiman. Revival, reinvention, and care are crucial collective acts to ensure that our intangible and physical heritages are nurtured and live on in creative and robust ways.

Featured artists are :

UP College of Music Voice students: Vyktoria Baile, Filianne Villaflor, Carmelite Salvador, Kzee Delos Santos, Ivanna Cruz, Marcus Mallonga, Jhon Michael Mauricio, Mark Nicholson Jaluag, Krisleen Andya Bareng, Jedidiah Retuta, Arianna Rodavia, Althea Domngal, Samuel Silvestre, and Lorenzo Esguerra

Maestro Lester Demetillo

Faculty guitarists Nathan Manimtim, and staff guitarists RJ Balledos and Mon Nerval

Voice Faculty Stefanie Quintin and Raymond Leslie Diaz

Keyboard Faculty Albert Roldan

Asian Music faculty Mlou Matute and UP TUGMA, and more.

Special guest is Joey Ayala. Artistic direction is by Joey Vargas.

Free and open to the public, this event marks the start of a yearlong partnership with the Pasig local government, with plans for more concerts and cultural activities in 2027. – Rappler.com

World.title: US urges PH to resolve Pax Silica issues first, says Gathalian
World.content:
Sen. Sherwin Gatchalian —NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines – The United States wants the Philippine government to resolve issues related to the controversial Pax Silica initiative first before proceeding with an agreement, according to Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian.

He said US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told him that the Philippines should be given enough time to address the various concerns surrounding the initiative.

“He said he knows there are many issues and problems. We should not rush things and should give the Philippine government time to address these issues,” Gatchalian said in an interview with radio dzBB on Sunday, recounting the conversation he had with Rubio during a state luncheon in Malacañang Palace on Nov. 18.

Article continues after this 

The state luncheon was hosted by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in honor of US President Donald Trump, who was in Manila last week for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean)-US Special Summit and bilateral meeting with the country’s chief executive.

“I’m sure they are monitoring the situation and they have seen that there are many issues. It is just right that we first resolve these issues concerning Pax Silica and Luzon Economic Corridor so that before we move forward, we can provide solutions to the problems,” added Gatchalian.

Marcos and US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton earlier confirmed that the signing of the Pax Silica initiative was not part of Trump’s visit to the Philippines.

During his visit, Trump was asked about the initiative, but he referred the matter to Lipton, who said, “There will be no signing. There is no signing.”

Marcos was also quick to respond to the reporter’s query, saying, “No, not on this trip. We are not covering that on this trip.”

Article continues after this 

READ: President ‘perplexed’ by protests vs Pax Silica

Trump’s visit was met with protests from various groups opposing the US-led Pax Silica Initiative, particularly the proposed high-tech manufacturing and semiconductor hub in New Clark City, Capas, Tarlac.

Article continues after this 

Pax Silica seeks to strengthen supply chains for semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, critical minerals and other technologies while reducing dependence on China.

The Philippines joined the initiative in April 2026, with the proposed technology hub expected to position the country as a key player in the global semiconductor and AI industries.

World.title: Ombudsman: Romualdez’s case can be finished in a year
World.content:
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla in a file photo.

MANILA, Philippines — Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla has expressed confidence that the plunder case of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez can be completed in a year as he emphasized that there will not be delaying tactics in resting their cases.

Last September, the Ombudsman filed a plunder case against Romualdez and two other co-accused before the Sandiganbayan over alleged kickbacks worth at least P7.44 billion. Romualdez is currently detained at the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology Jail Male Dormitory in Quezon City.

“Within a one year period, pwedeng tapusin namin ang case namin. Kasi umaabot nga ng 15 years sa nakaraan eh. Ngayon, because we’re ready before we file, ready talaga kami mag-file ng ano, mag-present ng evidence. That’s the difference now in our justice system,” Remulla said in his radio program in DZRH on Saturday.

Article continues after this 

(Within a one year period, we can finish the case. It could take up to 15 years before. Now, because we’re ready before we file, we’re ready to present the evidence. That’s the difference now in our justice system.)

READ: Romualdez co-accused surrenders to NBI, says Ombudsman

This pronouncement came after Romualdez’s co-accused, Felicito Guevarra surrendered to the National Bureau of Investigation last Friday. Guevarra is the president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corp.

The Ombudsman said that Guevarra surrendered after the prosecution moved to cancel his passport. Following his surrender, the Ombudsman noted that Guevarra was granted conditional immunity under Section 17 of Republic Act No. 6770 or the Ombudsman Act of 1989.

Remulla described Guevarra’s surrender as “significant,” noting that his commission on the transaction worth around P324 million is already restituted to the Bureau of Treasury.

Article continues after this 

READ: SC dismisses Romualdez petition vs Ombudsman’s prelim probe

“Kaya nga we’re looking at the case now of the former speaker. Parang kung bail hearing ang kanilang habol, ang gusto sinasabi ko talaga, let’s present our evidence in chief already. Tapusin na natin ito,” Remulla expressed.

Article continues after this 

(That’s why we’re looking at the case of the former speaker. If they are after the bail hearing, what I am saying is let’s present our evidence in chief already. Let’s finish this one.)

“At least we can do it in record time. Nobody can delay it. Ang problema kasi, kaaway natin sa justice, delay eh. Eh andyan na, chinallenge nila yung evidence namin. So now we’re ready to lay out everything,” he added.

World.title: Eastern Visayas youth groups warn Pax Silica may spur exploitation
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

TACLOBAN CITY — Youth groups across Eastern Visayas have strongly opposed the proposed Pax Silica initiative, warning that it could pave the way for the exploitation of the region’s mineral resources and intensify foreign military presence in their communities.

In a joint statement on Nov. 21, the groups accused the Marcos administration of prioritizing US economic and military interests over national sovereignty.

The said Eastern Visayas could become a target for resource extraction because of its deposits of bauxite, manganese, and chromite.

Article continues after this 

“Our land is not yours to plunder,” the groups added, calling on students and youth organizations to unite against the initiative and what they described as policies that threaten the country’s sovereignty and the livelihoods of local communities.

The groups expressed concern that Pax Silica, which seeks to strengthen US supply chains for semiconductors, artificial intelligence, and critical minerals, could have implications beyond its proposed industrial zone in Capas, Tarlac, reaching resource-rich areas such as Eastern Visayas.

READ: Four reasons Pax Silica may violate Philippine laws

They also criticized the growing military cooperation between the Philippines and the United States, citing the Balikatan exercises, the US Navy-led Pacific Partnership, and Kasangga 2026 as examples of increasing foreign military engagement in the region.

“Our region must not be transformed into a military staging ground or a potential battleground for wars driven by foreign interests,” the statement said.

Article continues after this 

The organizations also linked their opposition to the continuing difficulties faced by farmers and fisherfolk, including the effects of El Niño, declining agricultural productivity, inadequate government support, and threats of land displacement.

They said development should not come at the expense of communities whose livelihoods depend on the land and natural resources.

Article continues after this 

READ: Aeta, farmers face displacement over Pax Silica hub – HRW

The joint statement was signed by student councils and youth organizations from the University of the Philippines Tacloban, Leyte Normal University, Visayas State University, the University of Eastern Philippines, and youth groups in Tacloban, Baybay, and Ormoc, among others.

Separately, Kadayaw, a student organization of Holy Infant College, also in this city, declared its opposition to Pax Silica, stressing the importance of protecting cultural heritage, ancestral lands, and farmers’ rights.

“Progress should never come at the expense of our people, our heritage, and the land that sustains us,” Kadayaw said.

The organization added that modernization should not result in the displacement of communities or the loss of cultural identity.

The youth groups said the postponement of the signing of the Pax Silica framework during US President Donald Trump’s visit to the Philippines should not be considered the end of the issue, as efforts to advance the initiative could continue through proposed legislation in Congress.

World.title: Health advocates push funding for smoke-free, vape-free bill
World.content:
A man smokes a disposable vape, Newcastle-under-Lyme, Britain, September 14, 2023. REUTERS/Carl Recine/File Photo

MANILA, Philippines — Health advocates have urged lawmakers to retain the funding provision in a proposed measure seeking smoke-free and vape-free environments, warning that inadequate enforcement could leave Filipino families shouldering the rising costs of chronic diseases.

Social Watch Philippines (SWP) said House Bill No. 9603, or the proposed Smoke-Free and Vape-Free Environment Act, should include dedicated funding for local government units (LGUs) to implement tobacco-control programs and prevent smoking and vaping-related illnesses.

“Laws to protect Filipinos from cigarette smoke and vape aerosols will only work if local governments have the budget to enforce them,” SWP co-convenor Ma. Victoria Raquiza said in a statement.

Article continues after this 

“Every peso spent on stopping young people from starting to smoke or vape saves Filipino families from draining their savings on hospital bills,” added Raquiza, a professor of the University of the Philippines’ National College of Public Administration.

READ: DOH: 7 in 10 Filipino deaths due to noncommunicable diseases

The call comes after recent data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) showed that half of all health spending in the Philippines last year amounting to P1.87 trillion went to chronic illnesses like heart disease, cancer, and lung problems that require long-term treatments.

It also revealed that ordinary Filipino families had to pay 41.2 percent of these medical bills straight out of their own pockets.

According to the Department of Health (DOH), smoking, vaping, and breathing in secondhand smoke and vape fumes are among the top preventable causes of these costly chronic diseases.

Article continues after this 

The bill proposes allocating 3 percent of local health budgets for the operation of the Smoke-Free and Vape-Free Task Force, including research, benchmarking, smoking cessation programs and public awareness campaigns.

According to SWP, LGUs could use existing funding sources to implement the proposed measures, even if they lack the resources to create new budget allocations.

Article continues after this 

These include existing programs for noncommunicable diseases, the Special Health Fund under the Universal Health Care Act, and the 20-percent Development Fund for lower-income LGUs.

The group also suggested tapping funds earmarked for Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) programs under Republic Act No. 11467 to support tobacco-control initiatives, particularly SDG Target 3a, which seeks to strengthen the implementation of the World Health Organization’s Framework Convention on Tobacco Control.

READ: Push grows to raise vape, tobacco age limit to 25

SWP also welcomed the House committee on health’s approval of HB 9603, chaired by Manila 4th District Rep. Giselle Maceda on Nov. 11, in time for the National Children’s Month.

Raquiza urged lawmakers to preserve the bill’s funding provisions as it now advances toward plenary deliberation in the House and subsequent action in the Senate.

World.title: PNP chief vows impartiality after Sara Duterte’s criticism
World.content:
Philippine National Police chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. — Photo from Office of the Chief PNP/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. stressed that police must remain impartial and uphold due process in all operations after Vice President Sara Duterte described the agency as an “enforcement arm” of politicians.

“Impartiality is a principle that we strive to uphold in every police operation and public service,” Nartatez said in a statement on Sunday.

“Our commitment is to treat everyone with fairness, respect, and compassion, while providing equal protection under the law regardless of one’s position or political affiliation,” he added.

Article continues after this 

His statement came amid discussions over the reported incident involving former household staff members of Vice President Sara Duterte, who were fetched from a hotel in Bonifacio Global City, Taguig, on Nov. 17.

READ: Sara Duterte: PNP ‘enforcement arm’ of politicians

According to the PNP’s account, two lawyers sought assistance from Fort Bonifacio Police Sub-Station 1 and requested police officers to accompany them to the hotel.

Upon arrival, police found five individuals who were not being restrained and did not report any immediate threat to their safety.

The five voluntarily accompanied the officers to the police station, where they declined to execute affidavits regarding their alleged captivity.

Article continues after this 

They also did not identify anyone allegedly responsible for the supposed threats or coercion.

The PNP said their legal counsels later submitted an affidavit, which served as the basis for the police blotter.

Article continues after this 

“As an institution, we remain guided by the Constitution, the rule of law, and our commitment to serve all Filipinos fairly and impartially, with every action grounded in facts, evidence, and due process,” Nartatez said.

Nartatez emphasized that all Filipinos must be treated equally, regardless of political affiliation or personal circumstances.

“The PNP remains ready to listen, receive complaints, and provide appropriate police assistance to anyone who feels threatened or unsafe,” he said.

World.title: Ombudsman affirms preventive suspension order vs Dalaguete mayor
World.content:
Facade of the Office of the Ombudsman — File photo by Niño Jesus Orbeta | INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has affirmed its decision to impose a six-month preventive suspension without pay on Dalaguete, Cebu Mayor Ronald Allan Cesante and five municipal officials over alleged irregularities in the construction of a municipal warehouse.

In a statement on Sunday, the Ombudsman said it had dismissed the motion for reconsideration filed by Cesante and the five other respondents against its Aug. 29, 2025, decision ordering their preventive suspension.

READ: Romualdez co-accused surrenders to NBI, says Ombudsman

Article continues after this 

“A perusal of the Motion would show that it does not present any newly discovered evidence nor does it cite any grave error of fact or law, or any serious irregularity, prejudicial to the interest of the respondents. In fact, the arguments propounded are in essence a mere reiteration of the arguments already scrutinized and exhaustively discussed,” the Ombudsman said in its consolidated decisions.

The other five respondents are Municipal Assessor and Bids and Awards Committee (BAC) Chairperson Edmund Centeno, Municipal Budget Officer and BAC Vice-Chairperson Brenda Vergara, and BAC members Zoning Officer II Essandre Amprad, Municipal Government Department Head-I Donald Abraham Lara, and Administrative Assistant V Cristina Miranda.

The Ombudsman said the case stemmed from complaints filed by Jose Rene Moran and Braulio Moran, who questioned the municipal government’s construction of a warehouse on a lot covered by a Special Power of Attorney (SPA) executed by the heirs of Teodorica Severino and Pedro Moran in favor of Hetzel Moran.

The respondents argued that they acted within their authority in conducting pre-procurement proceedings, the Ombudsman said. It added that Cesante argued he could not be held liable for alleged procurement irregularities because these fell under the responsibility of the BAC.

READ: Ombudsman suspends Capiz town vice mayor over alleged inaction

Article continues after this 

The Ombudsman dismissed the arguments, noting that the SPA did not authorize Hetzel Moran to allow the municipal government to construct the warehouse.

“Respondents Mayor and BAC members should not have merely relied on the Permit to Enter but proactively verified from all the legal heirs if indeed Hetzel Moran had the legal authority to allow the Municipality unlimited access over the said lot,” the Ombudsman said.

Article continues after this 

The Ombudsman also said the respondents failed to present new evidence that would warrant reversing its earlier decision, adding that their arguments merely reiterated points already discussed in the assailed order. /mcm

World.title: DA: El Niño affects 12,595 farmers in Ilocos Region, causes P346M losses
World.content:
An agricultural farm in Ilocos Norte, where prolonged dry conditions brought by El Niño threaten crops and farmers’ livelihoods. The Ilocos Region has recorded 5,694 hectares of affected agricultural land and an estimated P346.12 million in losses. (Photo by Kenneth P. Tabin)

SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — The impact of El Niño has affected 12,595 farmers and damaged about 5,694 hectares of agricultural land in the Ilocos Region, causing an estimated P346.12 million in agricultural losses, according to the Department of Agriculture (DA).

The DA Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Operations Center (DA-DRRM OpCen) reported these figures in its latest monitoring update on the weather phenomenon’s effects in the region on Friday, Nov. 20.

READ: Agri losses due to El Niño up further past P10 billion

Article continues after this 

The Department of Science and Technology–Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (DOST-Pagasa) said very strong El Niño conditions were present in the tropical Pacific.

Forecasts indicated that the phenomenon could persist until the first half of 2027 and reach its peak before the end of 2026.

Meanwhile, water levels in major dams remained generally stable as of Nov. 20.

San Roque Dam recorded a water level of 279.62 meters above sea level, just 0.38 meter below its normal high water level of 280 meters.

The DA-DRRM OpCen said it would continue monitoring the effects of El Niño and providing updates on its impact on agriculture in the Ilocos Region. INQ

World.title: World’s largest rodent finds home at wildlife farm in Cavite
World.content:
Capybaras, the world’s largest living rodents, are now among the animals visitors can see up close at Yoki’s Farm in Mendez, Cavite. Native to South America, these semi-aquatic mammals are known for their webbed feet and calm, sociable behavior. (Photo from DENR-Calabarzon)

LUCENA CITY — Capybaras, known as the world’s largest living rodents, can now be seen up close at a wildlife farm in Mendez, Cavite, according to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR).

“The world’s largest living rodent can be seen in Cavite! This excellent swimmer and highly sociable animal can be seen up close at Yoki’s Farm in Mendez, Cavite,” the DENR-Calabarzon said on Friday, Nov. 20.

The DENR did not disclose how many capybaras were brought to the farm.

Article continues after this 

According to the agency, capybaras, which are native to South America, can weigh up to 65 kilograms. Their calm and sociable nature makes them popular among visitors, with even their natural predators sometimes seen resting near them.

READ: Patrons at Florida café play with capybaras

Yoki’s Farm began operating in the late 1990s as a holder of a Certificate of Wildlife Registration. It has since become a permitted wildlife farm, housing various animals on its four-hectare property along Tabluan Road in Barangay Palocpoc 1.

The DENR quoted Rommel Velasco, the farm’s operations manager, as saying that the facility aims to help shape future generations by promoting environmental awareness and conservation initiatives.

“Wildlife conservation begins with awareness, respect and responsible action. Small ways such as learning about nature and supporting responsible conservation efforts can help protect our environment,” Velasco said.

Article continues after this 

The farm offers tours and opportunities for visitors to encounter animals under its care for a fee.

According to information shared by the British Broadcasting Corp., the capybara belongs to the Caviidae family and is a semi-aquatic mammal often compared to a giant guinea pig.

Article continues after this 

Capybaras typically inhabit areas near bodies of water, including wetlands, open grasslands and forests. Their webbed feet help them swim, while their calm, sociable and relaxed behavior has made them popular among wildlife enthusiasts. /mcm

World.title: Rights Groups Demand Action Against Myanmar Junta After Historic Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
Rights groups are urging governments to step up diplomatic pressure, impose fresh sanctions and isolate the military regime following Thursday’s landmark International Court of Justice (ICJ) judgment that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017.

It was the first time in its 80-year history that the ICJ found a state responsible for committing genocide.

Rights advocates say the historic ruling must now translate into concrete measures to hold the regime accountable, rather than remain a symbolic legal victory.

“This is a big blow for [regime leader] Min Aung Hlaing at a time when he is trying to persuade the world to normalize relations,” Tun Khin, president of the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK (BROUK), told The Irrawaddy.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to investigate, prosecute and punish those responsible, and pay reparations, as well as ensure the safe return of Rohingya refugees to Rakhine State.

The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, although the court has no independent enforcement mechanism.

If Myanmar fails to comply with the ruling’s orders, the UN Security Council can act to enforce them, according to Article 94.2 of the UN Charter.

Tun Khin said his organization had called on the UK to organize a meeting of the UN Security Council. Though regime allies Russia and China would likely veto any resolution, they would be forced to explain such a move. London has called for a meeting.

“We hope it will result in new sanctions,” Tun Khin said.

Tun Khin expressed concern that the return of the Rohingya is still impossible due to the policies of both the Myanmar military regime and the ethnic Arakan Army (AA), an anti-regime armed group that controls 14 of Rakhine State’s 17 townships.

Lucky Karim, executive director of the group Refugee Women for Peace and Justice, said that as an initial step following the ICJ ruling, Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) member countries should stop engaging with the Myanmar regime.

She noted that this year nine countries have hosted self-appointed president Min Aung Hlaing, who oversaw the 2017 atrocities as military chief. She urged all countries to stop welcoming him. Despite the bilateral engagements, Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from ASEAN’s top-level summits.

“I think the regional states should apply the same rule [as ASEAN] and take a pause for now. Stop hosting him and rolling out the red carpet and engaging him,” Lucky Karim said.

The ICJ decision was welcomed by UN Secretary-General António Guterres, the UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch (HRW), along with foreign ministers from the United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland and Turkey, as well as Myanmar’s civilian National Unity Government (NUG).

As immediate actions, London ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s Defense Attaché from the UK and issued an urgent call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the judgment.

More than 190 local rights groups welcomed the ICJ ruling.

The regime rejected the verdict. Khaing Khaing Soe, a spokesperson for the military-appointed government, said on Friday: “The truth is we were wrongly accused.”

Emphasizing the fact that the verdict was not unanimous, she said, “Not all the judges voted for it, so it’s not a fair judgment.”

The ICJ ruled by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Meanwhile, the AA said it would act in the best interests of the state following the landmark ruling.

“We need to wait for the regime’s report to the Court. For example, will the regime deny it, or will they say they can’t pay compensation?” Rakhine politician Pe Than told The Irrawaddy.

Backed by the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), the Gambia brought the case in 2019, alleging that Myanmar’s atrocities against the Rohingya violated the Genocide Convention. It took seven years to reach a final verdict in the case.

The Myanmar regime has continued to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity across the country since the 2021 coup.

Since seizing power, the regime has killed more than 8,600 civilians and detained over 32,000 people, according to the Assistance Association for Political Prisoners. The group said the regime continues to hold political prisoners, including Aung San Suu Kyi, while millions of young people have fled abroad amid forced conscription, security fears, inflation, widespread crime, job scarcity and escalating conflict.

The NUG reaffirmed its commitment to justice, citizenship, and human rights norms for the Rohingya in a statement Thursday.

It said communities across Myanmar continue to face airstrikes, killings, arbitrary detention, torture and forced displacement, while hospitals, schools, monasteries and churches have also come under attack.

“The pursuit of justice for the Rohingya must be accompanied by action to end the military junta’s continuing violence against civilians throughout Myanmar,” it said.

Tun Khin said the ICJ judgment is good news for everyone in Myanmar. “Now they [the regime] are officially responsible for genocide and facing renewed international pressure instead,” he said.

World.title: U.S. Sanctions Two More Myanmar Regime-Allied Scam Warlords
World.content:
The U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned two more top leaders of the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA) on Thursday, accusing them of operating and facilitating cyber-scam centers on the Myanmar-Thailand border.

Commander-in-chief General Saw Shwe Wah and Phaya Thonezu town commander Colonel Saw A One join four other senior leaders of the regime-allied militia on the U.S. sanctions list.

Saw Steel, Saw Sein Win, San Aung and Sai Kyaw Hla were added last November as part of Washington’s crackdown on the multibillion-dollar border scam industry targeting Americans.

Also sanctioned Thursday was Cambodian national Zhao Hui and two of his scam-linked firms.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, Treasury has aggressively targeted overseas scam compounds to protect Americans from fraud,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. “We will continue to use all available tools to disrupt and dismantle the networks that enable scam compounds to operate.”

Thursday’s order was the U.S. latest action targeting Myanmar individuals in a crackdown on online scam compounds in Southeast Asia that defrauded an estimated $7.2 billion from Americans in 2025 alone.

The sanctions freeze any U.S.-based assets held by targets and make it illegal for Americans to do business or financial transactions with them.

Saw Shwe Wah took over protection of scam operations in DKBA-held Sone See Myaing, Kyauk Khet, Waw Lay, and Phaya Thonezu in December 2025 after replacing the blacklisted Saw Steel as DKBA’s commander-in-chief.

At least seven scam major compounds were under DKBA protection in 2025. However, staged regime raids on KK Park, Shwe Kokko, and Myawaddy in October and November last year forced a mass relocation to the DKBA’s Sone See Myaing headquarters, while others reportedly dispersed inland to villages under the group’s control.

“Shwe Wah has full oversight. The online scams are operating under his protection since he holds the highest position of the group,” a source familiar with DKBA administration told The Irrawaddy.

“Smaller scam sites are now scattered across DKBA territory. Despite their size they still have concrete buildings.”

He confirmed that DKBA-protected scam operations are concentrated in its Sone See Myaing stronghold, though others have relocated to villages in the Mulayit mountain range, roughly 20 km inside the border.

Following last year’s Myawaddy crackdown — widely dismissed as a publicity stunt — scammers reportedly flocked south to the Thai-Myanmar border town of Phaya Thonezu (Three Pagodas Pass) under the command of Colonel Saw A One.

Washington added him to its sanctions list Thursday, claiming he oversaw an expansion of scam operations and buildings.

“Tens of thousands of fraudsters flooded in here during the crackdown over there [in Myawaddy], turning this place into a large scam hub,” a resident of Phaya Thonezu told The Irrawaddy. “Since then, the scam buildings have expanded.”

He added that restrictions on movement make it difficult to determine the exact number of scam compounds and workers, though he confirmed the presence of two major compounds in the town and many more hidden nearby in restricted forest

The U.S. escalated its border scam crackdown in 2025, sanctioning leaders of the regime-allied Karen National Army (formerly the Karen Border Guard Force) including Saw Chit Thu and his two sons.

Washington has since formed the Scam Center Strike Force with Thailand to seize evidence, intercept fleeing scam bosses, and cut off cross-border supplies to compounds.

Jeanine Pirro, who oversees the Strike Force, met with Thai officials in Bangkok this week to discuss strengthening bilateral intelligence sharing, joint operations, and cross-border crackdowns against the scam syndicates.

The Irrawaddy could not reach DKBA headquarters for comment.

World.title: ‘Ungrateful and Two-Faced’: Why a Chinese Analyst Slammed Myanmar’s Junta Chief
World.content:
Following Myanmar regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks that appeared to blame China for the initial success of Operation 1027, a Chinese commentator responded that the junta was attempting to dodge its own political failures by simply attributing its opponent’s combat effectiveness to external assistance.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on Operation 1027, the Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that resulted in the seizure of the Myanmar military’s Northeastern Regional Military Command in Lashio and eventually left the regime stripped of control over most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State. The offensive brought about one of the most humiliating defeats in the Myanmar military’s modern history.

The regime chief insisted the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), one of the alliance members, did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

“There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” Min Aung Hlaing said, his voice filled with rage.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country involved, few observers were left in doubt about the target of his remarks. Among Myanmar political watchers and the public alike, the comments were widely interpreted as a thinly veiled swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance during the northern Shan offensive.

On Friday, the Chinese commentator, who claims to “specialize in Myanmar and Southeast Asia”, made the comments on Chinese social media platform WeChat under the title “The Myanmar Military’s Misunderstanding of China: An Analysis of Min Aung Hlaing’s Unspoken Accusations”.

The commentator, whom The Irrawaddy has learned is knowledgeable about Myanmar affairs and familiar with Naypyitaw, argued that Min Aung Hlaing’s remarks went beyond an assessment of the military’s battlefield defeats.

“He was not explaining his assessment of the enemy; he was assigning blame. He attributed the EAOs’ victory in Operation 1027 to ‘covert support from China,’” the author says.

The commentator also said the Myanmar military has never been on the pro-China end of the country’s political spectrum. From General Aung San, the founder of the Myanmar military, to successive generations of leaders like Than Shwe, Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing, all have been full of misunderstandings and suspicions toward China, the author said.

Regarding the junta’s loss in Operation 1027, the author said the Myanmar military failed to look inward for the cause of the collapse of its combat capability after 2021. “The real collapse occurred internally: troops were replenished through forced conscription, military officers’ families enjoyed special privileges, running businesses within the military was rampant, and grassroots morale was shattered. The Myanmar military has failed to rectify these long-accumulated bad habits,” the author pointed out.

“Shoving all the blame onto ‘external assistance’ is the easiest explanation, but also the one that solves absolutely nothing,” the author added.

China mediated a ceasefire between the alliance and the military in January 2024. In April 2025, under Chinese pressure, the MNDAA withdrew from Lashio, allowing the Myanmar military to re-enter the city.

The author says these developments should have encouraged the Myanmar military to rely more on China’s mediation efforts to facilitate negotiations and de-escalation. Instead, the junta leadership interpreted them differently.

“Instead, not only were they ungrateful, but they stubbornly believed: ‘Since the EAOs listen to China and stop fighting when told to, they must also be taking orders from them to attack the Myanmar military; therefore, any military action by the EAOs must be masterminded by China behind the scenes.’”

“If China were truly covertly supporting the EAOs, Lashio would never have been returned. This is the hardest evidence to refute the ‘covert support’ theory, but unfortunately, it is never mentioned in the Myanmar military’s narrative,” the author argues.

The commentator also pointed out that whenever the Myanmar military wants China to pressure ethnic armed groups, it invokes the concept of pauk-phaw, or fraternal, ties. When it needs China to support its economy, open border ports, or buy agricultural products, it repeats the slogan “China-Myanmar Community With a Shared Future.” Yet, the moment domestic governance goes wrong, it immediately shifts the blame to China, the author says.

“This two-faced mentality of simultaneous dependence and suspicion is currently the deepest rift in China-Myanmar relations.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Rejects ‘Unfair’ Rohingya Genocide Ruling at ICJ
World.content:
NAYPYITAW—A historic ruling by the top UN court that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority was “not fair,” the regime’s presidential spokeswoman said Friday.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday laid out searing evidence of Myanmar’s atrocities against the mostly Muslim Rohingya during a 2017 crackdown in Rakhine State.

Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed “widespread sexual violence” against women and “extreme violence” against children, the court’s president said.

Asked about the ICJ decision at a press conference in the capital Naypyitaw, spokeswoman Khaing Khaing Soe called it unfair.

“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” she said, noting the 9-6 vote.

“So this was not a unanimous decision,” she added. “I would say it is not fair.”

Myanmar had always denied genocide, arguing that its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

But the ICJ ruling dismissed Myanmar’s argument that it was carrying out counter-insurgency operations.

“There is no evidence before the court that, in the conduct of the clearance operations, Myanmar distinguished between civilians and alleged (Rohingya) fighters,” the judgment said.

It was the first time in the ICJ’s 80-year history that its judges have determined that a state committed genocide.

Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya were forced to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh during the crackdown, the court said.

Rohingya villages were “systemically destroyed” and replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, it said, ruling that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.

No enforcement

The court ordered refugees to be given safe passage home and awarded compensation, with specific sums to be determined later.

While the decisions of the ICJ are binding and cannot be appealed, the court has no way of enforcing its verdicts, and it remains to be seen whether Myanmar’s rulers will adhere to the orders.

But the ruling may heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing, who commanded the military during the Rohingya crackdown before ousting the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in a 2021 coup.

This year, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president following deeply restricted elections and is waging a diplomatic campaign for legitimacy.

China, an enduring partner after the coup, raised concerns of judicial overreach after the ICJ ruling.

One of the ICJ’s judges is from China and voted in Myanmar’s favour on all but one count.

The U.S. reacted with caution, stressing the need to avoid “politicization” of the international court.

Despite determining in 2022 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, Washington has more recently pushed back on another case before the court, involving accusations by South Africa that U.S. ally Israel perpetrated genocide in Gaza.

World.title: Min Aung Hlaing Lashes Out at Beijing, Scammer Whac-a-Mole Continues in Shan, and More
World.content:
Min Aung Hlaing hints at Chinese hand in resistance’s Operation 1027

Putschist president Min Aung Hlaing is still groping for an explanation for Operation 1027, the humiliating Brotherhood Alliance offensive in 2023-24 that stripped his regime of most of its key trade routes with China in northern Shan State.

In a speech to the junta’s rubber-stamp parliament on Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing delivered one of his most pointed public comments yet on the offensive.

He insisted the ethnic Chinese Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) did not prevail through its own strength alone. “The MNDAA attacked with superior weapons, technology and manpower, and all their allies were involved,” he said.

Then came the interesting part: “There are some things we aren’t saying simply because it wouldn’t be appropriate. But there was some outside assistance involved,” he added.

Though he stopped short of identifying the country, few observers were left in doubt that it was a swipe at China, which has long been accused by regime loyalists of turning a blind eye to, or tacitly supporting, the Brotherhood Alliance.

The comments echoed Min Aung Hlaing’s complaints at the height of Operation 1027, when he publicly alleged that the MNDAA had used Chinese-made drones and advanced technology in attacks on regime positions.

They come after Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun delivered a body blow to Naypyitaw by urging “high-level autonomy” for ethnic minorities, a suggestion that flies in the face of the military regime’s centralization doctrine.

Regime chief fingers neighbors for sustaining ‘insurgents’

In the same outburst, Min Aung Hlaing also accused the two neighbors that have made the biggest effort to accommodate his regime—China and Thailand—of sustaining “insurgents” by encouraging trade through border crossings they control.

He started with Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and MNDAA, which now control much of Myanmar’s border with China. “In Kachin, the KIA runs border gates at the Chinese border. In northeastern Myanmar, the MNDAA runs Chinshwehaw gate,” he said.

“Taxation from illegal trade has sustained and financed insurgents,” he complained.

In Kachin, the regime has also lost control over the lucrative rare earth mines, which are now a major source of revenues for the KIA. The situation is not much different in northern Shan, where the regime has lost key border crossings with Yunnan as well as rare earth and other mineral resources.

On the surface, he was only accusing Thailand of directly facilitating trade through resistance-held territory at the Thaw Le Hta crossing in Hpapun, avoiding direct accusations against China except by inference and association.

Chinese Customs figures show a steady increase in cross-border trade through crossings controlled by the MNDAA and its allies. Trade through the Chinshwehaw border crossing alone reached 5.01 billion yuan (about US$700 million) so far this year. The central regime is reduced to heavy-handed efforts to “tax” this trade once goods reach military-controlled areas.

China steps up media ‘outreach’ in Myanmar to shape narrative

China stepped up efforts to shape Myanmar’s information space this week, gathering regime-aligned media figures, officials and commentators in Yangon to promote President Xi Jinping’s four flagship global initiatives.

Speaking at a symposium at the Wyndham Grand Yangon Hotel on Tuesday with over 160 participants, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia highlighted growing bilateral cooperation in security, governance and people-to-people exchanges. Myanmar is the first country to sign up to all four of Xi’s initiatives, which also include AI.

Ma listed the usual talking points, from law-enforcement cooperation to combat cross-border crimes, including online scam operations, to cultural and media exchanges aimed at strengthening “mutual understanding.” Echoing Chinese President Xi Jinping and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, she called for key projects of the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) to be hurried along.

The event brought together stalwart regime propagandists like Lower House MP Aye Chan, Myanmar Press Council Chairman Dr. Tin Tun Oo, Myanmar Narrative Think Tank chairman Ko Ko, plus figures from regime and regime-aligned media.

Days earlier, Myanmar Foreign Ministry-backed think tank MISIS and state-owned China Media Group gathered academics, media representatives and officials in Yangon to discuss future areas of China-Myanmar cooperation aligned with Beijing’s 15th Five-Year Plan.

The forums follow a similar gathering hosted by Ma in May, when she called on regime-linked media and opinion leaders to tell “beautiful stories” about China.

Chinese-run scam industry lives on in southern Shan

Myanmar’s regime says it arrested 23 Chinese nationals and seized three assault rifles in a raid on an alleged online scam and gambling operation in Laihka Township in southern Shan State on Wednesday.

They were detained at a makeshift compound deep in the forest comprising a workshop, living quarters and a kitchen. A tally compiled from regime media reports suggests some 90 Chinese scammers have been arrested in raids since February in Laihka, which has emerged as a new scam hotspot since 2025.

They take advantage of the lawless environment amid competing territorial claims of local militias as well as the Shan State Progressive Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), and the Restoration Council of Shan State/Shan State Army (RCSS/SSA).

Even as a docuseries on Myanmar’s scam industry broadcast on Chinese state media last month sold the 2024 crackdown on scam hubs in northern Shan State’s Laukkai as an unmitigated success, the criminal gangs simply scattered across eastern and southern Shan instead. According to the independent Institute for Strategy and Policy–Myanmar, operations have since been identified in at least 17 Shan townships including Tangyan, Tachileik and Muse.

Meanwhile, ASEAN and the U.S., meeting in Manila this week, adopted what was billed as a “partnership work plan” to tackle online scams and thereby increase international pressure on Myanmar’s regime. Regime leader Min Aung Hlaing was not invited to the summit.

Complied by Thurein Lynn

World.title: US Warns Against ‘Politicization’ of ICJ, Studying Myanmar Ruling
World.content:
WASHINGTON—The U.S. State Department reacted with caution to the International Court of Justice’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, saying Washington was examining the decision while stressing the need to avoid “politicization” of the body.

Washington’s wary response comes as the United States determined in 2022 that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people.

But it has more recently pushed back on another case before the top UN court, involving accusations by South Africa that US ally Israel perpetrated genocide in Gaza.

“The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ,” said a State Department spokesperson on Thursday.

“We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications,” the official added, referring to the Myanmar ruling.

The US statement comes as the top UN court ordered refugees to be given safe passage home and awarded compensation.

The decision marked the first time in its 80-year history that ICJ judges determined a state committed genocide. It is likely to be viewed as justice for Rohingya victims of Myanmar’s deadly 2017 crackdown on the mostly Muslim minority.

The US official said Thursday: “We express our support for the people of Burma and share the grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups.”

The official also called for more burden-sharing in the humanitarian response for Rohingya refugees.

For more than one million Rohingya living in the world’s largest refugee camp over the border in Bangladesh, the landmark ruling offered hope for accountability.

World.title: Five Key Points From Historic ICJ Rohingya Genocide Ruling
World.content:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands—The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority—the first time the UN top court has determined a state responsible for the world’s worst crime.

Here are the key points from the 191-page ruling, which took nearly three hours to read out in court and is the second-longest in the ICJ’s 80-year history.

Genocide

This was what the hundreds of thousands of Rohingya victims were waiting for: did the atrocities they suffered clear the high bar under international law to be labelled a genocide?

In the end, the ICJ—known for dressing up its rulings in impenetrable legalese—was refreshingly clear.

Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State,” said the ruling, which was passed by nine votes to six.

By the same margin, the court found Myanmar had failed in its obligations under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention to prevent the crime.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to take “immediate and effective steps” to prosecute and punish anyone suspected of genocidal acts.

Myanmar must stop any ongoing acts of genocide and prevent similar violations of the Convention in future.

To prove genocide, judges have to be satisfied not only that genocidal acts have occurred but also there was intention to destroy a given community—a notoriously tricky legal hurdle.

However, the judges ruled that the “only reasonable inference” was that Myanmar intended to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people.

Safe return

Having concluded that genocide occurred, the court also issued rulings on the consequences for Myanmar—so-called “remedies” in the legal jargon.

It ordered several actions from Myanmar.

The authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.

They must also “return or replace in kind all individual and collective property” that was lost in the violent crackdown.

The Rohingya must also be offered “physical and psychological rehabilitation” for the harms they suffered, the judges ruled.

Reparations

The Rohingya are entitled to “adequate compensation” for the harms caused by the genocide.

The ICJ did not set an amount, saying that would be determined at a later phase.

It gave Myanmar two years to file a report setting out the “amount and modalities” of compensation.

After receiving the report, the ICJ will decide whether Myanmar’s proposal is sufficient.

Investigations

The ICJ is a court that settles disputes between countries, unlike its neighbor the International Criminal Court, which weighs individual responsibility.

However, the ICJ ruling tasks Myanmar with conducting a “prompt” investigation into anyone suspected of committing genocidal acts.

Judges ruled that previous efforts in Myanmar to probe atrocities were insufficient.

“Myanmar has not genuinely investigated or, if warranted, prosecuted its soldiers and commanders and punished them,” the ICJ said.

Scale of killings

The court said that an estimate of at least 10,000 deaths in the crackdown, established by an independent UN fact-finding mission, was “supported by the record.”

“The evidence before the court demonstrates the pervasive and lethal nature of the violence… and establishes that thousands of Rohingya civilians were killed by the Myanmar security forces,” said the ICJ.

The court said there were approximately 815,000 Rohingya in Rakhine State at the time of the crackdown, meaning those killed constituted 1.2 percent of the population.

The majority of the survivors fled to neighboring Bangladesh.

The ICJ also said there were at least 1,834 acts of rape during the 2017 “clearance operations.”

World.title: ICJ Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
World.content:
The United Nations’ top court, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in 2017, in a historic decision.

In the case brought by the Gambia, the ICJ delivered the first ruling in its 80-year history finding a state responsible for committing genocide.

“The Republic of the Union of Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, in violation of its obligations under the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said, delivering the court’s verdict.

Iwasawa said around 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the 2017 “clearance operations,” which also involved widespread sexual violence and violence against children, as the Rohingya fled en masse to Bangladesh.

“Records also contain evidence of intentional targeting of the Rohingya population,” Iwasawa said.

The court found that Myanmar deliberately targeted the approximately 815,000 Rohingya who lived in northern Rakhine before the operation.

Rohingya villages were systematically destroyed and their populations replaced with non-Rohingya inhabitants, the ICJ said, ruling that the only reasonable inference was that Myanmar intended to destroy the population—a key test for genocide.
