World.title: CA says Cummins backing not a sign it is taking sides in sandpaper spat
World.content:
Todd Greenberg insists Cricket Australia has not taken Pat Cummins's side in the ball-tampering saga, adamant that keeping the quick as Test captain should not deter others from contributing to the upcoming truth forum.

Cummins is expected to train again at the SCG early this week, as he and the fellow pacemen press on with their preparations for the first Test against New Zealand starting on December 9.

The 33-year-old confirmed on Saturday he would contribute to CA's independent forum, and make his own submissions over the events of the 2018 South Africa tour.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

It is expected the quick will deny any prior knowledge of the use of sandpaper on the ball on that tour until Cameron Bancroft was caught in Cape Town, a position the bowlers have maintained since that day.

Officials will lay out the parameters for the forum in the coming days, but have already made clear there will be no further sanctions, regardless of the findings.

There had initially been a fear that only those with an axe to grind may contribute, following claims by Usman Khawaja and Bancroft that the entire team knew of the ball-tampering plot.

David Warner and Chadd Sayers have also backed the claims raised in Khawaja's book, which kicked off the renewed furore a month ago.

But Cricket Australia CEO Greenberg has now had to deny that the CA board publicly standing by Cummins to remain captain on Saturday had swung it back in the other direction, and dissuaded those with opposing views.

Cricket Australia boss Todd Greenberg says the organisation is not picking sides amid the reignited Sandpapergate furore. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke )

"I don't see it that way, because I support their version of events and their ability to share what they think happened at that period of time," Greenberg told the BBC.

"That's their version. Equally, that's Pat's version as well.

"I am not putting someone's version of events over somebody else's. That's the one thing we're not doing.

"Pat has been the captain for five years, we haven't made any changes.

"If we were to, that would believe someone's events over the others."

Then-Australian coach Darren Lehmann has repeatedly denied prior knowledge of the plot to use sandpaper in Cape Town. (Jason McCawley - CA/Cricket Australia via Getty Images)

Beyond Cummins, then-coach Darren Lehmann has also indicated he will contribute, after denying Bancroft's assertions that he was aware of the plot on Saturday night.

Greenberg also maintained that the board's unanimous support of Cummins did not mean they thought Khawaja or Bancroft were lying.

Asked what would happen if the majority of the 2018 touring party — including staff and players — claimed everyone knew, Greenberg suggested nothing would change.

"Then so be it," Greenberg said.

"We're going in with an open mind and without providing sanctions."

Steve Smith received a heroes welcome at the SCG when he lined up for New South Wales in the Sheffield Shield on Sunday. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Former CA board member Michael Kasprowicz reiterated on Monday that the 2018 bans handed down to Steve Smith, Warner and Bancroft were not solely related to tampering.

Kasprowicz was a director in 2018 when CA's investigation found the trio were the only three to know of the plot.

"I am not sure it is actually about sandpaper, because the umpires didn't even change the ball," Kasprowicz told AAP.

"I know from a board point of view at the time, it wasn't about damaging the ball. It was about damaging the brand.

"That's why steps had to be made in those circumstances."

Usman Khawaja (left) will link up with Darren Lehmann (right) during an exhibition T20 clash in Cairns on Sunday night. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Kasprowicz is due to link up with both Khawaja and Lehmann in the celebrity cricket Gold Clash in Cairns on Sunday night.

Asked if he believed the sanctions may have been different had Khawaja or Bancroft given their most recent accounts then, Kasprowicz was uncertain.

"I don't know, eight years ago is eight years ago," the 38-Test seamer said.

"Your receipts and tax records only last for seven and you have to chuck them.

"That's why I am thinking what is going on right now is even more extraordinary."

Cricket on Sunday attempted to move on from the Sandpapergate saga, with Steve Smith returning from his neck injury to the Sheffield Shield alongside Nathan Lyon.

Smith spent most of the day fielding at slip for NSW, taking a catch to remove Test hopeful Jack Clayton on 10 in the middle session at the SCG.

He also bowled two overs of leg spin in the final session, to strong applause from a crowd of just under 2,000 at the SCG.

AAP

World.title: Live: Join us as Australia's Recipe of the Year is revealed
World.content:
Jimmy: The camaraderie between us all was the cherry on top for me. In and outside the barn, everyone made sure to check up on and take care of one another, we all had to become best friends in such a short amount of time, and I'm glad we did. Almost every night after filming, there would be a debrief in someone's room (maybe over a bottle of wine 😏) with plenty of laughs. No matter the time, we would all find an excuse to hang out with each other... even if Ray was falling asleep as soon as he sat down.

Cooking and trialling for each other on and off screen was another highlight, as we saw each other's recipes develop from ideas to fully fledged meals, especially in the blue ribbon challenges. There would be endless discussions about the food afterwards and a couple of heads shaking (especially mine 😂). Everyone is such a great cook and would give pointers or advice if something needed tweaking or adjusting, and everyone took it on board because we all wanted to see the best from each other's cooking. For me, it isn't about winning; it's about seeing each other succeed.

World.title: Horne-Francis planning to recruit Nasiah during AFL Origin camp
World.content:
Jason Horne-Francis is open to throwing his weight around in South Australia's AFL Origin camp to recruit St Kilda superstar and friend Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera.

South Australia and Western Australia today named their first five representatives for next year's Origin match, to be played at Perth Stadium on February 27.

Wanganeen-Milera and Port Adelaide's Horne-Francis were picked by SA coach Craig McRae, along with Saints co-captain Callum Wilkie, Adelaide skipper Jordan Dawson and Collingwood boom recruit Lachie Neale.

Players committed to 2027 AFL Origin SOUTH AUSTRALIA: Jason Horne-Francis, Callum Wilkie, Lachie Neale, Jordan Dawson, Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera WESTERN AUSTRALIA: Patrick Cripps, Charlie Cameron, Kysaiah Pickett, Luke Jackson, Tom Barrass

Wanganeen-Milera rejected massive interest from his native South Australia in 2025 to re-sign on a two-season, $4 million deal with the Saints.

Locking away the silky 23-year-old playmaker on an extension is top of St Kilda's agenda.

This year's Origin revival match between WA and Victoria allowed Western Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli to build a connection with Zak Butters, who crossed from Port Adelaide in the off-season.

While already mates with Wanganeen-Milera, Horne-Francis is mindful of the recruitment opportunity Origin camp presents.

"That worked, didn't it," he told reporters, referring to the Butters-Bontempelli connection developed through Victoria's Origin team.

Marcus Bontempelli (background) successfully recruited Victorian teammate Zak Butters (foreground) to the Western Bulldogs. (Daniel Carson/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

"So maybe I've got to try to do the same thing. Not that we need any more bonding time — we see each other bloody all the time anyway.

"We ran out together in the [Indigenous] All-Stars as well, so it will be good to run out with him again and see what he's got for us."

The 23-year-old admitted he might have to battle with Crows rivals to wrap an arm around Wanganeen-Milera, who finished fourth in St Kilda's best-and-fairest this season.

"There might be a bit of push and shove there," the Port ball-winner said.

St KIlda star Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera is once again in high demand as he comes out of contract. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Horne-Francis and other Adelaide-based SA representatives may have to go through Wilkie to get some alone time with Wanganeen-Milera.

"I won't let him talk to Dawson or anyone from Port," Wilkie joked.

"He'll stay right under my wing.

"Nas is amazing at putting that [contract speculation] to bed and focusing on us and what he brings to the club on field and off field."

Wilkie said he and Wanganeen-Milera had been speaking about the possibility of donning the SA jumper all year.

Collingwood coach Craig McRae will lead Wanganeen-Milera and South Australia in the Origin clash. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"That's what's so special about it," he said.

"You think when you're getting drafted you're never going to be able to pull the colours on again."

WA coach Dean Cox's first selections are Hawthorn defender Tom Barrass, Brisbane forward Charlie Cameron, Carlton skipper Patrick Cripps, Fremantle ruck Luke Jackson and Melbourne livewire Kysaiah Pickett.

Cripps, who captained WA against Victoria this year, is also due to come off contract at the end of next season.

Carlton captain Patrick Cripps has no plans to finish his AFL career in WA. (Getty images/AFL Photos: Matt King)

But the dual Brownlow Medal winner hosed down the possibility of finishing his illustrious career in his home state after the Blues made the finals under now-permanent coach Josh Fraser, despite starting last season 1-8.

"I've been here that long, you sort of become ingrained in the club," Cripps said.

"I sort of feel like a Carlton supporter these days … this is my 14th season.

"I've always loved playing footy at Carlton and been driven to try and build the club from the ground up, and I'm really excited about where we are right now."

AAP

World.title: India breaks New Zealand Test record with monster innings in Wellington
World.content:
India has broken the record for the highest Test score in a match played in New Zealand as it put itself in a commanding position to win the first Test in Wellington.

New Zealand reached 2-119 at the close of play on day four as it fought to save the first Test after India declared on a mammoth 9-720 with an imposing first-innings lead of 352.

India's assault was led by Rishabh Pant (128), whose six sixes took his career tally to 108 in just 53 Tests, now second behind all-time best Ben Stokes (138). Pant surpassed former NZ captain Brendon McCullum (107) during the innings.

New Zealand's hopes of a result rest on batting for much of the remainder of the match and forcing a draw, despite losing Tom Latham for a duck and first-innings centurion Henry Nicholls for 31.

Opener Devon Conway, who scored his 22nd Test half-century on his way to an unbeaten 59, and Rachin Ravindra (27 not out) will resume on day five with the Black Caps still 233 runs from forcing India to bat again.

India's pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah (1-33) again made an early breakthrough, sending Latham back on the second ball of the innings, the New Zealand skipper edging behind to take a pair.

Nicholls, whose 175 was the backbone of New Zealand's first-innings 368, got an edge and a bit of thigh pad on a Prasidh Krishna delivery, and Dhruv Jurel showed stunning reflexes to take the catch at short leg.

Jurel had earlier become the sixth batter to score a half-century in India's innings before being caught in the deep for 78, triggering the declaration an hour before tea.

India had resumed on 4-486 on another sunny morning at the Basin Reserve with the clear intent of pushing their 118-run lead out to the sort of tally that would take the possibility of a New Zealand victory out of the equation.

There are few better batters for such a task than Pant, and the swashbuckling wicketkeeper showed the full range of his shots as he approached his ninth Test hundred.

Pant was finally caught on the boundary for 128 off the bowling of Ravindra to bring up lunch, but the punishment for New Zealand continued into the second session.

Jacob Duffy finished with 1-201 off 33 overs. (Getty Images: Hagen Hopkins)

India's final score was well clear of its previous best innings tally in New Zealand of 520 all out in Hamilton in 2009 — a match they won by 10 wickets.

All-rounder Glenn Phillips (3-154) picked a couple of wickets as the Indian batters went for their shots ahead of the declaration to make his figures a bit more respectable.

Seamer Jacob Duffy, though, finished with unenviable figures of 1-201 from his 33 overs, only 28 runs shy of New Zealand's most expensive ever bowling display, which spinner Stephen Boock tallied against Pakistan in 1989.

Reuters

World.title: 'One-in-2,000-year weather' to be investigated post-blackout
World.content:
The SA government says the suggestion that a "one-in-2,000-year weather event" was responsible for the Eyre Peninsula blackout will be critically examined amid ongoing fallout from the incident.

Electricity supply to the peninsula and the state's West Coast was cut on Thursday afternoon when two transmission towers collapsed and a third was severely damaged during intense storms, leaving more than 20,000 properties without power.

Power was gradually restored to most of those properties over the following 24 hours, but the blackout has again raised the question of energy security, 10 years on from the 2016 statewide blackout.

ElectraNet — which is responsible for the state's high-energy transmission lines — on Sunday confirmed it was conducting a "complete and thorough review" into the recent outage.

SA's statewide blackout remembered after 10 years Energy policy has changed greatly since South Australia was left in darkness exactly 10 years ago today — but if there is a universal constant of the energy debate, it is that there is always friction over electricity.

On Friday, the company suggested the towers were likely brought down by a "one-in-2,000-year weather event" — a contention SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said would be considered during investigations into the incident.

"There are one of two possibilities here," Mr Malinauskas said.

"Either this was a genuine 'one-in-2,000-year weather event' here that understandably nothing can withstand — or, two, something went wrong in terms of the specifications of that infrastructure.

"That's what the investigation will examine, and that's what we're very keen to look at before we rush to make a judgement."

ElectraNet says two towers were downed and a third sustained major damage. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

The high-voltage transmission line along which the towers collapsed was completed only a few years ago, at a cost of $300 million.

ElectraNet executive Alex Trento told 891 ABC Adelaide on Friday the transmission towers were "built to a one-in-2,000-year weather event", and to withstand wind speeds of up to 172km/h.

"What we think has occurred is that the weather in this localised region has been even stronger than the winds that it was designed for," Mr Trento said.

He said ElectraNet was "always in contact with the bureau" but said there was no advance warning of an event on the scale of what occurred on Thursday.

But he added that what had occurred was "a very unique, very rare occurrence in a very localised area".

"I don't think we could have done anything better from that perspective."

'No evidence of tornadoes'

The Bureau of Meteorology said while wind speeds of around 100km/h were recorded at Roxby Downs on Thursday, gusts of around 170km/h were "unlikely".

"When we're talking wind gusts of more than 170km/h — those are the wind gusts you typically only see in tropical cyclones or associated with tornadoes," senior meteorologist Jonathan How said last week.

"There was no evidence of tornadoes that we could see [on Thursday] across the Eyre Peninsula.

" So certainly, 170km/h is something we couldn't really confirm. It's probably unlikely at this stage because the state record for South Australia is 167km/h. That was set in Woomera back in 1979. "

The images of collapsed and damaged towers at Wharminda on Eyre Peninsula are reminiscent of the scenes that accompanied the 2016 statewide blackout, when towers were felled in the state's mid north.

At a media conference on Friday afternoon, Mr Trento said that following the 2016 event, transmission line design standards were improved.

A fallen transmission tower near Melrose in South Australia in 2016. (ABC News: Dean Faulkner)

Asked whether there was a structural fault in the new towers, Mr Trento conceded that was a possibility, but expressed confidence that the towers had been constructed in accordance with the appropriate standards.

"We are investigating … but at this point in time, seeing the localisation of the event, we do think that the towers have been designed and constructed effectively," he said.

"We think the wind that has entered those towers has been above the specification that we've constructed it to.

"We could have been looking at a 250km/h wind session. We just don't know."

World.title: Major grassfire now under control in Victoria's north-west
World.content:
A major grassfire in Victoria's north-western region near Nandaly is now under control.

Firefighters battled the fast-moving grassfire, which started after 3pm about 55km south-east of Ouyen and burnt through around 1,300 hectares.

The CFA said more than 30 fire trucks and two aircraft helped control the blaze, which started soon after firefighters were also called to a header fire in a paddock.

An advice-level alert remains in place for Bimbourie, Daytrap Corner, Lake Tyrrell, Nandaly, Nyarrin, Pier Milan.

The CFA said smoke would still be visible from nearby communities and roads.

A fire has burnt through more than 1,000 hectares in Victoria's north-west near Nandaly. (Supplied: Terry Kiley)

Police closed off part of the Calder Highway, the main arterial route to the north-west of Victoria, in the affected area.

Manager of the Nandaly Community Hotel Tina Phillips said travellers along the highway were taking refuge at the pub.

"There are a lot of fire trucks going past and they've got planes going overhead as well," she said.

" The wind is very bad … so they're worried about the farmers. "

She said everyone was working together to help fight the fire.

"Everyone bands together and tries to help each other as much as we can," she said.

"One, it's dry. Two, everyone is harvesting and that's their life earnings isn't it? So, whatever they lose, really everyone loses."

World.title: Spirit of Tasmania operator told not to use autopilot for entire voyage
World.content:
Australia's maritime regulator has ordered the new Spirit of Tasmania ferries to stop using autopilot entirely, as a probe into steering issues on one of the vessels continues.

TT-Line previously suspended use of autopilot on the ferries during transits of Victoria's Port Phillip Bay, after the primary steering system on Spirit IV failed during a switch to manual mode.

This restriction has since been expanded to cover the whole Bass Strait voyage following a notice issued by the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA), which came into effect on Saturday.

"AMSA stipulated that both vessels are required to stay in hand steering [for the] full voyage," a TT-Line spokesperson said.

"[It is] important to note that there is another primary steering system available on both vessels, and additional back up systems that the crew are fully trained in."

Spirit IV docks late again after 'technical issue' It's the second time this month that the new Spirit of Tasmania ferry has dropped passengers off hours behind schedule. Tracking shows the new vessel spent hours performing loops in Port Philip Bay before being escorted by a tugboat into Geelong.

The directive was the result of an "intermittent fault" on the steering system on Spirit IV, but there was no similar issue on Spirit V, according to the spokesperson.

They said it was expected the directive would be lifted by AMSA as soon as the fault was rectified, and that it would not affect travel times for passengers.

State-owned TT-Line has reached out to Kongsberg Maritime, the Norwegian company that supplied the steering systems for the new vessels.

Technicians will be on site tomorrow to attempt to address the steering issue and the party responsible for funding repairs was "to be determined", the spokesperson said.

Spirit IV being escorted to Geelong by a tugboat earlier this month. (Facebook: Ferries of Tasmania)

Removing the use of automatic steering on the vessels increases the workload for staff, and TT-Line said an extra two crew members would be required to assist each vessel.

Since entering operations late last month, Spirit IV has docked hours late in Geelong because of technical issues on multiple occasions, including on November 5 and November 21.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau is investigating the steering issue on Spirit IV, as well as a separate issue on Spirit V which occurred during a trial voyage in October.

AMSA has been contacted for comment.

The new Spirit vessels came into service last month. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

'Teething problems' anticipated

The TT-Line spokesperson described the steering problems as "teething issues" and said they were "regrettable".

"We have said from day one that there will be issues uncovered and dealt with as they are identified," they said.

"The intermittent fault is an example of this, which could only be identified when the vessels entered service."

Martin Byrne from the Australian Institute of Marine and Power Engineers said he understood the issue was related to the electronic control system and the autopilot function.

"Ships not only move through the water but they have vibrations going through the ship at all times — the marine environment is not a kind one for electronic equipment," Mr Byrne said.

Martin Byrne says suspending the use of autopilot will increase the workload for deck officers. (Supplied)

He said it was "understandable" that AMSA would be taking a precautionary approach, given the vessels are passenger ships.

"I don't think there's any danger ... in reverting to a more manual style of operation, but it's going to place an additional workload on the deck officers," Mr Byrne said.

Tasmanian government minister Bridget Archer said it "was not unreasonable" for the brand new ships to be experiencing some early problems.

"We anticipated there may be some initial teething problems, as we have seen, because of the nature of the scale of these vessels that we're bringing into service," Ms Archer said.

State Labor MP Sarah Lovell said while it was understandable for major infrastructure projects to have teething issues, it was important for the public to be kept in the loop.

"What's important is that the government make sure that these instances are properly investigated and that they're open and transparent … about the causes and what's being done to fix it," Ms Lovell said.

World.title: COP31 struggles to reach deal with parties at odds over fossil fuels
World.content:
Global climate talks are continuing for a second day past deadline as a disagreement over explicit mentions of fossil fuels continues to divide countries and threatens to derail a final deal.

Nations have struggled to reconcile differences at the annual negotiations, against a backdrop of soaring energy prices, geopolitical tensions stemming from the war in Iran, and increasingly dangerous impacts of extreme weather.

Türkiye is hosting this year's conference, but Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen is the lead negotiator.

Chris Bowen is at the helm of climate negotiations in Antalya. (Reuters: Umit Bektas)

The organisers released a final deal early on Sunday morning, Antalya time, which keeps a call to electrify the global economy but makes no mention of fossil fuels despite a fierce backlash when they were stripped from an earlier proposal.

The burning of coal, oil and gas is the key driver of global warming, and in the lead-up to these talks, the UN announced the world would likely pass the most ambitious 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial temperatures.

"We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon," COP31 president Murat Kurum said.

"Outside of this hall there are people who are living with the effects of climate change," Kurum told negotiators early on Sunday. "The children, the parents are waiting for this."

Advisers surround Murat Kurum as nations struggle to reconcile differences. (Reuters: Murad Sezer)

Instead, the revised proposal by COP31 alludes to a 2023 agreement to shift from fossil fuels but stops short of naming them explicitly.

Head of political strategy at 350.org Andreas Sieber said last year's COP30 president Brazil had released a roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels, but this year's presidencies "chose to ignore it".

"The final draft confirms what has become increasingly clear throughout COP31; an indefensible failure of leadership by the Turkish and Australian presidencies," he said.

"They found room for a 2035 carbon capture target, yet struck the transition away from fossil fuels from the text and launched no initiative to take it forward.

"Brazil showed that such leadership was possible."

The latest draft retains a proposal to boost the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 alongside efforts to expand the use of "clean energy".

Facing pressure over fossil fuels, Türkiye and Australia had pitched "electrification" as a way to cut heat-trapping emissions and bolster energy security.

The push to replace technologies that burn fossil fuels directly, such as diesel cars and gas heating, with electric alternatives will cut emissions due to efficiency, but critics say they should be powered by renewable energy to reduce emissions further.

The globe is powering up The Iran war is turbocharging global electrification. But experts say the global grid needs to roughly double in size, as infrastructure bottlenecks prevent a clean energy revolution.

The text also calls for "accelerating" carbon capture and storage, a contentious technology championed by the fossil fuel industry. Its inclusion in a previous draft faced staunch opposition from countries that point to its high cost and meagre record in cutting emissions.

Director of the International Climate Politics Hub, Cat Abreu, said a focus on carbon capture and storage "came out of nowhere".

"It has been parachuted into COP31 by fossil fuel interests and must not be allowed to make it into a final global agreement," she said.

Because they require consensus from nearly 200 delegations, COP talks regularly run past planned deadlines, but only one so far has ended without an agreement.

Delegations have until 0300 GMT to raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled at 0600 GMT (5pm AEDT) to begin approving it.

AFP/AP

World.title: Four charts reveal how the PM built the biggest, best-paid office in 13 years while slashing crossbench support
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Four charts reveal how the PM built the biggest, best-paid office in 13 years while slashing crossbench support Nick Newling November 22, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has employed more advisers at higher salaries than Scott Morrison, Malcolm Turnbull and Tony Abbott, according to independent analysis of more than a decade’s worth of data, with the taxpayer-funded bill for his staff potentially exceeding $12 million per year. Analysis from the Centre for Public Integrity of staffing under the past four prime ministers shows Albanese has hired 70 per cent more advisers on top salaries than Abbott, and increased the size of his office by as much as 23 per cent, all while slashing the number of advisers given to the growing crossbench. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has the sole power to decide how many staff his political opponents can hire. Alex Ellinghausen The prime minister is facing growing criticism that he has politicised his power to decide how many staff his opponents can hire as experts and MPs from across the political spectrum demand the power be handed to an independent body. Centre for Public Integrity board member Geoffrey Watson SC said the power to make staffing determinations “must be out of the hands of the prime minister and moved to an independent body such as the remuneration tribunal”.





Additional staff – sometimes known as advisers or personal staff – can be employed only with the prime minister’s consent. They earn salaries as high as $317,152, attracting skilled candidates with expertise in policy, strategy and media. The prime minister can also authorise additional salary increases to attract top talent. These four charts show how Albanese and his predecessors have used this power. Record high staffing levels in the prime minister’s office The prime minister’s office employs more advisers than any other political office in federal parliament. Under Albanese, prime ministerial staffing hit a 13-year high when he employed 65 advisers in the months before the last election. Following the election, the number of Albanese’s staff shrank to 59, still above the average under the 2013-2022 Coalition government. Turnbull was the Liberal leader who employed the most advisers, peaking at 54, while Morrison at one point employed 51.8 full-time equivalent roles.



As soon as Albanese assumed power following the 2022 election, the number of full-time equivalent advisers jumped from 50.8 working for Morrison in his final days to 56. While individual salary packages are not publicly available, the maximum possible bill to the taxpayers for Albanese’s 59 staff totals $12,155,410 before entitlements. Most of them are very well paid Advisers are paid at a range of salary bands set out in their relative enterprise agreement. Every prime minister since Abbott has increased the proportion of advisers paid at the highest rates. Under Abbott, the proportion of staff earning top-band salaries (equivalent of between $156,510 and $317,152 in 2026) peaked at 45 per cent. Under Albanese, it has risen as high as 77 per cent.



Turnbull, Morrison and Albanese all increased the proportion of highly paid advisers in their offices after winning their first elections. However, only Albanese has maintained a steady upward growth. Significant cuts to staffing for crossbench MPs The number of independent and minor party MPs in federal parliament has grown from 23 politicians after the 2013 election to 34 now. This cohort includes One Nation, the teal independents and the Greens. As the crossbench grew over the course of the former Coalition government, so did their individual staffing allocations. However, after the 2022 election, when the crossbench grew to a record 34 MPs, Albanese immediately cut the number of advisers they could hire from four to one, sparking an uproar as the independent MPs argued they needed expert advisers to help them get across the national agenda’s many demands.



The prime minister has since granted more staff to some independents, but the ratio of advisers to crossbench MPs has not returned to the levels they enjoyed under Turnbull and Morrison. There are several unexplained staffing disparities among the crossbench. Senator Fatima Payman, who defected from Labor last term, is the only independent with no additional staff. Bradfield MP Nicolette Boele is the only teal independent with just one additional staffer, while her colleagues have two each. The Greens have more staff per MP than One Nation. If One Nation had the same proportional staffing as the Greens, their allocation of four advisers would more than double to nine. The growing divide



Currently, half of the advisers working for Labor and the Coalition are paid at the top salaries. By comparison, just one in nine crossbench advisers gets top-tier wages. Between February and March of 2025 – just weeks before the election – Labor ministers hired an additional 17 advisers, five of whom were in Albanese’s office. A government spokesperson said that when advisers were assigned, this is “done so with careful consideration”. “It’s been a longstanding practice that personal staffing allocations are made by the prime minister of the day – no matter what party he or she is from,” the spokesperson said. Abbott, Turnbull and Morrison were approached for comment. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Paine the peacemaker: Ex-skipper looms as key figure in Sandpapergate talks
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Paine the peacemaker: Ex-skipper looms as key figure in Sandpapergate talks Daniel Brettig November 22, 2026 — 7:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Former Test captain Tim Paine has emerged as a key figure in any possible peace talks between warring members of the 2018 South African tour party who became embroiled in the Sandpapergate scandal. As Cricket Australia works to finalise terms of reference for its truth forum, in which players and staff from the scandal eight years ago will be asked to share their honest recollections, a parallel line of private conversations are taking place. Usman Khawaja speaks with Tim Paine in South Africa in 2018. Getty Images While the positions of Usman Khawaja, David Warner, Chadd Sayers and Cameron Bancroft have been made publicly clear about collective knowledge, and therefore a need for collective responsibility, current captain Pat Cummins and fellow bowlers Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc have also made their differing views plain. Nathan Lyon has not spoken publicly, meanwhile, but was a signatory to the 2021 statement denying any knowledge of sandpaper being taken onto the field.



According to a source with knowledge of discussions, Paine, thrust into the captaincy by Steve Smith’s ban, remains a respected figure on all sides of the debate, in particular for how his leadership was shown in picking up the pieces from Newlands and the remainder of the tour in 2018. Importantly, Paine was the first player to publicly argue that the team should have taken collective responsibility in 2018, rather than allowing the full weight of CA’s penalties fall upon Smith, Warner and Bancroft. Loading Paine is the coach of the Adelaide Strikers in the Big Bash League and has also held numerous coaching roles for CA in recent times. He resigned as Test captain in 2021 after a sexting scandal. He declined to comment when contacted by this masthead, but his 2022 autobiography, The Price Paid, makes things clear.



“I have wondered if there was a point where we could have said something or done something differently,” Paine wrote, in a chapter on the saga that otherwise sticks closely to CA’s official version of events. Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket Australian young gun’s summer threatened by bizarre ankle infection “Everyone was a part of it to some degree – would it have worked out better for those three players if we had owned it as a team? I think it would have.” All-rounder and now white-ball captain Mitchell Marsh is held in similar regard by both sides of the argument, and his vexxed position has been made plain by a haunted visage in recent days, when he was also kept away from media duties after being persistently asked about the affair in his pre-series press conference in Perth. “I respect Uzzy for telling his story and for writing his book, and I don’t sit here coming from a place of judgement,” Marsh had said. “Everyone’s got their story. Some will be willing to share it, and others might not, purely on the basis of the fact that they’ve moved on. It’s really important that at some stage we do.”



Players Association boss Paul Marsh advocated in this masthead for collective responsibility to be taken by all players and staff from the 2018 tour, in addition to CA for leading the team in a win at all costs direction in the preceding few years. Editor's pick Australian cricket Marsh seeks sandpaper peace deal, calls on Cummins, bowlers and CA to share responsibility “They are a team, and you win, you lose as a team,” Marsh said. “I just think it’s something that maybe we need to be able to do collectively, so that, so everyone can find a way to move on here.” Those words found a sympathetic ear across much of the cricket community over the weekend, although some senior figures conceded, there is a significant amount of “scar tissue” that needs to heal before all players could be expected to get together and talk through matters. Captain Cummins was grateful to be supported both in private and in public by CA chief executive Todd Greenberg and chair David Boon, although he is still facing some harsh critiques, including by the respected former England captain Mike Brearley.



“It is hard to see Cummins remaining as captain for long, even if Cricket Australia is so far backing him,” Brearley wrote in The Times. “He has so much the bearing and look of a heroic and honourable leader, clean-cut, handsome, with the image of an outback hero. Another perspective Opinion

Ball tampering Cummins helped rebuild Australia’s cricket culture. It’s being tested now Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist “He has been a wonderfully consistent, top-level Test cricketer, and as captain has much modified the team’s bad reputation. But the cover-up, if it is so, has been worse for him than any crime or misdemeanour. Perhaps he should bow out with as much grace as he can find.” Greenberg and Boon have made it clear CA are in no mood to move Cummins on, but are aware he will need plenty of support in coming days and months. “I think he’s going need some help in that, and I think he’s going to need some other leaders to step up, and we’re gonna need to take the temperature down a little bit,” Greenberg told SEN radio on Saturday. “I think this has got very messy and very emotional very quickly, and it’s clearly it’s an emotional issue for a lot of people.

World.title: He left her for dead, then tattooed her name on his leg. Now her family want the law changed
World.content:
Tayla Richardson has spoken out about her mother’s death, calling for new legislation to criminalise those who leave people suffering from a medical episode to die.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Left to die, Narelle Simmons bore the unmistakable marks of domestic violence across her bruised frame, hidden under a blanket with a pillow over her face for over a week. Her daughter, Tayla Richardson, never got to say goodbye. When funeral directors warned her that viewing her mother’s decaying remains could traumatise her, she had listened. She was used to seeing her mother’s flesh brutalised. Trapped in an abusive relationship, Richardson says her mother had been duct-taped, degraded, trampled, kicked, burned and chased with a hammer. Tayla Richardson is calling for legislation change after her mother’s death in 2021. 60 Minutes Richardson says the last time she saw her mum alive in September 2021, Narelle had “been beaten from her forehead down to her chin. She was purple and yellow, and she had scratch marks all up and down her arms.” She gave her mum money, told her she loved her and said she would call soon. The following month, Narelle was left to endure a lonely death on a mattress in her Cranbourne home. Her partner, Craig Jennion, was nowhere to be found.



Now, five years later, Richardson is calling for legislation change that would protect other women from suffering the same fate, and punish those who leave their “loved ones” for dead. In Victoria, there is no specific law to criminalise the failure to alert Triple Zero when someone is in dire need of medical help. Gross negligence manslaughter is a charge – but it doesn’t capture the circumstances of some cases. It is a gap in the law the devastated families of victims of those who have been left to die alone without potentially life-saving medical treatment are fighting to change. In October 2021, Richardson, then just 21 years old, realised she hadn’t heard from her mother in over a week. When she couldn’t reach her on the phone, she called the Cranbourne police station and asked them to conduct a welfare check. Tayla and her mum Narelle. By the time officers entered Narelle’s home and found her body, she had been lying there for nine days. Richardson says she instantly knew Jennion was involved. When Jennion eventually handed himself in, he told them he’d beaten Narelle. He admitted he’d punched her twice in the face and elbowed her in the back of the head. He told them that the next morning when he woke, he had tried CPR before fleeing the scene.



He was arrested and later charged, but not with causing Narelle’s death – a post-mortem exam determined she had died as a result of drug and alcohol complications, pneumonia, chest injuries and haemothorax. Instead, Jennion was charged with common assault and failing to report a reportable death. He served five months in prison. “He’s living scot-free,” Richardson says. “I saw him. When I ran into him, he’s got a tattoo of my mum’s name on the back of his leg. “You have taken away, from an entire family, the right to say goodbye. How does that only deserve a couple of months?” A legislative blind spot As families rally for change – and with an election next week – the Victorian Labor Party has committed to introducing a specific law that would criminalise the act of abandoning a person who needs medical help in an intimate partner relationship. Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny says there is a gap in the legislation. 60 Minutes



Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny says a number of recent coroners’ reports had identified a “gap” in the justice system that allows perpetrators of domestic violence who abandon their partners in a time of need to avoid prosecution. “It’s terrible, and I think when you talk to people about this notion of a partner abandoning his partner when they need medical assistance or medical support in circumstances where there have been family violence, and you look at that act of abandonment as that final act of control, you know that is wrong,” she says. “You know it is wrong, and we need a justice system that can address that and hold that person accountable.” We need to create a criminal offence, she explains, that has never existed in the state. An offence that will send “a very strong message to all of the community that this is no longer acceptable, and we will be criminalising this kind of conduct in family violence circumstances”. Kilkenny says the act of abandonment is an “act of final control by a perpetrator”. The Liberals have also committed to the new legislation.



Shadow attorney-general James Newbury says it’s clear “we need action”. “The Liberals and Nationals will consider creating both a new offence where a victim in medical need is abandoned and establishing that such abandonment is an example of family violence, in relation to the Family Violence Protection Act 2008 (Vic),” he says. Parents fight a justice system they say let them down The new offence is something the family of 26-year-old Amy Bowden have also been calling for nationwide since their daughter’s death. In February 2024, Amy had overdosed on heroin. Instead of calling for help, her partner Ethan Ross injected her with methamphetamine. He told police he’d acted under the belief the combination of a downer and an upper would reverse the overdose. He was wrong. Michelle Sposito and Bryan Bowden with a picture of their late daughter Amy Bowden. Jason South For 24 hours, Ethan failed to get her the help she desperately needed. When he finally did decide to call an ambulance, it was too little too late.

World.title: The four schools that Melbourne parents, teachers and students rate highest
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation The four schools that Melbourne parents, teachers and students rate highest Jackson Graham and Craig Butt November 22, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Two schools in Melbourne’s growth corridors and two selective schools have scored the highest on average across surveys of parents, students and staff. Analysing the results of staff, parent and student surveys across more than 300 government secondary schools, this masthead found only four schools achieved results of higher than 75 out of 100 across all the three measures. The schools were Alamanda K-9 College in Point Cook, Cranbourne West Secondary College, select-entry Nossal High School in Berwick, and specialist school John Monash Science School in Clayton. Across all government secondary schools, about 50 per cent of student responses on average say their school is “good” or “very good”, while about 60 per cent of staff and 74 per cent of parents say the same.



There were two schools where parent and student survey results were above 75 per cent, but staff results did not reach the same level: select-entry boys school Melbourne High and Yuille Park Community College in Wendouree, near Ballarat. The data also shows specialist campus Victorian College of the Arts Secondary School in Southbank is a unique case among government schools – its student connectedness result was above 75 per cent, but neither its staff or parent survey results reached the same threshold. John Monash Science School was one of four schools to top survey results among students, teachers and parents. Principal Andrew Chisholm with students left to right Advik Palta, Alisa Krivulin, Amelia Bate and Jake Nuttall. Simon Schluter There were 16 schools where both parent satisfaction and staff endorsement survey results were above 75 per cent but student survey results did not reach this level, including Bayswater Secondary College, McKinnon Secondary College, Northern College of the Arts and Technology and Preston High School. The Age’s analysis excludes secondary or combined government schools with student and staff numbers below a certain threshold. School-level data is unavailable for non-government schools. You can view the data for your school using our searchable tables included further down in this article.



John Monash Science School scored 92.8 for parental satisfaction, 79 per cent on the staff survey and a 77.1 per cent endorsement from students saying they feel connected. The school’s results come back to its “team player” approach to learning, principal Andrew Chisholm said. Ninety-eight per cent of students enter STEM pathways – the main metric the school measures its success on. “We wanted to try to remove the competitive elements that sometimes influence how students perceive VCE in particular because we’re only a year 10 to 12 school. So collaboration we view as particularly important,” Chisholm said. “Our classes are team-taught, even specialist maths at year 12. It’s generally two teachers with 50 kids, and that also allows us to individualise some things for kids – there’s always another teacher there who can assist.”



He said this also helped teachers: “They can share the knowledge and the preparation, and they’re not just one person in one classroom by themselves.” At Alamanda K-9 College in Point Cook, parents gave an 87.5 per cent satisfaction rating, teachers an 82.1 per cent rating, and students 82.5 per cent for connection. The school’s principal Lyn Jobson said the school of 3335 students – which has seen the biggest raw growth in enrolments statewide in the past decade – went to great effort to make students, teachers and parents feel they were part of a whole-school family. “It’s creating a sense of belonging in that people believe that we care about them. The parent results are always influenced by what the student results are,” said Jobson, who has temporarily stepped away from her role on personal leave.



“And the priority we have and have always had at the school, and it’s an old-fashioned term, is the kids are front and centre.” The school is putting effort into maintaining contact with alumni, which Jobson acknowledged is not always the case for government schools. “They’re proud of their time at the school and they enjoyed it and it was beneficial to them in their life. So why would you give that up?” Jobson reinforces to teachers that they influence student lives, and the school’s success is due to their efforts. “They’re not just the staff, they are significant people in these students’ lives,” Jobson said. “We aim high all the time for our students. And we aim high because each one of the staff we have employed has the capacity to be highly successful educators.”



The Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools use a different survey to question staff, families and students, and therefore results are not comparable with government schools. Related Article Education The schools where teachers stamp out bullying – and those where they do not On average, teachers give a 74.3 per cent rating of their relationships with school leadership. Overall students rate their sense of physical and psychological safety at school at 55.1 per cent, up 2.3 per cent in the past three years. Independent Schools Victoria’s survey, which private schools voluntarily participate in, shows staff satisfaction rose 2.77 per cent, student connection 2.12 per cent and parent satisfaction 2.08 per cent between 2024 and 2025. World.title: Why we can’t forget the week’s other sports scandal
World.content:
NationalSpring racing carnival Editorial Why we can’t forget the week’s other sports scandal The Herald's View Editorial November 22, 2026 — 7:30pm

November 22, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Those involved in horse racing must be thanking their lucky stars that cricket exists. Thanks to the explosion of Sandpapergate, thoroughbred racing has been able to duck under the cover of being the second-biggest scandal to engulf Australian sport in the past week. For all the sound and fury that has accompanied the eight-year-old ball-tampering scandal, and the reopening of wounds that have never been allowed to heal fully, equal if not greater opprobrium should be meted out to those who have built an industry around horseflesh. So You Are, ridden by Rachel King, on its way to the barriers before competing in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington earlier this month. Racing Photos via Getty Images The cruelty of horse racing was laid bare in the last seven days. A dead horse was found in a skip with an old couch. It should have sent a chill through the heart of any animal lover. Any thinking, feeling human being. The carcass found at the Cleanaway Lucas Heights Resource Recovery Centre was a gelding that ran eighth in the Melbourne Cup, and this fact ought to shake the thoroughbred racing industry into action.



Two weeks after what Mark Twain described, during a trip to Melbourne, as a “delirium of colour, a vision of beauty” made its annual eruption at Flemington, the grim fate of So You Are in a bin on Sydney’s southern outskirts revealed the industry’s greatest flaw: its treatment of the animals it profits from. So You Are was a five-year-old whose winnings totalled $1.4 million, and owners, trainers, jockeys and punters alike were left horrified at learning the fate that befell him. Owner and breeder Stuart Ramsey described it as the “worst thing to happen in my lifetime” and described trainer Bjorn Baker as being distraught. For his part, Racing NSW chief executive Graeme Hinton called So You Are’s treatment after death “totally unacceptable”, promised a swift and decisive review to determine whether stricter standards were needed and vowed to push for a national approach. Hinton, who is due to start officially on December 1 but has the reins as outgoing chief Peter V’landys is on leave, offered strong words. These must be backed up with action if the state’s $3.3 billion industry is to maintain credibility. The message was certainly more encouraging than what we heard from the state government. Racing Minister David Harris last Tuesday afternoon described it as a “concerning incident” in a statement that distanced the government from welfare matters and offered that the investigation made it “inappropriate to comment further at this time”.



Related Article Opinion

Racing integrity So You Are’s horrifying final fate in a skip bin with an old couch is beyond unacceptable Neil Breen National sports editor Premier Chris Minns was better on Wednesday morning, acknowledging the discovery was distressing and urging a full investigation. “We expect these things not to happen,” he said. But Minns’ government has the chance to act. An independent review of the 30-year-old Thoroughbred Racing Act by former minister Brad Hazzard has been with the cabinet since July. While its conclusions remain under wraps, transparency, accountability, jockey and animal welfare were all within Hazzard’s scope. In NSW, thoroughbred racing has been ringfenced from scrutiny as political fights have centred on greyhounds. During the week, much focus has been on the cricket, but the racing industry should be placed on notice. The horses deserve better. World.title: Former Uber driver ‘who hated the rich’ guilty of starting deadly LA fire
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCrime Former Uber driver ‘who hated the rich’ guilty of starting deadly LA fire Lily Shanagher and Josh White November 22, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A former Uber driver who hates the rich has been found guilty of starting the deadly Palisades fire – the worst blaze in Los Angeles’ history. Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on New Year’s Day, 2025, that killed 12 people and destroyed nearly 7000 homes in Pacific Palisades, a wealthy neighbourhood in the city. Jonathan Rinderknecht will be sentenced in March. U.S. Attorney's Office via AP The fire burned undetected for six days before it was fanned by strong winds and erupted on January 7, spreading to more than 100 square kilometres and incinerating entire neighbourhoods, with the damage estimated at about $US150 billion ($226 billion). Rinderknecht had pleaded not guilty to two federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson after his first federal case ended this year in a mistrial.



Prosecutors cast Rinderknecht, a dual citizen of the US and France, as a resentful loner who hated the wealthy and “maliciously” started the fire. He was convicted on Saturday AEDT on both counts and will wait until March to be sentenced. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison. The January 2025 fire burned across over 100 square kilometres consuming thousands of properties. Bloomberg California central district attorney Bill Essayli said the defendant could face up to 40 years in prison. Jurors could not reach a unanimous verdict in the first trial, prompting prosecutors to present a more tightly organised case in the second.



They showed digital forensic data, expert testimony and scrutinised Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. Related Article California bushfires Man charged over deadly LA blaze asked ChatGPT to create image of burning city They zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire’s origin area, such as photographs showing his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and mobile phone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze was ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks. Prosecutors established that Rinderknecht acted erratically and angrily in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and text messages sent to his girlfriend at the time.



“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Mark Williams, an assistant US attorney. ChatGPT alibi attempt After the fire began, Rinderknecht called the emergency services more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented a video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?” The fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighbourhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu. AP



These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht had been trying to create for himself, prosecutors said. They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was caused by the initial blaze Rinderknecht started. Rinderknecht’s lawyer claimed his client had been wrongly accused. Steve Haney said he was disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process. “After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration,” Haney said. A car drives past homes and vehicles destroyed by the Pacific Palisades fire in Los Angeles. AP



The fire coincided with the deadly Eaton fire, which burned about 50 kilometres to the east. Nineteen people were killed in that blaze, which began when sparks from an electrical tower ignited flames that incinerated the Altadena neighbourhood. The Palisades fire destroyed many buildings in the Pacific Palisades neighbourhood, including a branch of the Los Angeles library and two elementary schools. A number of Hollywood celebrities lost their homes in the fire, including Sir Anthony Hopkins, Jeff Bridges and Mel Gibson. The flames also burned down the home of Ron Rivlin, an art dealer, destroying pieces by Andy Warhol. The Telegraph, London

World.title: ‘Is it worth it?’ The Sydney parents rejecting private schools for public education
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

After Marijana Rudan moved house from the inner west to Sydney’s north shore, she noticed conversations often started in one very direct way. “The first question anyone asks you is ‘What private school are we putting kids down for’?” Rudan said. Unsure of how to respond at first, Rudan began doing some research, quickly realising it might be too late for her kindergarten-aged daughter Madeleine to secure a year 7 place at a local independent school. “I was anxiety ridden because my daughter was 5, and I hadn’t put her down for any.” The family was offered a year 7 spot at Wenona at the last minute. Drawn to its highly regarded principal Dr Briony Scott, Rudan put her daughter down on the waitlist at Wenona in North Sydney. By year 6, Wenona had not called, and Rudan accepted a place at another private school. “Then, we get a phone call from Wenona, saying ‘We’ve got a place’,” she said. They dumped the other school and paid the enrolment fee. Two years later, they had absorbed sharp fee hikes and suddenly the school was an entirely different financial proposition. “We could afford it between the two of us. It was more [a question of] why? And is it worth it, based on what we could see?”



The plan was to switch to nearby Monte Sant’Angelo Mercy College, which was then about half the price of Wenona. But her daughter wanted them to consider Willoughby Girls High School, which Rudan thought was too much of a jump. She obliged her daughter by going on the school tour. The older students who led the tour were passionate, committed and proud of the school.“We just both walked out and we couldn’t fault it. We just couldn’t find any reason why we wouldn’t send her there.” So they enrolled. Related Article Private schools The waiting list war: The battle to become a private school parent The Rudan family’s move back to public education bucks a much bigger trend. Across the state and the country, thousands more families are shunning the public system in favour of private schools. In NSW, there are 70,000 more students last year in independent schools compared to 20 years ago and 35,000 more pupils in Catholic schools. Much of the non-government growth is in low-fee schools where tuition is less than $10,000 a year. At the other end of the spectrum, Sydney’s high-fee schools have become a different financial proposition. Scots College in Bellevue Hill charged $13,772 for year 12 tuition in 2005. If fees had increased in line with inflation, it would cost $23,671 two decades later. But in reality, fees are already double that. When choosing a school, parents can look for data points like NAPLAN results and facilities to get a sense of a school’s culture. If a parent chooses to judge a school on academic outcomes such as the HSC, Willoughby Girls outperforms at least a dozen high-fee schools in the Herald’s annual league table. But often other parents’ views of choosing a public school go beyond objective measures, veering into social perceptions and school gate chatter. Mosman High parent Ghislaine Vazquez moved from Mexico to Australia in part due to the reputation of Australia’s strong public school system. However, the private school panic started in the Sydney mother’s group before her son was born. “Everyone was just talking about Scots, Shore, Riverview, and Redlands … I started thinking the public system was not a good system for my kids.”



The pressure intensified when her son progressed through Mosman Public School as year 5 and 6 students began to decamp to private schools. She found the single-sex nature of many private schools unappealing. The facilities were impressive, but coming from Mexico, she found the uniforms with hats and ties slightly over the top. “This is too serious for a kid of 10, 12, 13 years old. They are kids,” she said. Ghislaine Vazquez with her son Sebastian, who attends Mosman High after going private for a couple of years. Wolter Peeters Her son, Sebastian, left public for private school for a period, but he wanted to return to Mosman High for year 7. Sebastian soon made friends and excelled in academics. The school facilitates trips to Balmoral and Manly to do extracurricular activities such as surfing. He is in year 9 and has been able to pursue his passion for football. “He has been able to do his sport at a very competitive level,” she said. Mosman High parent Tamara Neal sent her children to Redlands for primary but when her son reached Year 6, also opted for Mosman High. “Even when I was telling people my son had moved from Redlands to Mosman High, I suspected they were thinking: ‘Did you run out of money? Did you get divorced or did you get expelled’?” Extracurricular programs spanning music, drama, and arts, as well as the teaching staff, have impressed her.



“I would say the level of teaching is at least equal, if not better in the public system,” Neal said, singling out Mosman’s English department for praise. Related Article Exclusive

Selective schools Private school students blocked from last-minute selective spots Chatswood High School principal Robin Chand says removing the financial burden of private school fees can help some parents in ways that will tremendously benefit a child’s life. “That is something that will ease the family unit, have social impacts, psychological benefits, and people can breathe,” he says. When parents tour his school, he discusses the education on offer, as well as flow-on benefits to the family budget in an economy in which petrol costs $2.60 a litre and interest rates are high. “Why pay $30,000 a year when you can take your family to France look at the Louvre or whatever else – and get the best?” As some economists declare the country is heading for a recession, Sydney’s insatiable appetite for private schooling might be showing signs of cooling. Enrolment data has not been released for this year but at think tank The Centre for Independent Studies, federal opposition education spokesman Julian Leeser last week said principals had reported a drop-off from waiting lists. “I’ve had school principals recently tell me that because of the state of the economy at the moment, and the state of the government’s economic management ... there are schools that are having large numbers of families drop off their waiting lists because they simply can’t afford to have a non-government choice.”



But choice also goes beyond school sectors. For Randwick High School parent Katherine Hole, whose son started in year 7, the merger of two single-sex schools by the NSW government into a co-ed campus was a big factor behind their decision to choose the school. They toured other private options and noticed the difference in resources. But ultimately, Randwick was close to home, its two big grass ovals offered plenty of space and the academic and subject offering was excellent. “I look at friends at private school, they’re still paying extra for tutoring,” she said. After years of mulling over the decision, she says parents need to figure out what is right for them. “It is important to take a step back and look at what’s important for your kid, what made the decision for us was community, the impact on travel and what was going to make for a better family life.” Parents opting out of private schools for public education are bucking a broader trend. Edwina Pickles Concord High School P and C president Amber Hooker had also glimpsed local private school facilities before she toured the public school when deciding where to send her children. “We went on a tour, and it was a little bit confronting, to be honest, to see the building, especially in comparison to what there is available at other places,” she said. After enrolling, the campus was renovated to create a better learning environment, and she likes how transparent the school is with dealing with behaviour and other issues. There’s also a range of extracurricular activities, and her son has completed the Duke of Edinburgh Award. “I think the thing we have noticed over the years is it’s actually the passion of the teacher who makes the difference to the students,” she noted, saying they were excellent at Concord High.

World.title: Melbourne set to announce a $5 million loss after payouts to ex-staff, players
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLMelbourne Demons Melbourne set to announce a $5 million loss after payouts to ex-staff, players Michael Gleeson and Danny Russell November 22, 2026 — 7:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
