World.title: ‘Is it worth it?’ The Sydney parents rejecting private schools for public education
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

After Marijana Rudan moved house from the inner west to Sydney’s north shore, she noticed conversations often started in one very direct way. “The first question anyone asks you is ‘What private school are we putting kids down for’?” Rudan said. Unsure of how to respond at first, Rudan began doing some research, quickly realising it might be too late for her kindergarten-aged daughter Madeleine to secure a year 7 place at a local independent school. “I was anxiety ridden because my daughter was 5, and I hadn’t put her down for any.” The family was offered a year 7 spot at Wenona at the last minute. Drawn to its highly regarded principal Dr Briony Scott, Rudan put her daughter down on the waitlist at Wenona in North Sydney. By year 6, Wenona had not called, and Rudan accepted a place at another private school. “Then, we get a phone call from Wenona, saying ‘We’ve got a place’,” she said. They dumped the other school and paid the enrolment fee. Two years later, they had absorbed sharp fee hikes and suddenly the school was an entirely different financial proposition. “We could afford it between the two of us. It was more [a question of] why? And is it worth it, based on what we could see?”



The plan was to switch to nearby Monte Sant’Angelo Mercy College, which was then about half the price of Wenona. But her daughter wanted them to consider Willoughby Girls High School, which Rudan thought was too much of a jump. She obliged her daughter by going on the school tour. The older students who led the tour were passionate, committed and proud of the school.“We just both walked out and we couldn’t fault it. We just couldn’t find any reason why we wouldn’t send her there.” So they enrolled. Related Article Private schools The waiting list war: The battle to become a private school parent The Rudan family’s move back to public education bucks a much bigger trend. Across the state and the country, thousands more families are shunning the public system in favour of private schools. In NSW, there are 70,000 more students last year in independent schools compared to 20 years ago and 35,000 more pupils in Catholic schools. Much of the non-government growth is in low-fee schools where tuition is less than $10,000 a year. At the other end of the spectrum, Sydney’s high-fee schools have become a different financial proposition. Scots College in Bellevue Hill charged $13,772 for year 12 tuition in 2005. If fees had increased in line with inflation, it would cost $23,671 two decades later. But in reality, fees are already double that. When choosing a school, parents can look for data points like NAPLAN results and facilities to get a sense of a school’s culture. If a parent chooses to judge a school on academic outcomes such as the HSC, Willoughby Girls outperforms at least a dozen high-fee schools in the Herald’s annual league table. But often other parents’ views of choosing a public school go beyond objective measures, veering into social perceptions and school gate chatter. Mosman High parent Ghislaine Vazquez moved from Mexico to Australia in part due to the reputation of Australia’s strong public school system. However, the private school panic started in the Sydney mother’s group before her son was born. “Everyone was just talking about Scots, Shore, Riverview, and Redlands … I started thinking the public system was not a good system for my kids.”



The pressure intensified when her son progressed through Mosman Public School as year 5 and 6 students began to decamp to private schools. She found the single-sex nature of many private schools unappealing. The facilities were impressive, but coming from Mexico, she found the uniforms with hats and ties slightly over the top. “This is too serious for a kid of 10, 12, 13 years old. They are kids,” she said. Ghislaine Vazquez with her son Sebastian, who attends Mosman High after going private for a couple of years. Wolter Peeters Her son, Sebastian, left public for private school for a period, but he wanted to return to Mosman High for year 7. Sebastian soon made friends and excelled in academics. The school facilitates trips to Balmoral and Manly to do extracurricular activities such as surfing. He is in year 9 and has been able to pursue his passion for football. “He has been able to do his sport at a very competitive level,” she said. Mosman High parent Tamara Neal sent her children to Redlands for primary but when her son reached Year 6, also opted for Mosman High. “Even when I was telling people my son had moved from Redlands to Mosman High, I suspected they were thinking: ‘Did you run out of money? Did you get divorced or did you get expelled’?” Extracurricular programs spanning music, drama, and arts, as well as the teaching staff, have impressed her.



“I would say the level of teaching is at least equal, if not better in the public system,” Neal said, singling out Mosman’s English department for praise. Related Article Exclusive

Selective schools Private school students blocked from last-minute selective spots Chatswood High School principal Robin Chand says removing the financial burden of private school fees can help some parents in ways that will tremendously benefit a child’s life. “That is something that will ease the family unit, have social impacts, psychological benefits, and people can breathe,” he says. When parents tour his school, he discusses the education on offer, as well as flow-on benefits to the family budget in an economy in which petrol costs $2.60 a litre and interest rates are high. “Why pay $30,000 a year when you can take your family to France look at the Louvre or whatever else – and get the best?” As some economists declare the country is heading for a recession, Sydney’s insatiable appetite for private schooling might be showing signs of cooling. Enrolment data has not been released for this year but at think tank The Centre for Independent Studies, federal opposition education spokesman Julian Leeser last week said principals had reported a drop-off from waiting lists. “I’ve had school principals recently tell me that because of the state of the economy at the moment, and the state of the government’s economic management ... there are schools that are having large numbers of families drop off their waiting lists because they simply can’t afford to have a non-government choice.”



But choice also goes beyond school sectors. For Randwick High School parent Katherine Hole, whose son started in year 7, the merger of two single-sex schools by the NSW government into a co-ed campus was a big factor behind their decision to choose the school. They toured other private options and noticed the difference in resources. But ultimately, Randwick was close to home, its two big grass ovals offered plenty of space and the academic and subject offering was excellent. “I look at friends at private school, they’re still paying extra for tutoring,” she said. After years of mulling over the decision, she says parents need to figure out what is right for them. “It is important to take a step back and look at what’s important for your kid, what made the decision for us was community, the impact on travel and what was going to make for a better family life.” Parents opting out of private schools for public education are bucking a broader trend. Edwina Pickles Concord High School P and C president Amber Hooker had also glimpsed local private school facilities before she toured the public school when deciding where to send her children. “We went on a tour, and it was a little bit confronting, to be honest, to see the building, especially in comparison to what there is available at other places,” she said. After enrolling, the campus was renovated to create a better learning environment, and she likes how transparent the school is with dealing with behaviour and other issues. There’s also a range of extracurricular activities, and her son has completed the Duke of Edinburgh Award. “I think the thing we have noticed over the years is it’s actually the passion of the teacher who makes the difference to the students,” she noted, saying they were excellent at Concord High.

World.title: Laser shoot-offs in Utah, billions on offer, but NZ conserves its energy
World.content:
The NZ Defence Force (NZDF) has little on record about considering how it might use laser and other directed energy weapons in a future war.

Militaries around the world are rushing to develop, test and deploy new high tech weapons like lasers and high power microwaves that can destroy objects with beams of electromagnetic energy, including in space.

The Pentagon is putting more than $3.6 billion in 2027 into developing directed-energy weapons in the rush to counter drone swarms.

It has chosen seven lasers for a live-fire shoot-off in Utah next month.

They come with names such as Bullfrog, Archimedes, Locust and Firefly.

The demand for lasers to shoot down drones is rising rapidly, prompting industry recruiters to advise, "Smart professionals will monitor regulatory changes and technological advancements in directed-energy weapons, positioning themselves to advise organisations on emerging security threats."

But the NZDF has had little to say in response to an OIA this week requesting any reports, or trials or records of work with industry on this in the last three years.

It also asked for any recommendations or decisions since early 2023 on whether Defence should pursue directed-energy weapon research or capability development.

In response, the only activity the defence force mentioned in its two-paragraph response was that three personnel went to Canadian trials of counter-drone systems two years ago.

Yet NZDF forecasts have emphasised for a decade how crucial counter-drone systems will be, though for now efforts appear focused on jammers, not directed-energy weapons.

The government in Budget 2025 focused an undisclosed amount of funding on purchasing what it called a "credible" counter-drone system and a jamming system was bought from overseas this year.

The force's future fighting concept came out recently and did not mention directed-energy weapons.

In the Canada trial the NZDF went to,15 personnel from five countries competed in a 'sandbox' with a Canadian firm winning over a million dollars. The NZDF has talked about running such competitions in emerging technology.

It withheld a report on that visit in full but summed it up as a valuable opportunity to observe a range of systems and talk to researchers and operators that its science unit would use in researching autonomous systems.

Australia is buying locally-made laser weapons as well as mounting lasers on its Bushmaster vehicles to destroy drones."You need plenty of juice to do that," said a military leader earlier this year.

Australia tested its first directed-energy weapon in 2024.

NZDF's science and tech unit has been working closely with the Australians, and the NZDF has an aim to be interchangeable with them by 2035. New Zealand also runs Bushmasters now, but there is no sign of any lasers.

Europe's defence industry has laser weapons programmes that could help address the imbalance with cheap drones, by offering rapid, precise, cheap engagement, said a European Commission report.

The US is pursuing two types of direct-energy weapon: Lasers that focus a beam of light to burn a target and microwaves that deliver bursts of radio-frequency energy to overwhelm electronic systems.

It plans to use them in President Donald Trump's Golden Dome, though that project's funding momentum has begun to stall in fallout from the midterm elections.

Aside from the Dome and on the ground in Utah, the coming shoot-off shows the rush is on.

World.title: COP flop: Scientist warns countries are losing faith in UN climate summits as deal talks stall
World.content:
A climate scientist warns COP31 risks being seen as "a flop". OZAN KOSE / AFP

A New Zealand climate scientist says many countries are losing faith in the UN's annual climate summits, with the deal at COP31 teetering on collapse.

He said Pacific Island nations were among those who were deeply frustrated with this year's summit, as they face an "existential threat" of 1.5 degrees of global warming.

Fraught negotiations at COP31 in Türkiye have run more than a day over deadline, with international publications reporting a major deadlock overnight.

Talks stalled when a draft of the deal contained no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels, The Guardian reported.

EU, Pacific Island and African states were pushing for the wording, while Saudi Arabia was among those understood to be pushing against it.

Then, at a late-night session, COP31 presidents Australia and Türkiye announced a new package aimed at achieving consensus.

President Murat Kurum said he believed concerns around fossil fuel wording had been solved, as had those around providing funding developing countries' climate change adaptation programmes.

"I truly remain hopeful, I still believe that we can arrive at some excellent decisions here in this hall, here in Antalya.

"The gap between us is narrowing, and the political will required to build a bridge exists right here in this room," he told the BBC.

A third draft of the deal has been sent to delegates in the early hours of the morning.

COP31 had been dubbed the "Implementation COP", with a focus on action for climate change financing and adaptation, Victoria University's Professor of Earth Sciences Tim Naish, who attended the summit as Chair of the World Climate Research Programme, said.

Instead, it had been one of the least productive ever and would be a failure if no deal was reached.

"It was a given that we would continue this so-called roadmap of transitioning away from fossil fuels that people thought wouldn't be controversial.

"What can happen at this COP is, essentially it's a flop, and we don't get any traction on the core goals that were set going into this process."

Naish said even if a deal was reached, he did not expect it to be transformative as the summit had "backslid" on major issues. Meanwhile, the world was getting closer to the Paris Agreement target of 1.5C degrees of warming, he added.

He said Pacific Island nations, who had a very strong voice at COP, were especially frustrated.

Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown addresses leaders at PRECOP31 discussions in Fiji. Supplied / Cook Islands Office of the Prime Minister

"This is why they are at the COP, 1.5 degrees is existential for them."

One of the world's biggest polluters, the United States, was not there, and climate change was getting less public attention amidst other major geopolitical issues and a general sense the 1.5 degrees target couldn't be reached.

"Bottom line is I think people are losing faith in the process, they are not seeing the process working, but I think the majority would be very loathe to leave it, because it's all we've got at the moment."

Karan Titus, a researcher in renewable energy engineering at the University of Canterbury who also attended COP31, said lack of pathways for climate adaptation finance had been a big weakness in the negotiations up till now.

Titus said he thought carbon capture and storage was being used as a way to solve the fossil fuel wording deadlock, but in his view this technology risked lock-in of fossil fuel projects for many years.

Transitioning away from fossil fuels was the "crucial foundation" to any real climate action, Titus said.

"If it is to be the implementation COP, and these items are not implemented, then I think it will have failed in its mission.

World.title: Motorcyclist critically injured after crashing into police car on motorway
World.content:
Police are asking witnesses to come forward after a motorcyclist was critically injured when he crashed into a police car on Auckland's Northern Motorway.

Authorities say the police car was responding to an unrelated job when the motorbike came up the far-left lane, veering across traffic and colliding with the vehicle at about midday on Sunday.

The motorcyclist has been taken to hospital in a critical condition.

Inspector Matthew Laurenson said police were now hoping to hear from those who may have seen what happened.

"If you were travelling on the northern motorway between Tristram Avenue and Upper Harbour Highway, between 11.45am and 12.10pm today, and witnessed or have dashcam footage of the crash, or the motorcyclist's manner of driving prior to the crash, please get in touch," he said.

The crash had blocked part of the motorway, which was now fully reopened.

World.title: Letterbox port poisoning: Renewed push to solve death of Dave Davan
World.content:
Five years after Northland farmer Dave Davan died from downing a glass of poisoned port, his alleged murderer is still walking free and a $100,000 reward remains unclaimed.

Long-time mate Brett Evans told RNZ he had never given up hope of seeing justice done for the hard-case farmer and his family.

"I just can't let it go. It's the horror of the actual circumstances of his murder," he said.

Evans said Davan became severely ill after drinking a glass of port from a bottle left in his letterbox in remote Herekino, on the Far North's west coast.

He died of organ failure about three weeks later, on 9 December 2021, in Auckland Hospital - after naming the man he believed had murdered him.

Tests of the remaining port showed it had been laced with a restricted, and deadly, weedkiller.

However, police had so far been unable to prove who poisoned the port.

After Davan's funeral, a group of friends put up a $50,000 reward for information leading to a conviction - which Evans had since upped to $100,000.

It was a lot of money but would be worth every cent if it brought a result, he said.

"If there's anything I can do to help solve the case, I'll do it. Hence the reward really. There's quite a few people contributing to that, not just me, and we've been heartened by the fact that the police haven't ever stopped looking into it."

The poisoned port was left in Dave Davan's letterbox on remote Puhata Road in the Far North. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Evans said his hopes had been lifted in recent weeks when a new detective was assigned to lead the investigation.

He had already been to Kaitāia to meet him and was hoping new evidence would come to light.

Evans believed it was just a coincidence that the renewed push to solve the crime came as friends and family marked the fifth anniversary of Davan's death.

"But we're pretty happy that there's some action happening again," he said.

"We just want justice for Dave and his family. It's horrible to think of him lying there knowing that he'd been poisoned. He possibly didn't have the ear of the police at the right time and he became too ill and subsequently died. So it's a tragedy really."

Son Conrad Davan previously told RNZ his father, who was 67, found two bottles of port in his letterbox on isolated Puhata Road in November 2021.

He drank the first and, a week or so later, opened the second as he was cooking dinner.

He had barely finished the glass when he fell to the floor and was violently ill.

It took until the following morning before he could drag himself to the phone and call for help.

Conrad said his father was convinced from the outset he had been poisoned.

He had noticed the metal seal on the second bottle was broken but thought little of it at the time.

Also, in a rural area like Herekino, there was nothing unusual about people leaving gifts in their neighbours' letterboxes, often as a thank-you for work on their properties or favours done.

Puhata Road in the Far North. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Conrad said his father seemed to come right at first but four days later was admitted to Kaitāia Hospital with kidney failure.

As his condition deteriorated, he was admitted first to Whangārei Hospital, then flown to the intensive care unit at Auckland Hospital.

Before he lost consciousness, he was able to tell police and family what he believed had happened.

He had saved the second bottle as evidence.

Conrad described his father as "the best fulla I knew" and a wonderful grandfather to his boy.

Dave's brother, Grant Davan, said whoever killed him knew him well - the port was his favourite brand.

Evans said he got to know Dave in the late 1970s when he landed a job on a farm development in the Far North.

"Dave was the manager and I was his sidekick, and we just became very close mates. He taught me a lot about fencing and farming and all that sort of stuff," he said.

World.title: Competitor killed in crash during Whanganui motorsport event
World.content:
A person has died and another has been seriously injured in a crash at a Whanganui motorsport event.

Two competitors, a driver and co-driver, were involved in an accident on Sunday that saw their vehicle go off the road at the Brunswick Road Hillclimb.

Emergency services were called to the scene just before midday.

MotorSport NZ said one competitor died before crews arrived while another was taken to hospital.

MotorSport president Deborah Day said in a statement the whole motorsport community is shocked and upset by what has happened.

"Our thoughts are with the family and friends of the two competitors and all involved with the event," she said.

"We will be offering support to all those involved in the coming days."

World.title: The world's onto us now after All Blacks' defeat
World.content:
Analysis - Wow!

Or not.

That was dreadful, eh?

And perhaps the worst thing about it was the way one of sport's most remarkable identities has been publicly eviscerated, William Wallace style, in consecutive weeks.

By which I mean the character of invincibility. Once, so imposing, so persuasive, so effective for the All Blacks. Once, almost self-fulfilling.

Remember Dublin, in 2013? The All Blacks were trailing 17 - 22 going into injury time. But Richie McCaw knew that team wouldn't lose. And the team believed him. And they were right.

At that stage, the Irish had never beaten the All Blacks. Not once. In 111 years. And it wasn't going to happen under Richie's watch.

It's happened five times since.

Wales? They so deserved their victory two Saturdays ago (their time). But that was a team that had almost forgotten what the V was for. Losing had become a habit. Then they beautifully upended New Zealand. Whoopsie-daisy.

The terrible thing, as I watched the game against England in a kind of solitary penitence for all the victories I wasn't grateful enough for, is that I began to look at my phone. Then I turned the commentary down and listened to new music. Really. At 4am.

Not long ago, there was a certain inevitability about the narrative arc. The Northern Hemisphere teams would play like stink for sixty or seventy minutes, casting themselves as Robin Hood, and then the All Blacks would grind mercilessly past them, and the foregone conclusion would be manifest.

I mean, it wasn't always that simple. I'm being reductive. But the facts tell their own story. 111 years for Ireland. A 73-year gap for Wales. England now really, really having the measure of us (Ouch.) All of that happening in very recent years.

Remember when?

Yeah, I do. But that currency's not legal tender any longer.

There's nothing aberrant about this. It's not unusual, to cruelly use that famous Welsh songline. What were exceptional were the winning streaks, not their end.

But, gosh, we look flat-footed in our response. And skittish, too, if you can be both at the same time.

New Zealand players after the 3rd England try. England v New Zealand All Blacks, 2026 Nations Championship rugby union test match at Allianz Stadium, London, England on Saturday 21st November 2026. Photo: Matt Impey / Photosport Matt Impey / www.photosport.nz

Take the coaches. As opposed to taking to the coaches, which NZ Rugby likes to do.

Steve Hansen finished at the end of 2019.

Since 2020, Ian Foster, Scott Robertson and Dave Rennie.

Remember August 2022? NZ Rugby's CEO, Mark Robinson, actually flew to South Africa, during the tour, to knock on Ian Foster's hotel room door, death-row warden like, before the players mounted a passionate defence of their coach by winning at Ellis Park.

And then, it was Scott Robertson. Billed as the new messiah. Ridiculously oversold, the poor man. Who could possibly live up to that billing? Not him, as it turned out.

New Zealand Rugby conducted a review (the phrase, "physician, heal thyself" springs to mind here), which is seldom good news when the review is of you. Sure enough, it was agreed he should go. (Agreed. Lol.) It felt shabby from the top. Great teams aren't led like that. (And the players see it and know that bell tolls for them, too.)

It felt panicky.

Has that set-in at a systemic level?

Leicester Fainga'anuku as a back and a forward? Really? Why don't we just make him the best one-of-the above that that gorgeously gifted (but not superhuman) player can possibly be? Richie Mo'unga recalled to the All Blacks after a three-year absence. Ruben Love was injured, yes. But it still felt hopeful, a coin toss, rather than a meaningful investment in something long-term.

Fehi Fineanganofo, so brilliant with the Hurricanes that NZ Rugby lassoed him to hold him back from a lucrative deal with Newcastle. He got injured, sure. But if he was good enough to retain, he's good enough to play.

And if he's not, what's happened? It feels like a dice roll. And players aren't dice.

And now, I guess, discussions about Dave Rennie?

Codie Taylor (left) the New Zealand captain and head coach Dave Rennie face the press after the game. England v New Zealand All Blacks, 2026 Nations Championship rugby union test match at Allianz Stadium, London, England on Saturday 21st November 2026. Photo: Matt Impey / Photosport Matt Impey / www.photosport.nz

Three coaches since Steve Hansen and we might now want a fourth?

Wow.

What's needed, first of all, is some luck. The All Blacks without Ardie Savea are like fish and chips without fish. And chips. Ruben Love has to be supported to work.

That kid is still only 25. He'll deliver. If we let him.

Cam Roigard has to be given his head. Anyone can kick aimlessly, few people can create such defensive uncertainty on the fringes of tight play by passing like Aaron Smith and running like there's space where there's none.

It's the unpredictability that draws defenders and creates doubt and space. And, finally, or not, we have to stop telling hopeful stories about players we admire and are profoundly grateful for, beautiful servants of the game, but who maybe aren't, ultimately, a long-term solution in a rugby world not scared of us anymore.

Wallace Sititi and Pete Lakai (who's still only 23, for goodness sake) are so exciting. Back them, back them, back them. Quinn Puketahinga Claude Tupaea (I just wanted to use his whole magnificent name), get better, stay well, and be the boss!

New Zealand players performing the Haka lead by captain Codie Taylor. Matt Impey/Photosport

And beyond that, beyond the player Lotto, we have to understand that even great teams lose. And it's what you do next that defines you. Not what you used to do.

The world's onto us now. They know they can beat us and we know we can be beaten. Bummer, eh?

But also, c'est la vie. It really is.

Sure, these are psychologically shaky times. We haven't got a government (um, is that a hard thing, really?) and someone's misplaced the All Blacks.

I guess the former will be resolved, sooner or later. (Thank God, we closed enrolment early so we wouldn't have to wait so long for the specials. Lol.)

And the solution to the latter, surely, is to start from a position of rational humility, not panic, not hubris, not dice rolling, not nostalgia, and build a new self-belief that comes from an appropriate identity, and clear purpose, and trust.

NZ Rugby has to understand that its track-record of reactive appraisal is piss poor. (Really, those guys should keep calm and not carry on.)

We have to find the youngsters and really back them.

We have to look like we believe in our future sufficiently to stop scrambling through our past.

We have to look like we want to be there - and that we know who we want on the field when we are.

The sky hasn't fallen in. (I mean, not literally.)

The thing is, the sky used to be our limit.

World.title: One person dead, two airlifted to hospital after being trapped in house collapse
World.content:
One person has died after five people were injured, becoming trapped when a house partially collapsed.

The building in Tai Rāwhiti slid off its piles on Sunday morning as it was being relocated.

"One person received critical injuries and sadly passed away while enroute to the hospital," police said.

St John sent three helicopters, two ambulances and a rapid response unit to the scene on Te Huinga Avenue in Ruatoria.

Police said four other people received moderate to minor injuries.

Two of the four people were airlifted to Gisborne Hospital in moderate condition.

Police said the death has been referred to the coroner and inquiries were ongoing.

World.title: Fiji claims first win as Pacific three celebrate
World.content:
Fiji claimed their first win in the Nations Championship following their 21-16 win over Italy in Udine on Sunday morning.

The result meant all three Pacific Island teams Fiji, Samoa and Tonga recorded wins at the weekend in their respective World Rugby internationals.

Tonga had thrashed Hong Kong China 55-19 in Hong Kong on Saturday night in their Nations Cup clash, while Samoa walloped Spain 90-22 earlier today.

In Udine, the story truly belonged to Fiji and their second half resurgence as the islanders romp to the victory, silencing the Italian crowd that had cheered their side on.

The result means the two teams will go head to head again in London in the weekend, with the two both finishing sixth in their respective South and Northern hemisphere pools.

Italy had led 13-7 at halftime.

Fiji scored three tries to Italy's one, with captain Tevita Ikanivere claiming two, while flanker and 'Player of the Match' Kitione Salawa adding another.

Flyhalves Ben Volavola and his replacement Caleb Muntz added the extra six points between them.

Italy scored their only try through captain Lorenzo Cannone, with fullback Tommaso Allan adding 11 points through a conversion and three penalties.

Man of the match performer Salawa said post-match the Italians were tough and thanked his fellow players for staying in the fight until the end.

"First of all I would like to than the Lord Almighty for giving us the strength today," he said.

"I would also like to thank the boys for the great effort against the Italian boys.

"Thank the Italian boys for giving us a hard battle tonight and our boys for staying in the fight."

First half battle

Italy were fierce on defence and lightning on attack, keeping smiles on their fans' faces in the first half.

Fiji's Nathan Hughes was the first to receive the ball as Italy kicked off and the two teams tested each other out in the first seven minutes.

The Italians drew first blood in the game after captain Lorenzo Cannone crashed over the Fijians' line and planted the ball across, despite Hughes' attempted tackle.

That came in the eighth minute, following a good break from halfback Stephen Varney, that sliced open the Fijian midfield, and fullback Tommaso Allan's conversion gave them an early 7-0 lead.

Fijian captain Tevita Ikanivere was penalised for playing ball on ground in the 12th minute and Allan extended the home team's lead to 10-0 from inside Fiji's 22 metre zone.

But Fiji came back hard and a lineout take inside the Italian's 22 metres saw Ikanivere dive over for their try. Flyhalf Ben Volavola converted, as Italy led 10-7.

Italy's defensive efforts after the 20th minute saw them stop three scoring opportunities from their visitors, managing three good turnovers as Fiji attacked.

A second Allan penalty in the 31st minute saw Fiji trailed their host 13-7 at halftime.

Fiji's Tevita Ikanivere leads an attack against Italy. Photo: Fiji Rugby Union Fiji Rugby Union

Fiji resurgence

Fiji started the second half with a lot more determination, with prop Peni Ravai running on to a lineout win and driving his way through the Italian defence.

That saw Italy defending desperately on their line but they could not stop Ikanivere from diving over in between the posts in the 44th minute, with replacement flyhalf Caleb Muntz tipping the conversion over as Fiji claimed the lead 14-13.

That spurred Fiji into action with two consecutive bombs from Frank Lomani forcing errors in the Italian defence.

Taranaki Bulls reps Marika Parker in for his debut for Fiji, having played for Taranaki Bulls National Provincial Championship.

He replaced Luke Tagi and went straight into a scrum feed, that laid the platform for another Fijian attack.

That led to Kitione Salawa scoring a try after the flanker chased a loose ball that came off the Italians stripping the ball from Josua Tuisova's hands, in the 51st minute.

Muntz conversion gave Fiji a 21-13 lead.

Allan reduced the deficit with another penalty in the 64th minute after Tuisova was penalised for not rolling away in the ruck.

But Fiji held on and threw everything into their defence to claim the wind in the end.

Tonga show class

Tonga's John Tapueluelu dives over the Hong Kong China line to score a try on Saturday night. World Rugby

Tonga ran in eight tries against Hong Kong, five of those coming during a blistering opening 40 minutes which saw them lead 33-0 at the break.

The bonus-point success marked Tonga's third win of the campaign.

It also avenged the earlier loss in the day of the Tonga women's team, who went down 24-34 to their Hong Kong China opponents.

'Ikale Tahi captain Ben Tameifuna said post-match he hopes the win would inspire Tongan kids around the world.

"We expected a physical game in the first 20 minutes and just had to weather the storm," he said.

"There are a lot of Tongan kids around the world and it's great to be able to inspire them - boys and girls."

His Hong Kong China counterpart Joshua Hrstich said they were still learning and developing as they head into the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

The loss was their fifth straight loss in the Nations Cup.

"This was a massive opportunity for us to learn and the growth and development in the team has been awesome," he said.

"It's been a privilege to be a part of."

Tameifuna opened the scoring with a close-range effort.

That was followed by winger John Tapueluelu, who scored a double in the game, with other tries coming from when fullback Taniela Filimone, prop Siegfried Fisiihoi, another double from number eight Otunuku Jr Pauta and one from flanker through Sam Tuitupou Junior.

Flyhalf Manu Vunipola kicked five conversions for a personal tally of 10 points, while his replacement Patrick Pellegrini added a conversion and a penalty to the team's tally.

Seb Brien and Alexander Post scored tries early in the second half for courageous Hong Kong China, before second-row James Rivers went over late on for their third try.

Paul Altier added two conversions.

Samoa blitz Los Leones

Samoa emphatically claimed their third successive Nations Cup bonus-point victory to finish runners-up in Pool A behind USA, with 13 tries to their name in the huge 90-22 win over Spain at the Estadio Ciudad de Malaga.

Delighted Samoa captain Theo McFarland said it was the end to a strong campaign.

"I'm just very proud of the boys," he said post-match.

"At the start of the campaign, we got asked what we wanted from it and I think we've laid a good foundation, especially heading into next year."

Samoa centre Lalomilo Lalomilo put his side ahead early on when he burst over from close range.

Spain did respond through winger Alberto Carmona in the 17th minute.

However, the islanders took complete control before half-time and led 29-8 at halftime.

Their tries came through a double each from Latrell Ah Kiong (48', 61'), Jacob Umaga (50', 67') and Vaafauese Apelu Maliko (55', 76').

Other try scorers fro Manu Samoa were Lalomilo, Peter Umaga-Jensen, Theo McFarland, Ben Nee-Nee, Joel Lam and Irae Simone.

It was also a record-breaking night for Jacob Umaga, who set a new mark for the most points scored by a Manu Samoa player in a single international match.

Umaga's 33 points in the match sets a new Manu Samoa single-match record, previously held by Earl Va'a, at 31 points against Ireland in 2003.

Spain had number eight Raphael Nieto sin-binned on the stroke of half-time for a ruck infringement and early in the second half Samoa were awarded a penalty try for another offence as home winger Gauthier Minguillon was also yellow-carded.

The hosts scored through Alberto Carmona, who got a double and Valentino Rizzo.

Meanwhile, in the battle for the Nations Cup crown, Georgia reigned supreme against USA, with an emphatic 38-10 bonus-point win in Tbilisi.

Both teams had topped their respective pools with unbeaten winning runs in the group stages.

The Lelos prevailed in front of their jubilant home crowd to lay down an impressive marker heading towards Men's Rugby World Cup 2027 in Australia.

World.title: Wallabies still have a pulse despite nervous moments in win over Wales
World.content:
In Les Kiss's words, the Wallabies "earned their corn" with their gritty 29-26 Nations Championship win over Wales in Cardiff.

After ending a four-match losing streak, the Wallabies coach struck a relieved but proud figure when he and captain Harry Wilson fronted the post-match media conference.

It couldn't be described as a polished display on the field, nor was there a moment during the match where it seemed the Wallabies were dominating their opposition.

Each time they opened up an encouraging lead on the scoreboard, it never felt as though Wales was too far away from clawing its way back into the contest.

Wallabies defeat Wales The Wallabies hold on to defeat Wales 29-26 following a thrilling finish to their Nations Championship Test in Cardiff.

But winning breeds confidence, which had been in short supply for the Wallabies following losses to New Zealand (twice), England and Scotland.

"They had to work hard for it and I think tonight was a true Test match [and] they earned their corn and got what they deserved," Kiss said.

An improved defensive effort was among the positives in the Wallabies' performance.

While three of the four tries they conceded came from driving mauls off line-outs, they denied Wales more than once with their scramble defence deep inside the 22.

"When we do it [defence] well, it's a real point of difference for us," Wilson said.

"I thought our D-zone [inside 22] defence tonight was unbelievable."

The Wallabies' aerial game in attack also showed glimpses of its potential, with Max Jorgensen's second-half try an example of the pressure they can apply to opposition teams.

The line-out was strong (they enjoyed a clean sheet on their throw), highlighted by Josh Canham's clutch steal when Wales was camped inside the Wallabies' 22 during the first half.

Wallabies lock Josh Canham (right) enjoyed an excellent all-round performance. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

But the Wallabies let themselves down with poor discipline, especially inside their territory.

They conceded nine penalties in the opening 40 minutes, seven of which were on their side of the halfway line.

By full-time, the Wallabies had given 11 penalties away inside their half, with Wilson shown a yellow card in the 77th minute for one of those indiscretions.

If the Wallabies do the same against Ireland at Twickenham next weekend, they won't be shown any leniency.

Kiss admits the Wallabies' penalty count gave him "the shits".

"Discipline was a little bit disappointing, I must say … it kept them [Wales] in the game with field position and a few things like that," he said.

"So we're going to have to look at that as well."

Ikitau to the fore

Among individual performances, Carter Gordon looked assured at fly half.

The Wallabies were still pedestrian at times with ball in hand, however Gordon did enough to indicate he's the most suitable candidate to wear the number 10 jersey.

Wallabies fly half Carter Gordon looked solid against Wales. (Reuters: Andrew Couldridge)

Len Ikitau was deservedly named player of the match, again proving he's a world-class operator.

But the question remains whether he's better suited to inside or outside centre.

When the Wallabies pulled off their upset 42-38 win over the world champion Springboks in Perth in September, his performance at outside was superb until he left the field injured.

On that occasion, he was partnered in the centres by Hunter Paisami, who is unavailable for the Wallabies' Nations Championship campaign in Great Britain.

Ikitau played inside centre against Wales, with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii admirably slotting in at 13.

Len Ikitau was outstanding in the Wallabies' win. (Getty Images/CameraSport: Ian Cook)

A permanent Ikitau-Paisami midfield combination may be the Wallabies' best option at next year's Rugby World Cup, although Suaalii's stocks at outside centre rose in Cardiff, even though he appears more comfortable on the wing.

For now, the Wallabies will turn their focus to the Ireland Test, which pits the two third-ranked teams from the respective Nations Championship groups against each other.

Their spirits will be buoyed by halting their losing streak, but Kiss knows the pressure of Test rugby never lets up.

"Test match footy doesn't hand you things easy," Kiss said.

World.title: Bellamy to end Storm coaching stint after 2027 NRL season
World.content:
Melbourne can officially begin planning for life after Craig Bellamy, after the veteran coach confirmed the longest tenure in NRL premiership history would end in 2027.

After years of speculation about his future, Bellamy will officially finish with the Storm next year at the end of his 25th season in charge of the club.

The 67-year-old's call to walk away comes after he was diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder this year.

Craig Bellamy's coaching CV NRL - Brisbane Broncos (2002): Two matches, one win, one loss

NRL - Melbourne Storm (2003-current): 630 matches, 433 wins, 195 losses, two draws

NRL premierships: 2012, 2017, 2020 (all with Storm)

State of Origin - New South Wales (2008-10): Nine matches, two wins, seven losses

But he still hopes to play some role around the club after 2027, with the five-time premiership-winning coach the most powerful figure in the Storm's history.

"I love this club and everything it represents, the people, our history and our fans," Bellamy said.

"I still have huge passion for the job, and I'm excited about what we can achieve together in 2027.

"While 2027 will be my final season as senior coach, I'm determined to make the most of the opportunity and give everything I can to our club and our players.

"I've always said I'll continue coaching while I believe I can make a positive contribution, and I feel I can still do that.

"I also feel the time is right to make 2027 my final year."

Cameron Munster is one of several big-name Storm stars who are off-contract at the end of the 2027 season. (Getty Images: Pete Dovgan/Speed Media/Icon Sportswire)

Bellamy's decision to officially call stumps comes after chief executive Justin Rodksi admitted on Friday the uncertain future had complicated contract talks with the club's biggest names.

Harry Grant, Cameron Munster and Stefano Utoikamanu are all off-contract at the end of 2027, with the Storm facing an uphill fight to retain all three.

Melbourne hasn't been able to provide clarity on who will coach the club in 2028, unable to officially move on appointing a successor until Bellamy had decided his future.

Billy Slater remains the biggest name linked with Melbourne after he walked away from the Queensland State of Origin job in August.

Billy Slater is the highest-profile name tipped to be Bellamy's successor for the Storm. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Slater does sit on Melbourne's part-time staff, but has so far suggested he does not want to coach in the NRL.

Bellamy also declared in August that Melbourne's next coach should come from within, with Marc Brentnall, Ryan Hinchliffe and Bellamy's son Aaron his full-time assistants.

Brad Arthur, Michael Maguire, Anthony Seibold and Jason Ryles are among coaches to have come out of Bellamy's system in Melbourne.

Arthur is currently coaching Leeds in the Super League, but has signalled a desire to return to the NRL, while Maguire is under pressure at the Broncos.

Ryles is on the verge of signing an extension at Parramatta, while Seibold is a free agent after being sacked by Manly last season.

"Craig is one of the greatest coaches in the history of rugby league, and we're proud of everything he has achieved in the game," Storm chairman Matthew Tripp said.

"We're also delighted he'll have one final season in charge in 2027.

"While we would obviously love to have Craig coaching our team forever, we understand how significant this decision is and are incredibly grateful that we will have another season with him leading our club."

AAP

World.title: Piastri third, snaps at McLaren team, in Vegas GP with 352 overtakes
World.content:
Oscar Piastri has produced his finest performance of the 2026 season, claiming a sensational podium in Las Vegas after starting 17th on the grid.

Max Verstappen proved why he is one of the finest Formula 1 drivers of any era, winning a thrilling grand prix that will rank as one of the best this season. There were 352 overtakes on track, with 35 of those passes for the lead of the race.

Piastri took a 10-place grid penalty for using a new internal combustion engine, and was driving a McLaren described by team CEO Zak Brown as a "sitting duck" on the long straights, due to the car's lack of top speed.

But Piastri picked his way through the field across an action-packed 50 laps, crossing the line third behind Verstappen and McLaren teammate Lando Norris.

Piastri, who is notoriously cool under pressure, had an uncharacteristic snap at his team when they stressed the importance of being careful with his teammate Norris.

With a few laps remaining, and both drivers battling in a tightly packed top-five, Piastri was told he needed to be careful if he was battling his teammate, but Piastri was having none of it.

"Stop telling me to f****** be careful," he snapped.

Piastri would overtake Norris a few laps later, but his world champion teammate re-took the position on lap 48 of 50.

Neither McLaren driver looked set to finish on the podium, but the Mercedes duo of George Russell (off track) and Kimi Antonelli (energy deployment issue) both fell down the order.

"They say Las Vegas is the entertainment capital of the world, and I think that was pretty entertaining," Piastri said post-race.

"Everyone was just in such a big pack; it was bizarre to be a part of."

Verstappen wins after 35 lead changes

In 2025, Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix when there were 17 overtakes on track during the entire race.

In 2026, he won when there were 35 overtakes on track, just for the lead.

Verstappen was at his masterful best on Sunday (AEDT), converting pole position into the 75th grand prix win of his career.

The long straights at the Las Vegas Strip circuit resulted this year with a very powerful slipstream, meaning the car behind at the end of the straight would be going much quicker.

Verstappen drove a near-perfect race, losing the lead at the end of the long back straight several times, only to then smartly deploy his electrical power to retake the lead just a few corners later.

George Russell, Kimi Antonelli and Lando Norris all overtook Verstappen for the lead at the end of the back straight at some point, only for the four-time world champion to snatch the lead straight back.

"Crazy. Really, really surreal and something I have never seen before in Formula 1 myself," Verstappen said post-race.

Verstappen was ever present in the lead, while several drivers battled to be the next challenger to the Dutchman's position.

Russell, who started second, was Verstappen's main threat throughout the race, but while running third behind his teammate Antonelli late in the race, locked his wheels and went off the track.

Antonelli was shaping up to be Verstappen's challenger on the final lap, but an energy deployment issue on the penultimate lap led to the new world champion falling behind Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri. Antonelli would finish fourth.

Isack Hadjar, Verstappen's teammate, looked destined to be a contender as well. However, his race came unstuck when his front wing collapsed, without contact, on lap 26 during a restart after a safety car.

Alpine duo Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto were fifth and sixth, a terrific result to help cement the team into sixth place in the constructors' championship, and give them an outside chance of finishing fifth.

Lewis Hamilton was seventh for Ferrari, while Carlos Sainz secured a vital eighth place for Williams.

Russell was ninth after his late mistake, while Ferrari's Charles Leclerc dropped to 10th following a 10-second penalty for colliding with teammate Hamilton.

World.title: Dawn Fraser fired up for 1956 Melbourne Olympics reunion
World.content:
Amid the reunions and celebrations, Dawn Fraser is drawing some inspiration from the 70th anniversary of the Melbourne Olympics.

Australia's most famous Olympian has come to Melbourne for a lunch on Sunday at the MCG to mark the November 22 opening ceremony date of the 1956 Games.

Fraser is 89 and had to miss a commemorative 1956 Olympics dinner in Melbourne a few weeks ago because of a health issue.

Fraser says she will go from table to table in her wheelchair to meet old friends and make new ones at the lunch, which coincides with the opening ceremony at the MCG 70 years ago.

Asked if she might be there for the 2032 Brisbane Olympics — Fraser was also a key figure at the Sydney 2000 Games — there is a reminder of what made her an all-time sporting great.

TV memories of the 1956 Olympics Watching the 1956 Melbourne Olympic Games was many Australians' first experience of television.

"I would love to be there at '32, to support our athletes," Fraser told AAP.

"I think of my age — I just turned 89 — and, 'Oh well, that's so many years off.' But then when I look at some of the athletes who are coming to this testimonial, some of them are 95, 99.

"Then I'm thinking — excuse the expression — 'Shit! I can do that. If they can do it, I can do it.'"

Likewise, the 19-year-old from a hardscrabble Balmain upbringing had her eyes opened wide at the 1956 Olympics.

Until then, Fraser had only swum against other Australians.

"I never thought about it. [To me, the Olympics] was just another swimming event. But when I won my gold medal, I realised how big it was," Fraser said.

"It wasn't until after I won … competing against so many nations.

"To win a gold medal was something out of this world. You didn't think about it until a month later, that you were the best swimmer in the world."

Fraser won the 100-metre freestyle in Melbourne and was a member of the 4x100 women's freestyle relay team that also claimed gold.

Dawn Fraser (centre) began her Olympic reign in the 100m freestyle in Melbourne. She won her third straight gold in Tokyo in 1964. (Getty Images: Central Press/Hulton Archive)

She went on to become the first of only four swimmers who have won gold in the same individual event at three-successive Olympics. Somewhere in there, she became "Our Dawn".

Two days after the reunion, the Sport Australia Hall Of Fame annual dinner will feature the Dawn Award. It goes to an individual, team or organisation that shows courage, breaks new ground and changes sport for the better.

But as far as Fraser is concerned, she is just one athlete at the reunion.

"I'm an athlete among athletes, and I'm very proud to be among the athletes who I met and competed against in 1956," she said.

Just as the Melbourne Games dramatically changed Fraser's life, it also was a landmark for Australian sport. Only 11 years after World War Two, Australia was still an international backwater.

It has been 70 years today since Ron Clarke lit the Olympic cauldron at the MCG to kick off the Games in 1956. (Getty Images)

"Here we were, a small country, having an Olympic event that meant so much to a lot of sportsmen and women in our country … and throughout the world," Fraser said.

"We were holding the biggest sporting event ever in Olympic history.

"It was the start of not only my swimming career but for a lot of other sportsmen and women in Australia — the start of their international careers.

"It was a big stepping stone for all of us because we didn't realise we were competing against the best athletes in the world."

And so to 2032, where Fraser hopes Australia can raise the bar again.

"I want them to make it as successful as all the other Olympic Games — if not a little bit better. It's very hard to do that, but Sydney, I thought the same thing," she said.

"Sydney outshone Melbourne and I'm sure Brisbane will outshine Sydney."

AAP

World.title: Alcaraz digs deep to beat Shelton and reach ATP Finals decider
World.content:
Seven-times grand slam champion Carlos Alcaraz battled back from a set down to beat American Ben Shelton 3-6, 6-3, 7-6 (7-1) in their ATP Finals semifinal to charge into ​Sunday's showcase for the ‌second consecutive year.

Alcaraz, beaten by Shelton in the US Open quarterfinals on the Spaniard's return from a four-month injury break, stretched his winning run to 13 matches after ‌back-to-back titles in Vienna and Paris.

He will face Alexander Zverev, who beat Daniil Medvedev of Russia in the other semifinal.

"I was a ​little bit frustrated at ‌the beginning because I didn't start the match the way I wanted to," said Alcaraz, unbeaten on indoor courts this season.

"Just happy that I came back in the second set playing such great tennis, step by step, ​focused ‌on all my things and ended up playing good tennis. The third set was even closer."

Shelton, making his second consecutive appearance in the ⁠season finale, grabbed an early break to ‌race to a 3-0 lead.

Alcaraz, ‌whose fitness had come under scrutiny after he left the court with heavy ‌strapping on his left leg following Wednesday's win over Medvedev, had his thigh wrapped heavily against Shelton.

He upped his game and ‌started ​moving the American around ⁠more, engaging him in longer rallies. He earned two break points at 4-2 but could not convert either, with Shelton's booming serve getting him out of trouble.

The world number four fired a second-serve ace ⁠on his first set point to move ahead but Alcaraz went 5-3 up in the second before ‌serving out the ‌second set.

The pair traded blows in the third set ​before Alcaraz eased through the tie-break, sealing the win with a return winner.

Zverev beat Daniil Medvedev 7-6 (0), 6-4 in the second semi-final at the elite season-ending event for the year’s top eight players.

In their only meeting this year, Alcaraz beat Zverev in the Australian Open semifinals. The Spaniard also holds a 7-6 edge in career meetings.

"We had a practice before the tournament started. It was unbelievable. We played one set for one and a half hours. So I hope it’s going to be similar tomorrow," Zverev said.

"I hope both of us are going to be at our best and hopefully it’s a really entertaining match for everybody."

Reuters/AP

World.title: England thrash All Blacks after Moody faces haka with team
World.content:
England has roared to a record victory over New Zealand at Twickenham in the Nations Championship, after emotional scenes before the game involving former skipper Lewis Moody, who has Motor Neurone Disease (MND).

The English beat the All Blacks 37-12 to the delight of home fans, inflicting New Zealand's second-straight defeat after last week's loss to Wales.

Moody, who played 71 Tests for England between 2001 and 2011 and was part of the team's 2003 Rugby World Cup win, came onto the ground to a huge ovation and took his place with the team to face the NZ pre-match haka.

After the haka, various England players came to embrace Moody, who announced his MND diagnosis last year.

"Lewis is such an inspirational man, he ⁠was an inspirational player and, given his ‌diagnosis, the players jumped at ‌the opportunity to support him," current England captain Maro Itoje said.

"I think he and his family gave us that ‌extra lift today. He came to spend some time with us yesterday. He presented us our shirts for today's game.

"He addressed us ‌and there's no doubt that his ⁠presence, him joining us for the haka, him spending time with us, gave us an extra lift."

Itoje, though, played down the impact of how England responded to the haka.

"The most important thing is how you start ⁠the game against New Zealand," he said.

"You can do whatever you want. There are teams historically who've done different ‌things, different formations.

"It's ‌important, but the most important thing is how you start ​the game. I wouldn't pay too much attention to whatever anyone does to respond to the haka."

Ben Earl (second from right) scored one of England's five tries in their record win over NZ. (Getty Images: RFU/Steve Bardens)

The English ran in five tries against NZ, but Itoje was determined that his side must keep improving.

After four victories in a row over Fiji, Argentina, Australia and Japan, England were braced for a much sterner test against the All Blacks, who were hurting from a shock loss to Wales.

But ​England demolished NZ, ‌racing into an early lead and ultimately winning at a canter to record back-to-back victories over the All Blacks for the first time since 2003.

"I thought we took a step forward ‌today," Itoje told reporters.

"I thought we took advantage of the opportunity we ⁠had, but … we don't want this to be our ceiling, ‌we don't want this to be as good as it ‌gets for England.

"We want to push, we want to get better. We have an amazing opportunity next week, however the chips fall to do that."

In other matches in the Nations Championship, Ireland beat world champions South Africa 20-17 in Dublin, Scotland overwhelmed Japan 67-5, and Fiji defeated Italy 21-16 in Udine.

South Africa's losing bonus point meant they topped the Southern Hemisphere standings, and will play in next week's final.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Wallabies snap four-match losing streak with tense win over Wales
World.content:
The Wallabies have snapped a four-match losing run with a tense 29-26 win over Wales in their Nations Championship Test in Cardiff.

The result gives the Wallabies an injection of confidence and relieves some of the pressure on coach Les Kiss, although Wales did its best to deny the visitors in the shadows of full-time.

Wales scored a try through reserve hooker Ryan Elias in the 79th minute of the match, cutting the Wallabies' lead to three points.

Following the re-start, the home side launched an attacking movement from deep inside their 22, knowing it was the final play of the match.

But it came to nothing, allowing the Wallabies to celebrate victory after defeats to All Blacks (twice), England and Scotland.

The Wallabies claimed the James Bevan Trophy after defeating Wales. (Getty Images: Nations Chammpionship/Jan Kruger)

The Wallabies had entered the match low on morale, but their hopes were boosted when they established a 12-0 lead in the first half on the back of tries to Taniela Tupou and Brandon Paenga-Amosa.

But poor discipline proved costly, with the Wallabies giving away nine penalties to four, including seven inside their half.

Taniela Tupou opened the Wallabies' scoring with a first-half try. (Getty Images: Dan Istitene)

From one of those penalties, Wales scored its first converted try via captain Dewi Lake to reduce the Wallabies' lead to 12-7 at the half-time break.

The two sides traded tries early in the second half before Wales hit the front.

Wales hit the lead following Blair Murray's converted try. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Jan Kruger)

Fullback Blair Murray's converted try gave Wales a 21-19 lead, but the Wallabies struck back with Len Ikitau scoring a five-pointer and Carter Gordon adding the extras in the 65th minute.

Leading 26-21, the Wallabies extended their advantage through Gordon's penalty goal with six minutes remaining in the match.

Wales refused to roll over, however, setting up a grandstand finish with Elias's late five-pointer.

The Wallabies finished third on the Southern Hemisphere standings in the Nations Championship.

They play Ireland at Twickenham next Saturday, AEDT, as part of the Nations Championship's Finals Weekend.

Wales, fifth in the Northern Hemisphere standings, faces Japan on Sunday, AEDT.

South Africa and France will face off in the Nations Championship grand final at Twickenham on Monday, AEDT.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Lehmann denies knowledge of sandpaper plot despite Bancroft statement
World.content:
Former Australian cricket coach Darren Lehmann has once again denied knowledge of a plan to use sandpaper in the Cape Town Test against South Africa in 2018, revealing the fallout left him in a "dark place".

Speaking on ABC Radio before Australia's T20 against England at the MCG, Lehmann apologised for his role in the team's culture at the time, admitting that the team's attempts to find reverse swing during the tour "went too far".

Lehmann said he had not signed a Non Disclosure Agreement with Cricket Australia and therefore was permitted to talk about the subject freely.

Cummins to retain captaincy with CA board's 'unanimous' support Cricket Australia's board throws its support behind embattled skipper Pat Cummins as the sandpaper furore continues.

"I haven't changed my views from what happened in 2018," he said.

"It was a dark time, and we got a lot of things wrong, but my version still stays the same. It was just a bad time. We all made mistakes."

Lehmann said he could not remember being a part of a conversation where David Warner raised the prospect of using sandpaper on the ball, as Cameron Bancroft detailed in his statement earlier this week.

"I can't remember being present in that conversation," he said.

"But again, it is eight and a half years ago; you'll have to ask those people. That's the issue, I have my version, and that's where I stand."

Darren Lehmann said he felt 'empathy' towards Cameron Bancroft after his statement. (Reuters)

Bancroft's statement mentioned Lehmann speaking to squad member Peter Handscomb via a walkie talkie asking him to tell Bancroft to remove the sandpaper from the field.

However, Lehmann stated that he only knew sandpaper was on the field after seeing vision of Bancroft hiding it on the TV screen.

Lehmann denied intentionally not asking about how the players were tampering with the ball during the 2018 tour.

"With reverse swing, you throw it into the dirt, you rough up one side of the ball, you might pick at it; that's been happening for 100 years, "he said.

"For me, I didn't know, but you're always ball tampering to try and get the reverse swing happening, but you never go to that extent.

"In 2018, it went too far, and I'm [responsible] for that as the coach."

Lehmann hit back at suggestions he did not pay a price for his involvement in the saga as he detailed the mental toll it took at the time.

"People said I didn't lose anything. I actually lost the best job in the world, and I'm sorry for that, and I'm sorry for what happened. That's all I can say to the general public," he said.

"I went to a really dark place. I went to as dark a place as you can think about.

"It took me probably three to four years to actually get back to some sort of normality.

Lehmann described the job of being Australia's coach as 'the best job in the world'. (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

"I'm not going back to that dark place. I'm trying to move forward. I'm not going back.

"There's things I remember and not remember. It is eight and a half years ago, it was a traumatic time.

"I don't want to go back to that dark place, and I hope no one does. I feel for everyone and their families."

When asked what he felt towards Bancroft in particular after his statement, Lehmann said "empathy", adding that he felt empathy for all the players and staff involved.

The context you need to understand Bancroft's version of Sandpapergate If you feel like you missed a beat with the Australian cricket's sandpaper scandal and why its back in the news, this breakdown of Cameron Bancroft's article will bring you up to speed.

He also took aim at reporters doorstopping the individuals involved and the general media coverage of the sandpaper saga.

"Some of the things that have been said are just outright hurtful to a lot of people. That's what I care about," he said.

"There's a lot of people being hurt at the moment and I think people have forgotten about that aspect.

"Yes, we made mistakes, we apologise as best we can and you try and move on.

"I'm not going back to that place … but it feels like everyone is pushing everyone to these bad places."

Lehmann denied knowledge of a specific conversation Khawaja detailed in his book in which he claimed a coach told the players to get the ball moving by any means possible.

Lehmann says he trusts Australian bowlers' accounts of the events in 2018 despite having no evidence to back them up. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"I don't understand that statement as such, because at the end of the day, I didn't get that statement," he said.

"I didn't get that question posed to me, so I can't comment for anyone else."

However, Lehmann admitted the environment surrounding the team at the time was centred around winning at all costs.

"You're always trying to get the ball moving anywhere, in any Test match, whether it's normal or reverse," he said.

"It was an ugly series, that's what I do know. A lot of people suffered and paid the price.

" I just remember how volatile that series was … and we certainly could've handled it better. "

Lehmann also could not recall whether there were any meetings where an individual stood up and voiced their concerns against the use of sandpaper.

"Everyone talks about meetings at the moment; there [were] a whole heap of different meetings," he said.

"There are conversations going on and some people are privy to them and some people are not. I'm not privy to every conversation or meeting.

"So a lot of different conversations happen all the time, different meetings, not altogether, that's how it is."

Lehmann said he had no evidence to back up the fierce denials from Australia's bowling quartet at the time — Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon — but said: "I trust the bowlers. Everyone is entitled to their own opinion."

Lehmann confirmed that he would attend Cricket Australia's independent forum for those involved on the 2018 South Africa tour to tell their version of events.

Australian captain Pat Cummins has also stated his intention to attend the forum, as have Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

Tech.title: Amazon is complaining about NYC Council on shipping labels, too
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the New York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act. The company is now putting labels on shipments claiming that the Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order. The Delivery Protection Act would effectively ban the sort of third-party arrangements Amazon currently uses to deliver many packages, including small companies and independent contractors. Last-mile delivery firms operating warehouses would need to be licensed by the city and directly employ their workers.

Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the company is including an almost identical message on shipping labels.

Amazon claims that the bill, if passed, “would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City,” and has threatened to move its warehouses outside of the city. However, labor unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have countered that the company is attempting to “threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council” and is acting out of “greed,” pointing to Amazon’s market cap of nearly $3 trillion.

Tech.title: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.

According to NPR:

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.

The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”

Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.

According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:

On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

Tech.title: The FBI and USDA were reportedly hacked
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Friday, it was reported that both the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the FBI were hacked. In reporting on the FBI hack, CNN noted that this is the second such attack on the agency in the last few months, this time targeting the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which federal, state, and local law enforcement use to share information, including warrants and missing persons. President Donald Trump later confirmed the hack in an interview with Fox News. NBC first reported the USDA hack on Friday. According to Reuters:

While the payments ​database is the known extent ​of the intrusion so far, the former ‌officials ⁠warned that the compromised system could provide a backdoor to more sensitive information, including food safety ​data and ​research on ⁠animal-borne illnesses, according to the report.

The breaches come following a week of major outages across several sectors, including at the FAA and NSA, which the government has sought to reassure the public were not the result of a cyberattack.

President Trump suggested that the breach of the FBI might not be an entirely bad thing, telling Fox News that, “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place,” and “wouldn’t it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?” referring to investigations into his ties to Russia.

The FBI suffered a breach, reported in late September, that allegedly compromised personal records of “all FBI employees and applicants.” This was followed by a hack of DHS, reported in October, comprising 40,000 employee records. In the wake of these major outages, the White House national cyber director, Sean Cairncross, stepped down this week.

Update November 21st: Added President Trump’s comments.

You probably know John Roberts best as the voice of Linda Belcher on Bob’s Burgers. The show just wrapped up its 16th season and shows no signs of slowing down anytime soon. The show remains a reliable source of laughs, top-notch puns, and frankly wholesome fun.

Comedy is just part of Roberts’ life, however. In addition to his appearances on Gravity Falls and Comedy Bang! Bang!, he’s also a musician with deep roots in New York City’s queer nightlife scene. He just released his latest record, I Am, on Friday, and it dabbles in ’80s pop, ’90s house, and even dashes of ’00s rave. But while the record sounds made for the dance floor, it actually tackles some pretty heavy subject matter, like mortality, aging, and grief following the loss of his mother.

Despite that, Roberts is still having fun, as you can see in the video for “Complicated,” which revels in the queer cult camp of Scorpio Rising, William Friedkin’s Cruising, and The Wolf Man.
